# renderer (systems)

G87's authored-scene and viewer whole-scene streaming fixtures use 32 m tiles: ordinary trees,
including the wider three-plane foliage bounds, fit a tile while the deliberately oversized
renderer instance still stays outside streaming. The original instance, pair-accounting and
exact-pixel assertions remain unchanged.

The foliage fade fixture uses decoded level-zero images when comparing pixel IDs between ray
and raster paths. Raster alpha tests sample derivative-selected mips while ray alpha tests
intentionally sample level zero (see **The rays** below). The larger G87 atlases exposed that
pre-existing difference: cached images disagreed on about 0.27% of the fixture's pixels; with
matching level-zero images this falls below 0.008%, inside the unchanged 0.1% ID threshold.
The fade, mixed-block and popping assertions are unchanged. This fixture isolates fade decisions;
it does not claim that filtered raster masks and level-zero ray masks have identical coverage.

**Named tree motion (G85):** maple, oak, elm, walnut, beech and ash use the broadleaf stiffness
class; pine, spruce, cedar and juniper use the conifer class. Their species identity remains in
the container for materials and provenance. See [flora's shared growth rules](flora.md#shared-growth-rules-and-named-species-g85).

**Purpose.** The engine's renderer ([04](../plan/04-renderer.md), [02 §2.3](../plan/02-architecture.md#23-subsystem-boundaries-and-layering) L3): it turns a set of meshes and instances of them into a picture and into the numbers that describe how it was made. It owns the whole frame — source-mesh loading through the derived-data cache, the GPU-resident scene, two-pass GPU culling and LOD selection, the four rasterizers, the deformed-vertex pool, the per-frame cluster acceleration structures, the material resolve, the Hi-Z pyramid, the GPU timers, and the capture — and it does all of it **without a window**. `engine-view` is the command line over it and `engine-host`'s `render.*` methods are the protocol over it; neither is privileged, and a third consumer (the editor, a test, a benchmark harness) needs nothing new.

**Why it is a module and not an app.** Until this split every one of those passes lived in `apps/engine_view/main.cpp`, 2,654 lines of it, and the consequence was not that the file was long: it was that **nothing but engine-view could render**. The protocol had no `capture` and no `benchmark`, so the Phase 1 exit criterion ("agents can capture and benchmark", [10 §10.2](../plan/10-roadmap-risks.md#102-phases)) could not be met without either duplicating the frame in the host or driving a child process and reading its stdout. The renderer is the engine's own, in the same sense `gfx` is — not a capability a game adds ([ADR-0027](../adr/0027-additive-capabilities.md)) — so it is `engine_module(... LAYER systems)` with no `OPTIONAL`: a build without it could not draw at all, and every consumer of it would have to be switched off with it.

**The window is the app's.** `foundation/window` is not a dependency of this module, and nothing here touches a surface, a swapchain, or a present queue. A frame is recorded into a color image the caller names: engine-view acquires a swapchain image and hands it in with its two semaphores; engine-host renders into an offscreen target the renderer owns. That is the *only* difference between the two, which is why a picture captured through the protocol is the picture engine-view shows. `systems/renderer/tests/renderer_tests.cpp` opens with `#if __has_include(<foundation/window/window.h>) #error`, so the day the dependency comes back the build says so rather than a hosted CI run failing to open a display.

## Owned data

| Owner | What it is sized by | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `SceneDesc` | — | what to load: mesh paths, instances, the instance grid, which **procedural** scene an empty path builds (`Procedural::heightfield` or `shredded_atlas`, the UV-atlas LOD fixture of [geometry](geometry.md#the-shredded-atlas)) and its resolution, what the LOD builder is told (`lod`, which is part of the derived-data cache key), the derived-data root; and what a scene file adds — per mesh a name, the content hash its bytes must have and a fit, and the terrain an empty path then builds ([Scenes, camera paths and flythroughs](#scenes-camera-paths-and-flythroughs)) |
| `SceneData` | the content | one merged cluster LOD DAG, one `geometry::ClusterMeshPart` per mesh, each mesh's materials and images, the instance table, the bounding sphere, and the counts a summary reports; and, host side only, every cluster vertex's canonical id (`mesh_vertex_ids`, below); every mesh's source hash, and the terrain, names and file hash carried from the description, so a host holding only the loaded scene can fly a path over it and say what it measured |
| `GpuScene` | the **scene** | every device buffer whose size is a function of the scene: geometry behind device addresses, the material table and the bindless textures, the instance table, the deformed-vertex pool, the visible list (with a run per shadow cascade behind the views') and the indirect argument blocks, the pair table and the per-view pair-to-entry tables, the vertex path's indexed-draw regions, and the ray tracing chain — whose per-frame structures are the one thing here sized by the *frames* rather than the scene, and which `SceneRenderer` resizes ([The ray tracing chain's memory](#the-ray-tracing-chains-memory)); and, for a streamed world, the tail of instances that comes and goes between frames — each tile in a block of the instance table with a reserved run of pairs, the instance and pair tables in one set per frame in flight — with the per-pair buffers at a stride that grows with it ([Instances that come and go](#instances-that-come-and-go)) |
| `ViewSet` | the **layout** | N views over one scene: each one's rectangle of the target, its orientation and frustum shape, its source extent, and its quality tier |
| `SceneRenderer` | the **screen** | the shader library and its pipelines, the visibility buffer and the Hi-Z pyramids, the frame context, the GPU timers, the render graph, the per-slot parameter blocks, and `Stats` — and the sun's shadow atlas, which is sized by the settings rather than the screen and so survives a resize |

That line — scene-sized against screen-sized — is also the order the two build in, and it is not arbitrary: the `gfx::MeshDesc` array names the deformed-vertex pool, the deform table, and this scene's cluster templates, so it is uploaded last, after every address it carries exists. A `GpuScene` therefore finishes itself; a `SceneRenderer` is created against a finished one.

## Invariants

- **A picture does not depend on where the mesh came from.** `load_source_mesh` takes a glTF, a derived-data cache entry, or a `.clusters` container named outright, and all three have to reach the GPU upload with the same materials *and the same image bytes* — the loader hands on a container's carried bytes for an image the source embedded and its path for an image the source named, so that one `assets::MeshData` shape serves every route ([geometry](geometry.md#embedded-images-the-container-carries-them)). It is asserted in `engine-view`'s end-to-end test as four byte-identical captures, because the failure mode is a texture that quietly does not arrive and a cut that looks right. **The textures are the one input that a load may take from the cache instead**: a mesh whose images the content build has built draws them from `<ddc>/textures/` whether it arrived as a glTF, a cache entry or a container ([Built textures](#built-textures)), so those three routes still agree, and only `--no-cache` — which reads no derived data at all — draws the decoded source images; the two pictures differ by what BC7 and mips do, which `texture_tests.cpp` bounds.
- **A picture does not depend on which host drew it.** Every device- and scene-driven override lives in one function, `resolve_settings`, and nothing below it probes `gfx::DeviceFeatures` again. The order of the overrides is load-bearing and the function says so: the mesh-shader fallback decides which path runs, the path decides whether shadows can be traced or mapped, and traced shadows decide whether two-pass occlusion culling may run (the acceleration structures are built from one visible list, and pass 2's survivors are in a second one); the cascaded maps do not, because they are culled from the light into runs of their own. The chain's index space is checked before the path is settled, because a scene whose pairs in every view the device cannot name moves the ray path to the rasterizer and traced shadows to the maps ([The ray tracing chain's index space](#the-ray-tracing-chains-index-space)). Everything after that only ever forces a switch *on*.
- **The material map follows the merge.** A cluster draws with its own material whatever the scene's merge did to its index. `geometry::merge_cluster_meshes` puts each mesh's leaves first, and every mesh that came through the cache arrived in page order, leaves last, so the merge moves nearly all of its clusters; `load_scene` takes the merge's `source_of_cluster` and permutes each `SourceMesh::part_of_cluster` with it, which is the array `GpuScene::upload_materials` indexes by the merged position. Until 2026-09-24 it did not, and from 2026-09-17 every non-streamed scene of more than one mesh drew each cluster of a multi-material mesh with whichever material belonged to the cluster that used to sit at its index: rock on the dunes and sand on the ridges of the desert overlook's terrain, the FlightHelmet's leather in metal and glass, and — because every LOD cut draws different clusters — patches that changed as the camera moved, which is exactly what the first owner session reported ([the write-up](../experiments/first-interactive-session-2026-09-24.md)). The streamed path merges with `ClusterOrder::keep` and a single mesh is not merged, which is why neither the renderer's tests nor any single-asset capture showed it. `flythrough_tests.cpp` holds it on a glTF of two primitives side by side, whose every cluster's material is known from where its vertices are (the terrain was the fixture until it stopped having more than one material, below).
- **A cut change never changes a surface's colour beyond the cut's own geometric error.** A material is per cluster, so anything whose colour varies across a mesh must vary through the vertices' attributes — a texture over UVs, which every LOD level interpolates from the same source vertices — and never through which material a cluster was given. The terrain broke this until 2026-09-25: it chose one of four materials per cluster by a vote of the cluster's vertices, a coarser cluster votes over a larger patch, and the sand, rock and basin borders jumped by whole clusters as the camera moved (the second owner session, [its write-up](../experiments/second-interactive-session-2026-09-25.md)). It is one material over baked maps now ([Scenes, camera paths and flythroughs](#scenes-camera-paths-and-flythroughs), "The terrain"), and `flythrough_tests.cpp` draws it at the owner's six marker cameras from two cuts and holds the colour to within 8 of 255 on all but a sliver of the pixels.
- **What a summary reports is what ran**, not what was asked for: `ResolvedSettings::settings` carries the overrides, so a run whose `--raster hw` fell back to the vertex path says `"raster":"vertex"`.
- **The renderer never reads a buffer back inside a frame.** The visible-pair counts come from a per-slot copy of the indirect argument blocks, read one frame late; the GPU milliseconds come from `gfx::GpuTimer`, never from a CPU clock. The only blocking readbacks in the module are in `capture()`, which is not a frame path.
- Pass bodies are stored in the render graph's arena and capture by reference, so declaring, compiling, and executing a frame are **one function** (`record_frame`): every parameter block a body pushes has to still be alive when `execute()` records it.
- A capture's id buffer names the (instance, cluster, triangle) a pixel's visibility id led to, never the id itself — see below.
- **A picture does not depend on the order the GPU did anything in.** The visibility id is the scene's pair, so two surfaces at exactly one depth resolve to the larger (pair, triangle) whichever run, pass, rasterizer or thread drew them, and occlusion culling on or off gives the same id channel and the same colour, word for word ([gfx](gfx.md), "The tie rule"; the desert-overlook path checks it over 2,401 frames, [below](#scenes-camera-paths-and-flythroughs)). The visible list itself is still in append order, and the one place that order reaches a picture is a deformed-vertex pool past its budget ([What overflow costs](#the-deformed-vertex-pool)).
- **A view's cut does not depend on how many views there are beside it.** Every view culls, rasterizes and resolves against its own slices, and the only thing they share is the scene. The test that holds this is the one that renders a flat three-monitor surround at 3w × h and a single view at w × h from the same camera and requires the centre monitor to be *the same picture and the same ids, pixel for pixel* (see [Multi-view](#multi-view-a-viewset-over-one-scene)).

## The offscreen contract

```cpp
SceneData data;   load_scene(desc, data, error);
ResolvedSettings resolved;  resolve_settings(settings, device.features(), &data, resolved);
if (check_availability(resolved, device.features()) != RenderAvailability::Ok) { ... }
GpuScene scene;   scene.create(device, data, resolved, &error);
SceneRenderer r;  r.create(device, scene, resolved, {.width = w, .height = h}, &error);
```

`check_availability` is deliberately separate from `create`: a device that cannot render is not a caller's mistake, and the two hosts report it differently — engine-view exits 3 (which its tests treat as a skip) and engine-host answers protocol error 1007 (`RenderUnavailable`). It checks two things and not a third: 64-bit buffer atomics, without which nothing can write the visibility buffer, and cluster acceleration structures plus ray queries when a ray was **explicitly** asked for — the ray path, or `ShadowMode::RayTraced`. The second half used to cover only the ray path, and an explicit `--shadows rt` on a device that cannot trace drew the frame without shadows and a warning; it is refused now, like `--raster rt`, because a picture without the shadows somebody asked for reads as a shadowing bug. `ShadowMode::Auto` is the request that degrades quietly, and `--shadows rt` on a *path* that builds no structures (direct, sw, auto) is a settings conflict rather than a device one and stays a warning. **Presentation is not checked**, because presenting is the window's requirement and not the renderer's.

**A refusal says what the device lacks in the words of its own verdict.** `unavailable_reason(availability, device)` is what both hosts print — the adapter's name and, for a ray-tracing refusal, `gfx::ray_tracing_degradation(device.caps())`, the sentence `engine-cli gpu.adapters` carries in `verdict.degraded` ([gfx](gfx.md#what-a-device-has-to-have)). On the project's TITAN Xp that reads "NVIDIA TITAN Xp cannot trace rays: no VK_KHR_ray_query and no VK_NV_cluster_acceleration_structure: every ray the renderer traces is a ray query …". `reference_available` takes the device for the same reason and says the same. `availability_message` is the short phrase, for a caller with no device in hand.

**A path the device lacks is never compiled.** `SceneRenderer::create_pipelines` builds the two mesh-shader pipelines — the direct one and the visibility one — only when the resolved path draws with them, and does not even load `cluster_mesh` otherwise. It built both unconditionally until 2026-09-23, which nothing noticed while every GPU the suite ran on had mesh shaders: on the first device without them — the Pascal server — `resolve_settings` correctly chose the vertex path and `SceneRenderer::create` still failed in `create_mesh_pipeline`, so no renderer could be created there at all. The vertex path's indexed pipelines and its expansion pass follow the same rule — built, and `cluster_vertex_indexed` loaded, only when `ResolvedSettings::vertex_indexed` says they draw, since that module declares the `Geometry` capability a device without `geometryShader` cannot create. Everything else it builds runs on any device `check_availability` accepted, and is built as before.

**The vertex path draws its cut indexed where the device lets it.** `resolve_settings` sets `ResolvedSettings::vertex_indexed` for the vertex path with culling on, `DeviceFeatures::geometry_shader` and `DeviceFeatures::full_draw_index_uint32` (after every other override, since it changes how the path draws and not what), and that flag is the only thing that chooses between the baseline tier's two draws ([gfx](gfx.md), "Baseline tier"). With it, the cull pass runs `cull_vertex_main` instead of `cull_main`, an expansion pass runs before each hardware draw and is timed in its zone (`gpu_ms.hw` is the expansion plus the draw), and each view's draw is one `vkCmdDrawIndexedIndirect` of the cut's own triangles followed by one `vkCmdDrawIndirect` of whatever overflowed the index budget — an instance count of zero on every frame measured. `GpuScene::create_working_set` makes the three buffers it needs, one region of each per view and hardware run like the visible list: a 64-byte `gfx::VertexDrawHeader`, a 16-byte `gfx::VertexDrawRecord` per pair, and an index array of `k_vertex_index_budget` triangles (2^20, 12 MiB) **or the scene's own bound — every triangle of every pair — when that is smaller**, so a small scene can never overflow and pays only for what it could draw; the frame's reset writes each header with `vkCmdUpdateBuffer`. The largest cut measured, 64 FlightHelmets at LOD 0.25 and 3840×2160, is 0.85 M triangles of the 1.05 M. Everything downstream reads what it read before: the visible list the resolve, the Hi-Z build and the ray chain use is written exactly as it was, and the records are a second output of the cull pass beside it, not a change to it. The shadow casters' run (`gfx::k_caster_run`) does not meet it: a caster leaves the cull pass before the hardware survivor tail where the allocation is, and the draw reads only runs 0 and 1. The two draws are the same picture to the byte (the case below), and what the indexed one costs and saves is in [E1 on Pascal](../experiments/e1-pascal-rerun.md#after-the-vertex-path-draws-the-cuts-own-triangles): 42–48% of the raster pass on the TITAN Xp's helmet grid (6–19% of its frame), 6–24% *more* on its heightfield (at most 2.5% of that frame), and 7–22% more on the RTX 5090's helmet grid, which does not matter there because the 5090 draws the mesh path unless asked.

One frame is `begin_frame()` (wait for the slot, fold in the completed frame's statistics and timings), then `submit_frame(FrameDesc)`, then — for a presented frame — the caller's present. `FrameDesc` names the color image (a `gfx::ImageResource`), the layout to leave it in (a `gfx::ImageLayout`: `TransferSrc` offscreen, `Present` for a swapchain image), and the two semaphores (`gfx::SemaphoreHandle`s, the acquire and the render-finished); a null image draws into the renderer's own offscreen target. `render_offscreen()` is the three calls plus the wait, and `capture()` is `render_offscreen` plus the readbacks. The pipelines are built for one color format (`Desc::color_format`, a `gfx::Format`), which engine-view sets to the swapchain's so the picture is produced exactly as it is presented; the offscreen default, `R8G8B8A8Unorm`, differs from a typical swapchain's `B8G8R8A8Unorm` only in channel order and so reads back byte for byte the same.

**This module's public headers name no Vulkan type, and its sources include no Vulkan header** ([gfx](gfx.md#the-rhi-surface-and-the-backend-surface)). Since 2026-09-25 the renderer records every pass through `gfx::CommandList` (`bind_pipeline`, `push_constants`, `dispatch`, the indirect draws, `fill_buffer`, `update_buffer`, `copy_buffer`, …), creates its buffers with `gfx::BufferUsage`, its images with `gfx::Format` and `gfx::ImageUsage`, its samplers with `gfx::SamplerDesc`, and holds pipelines, views, samplers and semaphores as `gfx::` handles — `FrameDesc`, `SceneRenderer::Desc`, `GpuScene`'s buffers and `GeometryStreamer::record_uploads(gfx::CommandList)` included. Before that the public headers named Vulkan in 21 places and three of them included the RHI's Vulkan header, so every consumer of the renderer — both hosts, their tests — compiled against `vulkan_core.h`. The rule that it records into an image the caller names is what makes this possible: the renderer owns no device, no surface and no swapchain, so it needs nothing from the backend set, and `tools/lint.ps1`'s `vulkan-backend-include` rule and the build (only `engine::gfx_vulkan`'s linkers see `volk.h`) both keep it that way. The change moved no picture and no pass timing (the numbers are in gfx.md), which it could not by construction: every `CommandList` method is one Vulkan command, and every engine enumerator carries the Vulkan value it replaced.

The camera is a plain struct, and `orbit_camera(center, radius, distance, frame)` is the orbit engine-view has always used — distances scale with the scene's radius, and a `distance` of zero breathes between 8 and 36 radius-tenths. `orbit_camera_at(center, radius, distance, yaw, pitch)` is the same orbit at explicit angles, where `pitch` is the elevation above the orbit circle; its default, `k_orbit_pitch` (`radians(k_orbit_pitch_deg)`, 24.2277°, the protocol's `RenderOrbit.pitch_deg` default, atan(0.45) to four places), is the pitch `orbit_camera` holds too, and both rise `orbit_rise(pitch)` per unit of distance — tan worked out from the four operations in double, so a folded constant and a pitch off the wire round alike — which makes `--orbit 22` and `orbit {distance: 22}` **the same camera to the bit** and the two hosts' captures the same bytes. Until 2026-10-04 engine-view rose `0.45 · d` and the protocol `tan(radians(24.2277)) · d`, 32 float steps lower; the sky's exposure, metered from the eye's altitude, showed it ([One request, two hosts](#one-request-two-hosts)).

## The frame's origin

**The camera is a world position, and the frame's origin** ([ADR-0053](../adr/0053-world-positions-are-f64-and-the-gpu-sees-none.md), 2026-10-05; gfx.md, ["The frame's origin"](gfx.md#the-frames-origin)). `Camera::position` and `target` are `WorldPos` (f64), and a frame's one origin is the eye: `frame_eye(camera)` is the `WorldEye` every pass is given (`CullParams::eye`, `ResolveParams::eye`, the path tracer's, the top-level records' dispatch; the rasterizers read the view's cull block through `ClusterDrawParams::eye`). `ViewSet::update` builds every view's matrices with the eye at the origin, from the camera's direction (`camera_forward`: the f64 difference of its two points, normalized in f64, rounded once), so `View::view_proj` maps the frame's space to clip space and every pass's `camera` is zero. A scene's instances carry `WorldPos` translations on the CPU (`SceneInstance::origin` plus the float `transform`, added in f64 with the mesh's fit, `instance_translation`; a placement generator's placement sets `origin` to its `WorldPos` and the transform to its rotation and scale alone, in the scene reader's `expand_placements` and the world's placements consumer, so a prop stands within the local's rounding, 1.9 µm, of where its generator put it anywhere — [scene_gen](scene_gen.md#placements-far-from-the-origin), 2026-10-06) and `WorldCell`s on the GPU (`gfx::InstanceDesc`), and `SceneData::center` is a `WorldPos`, measured by `update_scene_bounds` in f64, each instance's centre placed in the frame of its own cell (T171). The centre and the radius place the stand-in lights, so a frame's rounding that depends on the instances moves them: framed at the first instance's cell, another order was lit from micrometres away (R164-3: two leaves a code apart); framed at the lowest cell, a scene read whole and the same scene streamed in framed from different cells (one pixel a code apart on the Titan Xp, `mesh room`'s case). In f64 neither the order nor an instance inside the bounds moves them.

**What the CPU rewrites each frame, and what it does not.** Nothing about an instance: the GPU measures each from the eye, the top-level records' transforms included, which `tlas_references.slang` writes in the dispatch that writes their bottom-level addresses. The lights are rebased on the CPU (`frame_lighting(..., eye)`: two stand-in point lights at the scene's centre plus an orbit, measured from the eye in f64, and the four fires nearest it, `add_fire_lights`), at most `k_frame_lights` (six) a frame, which costs nothing; each light's `WorldCell` on the GPU, as instances have, waits for a scene with many (roadmap W65, deferred). The rays' float offset (`FrameLighting::shadow_bias`) is sized by the scene's reach **from the eye**, `|center - eye| + radius`, since that is what a frame-space position's rounding scales with; it was `|center| + radius`, from the world's origin, which made it a metre 420 km out. The cascades are fit in f64 relative to the eye and snapped to whole texels in the world's light space, in f64, so a texel is fixed in the world (["Cascaded shadow maps"](#cascaded-shadow-maps)). The ground's detail frame is `gfx::ground_detail_frame(d, eye, eye)`: its lattices at the eye in double, its corner measured from the frame's origin. The sky is given the eye's height alone.

**The translation suite** (`tests/world_translation_tests.cpp`). Rigid cubes on a slab at whole 1024ths of a metre, drawn with the camera by the origin and moved by 6,548 cells (419 km), 156,250 (10,000 km) and 1,562,500 (1e8 m), and a second layout whose eye stands a millimetre short of a cell's edge with cubes either side of it: **byte-identical** ids, depth and colour on the mesh, software, indexed vertex and capacity vertex rasterizers, the ray visibility pass and with traced shadows; with the cascaded maps, byte-identical ids and depth, and colour outside a band two pixels either side of every shadow edge (a pixel is shadowed where it differs from the same frame unshadowed), because the maps' texels are fixed in the world and a whole-cell move moves the scene against them (["Cascaded shadow maps"](#cascaded-shadow-maps)). And twelve frames with the eye stepped a 1024th of a metre at a time, 10,000 km out against the same steps by the origin: the same twelve pictures, each different from the one before (a float32 eye there would not have moved at all). An absolute float32 anywhere on a path fails it by centimetres, which is why the rule is held by a test and not by reading the code.

**Seams** (ADR-0053, "one named helper per boundary"; each says `// ADR-0053 seam: <module> takes WorldPos after the merge`). **None is left after the third stage (2026-10-06)**: `scene_gen::Placement` holds a `WorldPos` and `expand_placements` puts it whole into `SceneInstance::origin`, `systems/scene_collision`'s `placement_position` is gone ([scene_collision](scene_collision.md#far-from-the-origin)), and the scene file's and the protocol's positions stopped being widened ([below](#positions-in-the-files-and-on-the-wire)); `origin` is zero only for `grid_instances`, a few metres round the origin by construction (a scene file's `scatters` joined the rest on 2026-10-07, when their centre became a `worldpos`). What went on 2026-10-06, when `domain/sim` took `WorldPos` ([sim](sim.md#positions-are-f64)): `instance_world_matrix` (`scene.h`), the float32 world matrix engine-view's animation LOD read its tier positions from, is deleted — the LOD reads an instance's cell and local (`gfx::instance_cell`, the 3x4 in the instance's own frame, `to_world`) — and so is `observer_position` (`apps/engine_view/anim_lod.h`), since the camera's `WorldPos` goes into the observer set as it is; and the float32 overloads of `terrain_tiles_round` and of `TerrainTileSet::build`, `next_layout` and `update` (`terrain_tiles.h`) are removed, since `systems/world` scores tiles from an f64 observer ([world](world.md)) and this module's tests hand the `WorldPos` forms a camera on the ground (`ground_at`). What went on 2026-10-05: `systems/scene_collision` read `instance_world_matrix` too and now reads an instance's cell and local ([scene_collision](scene_collision.md#far-from-the-origin)); engine-view's fly and walk controllers, which handed a float32 position over through `camera_point_from_controller` and `camera_point_to_controller` (`view_set.h`), hold `WorldPos` and hand the `Camera` theirs as it is ([apps](apps.md#far-from-the-origin)); and `terrain_eye`, where the ground's motion and tile layout took the eye in float32, since they take a `WorldPos` ([below](#the-grounds-tiles-are-placed-at-their-corners)). **Fields that stay `vec3` on the wire and on disk this batch** and are widened where they are read: the scene file's `Instance.translation` (`SceneInstance::transform.position`, with `origin` zero), a camera path's keys (`sample_camera_path` interpolates them in float32 as it always did and widens the result), the protocol's `RenderCamera.position`/`target` (`read_protocol_camera`) and, narrowed once, `RenderSceneInfo.center`.

### Positions in the files and on the wire

(ADR-0053 decision 5; picture-3, 2026-10-06.) Every position the renderer reads from a scene file, a camera path or a request is a schema `worldpos` — three f64, the same JSON numbers — so nothing is rounded to a float between the file and the frame's eye:

| Field | Version | Its reader | An older file or request |
|---|---|---|---|
| `engine.scene.Instance.translation` | 3 | `read_scene_file` puts it whole into `SceneInstance::origin` and leaves `transform.position` zero; `"ground": true` adds the surface at its whole millimetre (`GroundOps::height_mm`, at the terrain's time) | the same numbers, now not rounded to a float: a position a float held (anything a fragment writer wrote) is the same double; a decimal like `12.3` is its nearest double rather than its nearest float, a move of under half a float step, and a grounded instance at a millimetre-exact (x, z) stands on the same height |
| `engine.scene.CameraKey.position`, `target` | 2 | `parse_camera_path`: the keys as written; a key on the ground at its whole millimetre; an orientation key's target 100 m ahead in f64 | the same numbers, as above |
| `engine.scene.Scatter.center` | 2 (2026-10-07) | `read_scene_file`: each instance's place is the centre plus the float32 offset the seed draws (the angle, radius, scale and yaw stay float32: the expansion's content, the size of the annulus), added in f64, into `SceneInstance::origin` with `transform.position` zero; `"ground": true` adds the surface at its whole millimetre as a file's instance's does. The centre's `y` is not read | **refused with the field's path**: version 1 was two numbers, `[x, z]`, and is written `[x, 0, z]` now (the desert overlook's palms were). By the origin an instance moves by the float32 sum's rounding, at most half a float's step at its coordinate (7.6 µm on the palms 175 m out), and stands on the height at its millimetre |
| `engine.scene.RuinSite.origin` | 2 | written by the ruins' fragment writer (`domain/ruins`) from the site's f64 place as it is, read by nothing in the renderer | the same numbers |
| `engine.scene.SandDrift.from`, `to` | 2 (2026-10-07) | written by the ruins' fragment writer from a wall's `ruins::Drift` as it is — x and z the face's end in the world's centimetres divided once, y the building's base — read by nothing in the renderer ([ruins](ruins.md#far-from-the-origin)) | refused with the field's path: version 1 was `[x, z]`; write the fragment again |
| `engine.protocol.RenderCamera.position`, `target` | 2 | `read_protocol_camera` takes them as they are | the same numbers |
| `engine.protocol.RenderSceneInfo.center` | 3 | `render.load` writes `SceneData::center` as it is | — (a result) |

A `worldpos` outside the cells' reach (±1.37e11 m) or not finite is refused with the field's path, by the schema's reader, before any of these sees it ([schemas](../../schemas/README.md)).

**A scatter far out is its twin by the origin** (`renderer: a scene file's scatter far out is its twin by the origin, moved`, `scene_gen_scene_tests.cpp`, no device): two scatters of 16, one grounded and one not, read with their centre by the origin, at 419,072 m, 10,000 km and 1e8 m, and a 1024th of a metre short of a cell's edge 10,000 km out (11 of its instances west of the edge and 21 east): every instance is the origin's twin's place plus the centre, to the bit, its rotation and scale the same, and a grounded one stands on the test's sawtooth ground at the millimetre it is at. With the centre a float32 `vec2` the same scatter 10,000 km out stood on a metre's grid. A version 1 centre, two numbers, is refused (`flythrough_tests.cpp`'s scene file case).

**Counts a file states are bounded before they size anything** (T187, from [T13's reading](../experiments/fuzzing-design.md#what-the-reading-found); a client names a scene to `render.load` and a camera path to `render.benchmark`). A scatter's `count` is refused when the read's instances would pass `k_max_pairs` (2^24): every instance is at least one (instance, cluster) pair and the visibility id holds no more, so the rest could never be drawn, and before the bound the read pushed each one (16,777,217 of them, about 2.5 GB in a debug build) before the GPU scene refused the scene. A camera path whose duration times its rate passes `k_max_camera_path_frames` (100,000, `render.benchmark`'s own cap on a client's `path_frames`, 27 minutes at 60 frames a second) is refused by `parse_camera_path` with the number, where `frame_count` wrapped in `u32`; and a flight multiplies its warm-up, frames and repeats in 64 bits and refuses a flight a `u32` cannot count. Cases: `hostile_scene_tests.cpp`, no device.

**The camera path is interpolated in f64** (`sample_camera_path`): a sample is the segment's first key plus a displacement built from the keys' differences — `p0 + (p1 − p0) h01 + m0 dt h10 + m1 dt h11`, the Hermite basis with `h00 = 1 − h01`, and the tangents from differences too — so it rounds once, at the camera's own place, and a path moved by whole cells samples the same displacements. Where f64 holds the sum (keys at whole 1024ths of a metre and times on powers of two, as the file-based translation test writes them) its cameras move by exactly the cells; otherwise a far sample rounds at f64's own step there, 2 nm at 10,000 km. The field of view stays float32, eased by the same fraction. The path's hash is of the file's bytes and did not change. By the origin the samples moved by the float32 interpolation's rounding — a float's step at the path's coordinates, 0.12 mm at 1.4 km: on the erg's walk the eye moved in 1,136 of 1,201 frames, 0.05 mm on average and 0.22 mm at most — which moved a few percent of a picture's pixels by one level and changed no LOD level; the numbers are in [the experiment](../experiments/world-positions-renderer-2026-10-05.md#stage-3-picture-3-the-files-and-the-wire).

**The file-based translation test** (`apps/engine_cli/tests/render_tests.cpp`, "a scene file and its path written 10,000 km out draw the origin's bytes"): a slab and 28 cubes and a smooth three-key path, written by the origin and again 156,250 cells out by their own numbers, flown by engine-view over 17 frames (four between keys and the last key, colour, ids and depth) and captured by `render.capture` at two cameras named on the wire: the same bytes in every channel (15 engine-view files and 6 host files, `msvc-debug`, RTX 5090, 2026-10-06), and engine-view's last frame is the host's picture of the last key at each site.

### The ground's tiles are placed at their corners

(ADR-0053's consequence for terrain; picture-2, 2026-10-05.) Until then a terrain level's chunks — the world's tile levels, the far levels and a scene terrain's ring set — were world-space float32 vertices under instances at cell zero, so 420 km out every vertex reached the frame as `vertex + (−eye)`, both terms the size of the distance from the origin, and the endless desert drew its edges centimetres off. Now **a chunk is placed at its corner**:

- **Its vertices are metres from its corner.** A world tile's mesh (`build_terrain_tile_mesh`) writes `(i · spacing_mm − corner_mm) / 1000` for each lattice point, rounded to float32 once at the size of the tile; `TerrainTileMesh` and `TerrainChunk` carry the corner in whole millimetres (`corner_x_mm`, `corner_z_mm`), the tile's lattice point (0, 0). **A ring's chunk is built in its corner's frame by the ground provider** (2026-10-07, roadmap W63): the dunes' rings set `terrain::RingParams::chunk_frame`, so `build_ring_chunk_mesh` writes the lattice point less the chunk's corner — `(i, j) · k_ring_chunk_cells · spacing`, the chunk's lattice corner whether or not the ring's square clips it — in integers, rounded once, and measures the UVs from the same corner (`scene_gen::RingChunkRef` says so for every provider's rings); the ring set stands the chunk at that corner and reads its rest heights off the DAG as the corner's lattice index plus each vertex's own (`rest_of`). Until then the provider built in the world's frame and the set moved the DAG to the corner afterwards (`place_at_corner`: positions, spheres, cone apexes and the grid's origin), which was exact on the default dyadic lattices by the origin and a rounding on any other, and left the DAG simplified from world positions and the grid frame's UVs — a function of where the chunk stood. `TerrainRings::reset` refuses `chunk_frame` together with `merge`, which joins a ring's chunks into one DAG and so needs one frame; the renderer draws chunk by chunk (`merge` false) and never asked for it.
- **Its slot's instance carries the corner as a `WorldCell`**, set from the millimetres and never through a float32 metre (`gfx::set_terrain_corner`: the cell `floor(mm / 64000)`, the local the rest in metres), and written when the slot is turned on, in the same frame as the record that names the chunk's clusters (`GpuScene::terrain_chunk_show` and the first fill; the records go through the frame's record upload, `GpuScene::prepare_records`, with the mesh records — since 2026-10-22 out of the frame slot's own record staging rather than the staging ring — and the frame declares the instance table among the buffers it writes and reads: [Moving an instance](#moving-an-instance)). Turned off, it stays where it was. **Nothing is rewritten when the eye moves**; a tile moved into a slot is one 96-byte record.
- **The pool pass works in millimetres** (`deform.slang`'s terrain stage, `gfx::TerrainLevelDesc::spacing_mm`): it reads the corner back off the instance (`terrain_corner_mm` in scene.slang and cluster_cull.h — a local of whole millimetres is within 3.8 µm of them in float32, so the local times 1000, rounded, is exact), finds the vertex's lattice point as the corner's whole spacings in integers plus `round((remainder + rest) / spacing)` in float32 the size of a tile, and writes the point back relative to the corner. A world tile's border drawn from a coarser level's description works the same way with that level's spacing and the tile's own corner.
- **The scene's grid stays where it was**: level 0 is one mesh on the grid's float lattice in its own mesh space, which is the world, under the identity at cell zero (`GpuScene::create_terrain` refuses anything else); its hole, the only hole a level has, is in that space, and the cull pass tests it only for the grid (`spacing_mm` 0). The grid is the scene terrain's own, kilometres across round the origin.
- **A world tile's UVs are from its corner too** (picture-4, 2026-10-06). The terrain's material is two maps baked over the scene grid (`bake_terrain_maps`: base colour, and metallic-roughness with the sand share in alpha), clamped at its edge, and its UVs are read by nothing but that material — the ground's detail has its own frame. A tile's mesh writes `(lattice point − corner) / side` in millimetres, the grid's UV scale (`TerrainTileMeshSpec::uv_size_mm`, the spec's only UV field: the frame's corner left it), its slot's instance is flagged `gfx::k_instance_uv_from_corner` when it is placed (every level's slot since 2026-10-07, when the rings' chunks came from their corners too; `TerrainLevelSet::uv_from_corner`, which said which sets did, is gone), and the resolve and the reference path tracer add the corner's place in the grid's frame before `material_uv` (`gfx::terrain_uv_offset` from the frame in `ResolveParams::terrain_uv_*` and `PathTraceParams::terrain_uv_*`, which the GPU scene fills from `terrain_uv_frame`: the grid's corner, −extent on both axes, in millimetres, and one over its side; a half-side past 2,147 km, which those 32-bit words cannot hold, is refused). **Why**: the cluster DAG's simplification weighs UVs, and UVs in the grid's frame were a tile's absolute place in disguise — a tile 420 km out simplified from UVs in the thousands, its twin by the origin from fractions — so a tile's level-of-detail tree, and every cut but the finest, depended on where it stood. Now a tile's whole DAG is a function of its key and its heights. The UVs are far finer too: a half float steps by 2⁻¹¹ between 0.5 and 1, 3 m on the erg's 6 km grid, and a tile's UVs are a tile wide at most, near zero. `terrain_tile_key` never held the UV frame and did not change, and a tile set built ahead stores heights, so its cache is unchanged. A ring's chunk followed on 2026-10-07: its UVs from its corner in the grid frame's scale (the dunes' rings' UV frame is `ring_params_from_tunables(0, 0, extent, spacing)`'s, corner −extent and side 2 · extent, the frame `terrain_uv_frame` hands the resolve), its slot flagged, and the picture by the origin moved only through the rounding of the UVs and the DAG simplified from them ([the experiment](../experiments/world-positions-renderer-2026-10-05.md#stage-5-the-grounds-leftovers) has the numbers).
- **The ground's layout takes the eye as a `WorldPos`**: `TerrainMotion::frame`, `TerrainLevelSet::next_layout` and `update`, `TerrainRingSet::build` and `TerrainTileSet::build` choose windows, squares and ring centres from it in f64 and whole millimetres; the renderer's own first fill (`terrain_tiles_round(desc, WorldPos, ...)`) measures each tile's centre from the camera in f64. Stage 1's `terrain_eye` is gone.

**What holds it.** The translation suite's terrain (`world translation: the world's tiles moved by whole cells with their ground draw the same bytes`, terrain_tiles_gpu_tests.cpp): small world tiles with and without far levels, over a tile source of the test's own whose heights are a function of the lattice point measured from its own origin, moved with the camera by 6,548, 156,250 and 1,562,500 cells — ids, depth, normals and colour byte-identical on the mesh, software, both vertex rasterizers and the ray visibility pass, **at the finest cut and at the default one** (the default since 2026-10-06, when a tile's UVs became relative to its corner; before, about 22,400 id words, 10,100 depths, 18,900 normal bytes and 5,700 colour bytes of 24,576 pixels differed at the default cut on every path and move). Under it, `world tiles: a tile built far out is its twin by the origin, cluster for cluster` (CPU) builds a tile and its ground moved by 6,548, 156,250 and 1,562,500 cells, writes each DAG as a `.clusters` container, and finds all 33 sections' hashes equal (before: positions equal, all 281 vertices' UVs different, and 7 sections — clusters, LOD records, vertices, attributes, triangles, vertex sources and the 16-bit grid — differed). `terrain corner: a tile's corner placed from millimetres reads back to the millimetre` (domain/gfx) round-trips 1,260 corners from the origin to 1e8 m on lattices of 25 cm to 64 m. A ring's chunk has the same pair (2026-10-07): `terrain rings: a chunk built in its corner's frame far out is its twin by the origin` (domain/terrain, CPU) moves rings and their ground to 419,072 m, 10,000 km and 1e8 m, with the camera inside a chunk and a millimetre short of a cell's edge, and finds every chunk's mesh the same in every stream and a chunk's DAG the same in all nine (in the world's frame the positions and UVs of every chunk differ, and a far chunk's DAG had 38–50 clusters where its twin had 40 or 47); `terrain rings: a chunk in its corner's frame is the world's chunk at its corner` holds the corner's chunk to the world's less the corner to the bit by the origin; and this module's `terrain rings: a chunk stands at its corner, its DAG from it, its rest on the lattice` (CPU) holds every chunk of a ring set at its chunk's corner, every DAG vertex on the ring's lattice inside the chunk, and every rest height to the ground at the lattice point it is filed under. The erg drawn from tiles against the grid (`world tiles: the erg from tiles is the grid's picture inside its extent`) is now held to the same colour and to depth within 16 float steps, with at most one pixel in 5,000 past that: the grid's vertices are world coordinates at cell zero and a tile's are from its corner, so the same lattice point reaches the frame through two different roundings (6,690 of 156,172 pixels differ in some bit of depth, 11 by more than 16 steps — silhouette pixels whose edge moved by that rounding — and none in colour, RTX 5090).

**What it gives up.** Two tiles that share a border vertex reach the frame through two instances, so the vertex's two copies round differently by a float step at its distance from the eye — where every tile under one identity instance drew them bit-identical. The rasterizers snap to a sub-pixel grid far coarser than that, and the rings' and the far levels' seam tests (no crack, no T-junction, no lighting seam) pass as before.

## Multi-view: a `ViewSet` over one scene

[04 §4.6](../plan/04-renderer.md#46-extreme-displays) asks for multi-view rendering as a first-class concept: *N views sharing one scene, one culling hierarchy, one TLAS, one residency budget.* `systems/renderer/view_set.h` is that concept. `ViewSet::build` lays a `ViewLayout` — `single`, `surround3`, or `panini` — out over the color target and fixes everything the screen sizes; `ViewSet::update` turns one frame camera into N view-projection matrices. A `View` carries its rectangle of the target, its **source** extent (what the rasterizers run at, which is wider than the rectangle only for a Panini view), the yaw its camera is turned by, its frustum as tangents at unit distance, and its `ViewQuality` tier.

**What is shared and what is per view.**

| Shared by the set | Per view |
|---|---|
| the `GpuScene`: geometry, materials, textures, instances, the deformed-vertex pool | the cull params (frustum, Hi-Z, flags and prev_flags, LOD threshold) |
| one top-level acceleration structure, built from the **union** of the views' cuts | its run of the visible list, its indirect argument blocks |
| one CLAS set and one set of cluster bottom-level structures, sized by the frame's union | its region of the visibility buffer and its own Hi-Z pyramid |
| the eye position, the near plane, the lights, the residency budget | its viewport, its resolve, its ray dispatch, its statistics |
| | its view-projection, and its `clip_to_ray` — the projection times the view's rotation, inverted, with no eye in it — which every pixel's direction is made from ([the sky](#the-sky)) |

**Why the per-frame working set is slices of shared buffers and not a set per renderer.** The [Not yet](#not-yet) note this replaces said a second `SceneRenderer` on one `GpuScene` would need its own visible list, argument blocks and flags. Duplicating them per renderer was the wrong half of the choice. A visibility id is an *index into the visible list*, so if two views had two lists an id would be ambiguous and the resolve could not decode one without knowing which view wrote it; the ray tracing chain builds one set of structures from the union of the cuts, and a union is a contiguous range of one array rather than a gather over N; and §4.6 asks a `ViewSet` to share *one residency budget*, which one allocation that scales with the view count is and N allocations are not. So `GpuScene` takes the view count from `ResolvedSettings` and every per-frame buffer carries a slice per view.

**The entry space, and the id beside it.** The visible list is **run-major**: run *r* of view *v* starts at entry `(r * views + v) * pair_count` (`GpuScene::visible_base`). There are `k_visible_runs` = 3 runs — occlusion pass 1, pass 2, the software rasterizer (which a frame that traces shadows uses for its shadow casters instead, `gfx::k_caster_run`) — so the list is `3 * views * pair_count` entries, and an entry index is unique across the whole frame: it is what the deformed-vertex pool's slot table, the indexed draw's records and a CLAS record's base geometry index are indexed by. Within a run the entries are in the order the cull pass's append handed out slots, which is not the same twice ([gfx](gfx.md), "The visible list's order", has why it stays that way). The **visibility id is not an entry**: it is the scene's pair ([gfx](gfx.md), "The tie rule"), the same in every run and every view, and the cull pass also writes each view's **pair-to-entry table** (`GpuScene::pair_entries`, `pair_count` words a view) for every pair it draws — a pair is drawn at most once per view per frame — which is how the resolve gets from a pixel of a deformed instance back to the entry its pool block belongs to. Every other pixel decodes through the scene's **pair table** (`GpuScene::pair_table`, the {instance, cluster} of every pair, written once at upload), one load as `visible[entry]` was; reading the per-view table for every pixel cost the TITAN Xp's resolve 2–3% ([visible order](../experiments/visible-order.md)). Run-major rather than view-major for one reason: it puts the **first** run of every view in one contiguous range at the front of the list, and that range is exactly what the ray tracing chain consumes, so `records_main` covers every view's cut in one dispatch reading each view's own count word out of its indirect block (`gfx::k_draw_args_bytes` apart). With one view the layout is the same three runs it has always been, at the same offsets.

The records chain widens by the same factor: an instance's slice of the bucketing scratch is `views` times its mesh's cluster count, because in the worst case every view draws every cluster of it, and the view count in `gfx::ClusterRecordParams::mode` is what says so. The largest geometry index is `views * pair_count - 1` (three times that, less one, with shadow casters), which the device bounds — a surround is where a large scene meets it ([The ray tracing chain's index space](#the-ray-tracing-chains-index-space)). The CLAS set **was** sized `views * pair_count` too, which is capacity and not traffic: on a surround the views see nearly disjoint thirds of the world, so a frame builds about as many records as one view would while the allocation was three times it ([E9](../experiments/e9-multi-view.md) has the numbers). Since 2026-09-24 it is sized by what the frames build instead ([The ray tracing chain's memory](#the-ray-tracing-chains-memory)), and a surround costs what its union of cuts costs.

**What each shader had to learn, and what it did not.** The rasterizers and `hiz_build.slang` learned *nothing*: a view's raster pass sets a viewport at the **origin** of its own source rectangle, so `SV_Position` is already view-local, its `visibility` address is its own region of the buffer, and its Hi-Z pyramid is built from that region and indexed from element zero. Only the resolve had to learn where it is — `ResolveParams::view_x`/`view_y` are the rectangle's origin, which it subtracts from `SV_Position` — because the resolve is the one pass that writes the shared color target. Every one of those fields is zero for a single view and the arithmetic reduces to what it was, which is why the single-view pictures are byte-identical before and after (verified on the FlightHelmet through `--raster hw`, `--raster vertex`, `--raster rt --shadows rt` and `--deform wave`: PSNR null, SSIM 1, FLIP 0 on all four).

**Surround3.** Three views over a target divided in three, with per-monitor off-axis frusta. The eye distance is the one that makes a monitor subtend the field of view; `Surround3::bezel` is bezel *correction* (the rectangles always tile the target, because a driver-surround surface has no pixels behind a bezel, so the gap widens the angle between the monitors instead); `side_yaw` turns the side monitors inward, which turns their cameras and reshapes their frusta. The centre monitor is centred whatever the arrangement, so it takes the symmetric projection rather than the off-axis one — deliberately, because that makes the centre view of a flat surround **bit-for-bit** the single view of one monitor, which is the identity the multi-view cull is tested against. At `side_yaw` 0 the three off-axis frusta are exactly the three thirds of one wide rectilinear frustum, so a flat surround and a single wide view are the same picture.

**Panini.** One view, rendered rectilinear into an oversampled source and resampled in the resolve. The source is the *same frustum* the single rectilinear view would have used, at a wider resolution: `(d + cos t) / ((d + 1) cos t)` times as wide at the half horizontal field of view, which is what it takes for the resample never to magnify (about 2× at d = 1 and 48:9). The resample happens **inside the resolve**, in the visibility domain: an output pixel maps back through the Panini inverse to a fractional source position, reads the visibility buffer there, and reconstructs its barycentrics at that same fractional point, so it stays sub-pixel accurate. That is the cheapest form — no intermediate color image, no second full-screen pass, no bindless slot for it — and it is the honest one, because a visibility id cannot be filtered anyway. Its cost is that the periphery, where the source is several times denser than the picture, is point-sampled and aliases; a filtered color-domain resample plus TAA is the fix and both are open ([E9](../experiments/e9-multi-view.md)). At d = 0 the Panini projection *is* the rectilinear one, and the picture comes back identical to the single view's (measured: not one pixel of 49,152 differs at 384 × 128).

**Foveation, as far as it goes.** `ViewQuality::lod_scale` multiplies the view's LOD pixel threshold, so `--peripheral-lod 4` lets a cluster be four times as wrong in screen space on the side monitors before its parent group is drawn instead. That is the whole of §4.6's foveation that is built. `ViewQuality::shading_rate` is **stubbed**: it is set, carried into the statistics and reported, and nothing consumes it — a real rate needs `VK_KHR_fragment_shading_rate` in the RHI and either a per-view rate attachment or `vkCmdSetFragmentShadingRateKHR` per draw, neither of which `domain/gfx` has. Per-view internal resolution, ray budget and effect cutoffs are not built either; the `View` carries a source extent per view, which is the seam a resolution scale would use.

**Per-view statistics, and what the milliseconds mean.** `Stats::views[v]` carries the view's rectangle, its tier, its visible pairs by draw, and its GPU milliseconds by pass; `Stats::view_ms(v)` divides. The acceleration structure chain is deliberately *not* attributed to a view: it is built once from the union and belongs to the frame. Each stage is one render-graph pass with a loop over the views inside it rather than a pass per view, because the views write disjoint slices of the same buffers and the graph tracks whole buffers — a pass per view would make it insert a barrier between views that have no hazard. The Hi-Z build is the exception: one dispatch of it folds six mips and the next one reads the last of those, so its dispatches must be barriered anyway, and the views' pyramids are therefore built one after another and a view's pyramid is one timer zone. **A zone's timestamps are written at ALL_COMMANDS on both ends**, which was taken to order the views of a pass on the queue, so that the per-view numbers were what each view costs alone and the frame's total an upper bound on what overlapping views would cost. **Measured, it costs nothing that shows** (R195, 2026-11-21): the forest staging's walk at 11520×2160 with the views of each pass timed as one zone ran 52.19 ms of GPU at the median against 52.77, and its frames' wall 54.08 ms against 53.31 — under the flights' spread — so the per-view numbers are each view's share and the sum is the frame's. **`renderer.timing.view_zones`** (true; R195) is the comparison: false times each multi-view pass — the cull, the deform pool, the index expansion, the hardware and software rasterizers, the primary rays and the resolve — as one zone, the first view's, so the views of a pass may overlap; the frame's buckets keep their meaning, `Stats::views[0]` then carries the pass and the other views' milliseconds are zero, and the picture is the same bytes (`renderer: a surround's views timed as one zone a pass draw the same bytes`). One view is one zone either way. The pair is [the wide frame's page](../experiments/wide-frame-and-long-frames-2026-11-21.md#the-views-timed-as-one-zone); a weaker card or another driver is asked the same question with the one flag.

**What multi-view does to ray tracing, which is the finding worth carrying.** One TLAS over the union of per-view *cuts* means two views that take different LOD levels of the same surface put both levels in one structure, and a ray from either view may hit the other's level. E9 wrote that with the peripheral LOD multiplier at 1 the views agree; they do not whenever their projection scales differ, which a turned surround's do by construction (a side monitor stands further from the eye along its own axis) and a flat one's did whenever the camera's field of view was not the layout's, until the surround followed the camera (below). **Since 2026-10-09 a frame that builds acceleration structures gives every view the finest view's LOD** ([One cut for every view](#one-cut-for-every-view)), so the union is one cut and §4.6's "RT is view-agnostic" holds; the price is that `--peripheral-lod` does not coarsen the side monitors in such a frame. A consequence of the union that remains: with more than one view a ray may name a pair through *another* view's entry, which resolves to the same (instance, cluster, triangle) and so is invisible to a capture, but means E2's word-for-word "ray-traced visibility matches the rasterized cut" invariant is a single-view statement.

**A surround follows the camera's field of view** (2026-10-10, the roadmap's F18). The three frusta are computed in one place, `ViewSet::lay_out_surround(fov_y)`: the eye distance that makes one monitor subtend that field of view, then the bezel correction and the side monitors' turn as similar triangles. `build` calls it with `ViewSetDesc::fov_y`, so a set is laid out before it has seen a camera, and `update` calls it again with the **camera's** `fov_y` whenever that is not the one the frusta were laid out from (`ViewSet::fov_y()` says which), before it builds a projection. The centre monitor's symmetric projection always came from the camera's field of view, so the three views are now one field of view on every frame, whatever a host put in the desc or a path does to the camera. Nothing a surround allocates depends on it — its rectangles are the monitors' — which is why it can follow the camera where a Panini view cannot: a Panini source's width sizes the visibility buffer, so `ViewSetDesc::fov_y` is still what a Panini view is sized from, and for a surround it is only the layout until the first `update`. No host sets it today; every one gets the 55° default.

Until then `update` built the side monitors' off-axis frusta from what `build` had fixed at 55°, and the erg's walk and camera paths are at 60°: a centre monitor at 60° beside side monitors at 55° was a step in scale at both seams — by the projections' arithmetic, a metre-tall post ten metres out at the seam was 93.5 pixels tall on the centre monitor of a 5760×1080 surround and 103.7 on the side one — and side views 1.109 times as fine in LOD as the centre one, which is what put two cuts into the structures on the erg ([the shards](../experiments/shadow-shards-2026-10-09.md)) before every view took the finest view's cut under traced shadows ([One cut for every view](#one-cut-for-every-view)). With the views at one field of view a flat surround's three projection scales are equal again, so that rule no longer changes a flat surround's cut at all; a turned surround's side views still stand further from the eye along their own axes and still need it. The test is `view set: a surround follows the camera's field of view across both seams` (`renderer_tests.cpp`): a 55° layout, flat and turned 30°, updated with a 60° camera — the post at either seam is the same height on both monitors within a pixel and lands on the seam on both, the views are bit for bit the views of the same layout built at 60°, a flat surround's three LOD scales are one, and a single view is the camera's projection to the bit. What it did to the owner's two surround budgets is in [the shards page](../experiments/shadow-shards-2026-10-09.md#2026-10-10-the-census-again-f17-and-the-surround-at-the-cameras-field-of-view-f18).

## Morphed instances

A mesh with morph channels ([geometry](geometry.md)) is **deformed whatever the flags say**, exactly as a skinned one is: `SceneData::morphed()` joins `skinned()` in what makes `resolve_settings` turn the deform pass on, and every instance of such a mesh gets a `gfx::DeformDesc` with the two morph stages in its mask ([gfx](gfx.md), "The deform chain"). What this module adds is the three things the chain needs and only a renderer can supply.

**The stream, once per scene.** `GpuScene::create_morph` uploads the six arrays `merge_cluster_meshes` concatenated — the channel records, the per-cluster slice directory, the slices, the delta indices, and the two delta streams — and one `gfx::MorphParams` block naming them. They are the *scene's*: the slices are keyed by the global cluster index and the channels by the global channel index, so one block serves every mesh and every view of a frame, the way `StreamParams` serves the page table.

**The weights, on the same contract the joint matrices travel on.** Each deformed instance has `2 x channel_count` floats: the **static** half and the **pose** half. The static half is the scene's — `RenderSettings::morph_static_weights`, written at create and again through `GpuScene::set_static_weights`, which marks the caches dirty — and the pose half is the frame's, `FrameDesc::morph_weights`, one plain span the caller samples from a clip's weight tracks (`anim::Clip::sample(time, pose, weights)`) and the renderer copies into this slot's region. A morphed scene therefore always has the **per-frame** copy of the deform table that skinning already forced, because each record has to point at this slot's weights.

**The caches, budgeted.** `RenderSettings::static_shape_kib` (4 MiB by default, 16 bytes a mesh vertex) is handed out in instance order; an instance that gets none runs its static stage every frame over the cut, which is the same picture for more work. When the weights change, the frame dispatches `deform_cache_main` once per cached instance — over the whole mesh, not the cut — and the next frames read the cache. The summary reports `morph_channels`, `morph_static_cache_bytes` and `morph_cached_instances`, so "did this character get a cache?" is a number rather than a guess.

**Bounds.** A morphing instance's vertices leave their rest positions, so its `bounds_padding` gains `geometry::morph_bounds_padding`'s bound — the sum over the mesh's channels of |weight| × the channel's largest displacement — computed with the **static** weights as they are and every **pose** weight priced at 1, which is the range a glTF weights track lives in. It is conservative in the honest direction: a sphere too big draws a cluster that might have been culled, a sphere too small drops a limb off the screen. The three spheres it inflates are the cluster's and both LOD spheres, for the reason skinning's does — one constant on all three is what leaves exactly one cluster per DAG path passing.

**One instance's static weights** (2026-11-01, roadmap P52's creator; apps.md, "Actors"). The static half was the scene's alone — `RenderSettings::morph_static_weights`, indexed by the scene's channel, every instance of a mesh taking the same run of it, and `set_static_weights` rewriting every instance and marking every cache dirty. A game's actor needs a shape of its own, so `SceneRenderer::set_instance_morph_weights(instance, weights)` (`GpuScene::set_instance_static_weights`) writes **one** loaded instance's static half — `weights[c]` for channel c of its own mesh, the rest 0 — in every frame slot, as the scene-wide form does, and leaves every other instance's alone. The cache's dirty flag is now **per deform entry**: a scene-wide change marks them all and an instance's change marks its own, `take_static_cache_rebuilds` moves the marks to the frame's set as the frame is recorded, and the `deform cache` pass dispatches `deform_cache_main` for the marked entries only — so a change costs one dispatch over that instance's mesh on the next frame and the frames after it nothing, however many morphed instances the scene holds (until then a change re-ran every cached instance). The instance's cull padding is priced again from the new weights as the load priced the scene's (|static| + 1 for the pose half, times each channel's reach) on the padding it had before any morph, and its record re-uploaded with the next frame's (`mark_instance_written`), so a shape pushed past the load's padding is never culled away; that is also why the ABI holds a weight to `k_morph_weight_limit`. Refused, with nothing written, for an instance without channels or with more weights than it has. Never between `begin_frame` and `submit_frame`. The cost is measured in apps.md ("Actors", "Testing the shape").

**A single morphed mesh carries its own channel run, and until the Khronos samples nothing checked it.** A part's `first_morph_channel`/`morph_channel_count` is what gives an instance its morph stages and its deform record, and `merge_cluster_meshes` fills it for every part it concatenates — but a one-mesh scene never goes through the merge, and `load_scene`'s single-mesh branch left the run at zero while the stream (which `resolve_settings` reads) said otherwise. The deform pass was turned on for a scene with no deform record, the pool was sized for no vertices, and **every single morphed glTF failed to load** with `vmaCreateBuffer: VK_ERROR_INITIALIZATION_FAILED`. The morph case in this module's tests had never seen it because it builds its `SceneData` by hand and fills the part itself; `renderer: a single morphed glTF loads, draws, and moves through load_scene` goes through the loader, the way both hosts do.
**Streaming refuses a morphed mesh, and says so.** `resolve_settings` turns `--stream` off with a logged reason when the scene has channels. A page's payload is the cluster's positions, attributes, triangles and bindings; the morph stream is keyed by cluster too, but its slice directory indexes a scene-wide delta array whose offsets a page copy would have to patch the way it patches `ClusterDesc::vertex_offset`. That is the same work and belongs with it, so until then the whole stream is resident — `ClusterFileReader`'s resident list says so — and a caller that asks for both gets the one that draws the right picture.

## Skinned instances

E25 built the deformed-vertex pool and `deform.slang` grew a skinning kind; [animation](animation.md) produced the matrices as one contiguous span; nothing joined the two. This is the join, and it is deliberately small: **the renderer knows about bone matrices and knows nothing about clips.**

**What a caller says.** A `SceneInstance` names a joint count — `joints > 0` is what makes an instance skinned — and a bound on how far skinning moves its vertices (`bounds_padding`, below). Every member after `transform` carries a default, so `SceneInstance{mesh, transform}` is the whole of a rigid, unanimated instance and is the spelling the loader and the tests use; `animation`'s default is written `SceneAnimation animation{}` rather than left implicit, because a member of class type with no initializer of its own makes that spelling a `-Wmissing-field-initializers` error on Clang and the Windows build never said so. `SceneDesc::max_joints` is the longest matrix span a frame will hand over, which is what the joint buffer is sized by; a longer one is clamped with one warning rather than overrunning it. Two fields are the caller's to fill in **after** the load rather than before, and both for the same reason — they are lengths in a space the load is what reveals. `SceneData::max_joints` is final only once the population is attached, because it is the pose pool's capacity; `InstanceDesc::bounds_padding` needs the mesh's own bounds. A host that skins therefore loads, attaches, writes both, and calls `update_scene_bounds` before creating the `GpuScene`, which is what `engine-view --animate` does. Everything else is per frame: `FrameDesc::joints` is `std::span<const anim::JointMatrix>`, every animated instance's matrices in one run, and `FrameDesc::instance_joints` is one `{first, count}` per scene instance saying where each one's run is.

That is the whole interface, and it is spans rather than a system because **the renderer must not depend on `systems/animation`, on `domain/ecs`, or on flecs**. What it does depend on is `domain/anim`, for `anim::JointMatrix` alone — a domain module, not a capability, so the dependency cannot be switched off, and copying the 48-byte record here instead would be exactly the drift `domain/anim` took its own `geometry` dependency to avoid. The tick is the app's: `engine-view --animate` owns a world, steps it at the fixed rate, and hands over the span ([apps](apps.md), [animation](animation.md) has the pattern a game copies).

**An instance with no matrices this frame draws its rest pose.** A `count` of zero, or an instance the array does not reach, leaves `DeformDesc::joints` at zero, and `deform_skin` then writes the rest position into the pool. That is what an instance at animation LOD3 — no pool slot — looks like from here. The alternative, marking it `k_invalid_deform` for the frame, would mean rewriting the instance table mid-frame, which is a per-instance upload to save a pool write the cut had already paid for.

**The upload: one memcpy, and two deform tables.** `GpuScene` allocates a host-visible, persistently mapped joint buffer with `k_joint_slots` regions, one per frame in flight, so the host write never races a device read and needs no staging copy and no barrier; `SceneRenderer::create` refuses more frames in flight than there are regions rather than letting a character twitch one frame in ten. A frame copies the whole span into its slot's region with **one memcpy** and then walks the deform table once, rewriting the two words that change.

The two words are the problem that shapes the rest. `MeshDesc::deform` is baked into an array uploaded at create, and `scene.slang`'s `load_position` reads it on every position read of every rasterizer — for `pool_offset` alone, which never changes. Only `joints` and `joint_count` change per frame, and only `deform.slang` reads them, through a push constant. So the static table stays exactly what it was (device-local, written once, what a `--deform` run without skinning still uses) and the per-frame one is a **separate** host-visible buffer with a region per slot, whose address goes into `DeformParams::deform`. A skinned scene therefore has no host write racing a device read; a rigid one has no second table at all, and no allocation, and no changed instruction.

**Which instances read the pool.** Every instance under `--deform`, the skinned and morphed ones otherwise, and a moving terrain ([The dunes in time-lapse](#the-dunes-in-time-lapse)) — so a scene of one character and a hundred props deforms the character and leaves every prop on the rigid path. `ResolvedSettings::deform_pass` is the one flag that says the pool pass runs, and `resolve_settings` is the one place it is decided, because skinning is a *kind* of `deform.slang` and not a second pass.

## The deformed-vertex pool

**The pool holds what the frame deforms, not every instance's whole mesh.** E25 built it the other way: a deformed instance owned a block as long as its mesh's cluster-ordered vertex range, whether the cut touched it or not. That is what kept a cluster's vertices contiguous — a cluster acceleration-structure record points straight at them — and it is what made the pool the binding memory constraint the moment there was a crowd: **12.2 MB for 1,024 foxes, 110 MB for 64 FlightHelmets, 1.7 GB if the 1,024 had been helmets**, to write the 1,325 clusters the frame actually draws. The pool is now a **budget** (`RenderSettings::deform_pool_mib`, 8 MiB by default, `--deform-pool-mib`), suballocated per frame from the visible list.

**The block is the (instance, cluster) pair, because that is the smallest unit that stays contiguous.** A cluster's vertices have to be one run in the pool or the ray side needs a gather it cannot do (E25 decision 2). One instance's cut is a scattered set of clusters in its mesh's vertex stream, so an instance-sized block would have to be the whole mesh again — which is what it was. A per-**visible-entry** block is exactly one cluster's vertices, and the entry is the one name every reader already has in hand: the mesh shader's workgroup, the vertex path's `SV_InstanceID`, the software rasterizer's group, the resolve (through the pair-to-entry table, since the visibility id became the pair), and the CLAS emit pass's `visible_index`. So the address moved from the instance to the entry: `MeshDesc::deform_slots[entry]` is that block's first pool vertex, `gfx::k_no_pool_slot` if it has none. That word replaced the `DeformDesc[]` address in `MeshDesc`, so the struct is still 64 bytes, `DeformDesc` fell from 24 bytes to 16 (`pool_offset` and `vertex_count` were the per-instance block), and a position read is **one indirection shorter**: the base is resolved once per cluster by `deform_base` rather than a `DeformDesc` being read per vertex.

**Why the allocation is on the GPU.** The cut is the cull pass's output and the renderer never reads a buffer back inside a frame (see [Invariants](#invariants)); an allocation computed on the CPU would be a round trip, or a frame late, or an allocation for a cut nobody drew. `deform_alloc.slang` is a prefix sum over the visible entries' vertex counts, dispatched once per run of the list before the pool pass that consumes it, covering every view of the run, so the three runs and every view share one budget through one cursor in `gfx::DeformAlloc`. The cursor advances by what was *placed*, not by what was asked for, which is what keeps a refused large cluster from charging the budget and starving every small one behind it. `gfx::DeformAlloc` (the cursor and three counters) is copied into the per-slot statistics block beside the visible counts and read one frame late, the same way and for the same reason.

**The runs it serves.** Every run of the visible list a deformed entry can be in gets an allocator dispatch, all on the frame's one cursor in the order the render graph runs them: the camera's run 0 (which resets the record), occlusion pass 2's run, the software run, **the shadow casters' run** under traced shadows (`gfx::k_caster_run`, which is the software run's place, since such a frame has none; 2026-10-18, roadmap R84 — [Shadows](#ray-traced) has why and the casters' own overflow rule), and the shadow cascades' runs behind every view's three. Each is the same three-pass allocation (below) with `DeformAllocParams::first_entry` the run's base and `views` its views, followed by the pool pass over the same run. **The small-scene clamp** allows the whole meshes once per view and once per cascade (`whole × (views + cascades)`): within one view a pair is drawn by one run, a caster, or neither, so the caster run shares its view's allowance, and every cascade deforms its own copy. Until 2026-10-18 the views were left out of it — one allowance for every view of a surround — which a scene small enough to promise it never overflowed could break from its second view.

**The overflow rule: the rest pose, counted.** An entry the budget cannot fit gets `k_no_pool_slot`, and every position reader turns that into the cluster's **rest pose** — off the 16-bit grid in the rasterizers and the resolve, off the float positions in a CLAS record, which is the same fallback a rigid instance takes and the same code path. So overflow is a character momentarily drawn at rest: never garbage, never a wild address, never a crash. **A shadow caster is the one exception**: one the budget refuses is not built at all, because a rest pose that casts where the pose does not is a wrong shadow, and a missing one is the lesser error ([Shadows](#ray-traced)). It is also never silent: the renderer logs it once and `Stats::deform_overflow_entries`/`deform_overflow_vertices` reach both hosts' summaries. Measured at the pathological end — 64 FlightHelmets at `--lod 0.05`, a 24,619-pair cut, 8 MiB of budget — 11,508 entries got blocks and 13,111 fell back, and the picture is 0.0040 FLIP (35.2 dB) from the same frame with a 256 MiB pool: a picture, not a failure.

**The allocator is a device-wide scan with the one-workgroup allocator's answer** (2026-10-26, roadmap R104). Until then one workgroup walked the whole run, 256 entries a step: about 5 µs per 1,000 entries, which was nothing at E25's 1,300 clusters a frame and **15.0 ms** of the grass clearing's frame at 11520×2160 once the flora's field kind put its sward's 115,629 instances in the pool ([The field kind](#the-field-kind)) — more than the pool pass it feeds and more than the culling, the Hi-Z and the rasterizer together. The rule it implemented is kept exactly, so the allocator's answer is defined by it and not by the scheduling: the entries are taken in **tiles** of 256 per view, views in order, runs in the order the render graph runs their dispatches; a tile's entry is placed when the cursor plus its exclusive prefix within the tile plus its own count fits the budget, and the cursor then advances by the largest inclusive prefix that fitted. That is not a plain prefix sum once the budget is crossed — an entry after a refusal in the same tile is refused, a small one in the next tile is placed in the room the refused one left — so the scan is three passes, each a render-graph pass so the graph puts the barriers between them, under the one timer zone (`deform alloc`, and `shadow` for the cascades' dispatch):

1. **The tiles' scans** (`deform_alloc_tiles_main`, one workgroup per tile, up to `gfx::k_deform_alloc_max_groups` = 2,048 striding over the rest): every entry's vertex count, the tile's inclusive scan written into the entry's own `deform_slots` word as scratch, and two words per tile in `GpuScene::deform_blocks` — the tile's total and its first non-zero prefix.
