The software block's count goes there instead of `visible_sw` in such a frame, so `visible_pairs()` still counts only what is drawn. engine-view's summary prints `shadow_casters` (the setting) and `shadow_casters_last`, and `render.benchmark` returns `shadow_casters`. `--no-shadow-casters` and the protocol's `shadow_casters: false` restore the old behaviour, to measure against.

At the default cut the casters are 0 to 19% of the cut on the Khronos samples, and building them costs nothing measurable. At the FlightHelmet's finest cut, 74 casters beside 1,028 drawn pairs cost the chain 0.011 ms, about 0.14 µs a caster. `--rt-templates` keeps no casters, because an instantiated cluster is opaque whatever its record says.

**A caster outside the camera's frustum casts too** (2026-10-18, roadmap R54). Until then the frustum test dropped such a pair outright, so it was in no structure and cast nothing: a tree behind the camera threw no shadow forward, and an object walking out of the picture had its shadow cut by the frustum's edge, cluster by cluster, while the shadow was still in view — what the owner saw on the RTX 5090 in the desert proof of concept and the first game. The cascaded maps never had the gap, because their cull is from the light. Now, with `casters` on, a pair the frustum rejects is tested against **the view's caster volumes**, and one inside them is a caster: it takes the camera's cut (the LOD the cascades draw an off-frustum caster at) and the page residency like any caster and goes to the same run, built non-opaque, counted in `Stats::shadow_casters`, and dropped first by the capacity rule. The picture is unchanged on every path, because a caster is never drawn and primary rays pass through it.

- **The directional light's volume** (`fit_directional_caster_volume`, `caster_volume.h`) is the view's frustum swept towards the key light — the sun, or on a sky's night the moon, the light the maps follow — over a cap distance: every point from which a ray towards the light can reach the view. It is convex, and with the cull's inward planes it is the frustum planes that face the light (`dot(n, L) >= 0`: moving towards the light never leaves them), a plane through each **silhouette edge** between a kept and a dropped plane that contains the light's direction, and one **cap** perpendicular to the light. At most 6 + 6 + 1 = 13 planes (10 or 11 in practice: a perspective frustum's silhouette is a cycle of at most six edges); every plane's offset is the support of the hull's own sixteen corners, so whatever the float rounding the volume holds the whole sweep.
- **The cap** is `RenderSettings::shadow_distance` (`--shadow-distance`) past the frustum's farthest corner along the light where it is set, and otherwise — and never past it — the far side of the scene's bounds towards the light, exactly where a cascade's depth ends: a caster beyond that casts on nothing the frame shows. The camera's projection has no far plane, so the frustum is first closed at the depth of the scene's far side (`closed_frustum`), which leaves out no receiver. `shadow_distance` is therefore the owner's knob for the volume's reach under rays as well as for the maps.
- **The caster horizon** (2026-10-25, roadmap R94; `RenderSettings::rt_caster_horizon`, the `renderer.rt.caster_horizon` tunable, off by default, and always on with the hybrid at the rays' reach, [Rays near, maps far](#rays-near-maps-far)): with a `shadow_distance`, a caster of either kind — cone-culled or outside the frustum — whose sphere lies farther from the eye than that distance is not built (`CullParams::caster_horizon`, 1,728 bytes; `beyond_caster_horizon` in `cluster_cull.slang`, after every other test, so what it drops is exactly the casters there would have been). The drawn clusters are never touched, so the picture and the ray path are unchanged; what it costs is the shadow a far surface facing away from the camera, or a far object outside the view, would have cast — onto receivers at least that far away, where the cascades would not have drawn a shadow at all. It is the cascades' own reach for the rays. Without a `shadow_distance` the horizon is the far side of the scene's bounds, which no caster passes, so it is not resolved on. Each dropped caster is counted in the second word of the view's software argument block, which a frame with casters fills with 1 and never dispatches (`Stats::horizon_casters`, `RtStats::horizon_casters`, the flythrough summary's `rt.horizon_casters`). On the dense test grove (800 trees, 16 m tiles in rings of 4 and 8, 640×360, the camera low across it) a 30 m horizon keeps 1,283 of 7,051 casters and counts the other 5,768, and no pixel of the traced shadows changes (`engine-view: a shadow caster past the caster horizon casts nothing and is counted`).
- **A point or spot light's volume** (`fit_point_caster_volume`): under `rt` every light of the array casts a traced shadow, so its off-frustum caster is the same gap with another volume — the convex hull of the frustum and the light's position (the frustum planes with the light inside, and a plane through each silhouette edge and the light, at most 5 + 6), inside the light's sphere of influence, and no volume at all for a light inside the frustum, since the segment from it to any receiver in the view is in the frustum too. One per light behind the key light's, up to four (`gfx::k_max_caster_volumes` is five); the stand-in lights are two, and a scene with a sky has none — its array holds the moon, which is the key light's volume on a moonlit night and casts no off-frustum shadow by day.
- **One volume per view**, fit on the CPU each frame from the view's own view-projection in the frame's space (ADR-0053), and carried in the view's own cull block (`gfx::CullParams::caster_planes`): a surround's three views sweep three frusta. Nothing is allocated for it.
- **What it costs** (RTX 5090, `msvc-release`, before → after on 2026-10-18, every run under the GPU lock with `--wait-quiet 120`; the GPU 4–5% busy at the start of each and 45% at the end of the erg's second, other processes 8.0–24.9% of the CPU, so by the harness's rule every number is an upper bound). The **desert overlook**'s path at 1080p with `--shadows rt` builds **66 → 294 casters** at the median (p99 158 → 1,036, at most 167 → 1,151) from the sun's volume, and **943** (p99 2,072) with its two stand-in point lights' as well; the medians moved by cull 0.013 → 0.016 → 0.019 ms, the cluster build 0.109 → 0.112 → 0.133 ms, the bottom-level build 0.149 → 0.131 → 0.131 ms, the resolve 0.150 → 0.151 → 0.153 ms, and the frame 0.542 → 0.526 → 0.549 ms — the volume test costs the cull pass about 3 µs a volume, and a caster about 0.03 µs of the cluster build. The two surround traced budget runs (`erg-walk-surround3-rt`, `endless-surround3-rt`, 11520×2160) **build no casters before or after**: their ground is terrain levels, which were deformed instances and so never casters of either kind until the caster run had pool blocks (below, where they build 540 and 1,550), and they hold nothing else. Their medians stayed inside their noise — the erg's cull 0.092 → 0.087, clas 0.227 → 0.226, blas 0.174 → 0.176, the chain 0.643 → 0.591, the resolve 2.325 → 2.325 and the frame 3.458 → 3.397 ms; the endless desert's cull 0.049 → 0.051, clas 0.282 → 0.282, blas 0.270 → 0.264, the chain 0.929 → 0.924, the resolve 1.893 → 1.918 and the frame 4.335 → 4.361 ms — and both pass their budgets. A scene with a sky has no point lights, so the third stage changes nothing on either. The capacity is unchanged: a pair is a caster of one kind or the other at most once per view, so the casters' run still holds them.
- **A deformed caster casts its pose** (2026-10-18, roadmap R84, R54's remainder). Until then a **deformed** instance outside the frustum — a skinned or morphed character, a `--deform` mesh, and **every terrain level**, whose vertices the pool's terrain stage moves — was no caster, because the caster run had no pool blocks and its rest pose would have cast where its pose did not; so the dunes behind the camera threw no traced shadow into the view, and the two surround budget scenes, whose ground is all terrain levels, built no casters at all. Now the caster run gets blocks the way the cascades' runs do: **one more dispatch of the allocator over it** — `DeformAllocParams::first_entry` the run's base (`visible_base(0, k_caster_run)`), every view in the dispatch, its count words the software argument blocks the cull counted the casters in — on the frame's one cursor, behind run 0, then the pool pass over the same run (the terrain stage for a level, skinning and morphs for a character), and the records pass points a caster's CLAS record at its block exactly as it does a drawn deformed entry's. The cull pass's off-frustum test no longer leaves deformed instances out; the cone test still never runs on one, so a deformed instance's casters are all off-frustum ones.
- **The overflow rule: a caster the pool has no room for casts nothing.** A drawn entry the budget refuses draws its rest pose — a character momentarily at rest is better than a hole ([the pool's rule](#the-deformed-vertex-pool)). A caster it refuses is **not built at all**: `clas_records.slang`'s bucketing pass leaves out a caster of a deformed instance whose `deform_slots` word is `k_no_pool_slot`, before it is counted, so it is in no range and no record. The rest pose would cast a shadow where the pose has none — a terrain level's rest heights can be metres from the field it draws, a character's bind pose stands where it is not — and **a wrong shadow is worse than a missing one**. The cull still counts it (`Stats::shadow_casters` counts the casters the cull kept, as before); the pool counts it among `deform_overflow_entries`. Which casters overflow, past the budget, follows the cull's atomic order like every overflow ([the pool's reproducibility](#the-deformed-vertex-pool)). The small-scene clamp makes it impossible where the pool is the whole meshes: within one view a pair is drawn, a caster or neither, so the caster run shares its view's allowance.
- **What the deformed casters cost** (RTX 5090, `msvc-release`, before → after on 2026-10-18 with `tools/frame-budget.ps1 -WaitQuiet 120`, the after runs taken twice, every run under the GPU lock). The machine was not quiet: before, 9.9–17.9% of the CPU in other processes and the GPU idle; after, 23.7–71.4% at the starts, 50.5–99.7% at some ends, and another job holding the GPU at 99% at the end of the erg's first — so every number is an upper bound, the after ones the more so, and the two after runs' medians are both quoted. **`erg-walk-surround3-rt`** (the stand-in sun 53° up): casters **0 → 540** at the median (p99 976, at most 983), the chain building 4,087 → 4,756 structures; cull 0.090 → 0.097 / 0.100 ms, the pool's allocation 0.022 → 0.028 (its one more dispatch), the pool pass 0.022 → 0.027, the cluster build 0.227 → 0.236 / 0.236, the bottom-level build 0.174 → 0.188 / 0.186, the chain 0.632 → 0.622 / 0.619, the resolve 2.320 → 2.365 / 2.360, the frame **3.382 → 3.504 / 3.494 ms**. Every GPU line is inside its budget; both after runs were marked inconclusive on `cpu_ms` alone (0.250 → 0.445 / 0.357 ms, beside 44–100% of the CPU in other processes), which this change does not touch. **`endless-surround3-rt`**: casters **0 → 1,550** (p99 2,189, at most 2,231), structures 9,400 → 11,044; cull 0.066 → 0.056 / 0.055, allocation 0.052 → 0.062, pool pass 0.032 → 0.032, cluster build 0.281 → 0.326 / 0.324, bottom-level 0.271 → 0.270 / 0.270, the chain 0.934 → 0.978 / 0.971, the resolve 1.881 → 1.999 / 1.951, the frame **4.344 → 4.555 / 4.471 ms**; it passes its budget both times. The resolve's growth is the shadow rays now meeting the dunes outside the view, which is the point. **Neither scene's pool came near its budget**: a scene with terrain levels takes at least 768 MiB (`renderer.terrain.pool_mib`, 67 million vertices), and the frames' chains built at most 5,082 and 11,491 clusters of at most 64 vertices each, drawn and casters together, so the overflow rule never fired and nothing called for `--shadow-distance`'s cap. The far levels are in the sweep like the near ones — the volume's cap is the far side of the scene's bounds towards the light — and at a 53° sun the volume behind a view is short, which is why the casters are 11 and 14% of the structures and not more; under a low sun on these scenes they would be a larger share, and `shadow_distance` is the knob that bounds them, as it bounds the maps. Nothing was rebaselined.
- A key light past the end of its twilight sweeps nothing. `RenderSettings::off_frustum_casters` (no flag) turns the volumes off, which is the old behaviour, for the test that the picture is unchanged and to measure what they cost.
- **A reflection ray's volume is the whole scene, not a light's.** A sweep towards a light bounds what can shadow the view; what a mirror or water's surface reflects can stand anywhere in front of it, so the water's reflection (roadmap R129, 2026-11-08; [water](water.md#reflections-of-the-scene)) cannot reuse a light's sweep. For one plane it does not have to: what a level surface reflects is what a camera reflected in its plane sees, so it is **one more caster volume** in the view's block, `fit_water_reflect_volume` (`water_reflect.h`) — the closed frustum reflected in the water's level, cut by the level itself (only what stands above the water is in it) and held inside `gfx::k_water_reflect_m` (4 km) of the eye. Its pairs are casters like the others: the camera's LOD, built non-opaque, counted in `Stats::shadow_casters` (the cull does not tell the three sources apart) and in the chain's capacity, dropped first by its rule. It goes in behind the lights' volumes, so a block they fill (four point lights and the sun) leaves the water what the frame's cut holds. `Stats::water_reflect_views` counts the views that carried it. **What is under the water** (S86; [water](water.md#what-is-under-the-water)) adds one more behind it, `fit_water_refract_volume` (`water_refract.h`): a frame that traces has no two-pass occlusion culling, so what lies under the water inside the frustum is in the cut already, drawn behind the surface; what the refracted view reaches outside the frustum — under its bottom edge, where Snell bends the view nearer and deeper — is a vertical prism over the frustum's cross-section at the level, pushed out by how far a refracted view can run sideways (the critical angle's tangent times the depth, or its sine times the water's reach), between the level and the deepest bed. `Stats::water_refract_views` counts the views that carried it.

**`--view shadow`** (`gfx::ResolveMode::Shadow`) draws the sun's shadow query alone. White is lit, black is blocked, and mid grey is a surface facing away from the sun, where nothing is asked. It asks the shaded view's exact question, which makes it the picture to count a shadow difference on, and the shadow tests do. A ray answers black or white; the cascaded maps answer the filtered fraction, so their penumbra is grey between the two.

### One cut for every view

**A frame that builds acceleration structures culls every view at the finest view's LOD** (2026-10-09, the roadmap's F4). The structures hold every view's runs in one bottom-level structure per instance ([Multi-view](#multi-view-a-viewset-over-one-scene)), and a shadow ray from one view's surface meets everything in them. Each view's cull used to take its own projection scale and threshold, and a surround's views do not share a projection scale: a turned side monitor stands further from the eye along its own axis than the centre one, and on a flat one the side monitors kept the layout's field of view while the centre took the camera's (until 2026-10-10, [Multi-view](#multi-view-a-viewset-over-one-scene)). So the views chose different levels of the same ground, and wherever a cluster's sphere passed two views' frusta — a band many metres wide on the far ground, where the clusters are large — both levels were in the structure. Where one stood above the other, a ray leaving the lower surface met the upper one from below within a few centimetres: **the dark shards on the far sand** of the owner's surround, which the sand-detail captures had put down to the rings' skirts. They were not the rings': the same shards drew without them.

Now `cull.lod` is the finest view's (largest projection scale over threshold, the view the cascades already take their LOD from) in every view whenever `ResolvedSettings::rt_chain` is set, so the views' cuts are parts of one cut, bit for bit, and the picture every receiver is drawn from is in the structure its rays are traced against. The same scale is also the software split's and a streamed page's priority scale, and such a frame has no software pass. What it gives up: **`--peripheral-lod` does not coarsen the side monitors under traced shadows or the ray path** (their ratio is the coarser one, so the centre's is taken), and a side monitor whose projection is coarser than the finest draws finer than its own pixels ask. A frame without the chain — maps or no shadows — keeps each view's own cut. Measured on the erg's western floor at 11520×2160 `surround3`, the stand-in sun 53° up (no part of the erg's sand is that steep): 3,766 sun-facing pixels drawn black before, 6 after; a single view is unchanged to the byte; the frame drew 1.4% more pairs and its GPU time moved by less than its noise ([the experiment](../experiments/shadow-shards-2026-10-09.md)). The test is `renderer: a turned surround traces its shadows against one cut and not three` (`renderer_tests.cpp`): a heightfield under a sun straight overhead, which nothing in it can shadow, in a 35° surround from low over its edge, every pixel lit.

### Cascaded shadow maps

`ShadowMode::Cascaded`, or `Auto` without ray queries (and, far from the eye, the hybrid: [Rays near, maps far](#rays-near-maps-far)): the sun's shadow from depth maps drawn **from the light by the same cull pass and the same rasterizers the visibility buffer uses**, filtered by the resolve. `ResolvedSettings::csm` and `shadow_cascades` say a frame draws them; `RenderSettings::shadow_cascades` (1–4, default 4), `shadow_map` (texels a side per cascade, a power of two, default 2048) and `shadow_distance` (how far from the camera they reach; 0 is the far side of the scene's bounds) size them — `--shadow-cascades`, `--shadow-map`, `--shadow-distance` and the protocol's fields of the same names.

**The fit** (`fit_shadow_cascades`, `shadow_cascades.h`, on the CPU once a frame). The camera's depth is cut into slices **logarithmically from where geometry can begin** — the near side of the scene's bounds, or the near plane when the camera is inside them — to the shadow distance, with the logarithm's base never under a thousandth of that distance, so a camera standing in a 5 km terrain does not spend its first cascade on its own feet (on the desert overlook's scale the splits are about 11, 63, 356 and 2,000 m for 2 km of shadow). Each slice's cascade is the **smallest sphere centred on the camera's forward axis** that holds the slice's corners in every view of the layout — a sphere because it is the same size whichever way the camera turns, so a turning camera keeps its texels and a static shadow does not swim; its radius is rounded up to a 64th of its power of two so float noise cannot change a texel's size between frames; and its centre is **snapped to a whole texel across the light in the world's light space, in f64** (`snap_in_world`): the centre is put back in the world (the eye plus its frame-space offset, in f64), projected on the light's right and up, rounded to whole texels there, and the move that took is applied to the frame-space centre, which is then rounded to float32 once. **A texel is a fixed piece of the world for as long as the sun stands still**, wherever the eye is, so a camera that moves moves the grid by whole texels and a static shadow never steps. f64 because the coordinates are as large as the distance from the world's origin: a centimetre's texel 10,000 km out is 1e9 texels from it, where f64 still resolves a hundred-millionth of one and a float32 had resolved 3 cm. The fit is otherwise in the frame's space (["The frame's origin"](#the-frames-origin)). **What it replaced** (picture-2, 2026-10-05): stage 1 had anchored the snap at the corner of the eye's 64 m cell (`snap_from_cell`), the one anchor that moves with the scene under a whole-cell move and so kept the translation suite's maps byte-identical; its price was that every cascade took a sub-texel step each time the eye crossed into another cell — a shimmer of every shadow edge every 0.64 s at 100 m/s, near the origin too. `renderer: a cascade's texels hold their place in the world as the eye crosses a cell` steps the eye a 1024th of a metre at a time across a cell's corner by the origin and 10,000 km out and holds every cascade's grid to within 4e-5 of a texel (the centre's float32 rounding) of where it was; the cell anchor moved it by 0.14 to 0.48 of a texel at the crossing. The trade is the translation suite's: a scene and camera moved by whole cells now fall on the texel grid differently, so the maps there are held to the same bytes outside a band round the shadows' edges as wide as the filter's footprint, and to the same ids and depth everywhere. A cascade whose sphere would hold the scene's whole bounds is replaced by them and is the last: every receiver is inside it. That is the common case for a camera framing an object — engine-view's orbit frames a mesh with a frustum wider than the mesh, so its first slice already holds it and the frame draws **one** cascade with every texel on the scene (about a 1,024th of the scene's diameter a texel at 2048). A cascade's depth runs from the sphere's far side, away from the light, **to the far side of the scene's bounds towards the light**, so it holds every caster between the light and its receivers — including one outside the camera's frustum.

**The light-view cull.** Each cascade is one more **run of the visible list, behind every view's three** (`GpuScene::cascade_base`), with its own indirect block (`shadow_args`) and, on the vertex path's indexed draw, its own header, records and index array behind the views' two runs; the camera's runs, and everything indexed by them — the ray chain's union, the census, the pool's allocation of the camera's runs — are exactly where they were. The cull pass runs once per cascade (`cull_main` or `cull_vertex_main`, whichever the picture uses) with the cascade's six planes, **no normal cones** (a caster's facing to the camera says nothing about the light), **no occlusion** (there is no Hi-Z from the light), no pair-to-entry table (the resolve decodes the picture's pairs, never a cascade's), everything to the hardware run, and **the camera's own LOD**: its eye, its projection scale and its threshold (the finest view's under a multi-view layout). The cull pass needed no change for it: its LOD test never looks at the frustum, so for every pair in both a view and a cascade it makes the same decision it made for the picture. **A shadow's LOD is therefore the picture's LOD**, or since R103 coarser than it by at most half a texel (the next paragraph) — a receiver's own triangle is in the map at exactly the depth the resolve reconstructs it at, or within the bias of it, which is what lets the bias be the receiver's plane rather than a guess — and a caster outside the frustum is drawn at the LOD the camera would draw it at from where it stands. The alternative, a cut chosen from the light's own view, would put a different triangle of the receiver in the map; `RenderSettings::shadow_lod_scale` (measurement only) coarsens the cascades' cut against the picture's, and the Khronos measurement below says what that does. A streamed scene's cascades read the frame's residency and ask for the pages they miss, like the picture's cull. A deformed or skinned instance's cascade entries get **pool blocks of their own**, allocated behind the camera's runs by one more dispatch of the same allocator (`DeformAllocParams::first_entry`) and deformed by the same pass, so a moving character casts its pose; the pool's small-scene clamp allows the whole meshes once per cascade as well.

**The cascades' own texels** (2026-10-27, roadmap R103). The camera's LOD in every cascade is the picture's cut wherever a cascade reaches, and the far cascades of a wide frame reach a great deal the picture does not need finely: on the forest proof of concept's expanded forest at 11520×2160 the four 2048² maps drew 7.33 million pairs a frame (471 k, 1.87 M, 2.49 M and 2.50 M by cascade) where a texel is 5.7 to 32 of the picture's pixels ([the cascades against the pixel](../experiments/shadow-hybrid-2026-10-26.md#the-cascades-against-the-pixel)), and every swaying tree in each of them asked the pool for a block — 1,591,523 entries a frame refused. So a cascade's cull block also carries the lengths its texels accept (`gfx::CullParams::cascade_error_m` and `cascade_cover_m`, two of the block's pad words): `k_shadow_texel_error_texels` (half a texel) of world error and `k_shadow_texel_cover_texels` (two texels) of coverage error, both times `shadow_lod_scale`. A transition is acceptable when the camera's test accepts it **or** its error times the instance's `scale_max` is at most the first (its coverage error at most the second) — `cascade_accepts` in `cluster_cull.slang`. An orthographic error is the same number of texels wherever it stands, so no sphere and no observer enter it, and since each of the two acceptances holds for a cluster whenever it holds for its parent, so does their union: one cluster on every path, as before. It is **the coarser of the picture's cut and the texels' cut, never a finer one than the picture's**. Where a texel is finer than the picture's threshold — a heightfield's 2048² maps at the tests' orbits, every texel under a pixel — a cascade draws the picture's cut to the byte and a receiver's own triangle is in the map exactly as before. Where it is coarser, the map holds a receiver within half a texel of the triangle the resolve reconstructs, which is the constant half of the depth bias (`k_shadow_bias_texels`): a whole texel moved the forest's near dapple about twice as much, and a coverage of five texels three times as much (the [ladder](../experiments/cascade-budget-2026-10-26.md#the-threshold-ladder)). **The cross-fade is off in a cascade cut by its texels**: the cascades share one fade table per pair (`GpuScene::fade_cascade_block`), which held while every cascade took the camera's transitions and does not once each has its own, and a table per cascade would be eight bytes a pair four times over, 537 MB at the forest's 16.8 million pairs. So a cascade switches a transition at once; the picture's own fade is untouched. That alone is 0.0057 FLIP of the forest's 1600×900 frame (44.4 dB), most of the texel cut's 0.0065 (43.9 dB), so a fade table of the cascades' own would buy back 0.0057 FLIP for half a gigabyte. `RenderSettings::shadow_texel_lod` and the `renderer.shadow.texel_lod` tunable, both true, are the way back to the picture's cut alone (`ResolvedSettings::shadow_texel_lod` is their and); `renderer.shadow.texel_error` and `renderer.shadow.texel_cover` are a measurement's knobs.

What it gave on the v18 expanded forest's standing path (`msvc-release` engine-view, offscreen, a scratch copy of the proof of concept's derived data, 600 frames, `--wait-quiet 120` under the GPU lock; the machine state of every row is in [the write-up](../experiments/cascade-budget-2026-10-26.md#the-default-2026-10-27)):

| frame | cut | pairs in the maps (by cascade) | shadow ms | frame ms | pool entries refused |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 11520×2160 | the picture's | 7,330,300 (470,964 / 1,869,858 / 2,494,402 / 2,495,076) | 21.01 | 36.58 | 1,591,523 |
| 11520×2160 | its texels' too | 1,484,413 (174,837 / 1,132,523 / 98,720 / 78,333) | 9.04 | 24.24 | 0 |
| 1600×900 | the picture's | 1,771,028 (84,984 / 319,424 / 643,469 / 723,151) | 10.48 | 12.78 | 0 |
| 1600×900 | its texels' too | 601,178 (75,125 / 225,434 / 221,726 / 78,893) | 6.10 | 8.32 | 0 |

**What holds it.** `domain/gfx`'s cull test holds the GPU's cut to the camera's projection ORed with the two lengths, cluster for cluster over the whole DAG at five lengths with and without coverage (the shortest leaves the camera's cut exactly). `renderer: a cascade cut by its texels shadows a simplified receiver as the picture's cut does` (`shadow_map_tests.cpp`): a 129² heightfield from three orbits at 64², 256² and 2048² maps, the texel cut never drawing more pairs than the picture's, no opposite answer outside a band round every shadow edge as wide as the filter's footprint at the pixel's own depth (0 of up to 81,408 interior pixels; since T140 on a skirted heightfield, where the bound says one is owed, below at S105), the picture's ids unchanged and the vertex path's shadow the mesh path's to the byte. `renderer: texel LOD preserves the near fixture on both cascade raster paths`: the fixture's casters are their own roots, so the four of them draw the same bytes either way. The Khronos case (below) gives the same interior answers against the rays with and without it.

**Far casters at rest, per cascade** (2026-10-27, R103 stage 2). A deformed instance's cascade entries take pool blocks of their own, one per cascade, so a swaying tree is deformed into every map it is in — which is what overflowed the forest's pool before the texel cut. Its shadow in a cascade whose texel is coarser than the tree's whole sway cannot show the sway, so the cascades' allocation dispatch carries one length per cascade (`gfx::DeformAllocParams::rest_padding_m`, 96 → 112 bytes): past the nearest cascade, the cascade's texel times `renderer.shadow.rest_texels` (`k_shadow_rest_texels`, 1). An entry of a deformed instance that states its reach from the rest pose (`InstanceDesc::bounds_padding` × `scale_max`, the bound its cull already trusts: for a tree, every part's largest bend at the saturating wind times its distance from the pivot) and whose reach is under that length asks for no block, gets `k_no_pool_slot` and is drawn from the grid in that cascade — the same read as a rigid instance's, and no overflow, since it asked for nothing. The nearest cascade always poses, an instance with no stated reach (0) always poses, and **a terrain level never rests**: its pool stage draws the moving field its rest heights can be metres from, which is no pose a texel hides. That last also fixes the older `renderer.flora.rest_pose_cascades_m` ([The caster policy](#the-caster-policy)), which had put every deformed instance past its distance at rest, the terrain's rings included. **How far a tree's shadow still sways** is the far end of the last cascade whose texel is under its reach: on the v18 forest at 11520×2160 the cascades are 0.1–26.7, 26.7–150, 150–844 and 844–4,745 m with texels of 7.4 cm, 41 cm, 2.34 m and 4.44 m, so a tree that can sway 1.8 m (the young palm's bound) or 2.6 m (the grove's broadleaves') shadows its sway to 150 m or 844 m and its rest pose past it; at 1600×900 (2.8 cm, 16 cm, 88 cm, 4.94 m) both sway to 844 m. On that forest the texel cut had already left most far trees to their rigid distance forms, so the rule gives back little pool (426.0 → 422.6 MB a frame at 11520×2160, 278.8 → 274.3 MB at 1600×900, nothing refused either way) and the shadow passes 9.07 → 7.88 ms and 5.86 → 5.12 ms (medians, under the GPU lock, a shared machine: [the write-up](../experiments/cascade-budget-2026-10-26.md#far-casters-at-rest-2026-10-27)). `domain/gfx`'s allocator test holds the scan and its reference to the rule on the CPU with reaches of 0 to 8 m, cascade lengths of 0, 0.5, 2 and 6 m and a few terrain levels among the instances, and checks the rule leaves entries out; the fixture's shadows, one cascade each, are the bytes they were.

**The far side costs little once the cascades are cut by their texels** (2026-10-27, R103 stage 3). `shadow_distance` is a receiver horizon: it ends the last slice, and with it the receivers the maps shadow, but not the casters — every cascade's depth still runs to the far side of the scene's bounds towards the light (the fit, above), so a tall far caster's long shadow under a low sun still reaches a near receiver and the maps leave out no caster for it; the count of casters omitted is zero by construction. (The rays' caster horizon is the one that omits casters, and it counts them, `Stats::horizon_casters`.) Whether its default should become a stated distance rather than the scene's far side was a question of cost, and measured after stages 1 and 2 on the v18 forest the answer is no: 1,280 m (the proof of concept's tree residency radius) takes the shadow passes from 7.88 to 7.39 ms at 11520×2160 and from 5.12 to 5.21 ms at 1600×900 (1.48 → 1.26 and 0.60 → 0.61 million pairs), so the far side is half a millisecond of the widest frame and nothing at 1600×900, while a 1,280 m distance moves every split nearer (26.7 / 150 / 844 m become 7.2 / 40 / 228 m) and changes every cascade's texel. So `shadow_distance` stays 0 by default ([the write-up](../experiments/cascade-budget-2026-10-26.md#the-far-side-2026-10-27)).

**Drawing.** One raster pass draws every cascade into its tile of a single **D32 atlas** (`shadow_map × cascades` by `shadow_map`, 64 MiB at the defaults; reversed depth, cleared to 0, greater-or-equal) through **the picture's own rasterizer with no fragment stage**: the mesh path's mesh stage, or the vertex path's indexed draw and its fallback (or the capacity draw), with each cascade's viewport flipped like every raster pass. The triangles come off the same 16-bit grid or the same pool block through the same arithmetic as the picture's, and the mesh and vertex paths write the same map — the tests hold their shadows equal to the byte.

**Reading** is gfx's ([gfx](gfx.md), "The sun's cascaded shadow maps"): the first cascade whose tile holds the filter's footprint, a **3×3 bilinear PCF** (a 4×4-texel footprint, weights (1 − f, 1, 1, f)/3 per axis) evaluated as four gathers, and a **receiver-plane bias** — each texel compared against the receiver's own plane at that texel's centre, plus `k_shadow_bias_texels` (half a texel) for what is not flat, with the slope clamped at `k_shadow_max_slope` (tan 83°); and a **normal offset** — the point looked up leaves the surface along its geometric normal by `k_shadow_normal_offset_texels` (three eighths of a texel of the cascade read; three until F23) times (1 − N·L), for the concave creases and the terminator of a low-poly curved surface, which a plane cannot describe. `RenderSettings::shadow_normal_offset` overrides it for measurement. The maps shadow **the sun alone**: the two orbiting point lights are unshadowed under them.

**Measured on the Khronos samples** (the skipped case `renderer: cascaded shadow maps on the Khronos samples`; the tables are in [the experiment](../experiments/cascaded-shadow-maps.md)). Seven samples, each on a ground six radii wide, from sixteen cameras at 1280×720, in the shadow view, mapped against ray-traced on the RTX 5090: a pixel is interior when the rays give it and every pixel within three of it the same answer, and there the maps must give that answer too. **At the picture's cut, with the normal offset, the two never give opposite answers: 0 of 6.35–7.40 million interior pixels on every sample**, which the case asserts; the maps answer grey (partly shadowed) on 0.03–0.3% of them, where the 4×4 footprint of the last cascade reaches past the three-pixel band. Without the normal offset the maps shadowed 162–21,627 interior pixels that the rays lit, every one on a sample's own surface — at the terminator of its low-poly curves and in its concave creases — and an offset of two texels left 0–3, three 0, four 0 with less grey; three is the default, the smallest that gave 0 everywhere. **A cascade cut coarser than the picture's brings the self-shadowing back**: with the cascades' LOD threshold doubled, 16–8,436 interior pixels are shadowed that the rays light, quadrupled 113–38,888, and the first leaks appear (34–104 lit where the rays shadow). The receiver's own triangle in the map is then not the one the resolve reconstructs, and no plane predicts that difference. That is the measurement behind "a shadow's LOD is the picture's LOD". What they cost at engine-view's own camera: the maps' passes 0.013–0.021 ms, 0.010–0.011 ms of it the culls, and 0.009–0.010 ms more in the resolve for the filter. The frame is 0.088–0.107 ms, against 0.068–0.077 ms without shadows and 0.18–0.25 ms with rays (the chain before it was sized by the frame). A coarser cut saves at most 0.002 ms, because at these sizes a cascade costs its dispatches, not its pairs. **Why the case stopped passing, and the offset it took back (F23, 2026-10-28).** On dad55f90 it failed at the picture's cut as much as at the texels': 192 to 5,247 interior pixels the rays shadow were lit in the maps on six samples, and one the other way ([the write-up](../experiments/cascade-budget-2026-10-26.md#against-the-rays-on-the-khronos-samples)). **The maps had not moved; the rays had.** The normal offset above was chosen against rays that left their surface by a thousandth of the scene's radius, which skimmed a crease or a terminator clear as three texels of lift did. c5d23997 (2026-09-26) made a ray leave by one step of its receiver's own grid ([Ray-traced](#ray-traced)), so the rays now see a low-poly crease's self-shadow — the Suzanne's brow over its eyes, the inside of its ears — and the maps, lifted three texels, did not. Put back to c5d23997's old offset on today's tree, the rays and the maps agree again (0 / 0 on six samples, 1 leak on the FlightHelmet); the cascades, the texel cut and the world-eye fit change nothing. Over the seven samples (acne / leaks, at 2048 texels): three texels 1 / 9,569; one 0 / 101; half 0 / 13; **three eighths 0 / 3, the default now**; a quarter 0 / 3; an eighth 6 / 1; a sixteenth 25 / 0; none 1,769 / 0. **The case still fails by three pixels**, all on the FlightHelmet, where the rays shadow the wooden base under the coiled hose and the maps have a 4×4-texel hole in it: the hose's wire is thinner than the last cascade's texel (3.6 mm), so where the rasterizer drops it from the map depends on where the texel grid falls; at 4,096 texels the FlightHelmet gives 0 / 0. That residual is the maps' resolution, not a bias, and is roadmap F25. A quarter gives the same counts here, but the world-translation cases refuse it: their cubes' grazing faces then answer by where the texel grid falls, and a scene moved by whole cells drew 26–55 colour bytes away from the shadows' edges; three eighths holds them to zero. **The case's comment expected one cascade, the scene's bounds; that was never this camera's fit**: the orbit stands 2.4 sample radii from the sample, inside the bounds (4.24 radii), so the fit has always cut four slices from the near plane, and the sample sits in the last, a sphere of 7 radii.

**Statistics.** `Stats::shadow_pairs` (the pairs drawn into the maps, summed over the cascades), `Stats::shadow_fallback` (the cascades' survivors the indexed draw's budget sent to the fallback, logged once), `gpu_shadow` (every pass that draws the maps: the culls, the cascades' pool and index passes, the depth raster) and `gpu_shadow_cull` (the culls' share); the filtering is in `gpu_resolve`. They reach engine-view's summary (`shadow_pairs_last`, `shadow_fallback_last`, `gpu_ms.shadow`, `gpu_ms.shadow_cull`), `render.benchmark` and the flythrough's per-frame records. `Stats::shadow_pairs_per_cascade` splits the first by cascade (engine-view's `shadow_pairs_per_cascade_last`), and an offscreen flythrough with maps prints a last `engine-view: shadow cascade summary` line on stderr with the four counts, the pool's bytes used and its refused entries and bytes. `SceneRenderer::shadow_cascades()` is the fit the last frame used.

**What it does not do.** Point and spot lights cast no mapped shadow (a cube map or a perspective map each, and the ReSTIR-sampled lights of §4.4 are the plan's answer for them); the RTX 5090's rays still shadow them under `rt`. There is **no blending between cascades**, so the penumbra's width steps where one cascade hands over to the next. Nothing is cached between frames: every cascade is culled and drawn every frame, even where the light, the geometry and the cascade have not moved. And the far cascade of a large scene covers its whole far side — at no finer than its texels since R103, but every cascade still holds whatever lies beside and behind the view inside its sphere. Along the desert overlook's path that is seven to fourteen times the picture's pairs with occlusion culling on. It costs the RTX 5090 0.10–0.26 ms of median frame; the ray-traced chain, sized by the frame, is 0.40–0.61 ms at 1080p ([The ray tracing chain's memory](#the-ray-tracing-chains-memory)). It costs the TITAN Xp 0.60–1.22 ms, and its maps' passes reach 1.9 ms at 4K p95 ([the flythrough's rows](../experiments/flythrough-desert-overlook.md#cascaded-shadow-maps-rtx-5090-and-titan-xp)). `--shadow-distance` bounds it; cached far cascades are the follow-up.

**A cascade draws only what can shadow a pixel** (R49, 2026-11-16; `renderer.shadow.cascade_volume`, on). Each cascade's cull also tests a pair against every view's frustum swept towards the key light ([caster_volume.h](#shadows), the traced path's own off-frustum volume), widened by what the resolve reads beside a receiver — the filter's two texels each side, one more for rounding, and the normal offset, all in that cascade's texels — and drops it when it is outside all of them: a caster there lies on no ray from a drawn pixel to the light. All or none: more views than the cull block's five volumes, or a view whose volume cannot be fit, leaves the cascade its box. **Never with water**: the water's refracted floor and the sun's exit through the surface read the maps at points off the frustum, so a scene with a body keeps the box. `the cascades' light-view cull never changes the shadow` holds the three cuts (box and volumes, box alone, nothing) to the same bytes and the volumes to strictly fewer pairs. Measured on main's 86b931f7 against this change, the session unlocked and the CPU 63–100 % others: the streamed forest at 3840×2160 `--raster hw --shadows csm` draws 26,862 pairs into the maps where it drew 61,437, the maps 0.476 → 0.228 ms at the median (p99 0.701 → 0.434) and the GPU frame 1.391 → 1.097; `endless-1080p-csm` 22,961 → 10,144 pairs, 0.222 → 0.164 ms (p99 0.376 → 0.223), frame 1.175 → 1.076; the tunable off reads main's numbers. It is the baseline tier's lever: the maps are what a card without ray queries shadows with.

#### The ground takes the picture's cut in every cascade

2026-11-04, roadmap R132 ([the diagnosis](../experiments/ledge-shadow-2026-11-04.md)). **A terrain level never takes a cascade's texel cut**: `cascade_accepts` in `cluster_cull.slang` is ORed into a transition's test only for an instance whose `InstanceDesc::terrain` is zero, so the ground in every cascade is the camera's cut over the cascade's box, as every receiver was before R103, and everything else keeps the cut by its texels. The texel rule rests on a cluster's DAG error being how far it stands off the finer cut, kept under the half texel of the maps' constant bias. A terrain level's error bounds its rest heights only — the pool's terrain stage draws the field, and a world tile its shared vertices from a coarser level ([The ground from the world's tiles](#the-ground-from-the-worlds-tiles)) — and a surface offset e along its normal is e / (N·L) deeper along the light, which the bias covers only for a sun overhead. On the forest proof of concept's v29 foothill ledge at 15:00 (the sun 34° up) a world tile's coarser clusters shadowed a ten-metre polygon of open ground in front of the ledge, 34,436 pixels of a 1920×1080 frame, which the rays never drew; it went with `renderer.shadow.texel_lod` off, with a tenth of the default `texel_error`, and with this rule, and not with the far levels off, a finer picture or the coverage half of the cut. The ground is a few thousand pairs a cascade: the reproduction's cascades drew 11,617 pairs before and 12,755 after. **What holds it**: `terrain shadows: the ground takes the picture's cut in every cascade` (`terrain_shadow_tests.cpp`) draws the moving dunes under suns 34°, 20° and 12° up with the texel cut and without it and holds the two to the same pairs, ids and bytes; before the rule they drew 58–66 pairs against 109–117 and differed on 9–36 sand pixels.

**And so does every mesh that faces the sky** (2026-11-13, roadmap S105). The rule above keyed on a terrain *level*, and the second half of its reason is not about levels: any receiver whose coarser cluster stands its error e off it is e / (N·L) deeper along the light, and the half-texel bias holds that only with the sun overhead. Batch 63's server leg found the two it missed, on the water suite's swash bay under a sun 53° up (N·L 0.80 on level sand) on the TITAN Xp, which draws with the maps: the scene's own ground grid standing still — not a level, so it took the texel cut — shadowed whole lit triangles of open sand, 0 in the shadow view where the rays light them, one of them right at the swash's edge; and the lifted water body, whose DAG error bounds its rest pose and not the sheet the pool lifts it to (the first half of the reason, word for word), put its coarser clusters over the sand at the waterline. Measured on this machine with the TITAN Xp's profile, by elimination: the swash case's failing pairs were the same bytes under `--shadows csm` on the RTX 5090 as on the stand-in, gone with shadows off, with `renderer.shadow.texel_lod` off, and on the ground at `texel_error` 0.4 (0.5 × N·L, the derivation's bound) but on the water only at 0.25; the vertex path with traced shadows matched the traced path. So **a mesh whose every triangle, as it was built, faces above the horizon takes the camera's cut by world error in every cascade**: `renderer::sky_facing_meshes` (shadow_cascades.h) measures it once at load — each leaf cluster by its normal cone where the cone can say (axis·up > cutoff), by its own float triangles where it has none or the cone reaches past the horizon, a triangle with no area passed over — into one word a mesh that `gfx::CullParams::sky_facing` hands every cascade's cull, where it takes the error half out of `cascade_accepts` for that instance (the coverage half stays: a leaf card lying on the ground keeps R103's foliage lever; an opaque mesh has none). The leaves and not the coarser levels are asked because simplifying a flat surface folds a triangle over in its own plane now and then — the bay's water has six such, one of 0.3 m², each facing straight down — which turns no surface to the ground. **What any asset gets**: an imported ground, a deck, a road, a water body of any source is one by the same measurement as the scene's grid; a closed mesh (a rock, a trunk) is not and keeps R103's trade; a paged scene's leaves live in its pages, so its meshes keep the cut; a mesh that arrives after the load (a tile's) is past the table and keeps it. Being wrong either way only moves pairs: a mesh taken for one draws the picture's cut, never a wrong one. **What it costs**: the ground's pairs a cascade, which R132 measured at a few thousand (11,617 → 12,755 on its reproduction), and a scene with no such mesh nothing — the table is empty and the cull reads no word; one u32 per mesh, built once in a pass over the leaves that stops at a mesh's first downward face. The bay's two meshes (the 257² grid, 2,913 clusters, and the water, 2,085) are both one. `renderer: a mesh faces the sky when every triangle it was built with faces above it` (`shadow_map_tests.cpp`) holds the measurement on the CPU; the swash suite's sheet case draws the bay on the GPU as it is and as the TITAN Xp (`water swash: the sheet on the sand is one surface across the mesh's edge`, [water](water.md#one-sheet)). The R103 heightfield case above (`a cascade cut by its texels shadows a simplified receiver as the picture's cut does`) drew its heightfield at the picture's cut in both halves after this, since a heightfield faces the sky (416 pairs to 416), so **its receiver is now the same heightfield with a skirt a metre deep round its edge** (T140, 2026-11-15), written as a glTF file by the case: vertical faces, so not a mesh that faces the sky, and the case holds that first and that the texel cut draws fewer pairs than the picture's (6 of its 9 map-and-view frames: 417 → 77 at 64², 541 → 319 at 256²; at 2048² every texel is under a pixel and the two cuts are the same). Its rule is the derivation above made a bound: a cluster the cut takes stands at most τ texels off, e / (N·L) along the light, under the bias's b = half a texel, so the texel cut can only darken a lit receiver where N·L < τ / b — everywhere but the sun overhead at the default τ of half a texel. The case draws at τ = ¼ and counts opposite answers where the captured normal's N·L is at least ½ plus its RGB8 quantization (0.0065): 0 of 71,375 such pixels outside the filter's band, 1,860 of them at 256² where the cuts differ.

**What it costs, measured** (2026-11-14, the row's pair). `msvc-release` engine-view, main at 0aa8e44a and the branch, each copied out of its build tree, offscreen, each scene's own camera path (three repeats after 240 warm-up frames), flown main, branch, main, branch for every setting inside one GPU lease on the RTX 5090. The machine was shared: other processes held 13–46% of the CPU at the start and end of each run (100% at the end of main's first vertex flight, marked \*, whose tail it spoiled) and 6.5 of the GPU's 32.6 GB; the alternation is what makes the differences readable. The desert overlook has one sky-facing mesh of 14 (its 2049² ground grid), the oasis pool two of three (its ground and its water). Every run drew the same pairs frame by frame in each repeat. Milliseconds are the path's median (p99), one figure per run; pairs in the maps the path's median (p99); the cascades the last frame's.

So on this machine the rule costs the desert's 4K frame under the maps **+0.016 ms at the median** (+0.018 at p99), all of it in the shadow passes and next to none in their culls (+0.001): the maps draw twice the pairs, nearly all the added ones the ground in the far two cascades — the last cascade's 685 become 5,818 on the last frame, where a texel is 4.7 m and the texel cut had taken the ground at its coarsest. The vertex tier at 1440p pays +0.021–0.024 ms against main's undisturbed run (+0.018 in the shadow passes), the traced control does not move, and the pool pays +0.003 ms for its 518 more pairs. Between one side's two runs the median total moved by at most 0.005 ms, except the disturbed run. The TITAN Xp, the hardware the maps are for, was not flown: the cascades cost it 0.60–1.22 ms of this path's median frame (above), so the far cascades' ground is the figure to measure there first.
### Rays near, maps far

Roadmap R102 (2026-10-26). **A shadow ray through a forest is expensive and far from the eye mostly wasted.** The forest proof of concept's expanded forest at 11520×2160 spent 39.5 ms in the resolve under traced shadows against 5.0 ms under the maps, on the same pixels: about 34 ms of rays. The casters are alpha-tested leaves, so every candidate hit evaluates a mask, and the structures hold the cut to the horizon, so a ray towards the sun from a pixel 800 m away walks canopy for a shadow the pixel cannot show at its size. The rays are the right answer near the eye — a leaf's shadow on a trunk, contact-hard edges, no seams or acne — and the cascades far from it, where a texel is no coarser than the pixel it lands in.

**`ShadowMode::Hybrid`** (`--shadows hybrid`, the protocol's `"hybrid"`) is both, per pixel, by the surface's distance from the view's eye: nearer than `RenderSettings::shadow_ray_distance_m` the resolve asks the ray query, past it plus `shadow_ray_band_m` the maps, and across the band it blends the two **visibilities** (0 to 1, before the light is applied) linearly by distance, so a shadow crossing the band fades from one answer to the other rather than stepping as the camera moves. It is the same one function with its two implementations ([gfx](gfx.md), `shadow_visibility` with `k_shadow_hybrid`), and a pixel asks only what its weight needs: a near one traces and reads no map, a far one reads the maps and traces nothing. Near the eye the picture is therefore the rays' to the byte, and far from it the maps' — which shadow the light they follow and leave the point lights lit, as under `csm`. `ResolvedSettings::hybrid` is `shadows` and `csm` at once: the frame runs the chain and draws the cascades, and everything each needs is as it was (two-pass occlusion off, as under `rt`; the cascades culled from the light into their own runs behind every view's three, as under `csm`). It runs on the hw and vertex paths; the ray path has no maps and keeps its rays, and a device that cannot trace has the maps. The defaults are 100 m and a 20 m band (`k_default_shadow_ray_distance_m`, `k_default_shadow_ray_band_m`; `--shadow-ray-distance`, `--shadow-ray-band`, the protocol's `shadow_ray_distance_m` and `shadow_ray_band_m`).

**Why `auto` is not the hybrid** ([the measurement](../experiments/shadow-hybrid-2026-10-26.md)). It was built to be, and on the forest proof of concept it lost on every view, at 11520×2160 and 2560×1440, by two to three times the rays' frame. Three things the measurement found: **the rays' cost is near the eye, and it is the alpha-tested masks** — every caster traced opaque, a measurement switch (`renderer.shadow.opaque_rays`), takes the resolve from 29.2 to 6.0 ms on the clearing and from 36.8 to 9.1 on the expanded forest, while moving the rays in to 100 m takes it to 19.7 and 34.1, because the forest's view is mostly within 50 m; **the cascades cost twice their own beside the chain** — a frame with the chain draws the rigid forms at their frontier and without occlusion, so the maps draw the camera's finer cut (5.5 against 2.4 million pairs on the clearing at 2560×1440, 41 against 19 ms); and **the cascades' texel is nowhere as fine as the pixel** — the logarithmic split repeats one texel-to-pixel ratio per cascade, 5.7 at each cascade's far end and 32 at its start at 11520×2160, 1.44 and 8 at 2560×1440, so no ray distance meets "the maps no coarser than the pixel". What would turn it: cascades fit from the ray distance out and cut by their own texels rather than the chain's frontier, and a cheaper answer for an alpha-tested caster (opacity micromaps, or an opaque shadow proxy for a cluster whose coverage is high — the page weighs both). Until then the hybrid is asked for, `auto` keeps the rays, and the flip is one line in `resolve_settings`.

**Measured again over the texel-cut cascades** (2026-10-27, R103 stage 4; [the write-up](../experiments/cascade-budget-2026-10-26.md#the-hybrid-over-these-cascades-2026-10-27)), and `auto` still keeps the rays: the hybrid lost on all four views (121.1 against 90.9 ms on the expanded forest at 11520×2160, 31.9 against 15.3 at 2560×1440; 73.7 against 49.1 and 23.1 against 10.9 on the clearing), while `csm` became the cheapest frame on every one. The texel cut does not reach the hybrid's maps, because a chain frame draws a rigid distance form at its frontier by patching the form's LOD data, and the cascades read the same data: its far cascades draw five million pairs each. **`renderer.shadow.hybrid_fit`** (off) fits the cascades from the ray distance out (`ShadowFit::begin_distance`: the first slice starts at the least view depth a point that far from the eye can have, over the widest corner ray's secant, so every surface that reads the maps is in a slice; `renderer: the hybrid's cascades begin where its rays hand over` holds it), and it costs more while the forms are at their frontier, since the first two cascades then lie in their rings too; it is off also because `renderer: the hybrid draws the rays' shadow near the eye and the maps' far from it` holds the far pixels to the `csm` picture's bytes, and refuses it (12 to 21 far pixels and 2 or 3 in the band per caster differ, the maps being other maps). With the forms cut by the cascades' texels the hybrid would still be 2 to 41% over the rays, since the rest of its frame is theirs; the two levers are roadmap rows.

**A field species shows the seam.** The grass is untraced ([The caster policy](#the-caster-policy)) but drawn into the nearest cascades, so under the maps it shadows itself and under the rays it does not; in the hybrid the band is where the grass turns from the rays' white to the maps' grey, a strip about 100–120 m out on the clearing. That is the caster policy's choice made visible, not the blend's.

**The casters follow the rays.** No pixel past the distance plus the band asks a ray, so the rays' shadow casters — the clusters the cone test or the frustum kept out of the picture — end there: with the hybrid the caster horizon is on whatever `rt_caster_horizon` says, at `ResolvedSettings::caster_horizon_m` (the distance plus the band, or R94's `shadow_distance` where that is nearer), and every caster past it is counted in `Stats::horizon_casters` instead of built. The horizon is a sphere round the eye, so it has R94's one approximation: a caster past it can still be met by a ray from a near receiver — a tall far object's long shadow under a low sun — and that shadow is lost. The drawn clusters are not touched: the picture's cut is still built whole, far forest included, because the records pass builds what the views drew.

**What holds it.** `renderer: the hybrid draws the rays' shadow near the eye and the maps' far from it` (`shadow_map_tests.cpp`): on every caster of the shadow fixture, with the rays' distance at the median distance of the shadow the rays draw, every ground pixel nearer is the traced picture's byte (traced with the same horizon), every one past the band the mapped picture's, every one in the band between the two, the ids the same throughout, and with the distance past the scene the hybrid is the traced picture whole and with none the mapped one. `domain/gfx`'s `material resolve: hybrid shadows are the rays near the eye and the maps far from it` holds the same split against the CPU reference by each side's own rule (`brdf_ref::hybrid_side`), and the blend monotone and within a code of `gfx::shadow_hybrid_weight` across the band. `RayTraced` and `Cascaded` are the bytes they were: their flags never carry `k_shadow_hybrid`, and the function takes the branch it always took.

### A light too faint to test

**A traced light whose contribution is a negligible share of the pixel's light is not tested for its shadow** (2026-11-01, roadmap R115; [the measurement](../experiments/forest-resolve-2026-11-01.md)). This follows Ward's adaptive shadow testing ([Ward 1991](https://floyd.lbl.gov/radiance/papers/erw91/erw91.html)): test sources in decreasing order of potential contribution, stop when the rest is under a tolerance, and add an untested source in proportion to the visibility the tested ones found. In the resolve, with the lights' shadows traced (`k_shadow_lights` without `k_shadow_cascades`), the sun is always tested. Then each light of the array whose unshadowed contribution at the pixel (`brdf_direct` with its radiance, the sky's transmittance included) is, in its largest channel, at most `ResolveParams::light_tolerance` times the luminance of the rest of the pixel's light is skipped. The rest is the sun as its query left it, the ambient and the emission. A skipped light is added at the visibility the pixel's own sun query found (1 where the sun was not asked) and costs no ray. The sum keeps its order, so a pixel where the two visibilities agree is the bytes it was, and one where they do not moves by at most the tolerance.

**Why it exists**: the frame's light array holds the sky's moon whenever the scene's moon is on, day or night, and a fire's point light reaches 82 m (where it falls to 0.05 lux). Under `--shadows rt` every pixel facing either traced a ray to it: in the v24 forest at 11520×2160 at 15:00 that was 12.1–15.3 ms of a 33–41 ms resolve, for a moon a millionth of the sun and a fire a hundred-thousandth of it at ten metres. The rule returned 12.4, 15.0 and 15.4 ms at the three poses measured there.

**The tolerance** is `renderer.shadow.light_tolerance`, 2^-12 by default, and 0 traces every light exactly as before; a `ResolveParams` a caller fills itself has 0. 2^-12 is a thirty-sixth of the smallest code step of the 8-bit sRGB encode (0.87%, at white) and of the 10-bit PQ encode (0.90%, at 1,000 nits), so six lights skipped at the bound move a pixel a sixth of a step. At night the moon and the fires are the light and are traced. The cascaded maps (and the hybrid) answer for the lights as before: the rule applies only where a light's answer would be a ray. The sun below the horizon is still traced where a normal faces it. Extending the rule to the sun, with the ambient as the rest, is the night's measurement to make.

### What the sun ray's masks cost, and what does not buy it back

Roadmap R115 stage 2 (2026-11-01; [the measurement](../experiments/forest-resolve-2026-11-01.md#stage-2-the-walk-through-the-woods-and-the-sun-rays-split-2026-11-01)). On the owner's v25 walk through the woods the sun's ray is two thirds of the resolve — 14.6 of 22.5 ms at 11520×2160, 4.6 of 7.2 at 3840×2160 — and with every caster solid (`renderer.shadow.opaque_rays`) it is 2.4 and 0.7, so **the masks are 12 and 4 ms**. Counted per pixel (the stop word's counting bit, [Where the resolve's time goes](#where-the-resolves-time-goes)), the ray does little: at the walk's first marker, 3840×2160, 6.3 million pixels ask the sun, a ray meets 1.77 non-opaque candidates on average and samples 1.61 masks (median 1, 90th percentile 4–5, 99th 12–13), a ray that reaches the sun 1.1 and one that is blocked 2.3. So the cost is not the number of mask decisions but their shape: each is a chain of a dozen dependent loads (the hit's entry, its pair, the instance, the cluster's material, the material, the cluster, the triangle, three UVs, the texel) behind a hand-back from the traversal, and a warp waits for its longest ray, which is the tail's 5 to 13.

**Three levers were weighed against that, in the brief's order, and two lost.**

- **The mask at the ray's footprint** (sample the level the ray's cone selects at the hit instead of level 0, the ray-cone level of detail of Akenine-Möller et al., *Ray Tracing Gems* ch. 20, 2019) was built — a per-cluster level-0 texel baked beside the proxy's coverage, the receiver pixel's footprint across the ray, optionally widened by the sun's disc, 9.305 mrad, whose penumbra is the scale a sunfleck under a canopy is drawn at (the sun's disc; Anderson and Miller 1975, "Forest cover as a solar camera", is the paper on canopy penumbrae, found by title and not read here) — measured, and **taken out again** (it lived at f0f4ade7): it made the sun's stage *slower*, 14.6 → 16.4 ms at 11520 with the pixel's cone and → 25.1 with the disc's, and it moved 4.4% and 18% of the marker's pixels by more than 16 codes, because a coverage-preserving coarse level keeps the same share of a card but not the same holes. The texture fetch is one link of the chain; the lever added three (the texel table, the mesh's grid, the receiver's derivatives).
- **A stricter proxy for the sun** ([The opaque shadow proxy](#the-opaque-shadow-proxy)) buys time only by moving the shadow: on this forest even 0.5 changes 4.4% of the marker's pixels for 0.2 ms, 0.3 changes 4.9% for 2.7 ms, 0.2 changes 9.4% for 5.6 ms. The default stays off.
- **Opacity micromaps** remain, and the cluster structures take them: `VkClusterAccelerationStructureBuildTriangleClusterInfoNV` carries `opacityMicromapArray` and `opacityMicromapIndexBuffer` per cluster (VUID-10881 asks for `VK_BUILD_ACCELERATION_STRUCTURE_ALLOW_CLUSTER_OPACITY_MICROMAPS_BIT_NV` on the build). The micromaps are built once per mesh from its masks and UVs, so the per-frame cost is only the cluster build's with them attached; a two-state micromap would let the shadow ray's traversal decide a leaf card's interior and corners without the shader and leave it the edge. That is the next stage, the chain's, and R109's page has the bake and the memory arithmetic.

**`renderer.shadow.sweep`** (a measurement switch, off) is how the split was taken: frame f takes the sun ray's rule (f / 8) mod 6 — 0 the frame as set, 1 every caster solid, 2 to 4 the proxy at 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2, 5 the frame as set with the counting bit — so one flight under `renderer.resolve.stop_after=cycle` measures every stage of every rule interleaved along one path (`shadow_ray_rule`, `settings.h`). With it on, a scene bakes the proxy's table at load whatever the threshold (`ResolvedSettings::shadow_coverage_table`), and a frame whose threshold is 0 is never handed the table. `alpha mask: the shadow sweep steps the sun ray's rules eight frames at a time` holds the table the experiment's medians are read through, and `alpha mask: the sweep's coverage table is not handed to a frame with no threshold` holds the frame as set to the bytes it draws without the sweep.
### Opacity micromaps

Roadmap R120 (2026-11-02; working since R120b; **on by default since batch 53** with the shadow rays' two-state answer at level 6, where the device has `VK_EXT_opacity_micromap` beside the cluster extension, never under the opaque shadow proxy, read at load — `renderer.shadow.micromaps=false` is the one tunable that turns it back, [below](#opacity-micromaps-on-by-default)). The third lever above: a conservative 4-state opacity micromap per alpha-tested triangle, so the traversal decides the micro-triangles the mask decides the same way everywhere on them and the ray loops see only the rest. What stands:

- **The device.** `VK_EXT_opacity_micromap` is enabled only beside the cluster extension (`DeviceFeatures::opacity_micromap`, the requirements row of that name, `engine-cli gpu.adapters`); the RTX 5090 at driver 617.42 exposes it at revision 2 with both subdivision limits 12 (vulkaninfo; `ClusterAsProperties::max_opacity_*_level`), beside `VK_KHR_opacity_micromap` revision 1 and the cluster extension revision 4. The vendored headers (Vulkan-Headers 1.4.357) carry both.
- **The bake** (`gfx::bake_opacity_micromaps`, `opacity_micromap_bake.slang`), once at load by the first renderer over a scene read whole (`GpuScene::bake_micromaps`, after the proxy's bake): the alpha-tested clusters the proxy lists, one thread a triangle in two passes — classify (a level per triangle, the smallest whose micro-triangles cover at most `renderer.rt.micromap_texels` (4) of its mask's level-0 texels, then the cap `renderer.rt.micromap_level` (6 since batch 53, 4 before), and which states its micro-triangles took) and write (each data-carrying triangle's states) — with the budget `renderer.rt.micromap_mib` (1,024) lowering the cap a level at a time between them, a triangle wholly one state taking a special index and no data, and one `VkMicromapEXT` for the scene. **The rule is conservative**: `mask_keeps_level0` is a bilinear lookup at level 0 through the material's sampler, a convex combination of its 2x2 texels, so a micro-triangle is walked quad by quad with `GatherAlpha` over its UV box widened by 1/64 texel and is opaque only if every texel keeps by 1/512, transparent only if every one drops, unknown otherwise (the unknown sub-state follows the centre sample, for a later two-state reading). The micro-triangle order is meshoptimizer's (`rasterizeOpacityRec`), mirrored on the CPU by `gfx::micromap_micro_triangle`. A consequence worth knowing: a micro-triangle whose box edge falls on a texel boundary reads the next quad too, so geometry whose UVs are aligned to the texel grid (the alpha tests' quad) needs micro-triangles finer than a texel before anything is known.
- **The records** (`gfx::ClusterRecordParams::omm`, a `gfx::MicromapTables` block; `ClusterBuildInput::omm_array`/`omm_indices` on the CPU): a **drawn alpha-tested** record names the micromap and its triangles' 32-bit indices; a caster's did not until R140 (a primary ray would commit its opaque micro-triangles where the caster must be passed through) and does now that the casters have top-level records of their own the camera's rays leave out ([The casters in instances of their own](#the-casters-in-instances-of-their-own); with `renderer.rt.caster_instances=false` it does not), nor a pair inside a **cross-fade band** in any view (`omm_fade`, `fade_stride`: its hits are kept by the pixel, which an opaque micro-triangle would not ask), and a record with neither is the bytes it was. The cache keeps a fourth key form, alpha-tested without a micromap, for the fading pairs (`k_cluster_cache_forms` 4). The rigid forms' static structures are built again after the bake with them (a static form never fades). The templates never carry one: a masked scene builds records, not templates. Every set is built with `ClusterSetLimits::opacity_micromaps` (`VK_BUILD_ACCELERATION_STRUCTURE_ALLOW_CLUSTER_OPACITY_MICROMAPS_BIT_NV`, VUID-10881). The frame record says whether a frame's records named them (`rt_micromaps`).
- **What holds.** `alpha mask: opacity micromaps leave the shadow rays' and the ray path's picture alone`: 0 pixels differ (with the traversal using them since R120b, below), colour and ids, with micromaps and without, on the per-frame build and on the cache, under the shadow rays and the ray path (the bake: 576 opaque, 576 transparent and 7,040 unknown micro-triangles of the quad's two at level 6); `alpha mask: a device without opacity micromaps draws what it drew`.
- **What was wrong, and the rule that fixed it** (R120b, 2026-11-02). The probe that shows the micromaps in use — `renderer.shadow.opaque_rays` forces every caster solid, which the specification's traversal does not do to a micromap's transparent micro-triangle (it is ignored before the ray flags apply; "Ray Opacity Culling") — drew the same forced shadow with micromaps and without (21.4 % of the ground both ways) from R120's first commit. Neither suspect was it. Bisected in `rt_cluster_tests.cpp` on a one-cluster quad: the CLAS took the micromap in (384 bytes without, 512 with), and the same micromap failed on the **KHR** path too, so the cluster records and their address were right; then a probe shader with one ray query honoured it on both paths while `ray_visibility.slang` on the same structures did not — until its SPIR-V changed, after which even the original bytes did. **The driver (617.42) keeps compiled shaders in a cache of its own whose key leaves out `VK_EXT_opacity_micromap`, and a ray query from a compile it made on a device without the extension traces every micromap as absent.** Every ray-query shader of the engine had been compiled thousands of times on such devices before R120 enabled the extension. Shown directly: the probe compiled once on a device with the extension's row removed and then made from the same bytes on one with it hit the transparent quad on 1,998 of 1,998 pixels; a pipeline the driver had not seen hit it on 0. The rule: **every pipeline a device with micromaps makes carries one specialization constant no shader declares** (`micromap_key` in `device.cpp`; [gfx](gfx.md#the-pipeline-cache)) — behaviour unchanged by the spec's rule for an unused id, a different key in the driver's cache and in the engine's — and `cluster acceleration structures: a shader compiled without micromaps is not reused with them` fails without it. The bottom-level build's input also says `ALLOW_CLUSTER_OPACITY_MICROMAPS` now (`ClusterBlasSet::opacity_micromaps`), as the cluster builds' did; it was not the cause (the probe's coverage was the same with it alone) but a structure that holds such CLAS is built allowing them. With the key the forced shadow is 21.44 % without micromaps and 19.96 % with them: 6.9 % less, against the bake's 576 transparent micro-triangles of 8,192 (7.0 %), which is what the probe now checks.
- **What it buys, and what it costs** ([forest-resolve, stage 5](../experiments/forest-resolve-2026-11-01.md#stage-5-opacity-micromaps-on-the-walk-2026-11-03)). On the v25 walk (R115 stage 2's path and flags, `msvc-release`, the bake unbudgeted at the level cap 4) the sun stage is **14.79 → 13.29 ms at 11520×2160** and **5.20 → 4.26 at 3840×2160**, against the every-caster-solid ceiling of 2.18 and 0.79; the GPU frame 45.2 → 42.3 and 19.1 → 17.8. The bake is 1.5 s at load over 13.8 million masked triangles, and **79 % of the 3.3 billion micro-triangles come out unknown** at level 4 (the conservative rule unions every 2x2 texel footprint a micro-triangle of about four texels could read, so nearly every one straddles an edge of the mask), which is why a tenth of the masks' 12.6 ms comes back and not most of it. Two costs: the scene's micromap is **1.15 GB resident** (830 MB of states, the rest indices and the driver's micromap), and **`ALLOW_CLUSTER_OPACITY_MICROMAPS` raises the driver's worst case for a CLAS** from 6,144 to 8,832 bytes (124 triangles, 64 vertices), so the chain under the same budget holds 231,909 clusters where it held 338,115 — on v25 at `--rt-budget-mib 0` that drops more instances' structures (8,159 against 7,080 at 11520), which changes the picture, and part of the saving above may be that. So the switch is **off by default**; it is the coordinator's call whether a budget raised by the slots' 44 %, a finer level for fewer unknowns (at four times the memory a level), or the 2-state answer for the sun's ray (R126's resolve) makes it worth turning on. `renderer.rt.micromap_mib` defaults to 1,024, which holds v25 at level 4 (989 MB of states, indices and triangle records).
- **What the picture changes**: nothing under the frame as set (the identity above, now with the traversal using them). The rules that override a mask do change: `renderer.shadow.opaque_rays`, the sweep's every-caster-solid rule and the proxy's per-frame thresholds let the sun through a micromap's transparent micro-triangles, because the traversal never hands them to the loop that would make them solid — so the every-caster-solid row of a measurement is taken with micromaps off, and the opaque shadow proxy (`renderer.shadow.opaque_coverage` above 0) switches the micromaps off at load rather than leave holes in the clusters it makes solid.
- **Stage 3: the shadow rays' two-state answer, deduplication, the level** (R120, 2026-11-05; the numbers in [forest-resolve, stage 6](../experiments/forest-resolve-2026-11-01.md#stage-6-two-state-micromaps-for-the-shadow-rays-2026-11-05)). Three changes, none of which moves a pixel with the defaults:
  - **`renderer.shadow.micromap_2state`** (on by default since batch 53; read at load, only beside `renderer.shadow.micromaps`) sets `gfx::k_shadow_micromap_2state` in `ResolveParams::shadow_flags` where the scene baked micromaps, and the masked shadow query in `visibility_resolve.slang` then adds `RAY_FLAG_FORCE_OMM_2_STATE` (SPIR-V's ForceOpacityMicromap2StateEXT, 0x400; Slang's spelling) as a run-time ray flag. The traversal then decides an unknown micro-triangle by its sub-state — the bake's centre sample — and never hands it to the mask loop; every shadow ray (the sun's, the half pass's, the array lights') takes it, the primary rays never do, so the picture's ids are the rasterizers' to the word as before. The module does **not** declare `RayTracingOpacityMicromapEXT`: a device without the extension would refuse a module that did, and a variant per resolve module would double the eight ray-traced ones; the flag is a run-time operand the renderer sets only on a device that baked micromaps, and the RTX 5090 at 617.42 honours it without the declaration (the test below fails if it did not). The fallback, `VK_GEOMETRY_INSTANCE_FORCE_OPACITY_MICROMAP_2_STATE_EXT` on the top-level records, was not needed and would reach the primary rays.
  - **What two states can move, and how wide.** Only a micro-triangle the edge of the mask actually crosses answers differently: one that is unknown for the bilinear footprint's sake alone (the conservative rule's union of 2x2 texels) is one answer all over and its centre gives it. So a shadow's edge moves by at most one micro-triangle, whose leg is the card's side over 2^level: for a 0.10 m leaf card 6.3 mm at level 4, 3.1 mm at 5, 1.6 mm at 6, 0.4 mm at 8; for a 1.2 m merged card 7.5 cm, 3.8 cm, 1.9 cm and 0.5 cm. A grid-aligned mask on an aligned quad (the checker of the tests above) never moves at all, because no micro-triangle crosses a texel boundary; `alpha mask: two-state micromaps move only a shadow edge's band, never a primary ray` uses a bilinear disc instead and holds every lit/shadowed flip within one micro-triangle's longest side of the four-state picture's boundary (63 flips at level 4, 6 at level 7, none outside the band), fewer at the finer level, the ray path's ids unchanged and a device without the extension drawing what it drew.
  - **Deduplication.** A triangle's states are a function of its material and its UVs alone, and a forest's leaf cards repeat a few atlas regions, so the bake now stores one entry per distinct (material, UVs, level): the classify pass writes a 64-bit key (two 32-bit hashes of the seven words) beside each triangle's level, the host sorts the data-carrying triangles by key and level and gives each run one entry written once by its first triangle (`MicromapBakeParams::writers`, the write pass one thread an entry), and a **verify pass** compares every sharing triangle's words with its writer's, so a key collision costs an entry and never a wrong state (`MicromapStats::dedup_mismatches`). The micromap is built over the stored entries (`unique_per_level`); the per-triangle index buffer still scales with the scene. This is what lets a finer level fit: on v25 at level 6 the 12.5 million data-carrying triangles share **642,061 entries** (19.5 to one, no mismatch), 641 MB of states and **715 MB resident** with the indices and the driver's micromap — less than level 4 held undeduplicated (1.15 GB) — baked in 4.7 s; level 7 would be about four times the states and does not fit the 2 GiB budget the measurement gave it (a cap of 8 came down to 6). The shadow-proxy page's guess of "kilobytes per species" was wrong: the cards are many distinct UV sets (the LOD DAG's coarser triangles among them), so the states, not the 4-byte index, still scale with the scene.
  - **Why unknown, and how much at each level.** At the cap of 4, 79 % of the micro-triangles were unknown (stage 5), and the histogram says why: the texel target asks level 7 or 8 of 10.5 million of the 13.4 million masked triangles (level 5 of 1.6 million, 0 of 0.76 million), so the **cap** is the first cause — a level-4 micro-triangle spans 16 to 64 times the texels the target wants. At level 6 the unknown share is **20.1 %** (28 % of the level-5 triangles' micro-triangles, 19.8 % of the level-6 ones), and of those unknown ones **56 % are the filter's** — their corners and centre agree, so only the conservative union of 2x2 footprints made them unknown — which is the second cause, and exactly the share the two-state answer decides correctly.
