`texture_references()` the (mesh, image) pairs that reached one, `textures_shared()` those that took
one the scene already held, and `texture_bytes_saved()` what their own copies would have cost on the
device. The load logs it once (`scene textures`: `distinct`, `references`, `shared`, `bytes`,
`bytes_saved`, `sharing`). engine-view's summary has `"textures":{"built","decoded","distinct",
"shared","bytes","bytes_saved","sharing","normal_variance","normal_variance_bytes"}` and a flythrough's summary line the same block
(`engine.scene.FlythroughTextures`, through `summarize_textures`); `render.scenes` and
`render.unload` add `textures_shared` and `texture_bytes_saved` beside `textures` and
`texture_bytes`. `RenderSettings::share_textures` false — `engine-view --no-texture-sharing`, the
protocol's `"share_textures": false` — uploads every mesh's own copy again, which is the build
before this one, kept to measure against and to hold the picture to.

**What it measured** (RTX 5090, driver 610.88, `msvc-debug`, E33's ashlar kit from a derived-data
root of its own, 2026-09-25; the machine shared, other processes at 8–23% of the CPU and the GPU
0–1% busy with 7.1–7.9 GB of its 32.6 GB held by others at every sample of the two rows' runs).
*Kit grid* is the nineteen members five times each, 95 instances, at 1280×720; *E34's row* is E34's
"+ 100 ruins, E33 sections" scene, the desert overlook's terrain and 4,698 pieces, at 640×360.
*Each its own* is `--no-texture-sharing`; the build before this change gives the same textures and
bytes and the same device memory to within a megabyte. Device memory is `render.scenes`'s
`gpu_used_bytes` after one capture; *upload* is `GpuScene::create`'s geometry and material upload in
the debug build, from engine-view's log:

| scene | textures | texture bytes | process device memory | upload (debug) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| kit grid, each its own | 99 | 1,510,169,088 (1,440.2 MiB) | 1,868.2 MiB | 23.1 s |
| kit grid, shared | **6** | **83,899,392 (80.0 MiB)** | **332.1 MiB** | **1.3 s** |
| E34's row, each its own | 99 | 1,510,169,088 (1,440.2 MiB) | 2,203.4 MiB | 23.0 s |
| E34's row, shared | **6** | **83,899,392 (80.0 MiB)** | **668.0 MiB** | **1.3 s** |

`texture_bytes_saved` is 1,426,269,696 (1,360.2 MiB) in both, 93 of the 99 references shared.
Flown the way E34 flew its rows — 1920×1080, the desert overlook's path, shadows off, here 60 frames
and one repeat — E34's row holds **684 MiB** of device memory at the end of the flight where the build
before holds 2,220 MiB (E34 measured 2,219), and E35's streamed ashlar world (rings 1.5/6/10, mid
blocks near) **1,098 MiB** against 2,378 MiB at the same frame, the world having handed the
renderer 62 tails and the scene uploaded no texture after its load (other processes at 3–11% of
the CPU, 7.4–9.2 GB of the GPU's memory in use with ours).
**The pictures are the same bytes**: the captures through `render.capture` and through engine-view —
colour and the id buffer — shared, unshared and from the build before, in both scenes; and every
file `render.evaluate` writes for every scene of the corpus (the real-time picture, the reference,
the heat maps, at 32 samples), before and after, whose meshes have no image twice
(`textures_shared` 0). The 22 s the debug build spent was reading ninety-three copies of textures
it already had from the derived-data root and uploading them; a release build spends less on each,
and the same ninety-three fewer.

## Instances off the ground

A scene file's instance with `ground: true` stands `y` above the terrain's surface; one with `ground: false` stands at `y`, absolute. The second is how an author's landform can move under a scene unseen: the forest proof of concept moved its landform and left trees at the old heights, 26 m up (roadmap T74, engine-needs item 19). `read_scene_file` therefore compares, for every `ground: false` instance of a scene with a terrain, its `y` with the ground's surface at its x and z (`ground_at_world`, the query a grounded instance already makes, at the whole millimetre) and counts those more than `k_off_ground_m` = 1 m above (**floating**) and below (**buried**): a tree's roots and a rock's burial are within a metre, past it the author means it or the ground moved. The read keeps the count, the largest offset and the first instance's index of each (`SceneDesc::instances_floating`, `instances_buried`, `floating_max_m`, `floating_first`, ...), writes **one `instances off the ground` warning a scene** (counts, the largest, and the first one's name or index), and hands the two counts to the load summary as `load.instances_floating` and `load.instances_buried` ([apps](apps.md)). Nothing is refused and nothing moves. `ground: true` instances are never counted (their `y` is relative), and neither are scatters (their `y` is an offset by construction) or a streamed world's placements (their generators stand them on the ground). The cost is one more height query per `ground: false` instance, the same query a grounded one costs. Test: `tests/scene_gen_scene_tests.cpp`.

**An instance over a building is not floating** (2026-11-17, need 153 (f); roadmap P45). The forest's village props — a salt box on a dresser, a chest on an upper floor, a flitch hung from a joist, 1 to 3.5 m over the pads — were 53 `floating` in every v50 load, a warning that said nothing. What a building is, the read knows only from the placement entries: each says what it occupies as shapes (`Placements::shapes`, the footprints the entries after it and the exclusion are handed). So a lifted instance is set aside at the instance loop, and once the placements are read it is **held** when a disc or a polygon an entry occupies covers its x and z — a house's footprint, whose floors it stands on and whose timbers it hangs from — and counted in `instances_in_structures` (`SceneDesc`, the load summary's `load.instances_in_structures`, the warning's `in_structures`) instead of `floating`. A band (a lane, a tread) holds nothing up. A read-whole entry's shapes are the ones it hands anyway; a **streamed** entry expands nothing at the read, so its `tile` is asked for the tiles a lifted instance stands on and no other, once a tile, and only while some lifted instance is unheld — a scene with nothing lifted asks no tile and costs what it did. **What it does not judge**: the height. A prop 30 m over a house is held by its footprint as one on its floor is; the collision is what says whether it stands on something ([scene_collision](scene_collision.md#props)). Test: `renderer: an instance over a building's footprint stands in it and does not float`, read whole and streamed. **A footprint from the next tile** (2026-11-18, P45's review): only the tile holding the instance's point is asked, because a generator's `tile` hands **every shape that reaches the tile** (the contract on `scene_gen::Placements::shapes`), so a house whose footprint crosses into that tile from its neighbour is in that tile's answer — the village's `footprints` hands a shape to each tile its bounding disc reaches. A generator that broke the contract and handed a shape only from the tile of its centre would leave an instance over its far end counted floating; the read does not ask the neighbouring tiles to make up for it, which would multiply the tiles a lifted instance costs by nine for every generator to cover one that is wrong. Test: `renderer: a lifted instance over a footprint from the next tile is held by its own tile's answer`, with one generator that keeps the contract and one that does not.

## A tree seated by its footprint

G201 stage 2, 2026-11-12 ([tree base on slopes](../experiments/tree-base-on-slopes.md#stage-2-as-built-2026-11-12-branch-b63-g201-2), "Seating"). A grounded tree stands on the ground at its origin and its mesh carries its stem down below the collar as a skirt ([flora](flora.md#the-trunks-skirt)), deep enough for any plane of up to 45 degrees through the origin. What the skirt cannot reach is ground falling faster than that under the rim: a tread's fill face, a cutting's bank, a bench's edge, a step of the lattice. There the load lowers the tree until its skirt is under the lowest ground the rim stands over.

- **Who is seated.** An instance that **stands on the ground** (`SceneInstance::grounded`: a file's `ground: true` instance, a grounded scatter's, every placement generator's placement) whose mesh's container records a **seat** (section 42, `geometry::ClusterFileSeat`, read into `SourceMesh::seat`: the foot's farthest reach from the origin across the level plane, the collar's lowest point and the skirt's bottom; [flora](flora.md#the-seat) writes it for every tree, the deadwood for a standing remain) and no fit. Everything placed at a height of its own, every glTF and every mesh without a seat stands as it did.
- **The rule** (`scene_gen::seat_on_ground`, `domain/scene_gen/seat.h`): the drawn ground at the centre and at 16 points on the circle of the seat's radius times the larger of the scale's x and z, in **fixed world directions** (k 22.5 degrees from +x, each offset rounded half away from zero, so the set is symmetric and the answer is the yaw's in no way), in whole millimetres; a sample in a hole is not ground and is left out, and a centre in a hole seats nothing. The origin goes to `min(y, lowest + skirt - 0.05 m)`, the skirt the seat's depth times the scale's y: it never raises, an instance sunk deeper already (a scatter kind's `sink`) keeps the deeper, and seating twice is seating once. A plane fitted to the rim's samples by least squares (integer centred sums, one 2 by 2 solve in f64) is kept as its gradient in two 16-bit words of 1/8192, `scene_gen::GroundSlope`, **four bytes a placement** (scene_gen's size table), on `SceneInstance::slope` and `SceneData::ground_slopes` for the conformed foot of stage 3; nothing reads it yet.
- **The ground asked is the drawn one**: the terrain with the scene's edits and every edit its entries plan (`plan_scene_ground`), at the terrain's own time, the holes from the exclusion. The answer is the provider's (bilinear on a tile set's lattice); a ground drawn from a coarser grid than it is sampled at can differ from it by what the grid's spacing allows, which `engine-content ground sample`'s head line states ([apps](apps.md#engine-content-ground-sample)).
- **Where.** `load_scene` calls `seat_scene_instances` after the meshes load (their containers say the seat) and before the authored entry takes its instances, so a streamed authored tree is handed on seated (`StreamedPlacements::seated`) and every other streamed entry's placements are seated by the world's placements consumer at activation with the same function ([world](world.md#a-tiles-trees-are-seated)). A ground is made only when a load has an instance to seat on it: one more `TerrainSampler` over the scene's terrain description. The load's report counts `seated`, `lowered`, `lowered_max_m` and `seat_ms`, and logs one `instances seated by their footprints` line.
- **Determinism.** Every decision is whole millimetres, sums, products and one IEEE solve, and each instance is seated alone, so a seat is a function of the scene and the place, never of the thread count or the order tiles come in: `tests/seat_scene_tests.cpp` seats a bank's trees at one load thread and at every thread to the same instance table and pins the origins' bits; `systems/world`'s `seat_tiles_tests.cpp` builds the tiles in another order and finds every tree where the whole read put it.
- **What it costs.** 17 ground queries a seated instance where it made one, once, off the frame's thread. Measured: [the stage's page](../experiments/tree-base-on-slopes.md#stage-2-as-built-2026-11-12-branch-b63-g201-2).
- **Not built.** A tile's own meshes (handed with the tile, built after it) are not seated, because their seat is not known when the tile is built; the authored set does not carry an instance's slope across the hand-over, so a streamed authored tree's `slope` is zero (its height is seated). Both are stage 3's to close where it needs them.

What holds it on a GPU: `tests/flora_scene_tests.cpp`'s "a tree on a tread's edge or a cutting's lip is seated with no gap", on `content/test-scenes/tree-bases/seat.json`'s ground, read from the ids and the depth along each edge: seated, no pixel under any trunk is the sky, another tree or the ground far behind; the same trees loaded as the base placed them (not grounded, so not seated) show such pixels on both edges, so the scene asks what the skirt alone cannot answer.

## What the load reads

**The scene file is read with no tree of it** (D40): `read_scene_text` (`scene_text.h`) reads the text straight into `engine.scene.Scene` ([schema](schema.md#json-text-with-no-tree)), the tree path's verdicts word for word, and only `water_channels` as a tree, for its migration; `read_scene_props` the same. One startup stage, `schema read`; `renderer.scene.read_text` (`bench/scene_read_bench.cpp`) times it with no device.

**The two CPU stages by zone** (W150; [measured](../experiments/load-cpu-stages-2026-11-18.md)): every file instance's ground is asked by place (`scene_gen::heights_by_place`, stage `instance heights`; in the file's order the `tiles` cache read the staging's tiles 2.4 times over), `SceneData::streamed` is moved out of the load's copy rather than copied (the authored entry's tree of every streamed instance), and `stream_authored` names its parts (`authored sway`, `rings`, `set`, `params`).

The mask upload (W76, 2026-10-26) counts `GroundMasks::ops->present` from the provider's
manifest before its resident-budget check, then reads each present payload once into its final
slot. `terrain masks` is a startup-trace child of `gpu scene`; it includes provider opening and
the resident page table's construction. A missing/corrupt present tile now fails the copy with
its coordinates instead of being silently treated as absent during counting. Sparse slots keep
`k_terrain_no_mask_tile`; resident bytes and shader layout are unchanged. The
[matched measurements](../experiments/tile-archives-2026-10-24.md#one-mask-payload-pass-at-load)
separate payload reads from read-ahead I/O and report the machine state.

**A cooked scene's load reads derived data and the scene's own small files, and no source image**
(since 2026-10-24, roadmap W75; the measurements are in the
[startup trace's page](../experiments/startup-trace-forest-2026-10-24.md#after-w75)). **The
load's stages say where it is while it runs** (roadmap W79): every `ENGINE_STARTUP_STAGE` here and
in `GpuScene::create` feeds the live progress record whether or not a trace records
([profiling](profiling.md#the-trace-is-live)) — the scene file's expand, `meshes` and each `mesh`
stage as the current stage's detail, `trace_items` as the items — and a stage that runs on a thread
that owns a window pumps its messages as it begins and ends, as does each texture upload in
`GpuScene::create` (`profiling::progress_pump()`), which is how engine-view keeps its
window answering through `gpu scene` without the renderer knowing it has one
([apps](apps.md#the-loading-presentation)). `load_scene` itself can run on any thread; engine-view
runs it on a load thread. `load_scene` does its work in this order:

1. **The meshes, on the job system.** One job per mesh on one `jobs::JobSystem` made for the load
   (`SceneDesc::load_jobs` workers, 0 one per performance CPU), the calling thread helping: each
   mesh's source hash, container read, generator inputs, or — on a miss — import, repairs, DAG and
   cache write is its own and lands in its own slot of `sources`, `dags` and `tables`, so nothing
   depends on the thread count or on completion order (`cooked_load_tests.cpp` loads at one worker
   and at every one and requires the same tables, hashed), and the first failure reported is the
   lowest mesh index's, as the serial loop reported it. A path a later mesh repeats loads in a
   second wave, after the first wrote the entry they share, so it is a hit as it was serially and
   not a second build of the same entry. The trace's `meshes` stage holds the main thread's wait;
   each `mesh` stage is on the thread that ran it. **The pool gets one runner job a thread, never
   one job a mesh** (`run_jobs`, scene.cpp; T73): each runner takes the next mesh by an atomic
   index until none is left. The pool's queues hold 4,096 jobs each (the caller's guest deque and
   the inbox, `JobSystemConfig::queue_capacity`), and `schedule` runs a job that fits neither on the
   submitting thread at once — before it wakes a sleeping worker — so the v35 forest's 16,351
   meshes ran 8,159 of them one after another on the load thread, ~27 ms each, while every worker
   slept, and only then the queued 8,192 in parallel: 246 s of a 419 s load
   ([the measurements](../experiments/load-v35-2026-11-08.md)). `SceneLoadReport::inline_jobs`
   counts what the pool ran inline and is zero; `cooked_load_tests.cpp` loads 10,000 meshes and
   holds it there. The duplicate-path scan that splits the two waves is a hash of the path, not a
   comparison with every earlier one.
2. **The textures, once for the whole load** (`prepare_scene_textures`, scene.cpp; the trace's
   `cache textures`), where until W75 every mesh ran the content build's texture step on its own —
   a read and a hash of every image it named, and a job pool made and joined to do it:
   - every (mesh, image) a material samples, in mesh order: an image the container carries by the
     key its record says, one named by path by **one identity per distinct file for the load**,
     through the load's table of its source images (`content_build::ImageIdentities`): a material
     pack's file from the pack's index under the derived-data root without a read, any other file
     read and hashed once ([content_build](content_build.md#one-hash-per-image-and-a-packs-from-its-manifest)),
     the distinct files one job each (`texture identities`);
   - every distinct key's `.tex` **trusted from its header** — there, the size its header says,
     recording this key's identity (`texture::probe_texture_file`, a few hundred bytes;
     `texture probe`; [texture](texture.md#trusted-not-read));
   - only a key whose `.tex` is missing or refused built, all of them in one run of
     `content_build::run_texture_step` on the same pool (`texture build`), from the bytes the
     container carries (`TextureSource::view`, no copy) or the file read now — and a pack file whose
     bytes no longer give its index's hash built under the key its bytes give;
   - the keys written into every mesh's in-memory records (`SourceMesh::textures`), before the
     authored forms copy them, so the upload's `find_built_textures` finds every built texture by
     key and **never hashes a source again**. The container on disk is untouched: an image named by
     path still records no key there (geometry.md, section 32).
   The trace's `textures trusted` names the counts (`trusted=… built=… hashed=… from_index=…`), and
   `SceneData::load` (`SceneLoadReport`) carries them and the source images opened and their bytes
   for a test and for engine-view's summary (`load`, [apps](apps.md#the-summarys-load-block)).
3. The authored forms (`authored forms`), the merge (`merge`), the instances, as before — except
   that the per-mesh DAGs and page tables are released as soon as the merge has copied them
   (`release meshes`), not at the end of the load, and the instance list is moved out of the
   load's copy of the description rather than copied (T73). Each placement entry of the scene file
   is a `placement` stage whose detail is its generator, and the footprints handed to the entries
   after it a `footprints` stage, so `placements` says where its time went.

**The embedded image bytes go once the textures are built** (W51-3, 2026-11-18;
[the measurements](../experiments/start-commit-by-owner-2026-11-18.md#w51-3-what-the-stages-returned)).
An image a container carries (a GLB's, a data URI's, a generator's leaf and bark atlases) arrives
in `SourceMesh::data.images[i].bytes`, and until W51-3 it stayed there for the session: a second
copy beside its built `.tex` and its GPU texture, and a third, fourth and fifth in every distance
form, far-form level and placement form the load copies a mesh into — 9.8 GB of the forest
staging's host commit, two thirds of the host at its start. Right after the texture pass and before
anything copies a mesh, `release_built_image_bytes` (source_images.cpp) empties every image's bytes
of a mesh when **every image its materials sample has its `.tex` under the mesh's root** (so
`find_built_textures` takes the built path and decodes nothing) **and the mesh has a container**
(the file it was read from or this load wrote, which holds the bytes), and marks the mesh
`SourceMesh::image_bytes_released`; the load reports the meshes and bytes
(`SceneLoadReport::image_bytes_released`). A mesh with no derived-data root, no container, or an
image not built keeps every byte, exactly as before. The rule is the mesh's own state, never a
generator's or a scene's name, so a glTF kit with embedded textures is treated as a tree is.
**Who reads them after that, and what each does now**: `find_built_textures` and the prefetch read
records and keys only; the upload's decode — when the built path cannot be used (the device has no
BC formats, a `.tex` gone or refused between the load and the upload) — and the crowns' leaf masks
(`build_crown_priors`, one decode a distinct mask, its key the record's source hash, which is the
hash of the same bytes) read them back through `source_image_bytes`, which reads the container's
resident sections (`geometry::ClusterFileReader`, no paged stream) and checks them against the
record's source hash; a far forest's composite never copied bytes when records exist; a far tile and
a placement tile load their own members (`load_placement_mesh`) and never see a released mesh, so
the bytes a far tile writes into its container are unchanged. Every one of those readers runs in
`load_scene` or `GpuScene::create`/`SceneRenderer::create`, never in a frame, so the frame loop reads
no file for it. Nothing that is cached moved: no container, texture or key changes.

**What it still reads before the first frame**, warm, for the forest v7 (2,074 MiB of 4,498): the
`.clusters` containers (281 MiB) and the GLBs' own bytes for their source hash (195 MiB), every
`.tex` whole at the upload (357 MiB, its content hash checked), the scene file and the region's
tile files under every placement (174 MiB, `scene expand`, item (1) above), the animation clips
(131 MiB), the geometry's upload (112 MiB), and the ground's tiles and the walker's with the renderer's
sky and flora tables (about 640 MiB over `ground prepare`, `ground start`, `session` and `renderer`). **A GLB's source hash** is the one source read a
cooked load still makes: the container is found by the hash of the GLB's bytes, and nothing cheaper
names those bytes yet (a scene file's `hash` field is checked against it, not trusted in its place).

**The built textures are read ahead of their upload** (`TexturePrefetch`, gpu_scene.cpp; T73):
`upload materials` plans the `.tex` keys `find_built_textures` will read, in its order (mesh order,
each key once), and reads them in windows of 128 files on eight reader threads of its own job
system's efficiency pool — which a waiting main thread never helps, so it uploads while they read —
the next window while this one is uploaded; at most two windows' bytes are held beyond what the
upload held before. A key the plan did not hold (named by path, hashed at the upload), or one a
later mesh asks for after its window went, is read where it always was. The bytes are the file's,
so nothing uploaded changes.

**What did not move**: the uploads themselves are still serial on the main thread after the load
— each `gfx::upload_image_2d_levels` makes its own staging buffer and waits for its own copy —
and nothing is uploaded while the meshes load; that is the residency work's
([04 §4.9](../plan/04-renderer.md#49-streaming-and-residency), W47), which also bounds what is
loaded to the spawn's neighbourhood.

## Content classes at load

**Every instance of a loaded scene is decided under the scene's view policy when it is admitted, before its mesh's geometry is read** (roadmap C64; [content classes](../content-classes.md#what-decided-at-instantiation-means), [ADR-0073](../adr/0073-classes-travel-with-derived-data-and-policies-are-the-operators.md) decision 5; the vocabulary is [content_class](content_class.md)'s). **Built 2026-11-19** in `msvc-debug`; its CPU cases (`content_class_load_tests.cpp`, `content classes at load: *`, and `cooked load: a classified recipe has a cache entry of its own, carrying its class`) pass with no device; the capture case (`content classes at load: a capture holds the box or nothing, on every path`) needs one: on every rasterizer and the ray path an omitted grid is in no channel and a proxied one is the box in colour, ids, depth and normals alike, and, with the grid 24 m up on the line from a receiver's centre towards the stand-in sun, so that its shadow falls on the receiver and the eye sees the receiver beside it, under the maps and under traced shadows and through the reference integrator, an omitted grid casts no shadow either, while the receiver's own pixels that the eye sees in both shots (its instance's ids) are darker under a covered one, so that half's equality cannot hold only because no shadow could be seen. `SceneDesc::view_policy` (a `content_class::NamedPolicy`, `agent-default` unless the caller names another; a host's flag is C65's) is what the load decides under, and `PlacementMeshOptions::view_policy` carries it to a mesh built after the load.

**One door** (`admit_instance`, `systems/renderer/admission.h`): it joins the instance's mesh's own class, its textures' and its raise, decides the join through the scene's `DecisionTable`, and accounts for it. The load calls it once for every instance it makes, the implicit one and a grid's included, and the implicit one it makes when a streamed world's tail took every file instance (`admit_made_instance`, keyed on whether the load made the instance rather than on whether the file named none; before C64's mends that one was placed undecided, and drew mesh 0's box at the origin when mesh 0's own class refused it; test "content classes at load: the mesh-0 instance made after a streamed tail is decided", on the CPU); what admits an instance after the load (a world tile's placement, a placement's form, a game module's object) is the live re-decision's (C67), which calls the same function with the class `read_container_class` or `read_sidecar_class` gives its mesh, before it makes an `InstanceDesc`.

**Where each class comes from**, all before a mesh's geometry is read, so a mesh nothing would draw is never read at all, with one exception: **a refusal that only an image's class decides reads the mesh first**, because the mesh is what names its images (a container's section 32, a glTF's JSON), so its geometry is read and its own cache entry built, under its own key, before the second pass probes the images; nothing of it then reaches the scene (its slot becomes its box). Probing the images a container's section 32 or a glTF's JSON names in the first pass would close that, and is not built:
- **a container's own** (`.clusters`, named outright or found in the cache): section 54, looked up in its section table and read only when present, its ladders learned into the scene's `categories`; joined with a sidecar beside it. **The probe is a saving, not the decision**: when the mesh job reads a container named outright in full, its section 54 is taken from those bytes, and where it is not what the probe saw (or the probe could not open the file) the second pass decides the mesh again by it (`container_class_as_loaded`), so a container replaced or finished between the two opens is decided by what was loaded, and becomes its box if that refuses it (test "content classes at load: a container is decided by the bytes the load read", and through `load_scene` "content classes at load: a container replaced after its probe is decided as read", where a fixture generator's hash, taken while a later recipe's class is read, writes a classified container over one probed unclassified and the instance is left out). The probe's read is sized from the section table only after `ClusterFileReader::open` has held every section to the file's bytes, so a count the file cannot hold is refused before anything is allocated, and the load fails on it with the reader's sentence (test "content classes at load: a classes section the file cannot hold allocates nothing"). A game category such a container is the first to teach is decided under the table's policy as it was resolved before, where that category is `none` with `omit` whatever the policy names for it: the stricter reading;
- **a glTF's**: its sidecar, read once, before its key is taken, through the content build's own reader (`content_build::read_source_classes`), so nothing of that name is `none` and a sidecar there that cannot be read (a link or junction that leads nowhere included) is the unreadable class, as in the build; a classified glTF's cache key holds the class by name (`content_class::classified_key`, the content build's own rule), and the entry the load builds carries section 54;
- **a generated mesh's**: its recipe's sidecar (`<name>.flora.provenance.json` beside `<name>.flora.json`) joined with the pack sets it bakes and with the class of every mesh it reads, its hosts', found from the recipe alone (`content_build::read_source_classes`; [content build](content_build.md#content-classes)), so a host the policy refuses refuses the output before the host is read (test "content classes at load: a generated mesh over a refused host is left out, unread"); a classified recipe's cache key moves by its class as the content build's does, and the entry the load builds carries section 54 and records the moved key;
- **its textures'**: every image named by path probed once a distinct file for `<stem>.provenance.json` beside it (an image and a container that share a stem in one directory share one sidecar, which then classifies both), read by the same reader; a classified image's texture key holds its class, hashed over its materials as the content build's texture step hashes it, so the `.tex` the step writes on a miss is the one the key names, and a texture built at load from it is built from its file, so its `.tex` gets section 6. The `.tex`'s own section 6 is not read again at load: the key the load computes already holds the sidecar's class, so the `.tex` it finds by that key carries exactly that class. An embedded image's class is its container's;
- **its raise**: `SceneInstance::content_classes`, from a scene file's `Instance.content_classes` (version 4), read at the load, after the containers have taught the scene their ladders, so a raise naming a game category no data defines fails closed. **The scene file is read strictly** (`JsonParseOptions::refuse_duplicate_keys`, the mode the classes module's readers and a content manifest use): a key given twice anywhere in a scene refuses the load with a sentence naming the key, so a merge's appended `content_classes`, or a level given twice, cannot lose a raise (test "content classes at load: a scene file that gives a key twice is refused, naming it"); `read_scene_props` reads the same file the same way, and names the key the same way (test "content classes at load: the props read names a key given twice"). Every scene the renderer's scene cases read from `content/` still reads.
**A class that cannot be read is decided with what the scene knows at the decision**: reading it keeps only the fact (`ReadClass::unreadable`), and its levels are made after every mesh's class is in, from every category the scene knows then (`content_class::unreadable(categories)`), so every ladder the scene's data teaches is in it, whichever of the meshes is listed first (test "content classes at load: an unreadable class decides the same in either mesh order"); what the load builds for such a ground, glTF or recipe (its key's class term and its entry's section 54) is taken from that class too, so an entry a wide policy admits records every category its decision used (test "content classes at load: an unreadable glTF's entry records the class it was decided on"). **Every ladder of every container the probe opens is learned before any class is read**, in two rounds of teachers, each record learned by the same `content_class::decode_classes`, whole or not at all: first every container the scene lists, in the order listed, from its own section 54; then every recipe's container hosts, the whole chain, in the order the scene lists the recipes (`content_build::learn_source_hosts`). So **a host the scene does not list teaches only a category no listed container taught**: one whose ladder differs from one already learned is refused as a second listed container is, and its recipe is unreadable (test "content classes at load: a listed container's ladder stands over an unlisted host's"). Only then are the classes read, in mesh order, against the finished table: each recipe's own sidecar, its pack and its hosts', each glTF's sidecar, each listed container's sidecar, the ground's. A listed container the probe cannot open (locked, half written) teaches nothing in round one: it is decided, and its ladder learned, at its whole read, after the policy is resolved and every class is read, so a class that names a category only that container carries was read as unreadable, and that container's own sidecar is not read (roadmap C70). So **for a scene in which no two teachers disagree about a category, what is admitted, what is left out and under which row it is counted, and every asset's key, are the same under every order of its mesh list** (test "content classes at load: every order of a scene's meshes decides it alike", all 120 orders of a listed classified container, a cover over it with its own sidecar, a cover over an unlisted host of a second category, a glTF naming both and a ground naming the second, under two policies; and "content classes at load: a cover's own sidecar reads before its host, after, alone", "content classes at load: an unlisted host's ladder reaches a glTF in either order", "content classes at load: a recipe over a game-classified host decides in any order"). Between two listed containers that teach one category differently, the first listed still wins and the second is refused, as before (test "content classes at load: what cannot be read is omitted and counted apart").
- **the ground's** (the terrain an empty path builds): the join of what the sidecars beside its heightfield source (a tile set's `manifest` or `heightfield`) and beside **every** image its `terrain.materials` layers name (`base_color`, `normal`, `roughness`, `height`, `mask`) and beside every image its `terrain.masks` are painted from (each `paint[].image` and `index.image`, the weight maps the mask level is composited from) declare, read through the same reader before any of those files is embedded in the ground's render mesh, uploaded or drawn. **What is read before the decision**: the scene read (`read_scene_file`) reads the heightfield source, and cooks the tile set and the mask level into the cache, whatever the policy, because seating, collision, the scene read's own refusals (a mask tile over its layer budget, a level over `resident_mib`) and the placements that place by substrate (litter's and the sward's, through `Ground::masks`) stand on the ground, and the world is not an output; what the admission holds back for a refused ground is its render mesh, its textures, its upload and the picture. The ground is decided through the door's form for it (`admit_ground`): **a ground the policy refuses is left out whole**, never a box, since a box at a ground's bounds stands for nothing, and is counted in `SceneLoadReport::grounds_omitted`, beside the instances' counts. Left out, it is not built (nothing of it in the terrain's cache entry, the textures or the picture), and the load turns the terrain, its tiles and the world's ground off, so no ring or tile draws its shape; instances are still seated on the ground the file described, since the world is not an output. A sidecar beside any of its inputs that cannot be read refuses it, as it refuses a mesh. Its cache key takes the class hash as a mesh's does (`content_class::classified_key`, a term that is the key itself when nothing is classified), so a ground with no sidecar beside anything keeps exactly the key it had (test "content classes at load: a ground keeps its key with no sidecar, and fails closed" computes `load_terrain`'s classless key and finds the entry under it), and a classified one's entry carries section 54 (tests "content classes at load: a ground whose layer image is above the cap is left out whole", "content classes at load: a ground's painted mask above the cap leaves it out", and "content classes at load: a dangling sidecar beside a ground's paint map refuses it"). On a device, "content classes at load: a capture holds nothing of a refused ground" holds every channel of such a scene, on the hardware rasterizer and the ray path, to the bytes of the same scene with no ground at all. **Not built**: a neutral stand-in for one refused layer, so that the rest of a ground still draws; until then one layer refuses the whole ground.

**What each outcome makes.** `admit`: as before. `omit`: the instance is left out of the instance table, and the whole read's index follows ([below](#the-whole-reads-index): a read index whose instance was left out answers `k_not_loaded`); in a streamed world it is kept from the tail. `proxy`: the instance draws **the proxy box** (`build_proxy_box`): the engine's box at its mesh's finest clusters' sphere bounds in mesh space, so its transform and its mesh's fit place it where the mesh stood, a vertex per face corner, built by the same LOD builder as every mesh (one cluster, twelve triangles), with one mid-grey, rough, untextured material (`proxy_material`). It is an ordinary mesh (its CPU case holds that its twelve triangles face out and close it), so every path draws it alike, `--raster sw` within that debugging mode's limit: it skips a triangle whose pixel box is over 64 × 64 (`k_max_bbox_pixels`, [E1's follow-ups](../experiments/e1-pascal-rerun.md#follow-ups)), and a face's two triangles each have the face's box, so a near box loses its lid there, as any mesh of few large triangles does. From the capture case's first shot (40 m) the lid's were 9,328 pixels and `sw` drew 4,734 of the box's 9,125; the shot is 70 m up now (3,024), held on the CPU by `content classes at load: the capture's shot keeps the proxy in the software box`. **Substitution is the placer's, not the slot's** (C64): a mesh's slot is replaced by its box only when the mesh's **own** class (its own and its textures', never an instance's raise) is refused, so every placer, a streamed entry's tiles and a prop included, places the box; or when no admitted instance draws it and nothing else places it (what `open_scene_meshes` marks). An instance refused by its own raise is left out, or draws a proxy mesh of its own, and the slot the tiles, props and other instances place stays the mesh; a mesh some other placer places is read whenever its own class lets it be drawn (test "content classes at load: a raise refuses its instance, not the mesh others place"). A replaced slot is replaced before the texture pass and the merge: its geometry, images, container, motion, seat and far form leave the scene, so a capture, a page source or a form of it can only reach the box. A mesh admitted for some instances and proxied for others gets a proxy mesh of its own after the scene's meshes. A substitution keeps a streamed scene on the streaming path: in a scene that streams, the box gets a page table of its own (`geometry::build_cluster_pages`, one cluster, one page), so the merged table is still built and the gate the authored instances stream by is where it was (test "content classes at load: a streamed scene with a box in it still streams"); until C64's mends the box had none, which loaded such a world whole and resident and started its authored instances streaming where they had not.

**What the scene remembers**: `SceneData::instantiated_under` (the policy, its game caps resolved against `categories` once every container's ladder is in), `categories`, `decisions` (append-only; one entry, `none` admitted, for a scene with nothing classified) and `held` (the join of what it admitted). `SceneLoadReport::substituted` counts the instances each category omitted or proxied, by name (instances only: a mesh no instance names is decided outside the count, its class entering the table and `held` only when another placer draws it; test "content classes at load: a mesh no instance names is decided, not counted"), and `unreadable_omitted` and `unreadable_proxied` the ones decided on a class that could not be read, apart; `grounds_omitted` the grounds left out; `image_sidecars_probed` and `image_sidecars_found` count the probes.

**What a scene with nothing classified pays**: its keys and entries are the ones it had: the test "content classes at load: a scene with nothing classified loads what it loaded" holds the glTF's, each image's and the ground's cache keys to the plain key functions computed without any class, with their entries under those names, and "cooked load: a classified recipe has a cache entry of its own, carrying its class" holds a plain recipe's to the generator's own key; no GPU struct, shader or per-frame work; no field per instance (the raise is two bytes in what was `SceneInstance`'s padding); per mesh during the load only, a few words of the passes' state; per container one section-table read and a sidecar probe, per glTF one sidecar probe, per distinct image one sidecar probe; per distinct generated mesh whose generator can name a host (C72) a second read of its recipe and its generator's hash run once more under the class probe's hooks, and per host that recipe names a sidecar probe, and for a container host its open and section-table read (a recipe host's own recipe read and hash in turn); **the two teaching rounds add no read**: round one is each listed container's own section-table read, moved before the sidecars, and round two is each recipe's probe and its container hosts' opens and section-table reads, kept (`content_build::HostReads`) and taken from there by the class read, so each is still made once; they add a hash-map lookup per recipe and per container host, and the kept records' bytes, none for a host with nothing classified; per ground up to `2 + 5 × layers` sidecar probes, the tile set's two paths and each layer's five images, plus one beside each of its masks' paint maps and its index map; then the second pass returns before it looks at an instance. `SceneData` gains the policy, a categories table of the engine's three and a one-entry table, a few hundred bytes a scene. **Measured** (2026-11-19, `msvc-debug`, driverless, the line's tip against this branch, two alternating pairs, other processes using 0 to 66% of the CPU): a scene of 10,000 references to one container loads in 4.70 and 4.65 s before and 4.74 and 4.76 s after; two generated palms over a pack's images in 0.42 and 0.47 s before and 0.46 and 0.51 s after. **Before the passes read each distinct path once**, the 10,000 references cost 5.86 and 5.97 s against 10.59 and 10.46 s: a container's section-table read and sidecar probe cost about 0.46 ms each in `msvc-debug`, serially on the load's thread, which is what a scene of as many *distinct* containers still pays (about 7.5 s for 16,000 distinct containers in that build, not measured in a release one): a figure for one container named ten thousand times, the case the path dedup covers, and not a forest's, whose cost is thousands of distinct recipes (C72, below). The recipes' reads now run on the load's pool; the containers' sections are still read one after another. **The probes added since are not measured yet** (the recipes' second read and hash, the hosts' probes and opens, the ground's sidecar probes): the figures above were taken before them, and the page does not record the harness they were taken with, so they are taken again, by the same two scenes and a ground with layers and masks, when the load's measurement is next run.

**What the class read costs is counted, by kind of read** (roadmap C72): the first pass is the startup stage `content classes` (its items the distinct paths), and its reads are counted in the pass's own state (`content_build::ClassReads`, `class_reads.h`, handed to the content build's reads through `HostReads::counts`) and kept in `SceneLoadReport::class_reads`, `class_paths` and `classes_ms`, by kind: a listed container's section, a container's sidecar, a recipe's file, a recipe's sidecar, a pack's sets (asked once a set, its bytes the `pack.json` read), a host's probe (the generator's hash under the probe's hooks, no file), a host's record, a glTF's sidecar, the ground's inputs; for each how many were asked for, found a file, the bytes and the milliseconds. Apart from what those reads cost, two kinds count how the walk got each recipe's hosts: taken from a probe made ahead (`ahead_answer`) or probed in the walk itself (`walk_probe`), so a load that probed ahead can hold that it made no probe of its own and the parallel road was taken, not bypassed (the cost case and "content classes at load: one thread and many decide a scene alike" hold `walk_probe` at zero; with the ahead call taken out both fail on it). The pass ends with one line, `content classes read`, with those as typed fields (`<kind>.asked`, `.found`, `.bytes`, `.ms`, beside `paths` and `ms`); a procedural scene with no ground reads nothing and prints none. **Measured** (2026-11-22, `msvc-release`, the test `content classes at load: the class read's cost on a forest's shape` at its release size: 2,000 distinct palm recipes, 200 containers and 200 glTFs in eight directories over a pack of 40 sets, no sidecar anywhere; not a quiet run: the test records no machine state, and a sample minutes after read the whole machine 27 to 29% busy with other agents' compilers running, so the figures are upper bounds): the pass took 2.77 s for 2,401 distinct paths, 1.2 ms a path, and the calling thread's CPU was 2.64 s of the load's 2.89 s, so the read is **CPU-bound here, not waiting**. By kind: the pack's sets 1,253 ms (every recipe reads and parses the whole `pack.json`, 9.4 KB, again: 80,000 set reads for 40 sets), the recipes' files 747 ms, the hosts' probes 304 ms, the containers' sections 214 ms, the recipes' sidecar looks 208 ms, the other sidecars 31 ms; with a sidecar beside every 97th source, the same. With a pack of 400 sets (94 KB) the sets take 7.2 s of 8.8 s, linear in the pack's size times the recipes. A forest's load of 4,236 meshes waits 72 s here (17 ms a mesh, its thread mostly waiting, by its trace), which this scene does not reproduce; **its own line** (2026-11-22, `msvc-release`, that forest's scene of 4,236 meshes, 3,849 of them listed: 3,158 flora, 613 deadwood, 39 rock, 28 cover, a few others, 4,235 distinct paths with its placements', a pack of 23 sets and 33 generated ones, 40 KB) said where: the pass took **67.2 s**, of which **the recipes' files 54.7 s** (3,883 reads, 315 MB: the forest's recipes average 81 KB), their hosts' probes 8.6 s (each recipe parsed under its generator's hash), the pack's sets 3.1 s (89,562 set reads), the containers' sections 0.73 s (64), every sidecar together 0.15 s (none was there).

**What the pass reads once, what in parallel, and what stays serial** (C72). **Once a load**: the pack's sets' classes, read against the finished table after the teaching rounds (`content_build::keep_pack_classes`, kept in `HostReads::pack`), so every recipe joins the same classes without reading `pack.json` again; a read over another pack or table reads its own. **Not at all**: a recipe whose generator cannot name a host, since the answer, no host, is known without it: one with no host-aware hash (deadwood's, the rocks') and one whose registration declares that its recipes name none (`assets::MeshGeneratorDesc::names_hosts`, flora's and wetland's; on a forest most of its recipes are flora's). Its sidecar is still looked for and its pack's sets still joined. The declaration is checked where the recipe is hashed for its build, never trusted: a host such a recipe asks for anyway is refused there (`content_build::GeneratorHosts::identify`), so the whole load fails, with a sentence naming the generator, the recipe and the host, as it fails on a recipe that cannot be built; a class that cannot be read leaves out only its own mesh and the load goes on. Both fail closed, and nothing is built over a host whose class was not read (test "content classes at load: a generator that names no host and asks for one is refused"; [content build](content_build.md#content-classes)). The check sees the hooks that name and load a host, not the image hooks, so a generator declared to name none that read a container's bytes as an image would pass it; none in the tree does (roadmap C70). **In parallel**, on the load's pool, which `load_scene` now makes before the pass: every distinct recipe's file that can name a host (or its handed bytes) and its generator's hash under the probe's hooks, each into its own slot (`content_build::probe_recipes_ahead`, `HostReads::ahead`, keyed by the path and by whether its bytes were handed), then in waves every recipe host those probes name, to `k_host_depth`. **Serially and in listed order, exactly as before**: round one's containers, round two's walk, which takes each probe's answer from its slot instead of computing it and keeps, learns and refuses what it did, and the classes against the finished table, so the decision does not depend on the thread count (test "content classes at load: one thread and many decide a scene alike", the permutation case's scene in two orders at one job, two and the machine's, with a chain of two recipes over a container, so the probes' second wave is not empty, and a recipe whose hash refuses the probe, so a slot carries a refusal and the recipe is counted unreadable). The probe is a pure function of the bytes and the generator, so the answer is the one the round would have computed when it got there; only when it is read moves, as it moves for the mesh job's own read later. The containers' sections stay serial (0.73 s on the forest). **Not built**: a listing of each directory to learn which sidecars exist, since the forest's sidecar looks cost 0.15 s of 67. Measured on the test's scene at its release size after the change: the pass 1.47 s, down from 2.77, the pack's sets 40 reads and 0.8 ms; the recipes' reads summed over the threads came to 36.4 s against 0.75 s one after another, so on that machine, where every file here is small and already in the cache, their opens contend and the pool buys little: the pack read once is most of that scene's saving. **On a forest's scene of 4,236 meshes, the same flags: 67.2 s before, 4.38 s after** (the binaries before C64 took 0.4 s from `load scene` to `meshes`): the pack's sets 23 reads and 1 ms, the recipes' reads and probes on the pool (101 s and 27 s summed over its threads, about 3.6 s of wall), the containers' sections 0.67 s, still one after another. **Then 0.95 s**, once a recipe whose generator cannot name a host is not read at all (2026-11-22, the same scene, flags and build, not a quiet run: another checkout's tests held the card until a few seconds before it): the recipes' files 30 reads, 15 KB (the 28 cover and 2 vine recipes; 1.9 s summed over the pool's threads), their probes 6 ms, 30 answers taken from the slots and no probe made in the walk, the containers' sections 0.71 s, the recipes' sidecar looks 86 ms, the pack's sets 23 reads and 1 ms, every other kind under 25 ms; from `load scene` to `meshes` 1.35 s, against 72.0 s before C72 and 0.4 s before C64. The containers' sections, read one after another, are now most of the pass. Only the fetched pack's own `pack.json` is read for its sets, as before: the generated sets behind it in `generated/pack.json` join no recipe's class.

**Not built here**: a world tile's and a placement form's admission after the load, and a live edit's re-decision, `doc_scene` and the editor's viewport deciding an instance again when the change feed touches its record's class or its mesh (C67); the hosts' flags (C65); the capture's check, a capture drawn for a caller only when the caller's policy makes every decision in the scene's table, checked before the first frame and after the last is recorded (C66). The renderer's own nodes built from several meshes (far tiles, offered far forms, baked impostors) are built only from meshes the load admitted, since a replaced slot is a box by then.

## Materials

**An imported asset's own vertex streams** (roadmap G2, 2026-11-18; [gfx](gfx.md), "The author's tangent frame"; [assets](assets.md#what-g2-reads)). A mesh whose source stated tangents, a second UV set or colours carries `ClusterMesh::extra`, and the scene's merge keeps it parallel to the vertices, so `GpuScene` uploads it once as `extra` (12 bytes a scene vertex, `extra_vertices` of them) beside the attributes, and the resolve and the reference path tracer read the author's tangent frame from it. A scene none of whose meshes carries a stream uploads nothing and draws the bytes it drew; a streamed scene (pages) and a tile's mesh in the mesh room upload none yet (R204), and a terrain ring's slot vertices lie past the stream and read "none" — all of them draw the frame derived from the UVs, which since R202 has the author's handedness ([one tangent-space convention](../experiments/tangent-space-convention.md)), so the same asset shows the same relief whichever way it arrived. `renderer: an imported tangent frame draws the same picture on every raster path` (`imported_streams_tests.cpp`) holds the vertex, mesh and ray paths to one picture on a glTF quad written in the test, and `renderer: an asset draws one relief whether its tangents reach the scene or not` a curved patch loaded whole and streamed to 2 codes (measured 1). The ground's layers read their maps through fixed frames of the same handedness (`terrain_material.slang`: the bitangent -z on the ground, -y on a side), and `renderer: one normal map lights the same flank on a mesh and on the ground` holds a mesh and the ground under one map and one light to the same relief.

### Native authored terrain materials

`Terrain.materials` (scene schema version 8, W68) optionally puts authored layers on the native
heightfield, rings and world tiles. It adds no second floor and changes no height or collision.
Layers composite in array order over the existing ground palette, using `weight` times the
optional mask's R channel. Masks are linear, clamped in the scene terrain's map frame. A layer
may be colour factors alone or name base colour (sRGB), an OpenGL (+Y) tangent-space normal,
and linear roughness read from R. Image paths resolve against the scene file. Missing images,
invalid numbers, empty layers and a count exceeding the scene's `layer_budget` are refused.
`materials` and the legacy sand `detail` block are alternative surface-detail paths; naming both
is refused, so an authored block never silently disables requested sand ripples — unless a layer
is wind sand, which draws the ripples over its own share (R99, "Sand and snow" below).

```json
"materials": {
  "layer_budget": 4, "detail_near_m": 32, "detail_far_m": 128,
  "layers": [
    {"name": "painted landscape", "projection": "Map", "base_color": "ground.png"},
    {"name": "rock detail", "projection": "Triplanar", "tile_m": 1.5,
     "base_color": "rock.png", "normal": "rock-normal.png", "roughness": "rock-rough.png",
     "mask": "rock-coverage.png"}
  ]
}
```

`Map` preserves finite landscape paintings. `Triplanar` repeats at `tile_m` (rounded to whole
millimetres), blends the axis projections by the fourth power of the surface normal's absolute
components, and projects each normal map's slopes into the surface tangent plane. A flat normal
map preserves the input normal on every slope. Phase comes from integer world cells and the
frame-local point; map coordinates also come from that point, avoiding chunk-dependent half-UV
rounding at tile/LOD boundaries. A tiled layer's normals and fine colour/roughness fade across the
authored near/far eye distances to the layer's linear texel means (with a normal-variance chain only
its colour and height do: "Normal filtering", below); a stochastic layer does not
fade (below). `Map` retains its painting, filtered by the existing texture mips. These are content
settings, not geological altitude rules.

#### A layer's far colour

`TerrainMaterialLayer.far_color` (scene schema, layer version 6; G141) is a tiled triplanar layer's
colour past `detail_far_m`, linear RGB in [0, 1]: what its detail fades to in place of the image's
mean, for a layer that stands in for something it does not draw. It rides the container's transport
of the mean (`terrain_materials.cpp`), so the resolve reads it where it read the mean and nothing in
the resolve changed: no shader, no GPU-mirrored struct, no millisecond. **A layer without it draws
what it drew, to the bit** (the field is left out of the layer's JSON, so no scene's cache key
moves); a layer with it is keyed apart. A `Map` or stochastic layer naming one is refused, since
neither fades to its mean. The sward's ground uses it: the image is the floor under the drawn blades
near the eye, `far_color` the real canopy past the sward's reach, and the fade the terrain already
draws over `detail_near_m`..`detail_far_m` is the blend between them
([flora](flora.md#the-ground-under-the-sward-g141), "Near and far").

#### Stochastic sampling

A triplanar layer may name `"sampling": "Stochastic"` (R96, scene schema `TerrainMaterialLayer`
version 3; the default `Tiled` draws every scene before it byte for byte and keeps its cache key).
Each projection then reads its maps at three tiles of a triangle lattice, each tile at its own
random offset, blends them by Burley's exponentiated weights (power 7) and Heitz and Neyret's
variance-preserving operator — `mean + (Σ wᵢ (xᵢ − mean)) / √(Σ wᵢ²)` — applied to the texels
themselves, and saturates the result. **Every map takes the same three places and the same
weights**, so colour, roughness, height and normal stay coordinated; colour, roughness and height
blend about the layer's own means (colour and roughness as before; the height map's mean is carried
in the layer's container entry and moved by upload to `uv_offset.w`), the normal map's slopes
about zero, the mean slope of any tileable height field. The method, the four papers it is drawn
from and the numbers it was chosen by are in
[stochastic terrain sampling](../experiments/stochastic-terrain-sampling-2026-10-26.md); it needs
no lookup table, no second texture and no container section, and adds no texture residency.

- **No fade.** The lattice leaves no repeat for distance to reveal, so a stochastic layer keeps
  its detail to the horizon: far pixels read the lattice at the mip their footprint selects
  (`SampleGrad` with the pixel's own UV derivatives, turned with the tile, never the derivatives of
  the jittered UV), and `detail_near_m`/`detail_far_m` apply to tiled layers only. Past the
  distance where a pixel covers a whole repeat the mip is the image's average, and the ground is
  the mean colour there as before.
- **Anchored in integers.** The lattice is Deliot and Heitz's skew with 2√3 replaced by 97/28 so
  that a lattice point's integer part comes from the frame's integer cell in 64-bit integers and
  only the frame-local rest is a float (ADR-0053); the tile hash is integer-only. Every tile, ring,
  far level, cut and eye cell that draws a point reads the same three tiles. The lattice and the
  operator live in `hex_lattice.slang` since R131, shared with the mesh materials ("Stochastic mesh
  materials", below).
- **Direction.** `rotation_deg` (0 to 180, default 0) turns each tile by a hashed angle up to that
  bound, and its normal map's stored slope pair by the same rotation (the map's y is the image's up,
  opposite the UV's v, so in the stored frame the turn is R itself). With 0 nothing turns, so
  strata, a road's ruts or a directed needle bed keep their direction; a texture with a direction
  should keep 0 or stay tiled. A `Map` layer cannot be stochastic, and a turn on a tiled layer is
  refused.
- **Cost.** Three reads per map per projection where tiling makes one, but the stochastic branch
  skips a projection whose share is under 1/128 and renormalizes the rest: flat and gently sloped
  ground reads one projection, nine reads per layer (colour, metallic-roughness with height, normal
  at three tiles) — the nine a tiled layer makes reading all three projections; a 45° slope reads
  18 and a three-way corner 27. Past `detail_far_m` a tiled layer reads nothing (it is its mean),
  so on far ground a stochastic layer is 9–27 reads per layer where there were none: on the forest
  the resolve rose 0.2–0.7 ms at 2560×1440 and 1.7–2.3 ms at 11520×2160 with every layer
  stochastic (a loaded machine; upper bounds), and texture residency did not change. Since R136 a
  tile under 1/128 of the blend is not read ("What a far pixel reads", below): about a third
  fewer tile reads over a cell, a fifth of the resolve on the v31 fell.
- **What holds it.** `gfx: terrain material phases …` checks the GPU's lattice, weights, shifts,
  turns and blend against the double mirror in `domain/gfx/tests/terrain_hex_reference.h` at an eye
  100,000 km out (worst 9 × 10⁻⁶); the CPU cases on the mirror check the statistics (mean to 0.005,
  variance to 4%, histogram distance below the linear blends'), a directed texture's direction
  without a turn and the normals' turn against finite differences; `world tiles: a stochastic
  layer is one function of the world point …` renders albedo across rings, cuts and two eye cells
  and finds every pixel within 0.26 codes on average of the reference's read at its world point;
  `renderer: a stochastic layer shades the same ground in the resolve and the path tracer` holds
  the three readers together by FLIP.

#### What a far pixel reads

R136 (2026-11-07; [the measurement](../experiments/terrain-resolve-2026-11-07.md)) cuts a
stochastic layer's reads where the pixel cannot tell the difference. Five rules are written in
`terrain_material.slang` and selected at compile time by `TERRAIN_FOOTPRINT_LEVERS` (a bit each);
**the engine ships with one, tiles by weight**, because it is the one that paid:

- **Tiles by weight** (bit 16, on). Burley's power-7 weights leave a tile under 1/128 of the blend
  over about half of every cell (its barycentric under half the largest's, and 0.5⁷ = 1/128),
  where it moves the pixel by under 1/128 of its departure from the layer's mean — under a code
  step. A weight under 1/256 is dropped and the tile not read, one between 1/256 and 1/128 ramps
  to its own, and the kept weights are renormalized with the variance-preserving gain taken from
  them (`terrain_hex_kept`), so the blend stays the operator over the tiles it reads; a hex whose
  every weight is 1/128 or more is returned bit for bit. Every map of the tile goes together, so
  the maps stay coordinated. On the v31 fell it returns a fifth of the resolve (1.60 → 1.28 ms at
  1920×1080, 14.26 → 11.66 at 11520×2160) and changes 1.8–3.2% of the pixels, FLIP 0.0012–0.0018;
  on the v25 walk at the owner's width the resolve goes 13.73 → 12.73 ms. It acts on the near
  ground too, so it is a shading rule, not a culling one, and a sun glint can move by more than a
  code where a dropped tile's slope turned it (1,099 pixels of 24.9 million over eight codes at
  11520; a tighter band is the first thing to try if one is seen to flicker).
- **The four footprint rules** (bits 1, 2, 4, 8; built, tested, **off**): past a lattice cell a
  pixel (sqrt |du × dv| against the cell, 28/97 of a repeat) one tile, the nearest, instead of
  three, with a band from one cell to two; past a repeat's filter width (the larger of the
  footprint's minor axis and its major over the anisotropy's 16) the maps' means instead of the
  colour, metallic-roughness and normal reads, a band from half a repeat to one; the projection
  floor rising from 1/128 to a band of 1/32–1/16 past a cell; a mask layer under 1/128 of the
  pixel skipped past a cell of it (its coverage still counted). Each is exactly off under a cell,
  so with them the near ground draws its bytes. **They do not pay at these footprints**: on the
  fell at 1920×1080 they act on 0.47% of the pixels (the far mountain) and the branches and
  registers they add cost the whole frame 0.44 ms; the owner's width only has smaller footprints.
  A view whose far ground is most of the frame (a summit's horizon) is where to try them again.
- **What a far pixel reads**, then: what a near one does — the kept tiles of each kept projection,
  colour, metallic-roughness with height, the normal and its variance chain — with tiles by weight
  reading 1.5–2 tiles of 3 over most of a cell instead of 3.
- **What holds it.** `gfx: a stochastic tile under 1/128 of the blend is ramped out, the rest
  untouched` (the rule against its double mirror over a cell, bit for bit where it does not act);
  `gfx: the far terrain's read rules are bands, and exactly off under a cell` (the footprint rules'
  ramps and the projection band across a plane tilted a hundredth of a degree at a time: no share
  moves by more than 3.5 × 10⁻⁴ a step, where the near rule's step is 1/128);
  `renderer: the ground reads fewer tiles where a pixel cannot tell, within the bound` (a plane to
  the horizon drawn by the engine's module and by the footprint rules beside a module with every
  read made, loaded through a shader manifest: the near ground's bytes under the footprint rules,
  FLIP under 0.005 for both, and a frame drawn again the same bytes).

#### Normal filtering (R97)

A pixel's footprint averages the normals a normal map holds; the mip of a normal map is their
mean, renormalized, so far ground used to shade as if it were smoother than it is — a sheen that
grows with distance — and the old answer was to fade the normal to flat past `detail_far_m`, which
loses the bumps outright. **A built normal map now carries what the footprint stops resolving**: its
normal-variance chain (texture.md, "Normal variance"), read with the map's own sampler and
derivatives, becomes a slope variance `v = s²(1 − L)/L` (Toksvig; `s` the normal strength) that
widens the GGX lobe, `α′² = min(1, α² + 2v + g)`, where `g` is Tokuyoshi and Kaplanyan's bounded
projected-space kernel over the hit triangle's own normal derivatives (`screen_geometric_alpha2`,
from `screen_barycentrics`, never a neighbouring pixel's). The final roughness feeds the GGX
distribution and Smith's visibility alike (`brdf_filter_roughness` in `brdf.slang`;
`brdf_reference.h` mirrors it in double). Sources, the fit and its error are in
[normal filtering](../experiments/normal-filtering.md).

- **On terrain.** A tiled layer with a chain no longer fades its normal or its roughness at the
  detail distances — the chain does what the fade stood in for — and keeps the colour and height
  fade (`terrain_filter_sample`). A stochastic layer (R96) never faded; its three tiles are read
  unwidened and the widening applied once to their blend, the tiles' shortening a plain weighted
  mean. Layers combine after the fetch as a mixture: the weighted `r⁴` plus the variance between
  their mean slopes (`terrain_filter_combination`). The fit is isotropic: no anisotropic lobe, no
  covariance between triplanar projections.
- **What reads it.** The resolve's grad path (`sample_material_grad`, the terrain layers). The
  reference path tracer reads level zero, whose variance is zero: its jittered rays integrate the
  footprint themselves, which is why it is the truth the filter is held to.
- **The switch.** `renderer.material.normal_filter` (true since 2026-10-27), read once when a
  scene's materials are uploaded: false uploads no chain and sets no flag, and every material draws
  the bytes it drew before R97. A material without a chain — a decoded texture, an unmipped map, an
  older `.tex` — always draws them. The report's `textures.normal_variance` and
  `normal_variance_bytes` say how many chains a scene took and what they cost.
- **What holds it.** `renderer: normal filtering holds a grazing normal-mapped plane to its
  converged picture` (a bumped plane at 1, 4 and 16 m against the path tracer: RMSE 12%, 54% and 58%
  lower than unfiltered, the picture's light within 7% where unfiltered is 10–15% over);
  `gfx: normal filtering agrees with the double reference` (2 × 10⁻⁶); `gfx: variance footprint is
  monotone and continuous between texture mips`; `gfx: filtered GGX is closer to an 8 by 8
  normal-plane reference`.

The diagnostic views `sun-specular` and `sun-specular-legacy` (`gfx::ResolveMode` 11 and 12) are
R97's measurement entry points and return linear data: R is the shadowed sun-specular radiance
luminance of native ground before aerial scattering and exposure, G is 1 on ground and 0
elsewhere, B is roughness. Capture with `--present-format linear --capture probe.exr` and average
R where G is 1. The legacy view clears the variance flag in the shader on the same geometry and
textures, so it is the old normal and roughness fades; with the switch off the plain view is the
same answer. They change no shadow algorithm and exclude water, other meshes and sky from the
mask. Measurement views, not display colours.

The normal resolve, ray-shadow resolve and reference path tracer share `terrain_material.slang`.
The water volume tier evaluates it at the analytic bottom hit too; this does not add submerged
scene objects or reflections. Separate `_terrain` modules are selected only for scenes that
name layers. `ResolveMaterial` remains 112 bytes. **The root is an ordinary material plus its flag
and one word** (2026-10-24): `uv_offset.z` names the terrain's **record** (`gfx::TerrainRecord`,
`gfx::set_terrain_root`), a table entry after the layers that no cluster names, holding the
layers' range, the detail distances, the map frame and the mask level's addressing under names.
Until then (W68) the root bit-cast the layers' range into `uv_offset.zw` and kept the near/far
distances in its `normal_scale` and `occlusion_strength`, so any reader not gated on
`k_material_terrain_layers` — an occlusion view, a normal map on the root — read distances as a
material's; now only an alpha-tested material reads `uv_offset.z`, and a root is refused as one.
Each layer adds one table entry with ordinary texture slots, its terrain fields set and read by
name (`gfx::set_terrain_layer`, `terrain_layer_*` in the shader): its occlusion slot carries
coverage and is never applied as ambient occlusion; cold containers transport the decoded
colour/roughness means in the unreferenced layer materials' emissive and metallic factors (and a
stochastic layer's height mean in its alpha cutoff), and upload moves them into the layer's
otherwise-unused UV transform (the height mean and the turn into `uv_offset.zw`). `tools/lint.ps1`
(`terrain-ungated`) holds every shader call of `sample_terrain_material` behind the root's flag.
The map frame's offset is converted to float exactly to 17,000 km (split at whole 1,024 mm past
16.7 km from the map's corner, where a float no longer holds the millimetre; W68's arithmetic,
operation for operation, within it).

Sources and choices, costs and validation: [native terrain materials](../experiments/native-terrain-materials.md).
`terrain_materials.h` provides validation, source-image preparation and content hashing; every
image's bytes enter the terrain cache key, independent of its directory. Textures use the existing
embedded-image build, compression, mip and sharing path. Per-tile material-page streaming is the
remaining W25 work; this surface contract makes no claim of bounded texture residency for an
arbitrarily large coverage image.
Changing a layer or image currently rebuilds the grid's cached container too; geometry and material
cache identities are not split. A streamed terrain keeps that grid as its small material carrier.

### Stochastic mesh materials

**A mesh material may place its texels stochastically** (R131, 2026-11-04; the forest proof of
concept's v29 hand-off: a generated cliff repeated its one 1.8 m PBR set across 40 m of face, and
"enlarging the same small PBR to mountain scale is not the solution"). `gfx::k_material_stochastic`
on a `ResolveMaterial` makes every map of it — base colour, metallic-roughness, normal, occlusion,
emissive — read at three tiles of the terrain's lattice ("Stochastic sampling", above) **in the
material's own UV plane** (the mesh's UVs after the material's transform, in repeats: no
triplanar, no world position), each tile at its own hashed offset, with the UV derivatives turned
with the tile and `SampleGrad` at the footprint's level, and blends them by the same
variance-preserving operator: colour and roughness about the material's means, the normal map's
slope pairs about zero, metallic, emissive and occlusion as the tiles' weighted mean (no mean is
carried for them; a rock's metallic is a constant 0, and a widened occlusion would darken where the
tiles part). With a normal-variance chain the tiles' roughness is read unwidened and the widening
applied once to the blend, as the terrain does (R97). **Offsets only**: a mesh material takes no
turn, so a bedded or streaked set keeps its direction. The lattice is a function of the UV alone, so
every frame, view, cut and eye cell reads the same tiles.

- **One lattice, shared.** The hash, the tiles (`hex_tiles`, Burley's weights at power 7, Heitz and
  Neyret's gain) and the operator (`hex_blend`) moved from `terrain_material.slang` into
  `domain/gfx/shaders/hex_lattice.slang`, without changing an operation; the terrain keeps its
  names (`terrain_hash`, `TerrainHex`, `terrain_hex`, `terrain_hex_blend`) as wrappers, takes the
  skewed point's integer part from the frame's cell in 64-bit integers as before and hands the
  shared code its low 32 bits (all the hash reads), and every terrain test passes unchanged. A
  mesh's skewed UV is split into its floor and fraction in floats: its UVs are a few hundred
  repeats at most. `engine_shaders()` walks the include graph itself, so no `DEPENDS` names it.
- **Only a scene that has one pays for it.** The stochastic path is compiled only into modules that
  define `MATERIAL_STOCHASTIC`: eight `visibility_resolve*_stochastic.slang` wrappers, one per
  combination of shadow rays, water and terrain, and the reference path tracer, which always has it.
  Without the define `material.slang`'s reads keep their pre-R131 names and bodies and the
  dispatch does not exist, so the four plain modules without terrain materials compile to the bytes
  they did at efe7e9c5 (compared after an `msvc-release` build); the four terrain ones differ only by
  the lattice's move into `hex_lattice.slang`, the same operations. `GpuScene::has_stochastic_materials` is set at upload when a material row
  carries the flag, and `resolve_module` picks the `_stochastic` module from it, as it picks the
  water and terrain ones. The first build had the dispatch in every resolve: the frame budgets'
  `endless-surround3-rt`, which has no stochastic material, went from 2.11 to 2.24 ms of resolve
  (registers, not reads); the numbers are on the [experiments
  page](../experiments/stochastic-mesh-materials-2026-11-04.md#the-plain-kernel-the-frame-budgets-follow-up).- **The means.** `uv_offset.z`'s bits hold four bytes, the square roots of the linear mean colour's
  r, g, b and of the mean roughness, factors included (`gfx::set_stochastic`,
  `pack_stochastic_means`; the root spends the eight bits where a dark rock's colour is: a step of
  under 0.4% of 0.05). The upload makes them from the **built** textures: the first level of at most
  16 × 16 texels of the base colour and metallic-roughness `.tex`, decoded as the GPU samples it,
  sRGB to linear, averaged (`built_texture_mean` in `gpu_scene.cpp`) — the chain is filtered in
  linear light by a normalized kernel, so that is the image's mean to within the kernel's and the
  block coding's rounding, at the cost of decoding 256 texels. A texture shared with an earlier mesh
  carries its mean with its slot.
- **What refuses it.** `uv_offset.z` is an alpha-tested material's cutoff, a water material's and a
  terrain root's word, so `set_stochastic` refuses all three (and `set_alpha_mask` clears the flag,
  in either order), the shader reads a row carrying both as plain, and the upload draws plain —
  with a warning naming the mesh and the material — a material whose textures are decoded rather
  than built (no small mips to take the means from, no gradients for the tiles) or that belongs to
  the terrain mesh, whose layers have their own stochastic path.
- **Where it comes from.** A material set's `sampling` key (a pack role's `"sampling":
  "stochastic"`, a rock recipe's `material.sampling`; [materials](materials.md)) becomes
  `geometry::k_material_sampling_stochastic` in the container's material sampling record (section
  33's `flags` word, what was its `pad`, so every older container reads plain), which
  `adopt_container` keeps in `SourceMesh::material_sampling_flags` and the upload turns into the
  bit. A glTF material has no way to say it, and no scene-level override exists yet. The upload logs
  `stochastic materials` with the count when any are drawn.
- **The reference path tracer** reads materials through the same `sample_material` and
  `apply_normal_map`, which dispatch on the flag, so a stochastic material reads the same three tiles
  there, at level 0 as every material does in it.
- **Cost.** Three reads per map where tiling makes one — colour, metallic-roughness, normal (and
  the variance chain and occlusion where the material has them) — and the lattice's ALU, three
  times per pixel (the material, the normal map and the occlusion each compute it). On the v29 ledge
  repro at 1920 × 1080 the resolve rose 0.02–0.03 ms (+3%) with a third of the picture on the cliff
  and 0.09 ms (+17%) with three quarters, about 0.06 ns a stochastic pixel (a shared machine; upper
  bounds), and texture residency did not change: [stochastic mesh
  materials](../experiments/stochastic-mesh-materials-2026-11-04.md).
- **What holds it.** `material resolve: stochastic mesh materials keep the mean and lose the repeat`
  (`domain/gfx/tests/stochastic_material_tests.cpp`) draws a noise texture over eight repeats plain
  and stochastic: the stochastic albedo's mean within 1% of the plain picture's per channel, its
  deviation above 0.8 of the plain one's (contrast held), more than half the pixels different, two
  frames byte-identical, and an alpha-tested row carrying the bit drawn as the plain alpha-tested
  row; the helper's refusals and the means' packing on the CPU.

### Ground materials by place

**A palette, per-tile selection and authored regions** (roadmap W72, 2026-10-24; the grounding:
[ground materials](../experiments/ground-materials-grounding.md); the level's format:
