[tileset](tileset.md#the-mask-level)). With a `masks` block (`engine.scene.TerrainMasks`, `Terrain`
version 9) the terrain's `materials.layers` are a **palette** of any number of substrates (up to
254) and `layer_budget` is the **per-tile** budget, 1 to 4: each 32 m tile of the mask level names
at most that many palette layers and carries their weights at every metre, so a 10 km world has
fifteen substrates and a tile four. The `tiles` provider builds the level beside its set on first
ask (`scene_gen::GroundOps::masks`), the renderer uploads it whole at scene load
(`prepare_terrain_masks`: a page table over the level's tiles, then every tile's words) and names
its address in the record; a terrain without masks draws exactly as before.

```json
"masks": {
  "spacing_mm": 1000, "tile_cells": 32, "height_blend": 0.2, "wetness": 0,
  "priors": {"soil": "soil", "scree": "scree", "bedrock": "bedrock", "snow": "snow",
             "snowline_m": 150, "snow_aspect_m": 25},
  "paint": [{"material": "moss", "image": "moss-weight.png"}],
  "index": {"image": "zones.png", "materials": ["trail", "clearing_grass"]},
  "regions": [
    {"name": "alpine", "center": [179, 0, -179], "radius_m": 250, "base": "alpine_meadow"},
    {"name": "sandy pond", "water_body": "sandy-pond", "bed": "sand", "margin": "gravel",
     "margin_m": 3, "wet_m": 8}
  ]
}
```

**The authoring**: generated priors (soil, scree, bedrock, snow by slope, elevation and aspect)
under painted weight maps under the index map under the regions, each laid over the last; a
region gives a layer outright (`material`), stands in for the priors' soil (`base`), or, for a
scene water body named by `water_body`, gives its own `bed` and `margin` and wets the ground out
to `wet_m` — so two ponds at one height have different beds. `engine-content terrain-masks
--write-priors` writes the priors as images an author edits and paints back. Refusals, each a
sentence: masks without materials or without a tile set, a budget outside 1 to 4, a name the
palette lacks, a region with no outline or two, `material` beside `base`, a water body the scene
does not have, and **a tile whose points name more layers than the budget** (named, with its place
and its layers) — never a silent drop, which would show on one side of a seam only.

**The resolve** (`terrain_material.slang`, every path: the resolve, the ray-shadow resolve, the
reference path tracer and the water's bottom): the point's mask tile from the frame's integer cell
and its local millimetres — never a world float — its table, and its four weights filtered across
the two mips the pixel's ground footprint selects (the path tracer reads mip 0, as its texture
reads take level 0); each named layer is evaluated as W68 evaluates one (map or triplanar at its
own `tile_m`, faded to its means past the detail distances), the four are blended by weight, or by
**height** where a palette layer names a `height` map (its R carried in the metallic-roughness
map's B; Mishkinis' blend at `height_blend`, linear without one), and the blend is laid over the
ground palette by the weights' sum. **Wetness** is a separate scalar — the larger of the scene's
`wetness` and the mask's (a water region's `wet_m`) — that darkens the substrate by
`lerp(1, 0.2, porosity)` and multiplies its roughness by half that factor (Lagarde 2013), so wet
sand turns dark and a little smoother and wet rock barely changes; nothing turns glossy dry.
The sampler skips a layer only where its filtered weight is exactly 0; the bilinear weights leave
small shares across every transition, and R136's layer rule (a stochastic layer under 1/128 of
the pixel not read past a cell of it, its coverage still counted, so the root never shows) is
built but compiled off, with the other footprint rules ("What a far pixel reads", above).

**Why identity survives the levels.** The material is a function of the point and the pixel's
footprint alone: every geometry level, tile, chunk and cut that draws a point reads the same mask
tile at the same place, so a tile boundary or a level handover changes no material; a seam is
continuous because the two tiles hold the same edge points (tileset.md, "The mask level"), and the
mips' edge points are filtered along the edge alone so that holds at every mip.

**Costs** (`msvc-debug`, RTX 5090, 1600 × 900, the ground-by-place camera path, terrain tiles and
two far levels; machine state in [the costs](../experiments/native-terrain-materials.md#ground-materials-by-place-costs)):
the resolve's median per frame against the plain palette, and the level's bytes, are in that
section. The level is held whole (`resident_mib`, 256 by default, refused above): the 1 km test
scene is 1,089 tiles and 8.2 MB, 7.5 KB a 32 m tile; streaming it with the terrain's tiles is
W25's remainder.

**Sand and snow: a response per layer** (roadmap R99, 2026-11-02; the research and the numbers:
[sand and snow](../experiments/sand-and-snow-substrates-2026-11-02.md)). A palette layer may name a
`response` (`engine.scene.TerrainMaterialLayer` version 4, `Terrain` version 10) — `Default`, the
layer as its maps and colour draw it, to the bit; `Sand`; or `Snow` — with its block of numbers,
each defaulted from the page:

```json
{"name": "snow", "response": "Snow", "roughness_factor": 0.8,
 "snow": {"grain_mm": 0.25, "lobe": 1, "glints": 0.5, "thickness": 0.7}},
{"name": "beach_sand", "tint": [0.62, 0.55, 0.42], "porosity": 0.9, "response": "Sand",
 "sand": {"kind": "Beach", "wet_darkening": 1, "glints": 0.15}}
```

- **Snow** needs no maps. Its albedo is its grain's — Kokhanovsky's spherical albedo
  `exp(-sqrt(4πχ/λ · 16 d))` over Warren and Brandt's ice at 610, 550 and 465 nm, 0.977, 0.986,
  0.996 at the default 0.25 mm and bluer as the grain coarsens — times the layer's `tint` (an old
  snow's soot and dust) and, where the layer has a colour map, the map over its mean. `lobe` weighs
  the specular lobe in multiples of the dielectric F0 0.04, carried exactly through the metallic word
  with the diffuse kept (1, the default, is metallic 0: the visible's measured near-Lambertian snow
  at roughness 0.8). `thickness` is the snow's height in the height blend (a layer without a height
  map stands at 0.5), so snow lies on litter and soil and high rock shows through it.
- **Sand** of `kind` `Wind` draws the scene's `detail` block — W42's ripples and grain,
  [The sand close up](#the-sand-close-up) — over the wind-sand layers' blended share, which
  `sample_terrain_material` returns as the detail share the resolve already weights the detail by;
  a palette with a wind-sand layer is the one that may name `detail` beside `materials` (any other
  is still refused), and only its root keeps `k_material_ground_detail`. `Beach` draws no ripples
  and darkens where wet by Lekner and Dorf instead of by porosity: per channel, `0.4909 / (1 -
  0.4744 a)` of its dry albedo `a` at saturation, scaled by the place's wetness and by
  `wet_darkening`, so wet sand turns darker and more saturated (0.6 of a 0.4 sand, where porosity
  0.9 gave 0.28), and its roughness loses half that factor.
- **Glints**, both: the ground is cut into world-anchored cells of power-of-two millimetres (from
  the frame's integer cell, never a world float), at **two levels about the footprint**, the finer
  `floor(log2 footprint)` and the one above it (R125); each level's cell hash decides whether it
  holds a facet, the pixel's chance `p = glints × min(1, 4 mm / footprint)` split between them by
  the footprint's fractional log so that either drawing has chance p exactly, the finer facet
  winning where both draw, none past a 256 mm footprint. A curve of equal footprint (a screen row on
  flat ground) therefore never re-draws the facets: one level that doubled its cell there drew them
  in bands ([sand and snow](../experiments/sand-and-snow-substrates-2026-11-02.md#glints)). A facet replaces the layer's slope with its own normal,
  drawn from GGX of alpha 0.15 and turned at most 25° (a facet turned further would speckle the
  diffuse: it replaces the pixel's one normal), and its roughness with 0.1. The resolve's own GGX lights
  it for every light and shadows it as the pixel, so a facet flashes where sun, facet and eye line
  up and twinkles as the eye moves. The path tracer has no footprint and draws none.

**The composition.** Each layer's response is applied where the layer is sampled, once per layer on
its record's `flags` (`k_material_terrain_snow`, `_sand`, `_beach`), never per texel; the layers then
blend by their weights and the height blend exactly as before, so a response is weighted by its
layer's coverage at the pixel, faded with its maps by the footprint, and shared by every reader of
`sample_terrain_material` — the resolve, the ray-shadow resolve, the water's bottom and the path
tracer. The response's numbers ride in the layer entry's emissive rgb and, for snow, its occlusion
strength (`gfx::set_terrain_layer`): words a layer never read, so no record grows. A palette whose
layers all say `Default` writes none of them and sets no bit, and every added operation in the
shader sits behind an `any_snow`/`any_beach`/`any_wind` that such a palette never sets, so it
draws its bytes; the response is also left out of the container's key, so no scene rebuilds. How
many layers a tile may give a response is the per-tile budget's: any of its four. Not built (the
page's remainder): a wrap or forward lobe shaped otherwise than GGX's, which need the light and so
the resolve; the beach's swash marks and rills. **Measured** (the page): the test scene's old palette,
all Default, draws 0 changed pixels of 2,073,600 at every pose after the change, and the material
stage's median (`renderer.resolve.stop_after=material`) stays within the shared machine's noise,
0.41–0.44 ms at 1080p with or without the change and 0.29 ms with the responses.
**What a material table entry carries** (`gfx::ResolveMaterial`, 112 bytes; [gfx](gfx.md), "The
material table"): the factors, five texture slots — base colour, metallic-roughness, normal,
occlusion, emissive — a bindless sampler per slot, the occlusion strength, and one UV transform.
`upload_materials` fills it from `assets::Material`, which the glTF import or a container's
section 33 filled ([texture](texture.md#samplers-and-texture-transforms)).

**Samplers, one per combination.** A slot with a texture asks for the sampler its glTF texture
names — wrap s and t, the three filters — built (the whole chain, 16x anisotropic where the
minification is linear) or decoded (level 0 alone), and `upload_materials` makes one bindless
sampler per distinct combination the scene asks for, shared by every material after the first that
asked (`GpuScene::material_samplers()`, logged as `material samplers`) — keyed by that description,
as the textures are keyed by their content ([One upload per distinct image](#one-upload-per-distinct-image)),
so a kit whose members all ask for the glTF default draws through one. A slot with no texture asks
for none and borrows the base colour's slot word, which it never reads. The classic heightfield keeps
its own clamped tooling sampler, uncounted. Every sample in `content/samples` names the glTF default
sampler or none, so each of them draws through **one** material sampler.

**The UV transform is one per material** — the base colour's, or the first textured slot's — and a
material whose other textured slots ask for a different one is counted
(`GpuScene::transform_conflicts()`) and logged with a warning; it draws every slot with the one kept.
The container keeps them per slot, so carrying more is a table change and not a rebuild.

**The water class** (`gfx::k_material_water`, [water](water.md); 2026-10-17). A mesh the scene's `water` block made carries its body on its info (`SceneMeshInfo::water`, `SceneWater`: the block as the file gave it and the shading numbers the reader resolved — colours with their defaults, the waves' direction from the ground's wind or the block's own), and `upload_materials` packs those numbers into the mesh's one material with `gfx::set_water_material`: the colours, the fade, the waves, the shore and the seed in slots an untextured material with no UV transform never reads, and the flag the resolve branches on. Every reader that is not the resolve's water branch draws it as an untextured dielectric of the shallow colour. The mesh's UVs are data — x the distance from the edge, y the depth under the vertex — which is why the class keeps the UV scale at 1 and the transform off. **At `water_quality` high** (the default, 2026-10-18; [water](water.md#translucent-by-volume)) each body also takes the entry after its material — its optics, `gfx::set_water_optics`: extinction, scattering, transmission, and the terrain's material index with the body's centre in that material's UV frame, computed in f64 from the instance — and `gfx::k_material_water_volume` on the material, which the water modules read to see the ground through the surface; and each body with a **depth map** (`SceneWater::depth`, read from beside its GLB; [water](water.md#the-depth-map), 2026-10-19) is uploaded as an RGBA8 image the same entry names (`gfx::set_water_depth_map`, `k_material_water_depth_map`) at either tier, so at low a body with a map has that entry too, holding the map alone.

**The resolve draws water with modules of its own** (2026-10-18). `visibility_resolve_water` and `visibility_resolve_rt_water` are `visibility_resolve.slang` compiled with `RESOLVE_WATER` — the plain and the ray-traced resolve, each with the water branch — and the renderer makes its resolve pipelines (the frame's, and the frame passes' linear one) from them only when `GpuScene::has_water()` says a material of the table is the water class (`resolve_module` in `scene_renderer.cpp`; the table is uploaded once, so the choice is made once a scene, and again only on a shader reload). A scene without water draws with the plain modules, which have no water branch, draw a water material as the untextured dielectric every other reader draws, and compile to the SPIR-V the resolve was before water existed (SHA-256 `AD0A0386…` plain, `5C77B086…` rays, measured against `main`). Why: a fragment shader's registers are allocated for its largest path whether a pixel takes it or not, and the branch compiled into every resolve took `gpu_ms.resolve` on `erg-walk-surround3-rt` from 2.316 to 2.793 ms median with no water on screen, failing the frame budgets in that pass alone ([water](water.md#shading)).

**Emission** is the factor times the emissive texture, added after the lighting in the resolve and
wherever a ray lands in the reference. Before 2026-09-24 a material with an emissive texture drew
with no emission, because the resolve had no slot for the texture — which is what the Lantern's
glass did in both pictures, and what `thin-geometry`'s FLIP band was set against. **v1 treats
emission as radiance only** in the reference: seen directly and by bounce rays, never sampled as a
light ([texture](texture.md#emissive)).

**What it cost and what it changed** ([texture](texture.md#what-the-samplers-emission-and-occlusion-cost)):
the resolve 2–5% slower on the FlightHelmet at 1080p and 4K, about half of it the occlusion;
against the reference, `flighthelmet` from 0.0190 to 0.0172 FLIP and `thin-geometry` from 0.0051 to
0.0048 — both towards it — and every other scene of the corpus where it was.

**Occlusion** multiplies the resolve's indirect term — the hemisphere of sky and ground today,
[below](#the-sky-above-the-ground-below) — and nothing else,
and is never applied in the reference, which traces that visibility. `--view occlusion`
(`ResolveMode::Occlusion`, `render.load`'s `"view":"occlusion"`) shows the value unencoded beside
`--view albedo`: a captured byte is the occlusion times 255 ([texture](texture.md#occlusion)).

**What it measured** on the FlightHelmet (RTX 5090, `msvc-release`, 600 frames windowed at three
orbit distances and two resolutions; the table and the machine's state are in
[texture](texture.md#what-it-measured)): the fifteen images take **71.3 MB** of device memory built,
every level included, against **213.9 MB** decoded at one level; the resolve moved by no more than
3% against the parent commit either way (2–3% slower up close for the derivative pass, 3% faster
far away at 4K); and the decoded path's capture is byte-identical to the parent commit's.

### Formation bands

**A world formation drawn as a band layer** (roadmap W85, 2026-11-05; the grounding:
[formation field](../experiments/formation-field.md); the cliffs' side:
[rocks](rocks.md#geology-on-the-world-formation-w85)). A scene's `formation`
(`engine.scene.Formation`, `Scene` version 10) is one set of beds through the world: an origin, a
dip and an azimuth (rocks' convention: the beds go down along (cos az, 0, sin az)), up to two
cylindrical folds — the beds displaced along their normal by A sin(2π u / L), u the distance along
the dip direction, so the hinges run along the strike — a **bed sequence** of up to 512 beds
(each a thickness, a tint, a roughness offset and a resistance; eight until W94, which also draws
them from a seed and a list of members, below) and a **macro sequence** of members
at tens of metres, both repeating along the folded coordinate. A terrain layer opts in
with `formation: true` (`TerrainMaterialLayer` version 5; refused without a field): its sampled
colour is multiplied by the bed's tint and the macro bed's, and their roughness offsets are added.
So a band follows the ground's form — on a slope it is the line where the slope cuts a dipping,
folded plane, never a line on the screen or a contour — and a band on a steep face is as thin as
the bed is, which no plan-view mask could hold.

**The flag, the address and the one block.** The layer's flag is `k_material_terrain_formation`,
bit 18 of `ResolveMaterial::flags` (R131 took 17). The field is one 106,816-byte (T94; 98,624
after W94, 928 before) `gfx::FormationParams` block (`domain/gfx/formation.h`, pinned by the size table, mirrored once in
`formation.slang`), uploaded at scene load only when a layer asks for it, and named by
`TerrainRecord::formation`, a device address in two of the eight pad words the terrain's record
always had. **Beside the terrain record and not in `ResolveParams`**: the field is the terrain's
and fixed for the scene, the record is already the one entry every banded pixel has read, and a
`ResolveParams` field would be a per-frame word every resolve variant carries for the one that
reads it. A scene without a formation uploads the record with that word zero and the layers
without the bit, and the shader returns before any of its arithmetic, so **every existing scene
draws the bytes it drew** (`formation_scene_tests.cpp` pins a palette scene with and without the
unused field byte for byte).

**Where it is applied.** `terrain_formation_band` (terrain_material.slang) runs on a layer's sample
after the detail fade and the variance policy (`terrain_filter_sample`), at the two places a layer
is sampled (the masked palette's four and W68's layers): a band applied inside
`terrain_layer_sample` would be faded back to the layer's untinted mean by the variance policy past
`detail_far_m`, which is exactly where a mountainside's bands are wanted.

**The function and its twin.** `formation_coordinate` (`formation.slang`) gives the folded
coordinate reduced modulo each sequence's period and its gradient; `formation_bed` the bed, its
fraction across, tint, roughness and resistance; `formation_filtered` the sequence's value
**box-filtered** over a width, from the sequence's running integral (two lookups whatever the
width), so a pixel shows the mean of the beds it spans and a sequence finer than a pixel reads as
its mean. The width is the wider of the field's `soft_m` (default 0.1 m) and **two** pixels' footprint
across the beds, `2 max(|∇c · dp/dx|, |∇c · dp/dy|)` — the coordinate's change along the pixel's
edges, doubled because a box nulls only a period as wide as itself: the first v31 capture's far hill,
with a one-pixel box, kept a two-pixel period alternating row by row — from the same derivatives the mask sampler's footprint comes from; the path tracer, whose
rays carry no footprint, draws `soft_m`. `domain/gfx/formation.h` holds the f64 twin of all three,
which the rocks solver calls, and `formation_tests.cpp` holds the shader to it over a lattice round
the origin and 10 km and 10,000 km out.

**The sequence is drawn, and a bed's top moves** (roadmap W94, 2026-11-10; the grounding:
[formation sequence](../experiments/formation-sequence.md)). `Formation` version 2 takes `members`
and a `seed` in place of authored `beds`: each member (a thickness, `resistant` its share of
resistant beds, a median bed and a log deviation) is an embedded chain of a resistant and a
recessive lithology with lognormal thicknesses, drawn by `gfx::generate_formation` in whole
millimetres, integer hashes and `det::exp`, on the CPU at pack time. The members are the macro
sequence, so both tables have one period, the members' whole thickness: a section repeats after
hundreds of metres, not every few. **The table is the definition**: 512 beds of 96 bytes a
sequence (W85: 8 of 48), read by the shader and the twin alike, found by a **binary search** — over
the whole table as W94 left it, nine steps; over the few beds a slice of the period names since
T94 (below). The
integral a bed carries is of the value **less the sequence's mean**, a bounded walk where the plain
integral grew with the section, so a 4 mm box across a contact is exact to 1e-4 over a kilometre of
beds (W85's form: 2e-3 over 128 m). An authored `beds` and `macro_beds` still packs to the table
W85 packed and filters to the same value (`formation_tests.cpp`, "an authored sequence").
**Variation along strike**: bed i's base stands at `start_m + dot(base_amp_m, g)`, g two lateral
fields in [0, 1] at the point — value noise on a whole-millimetre lattice of `lateral_m` and 2.618
times it, each along its own horizontal direction 35 and 50 degrees off the strike, the lattice's
values from one 32-bit hash both sides compute, sharpened so a top rests at each end of its travel.
A top's amplitude is whole millimetres, under 0.45 of the thinner bed it parts, so tops never
cross; a **lens** is a bed whose top comes down its whole thickness, which pinches it out exactly
where its field is one. The filter is still two lookups: each bed carries, per field, the prefix sum
of `amplitude * (value below - value above)` over the tops under it, which is exactly what moving
the tops adds to the integral. A **fault** is a vertical plane beyond which the coordinate is a
throw greater, added in whole millimetres before the reduction. The first and last top of a sequence
and every member's top do not move, so the period — and the precision argument below — is the same
everywhere. The block was **98,624 bytes** a scene as W94 left it (106,816 with T94's two slice
indexes), uploaded as it was (one `upload_buffer` of the packed block); a pixel pays the two
lateral fields (an int64 division each, four hashes) and the fault's sign once, and nothing more
per lookup than two multiplies a step. **Measured as W94 left it** (2026-11-11, RTX
5090, 1920 × 1080, `--raster hw --shadows csm`, the escarpment's ridge as one banded rock layer,
the median of 52 frames a held pose; under the GPU lock with the GPU otherwise idle and every CPU
core busy with other agents' builds, so upper bounds): the resolve with W85's authored fixture
(four beds, three macro beds) against a drawn section (163 m, eight members, the tops moving, a
fault), both through this shader — **0.720 → 0.814 ms** at 50 m from the face, **0.197 → 0.219 ms**
from 500 m, **0.672 → 0.752 ms** from the valley floor: 11 to 13% of the resolve for the longer
search, the lateral fields and the fault. What the authored fixture cost under W85's own shader
on this view was not measured (no build of the base was made); its lookup has fewer steps now (two
of a binary search for four beds, where the linear one took three). **What the pictures show**
(`formation-sequence.md`, "What the pictures show"): the regular corrugation is gone and members
read as members, but at 100 m and beyond the tops are still ruled lines.

**The frame-only pack** (roadmap T94, 2026-11-11). The block is 106,816 bytes, and a caller that
declared one to read its frame — rocks' `make_fabric` did, once a rock — put that on its stack.
`gfx::FormationHead` is the block's first 192 bytes as a type of its own (the origin, the
directions, the folds, the lateral fields and the fault: all the coordinate and the lateral fields
read), `gfx::pack_formation_head` fills it from the scene's formation and its plans, and
`gfx::pack_formation_frame(formation, frame, error)` gives the 208-byte `FormationFrame` the twin's
`formation_coordinate` and `formation_lateral` take, with no table packed. `pack_formation` writes
the block's head through the same function, so the two frames are the same bytes
(`formation_tests.cpp`, "the frame-only pack"); whether the lateral fields are on is asked of the
plans (`formation_top_travel`, the one rule for how far a top moves, which the table's packer also
calls) and no longer read back from the packed tables. `gfx::check_formation` is the validation
with the table's bound and no block, for a caller that only wants to know a formation packs.

**What the formation costs the resolve** (roadmap T94, 2026-11-11). Measured three ways on W94's
views — W85's tree (44c80a0a, its own shader), W94's (b8eb339a) and T94's — each `engine-view`
copied out of its build, the same three scenes (the escarpment's ridge as one rock layer: W85's
authored fixture, W94's drawn section of eight members with its fault, and the layer with no
formation at all), RTX 5090, 1920 × 1080, `--raster hw --shadows csm --sun 120,35`, the resolve
pass's GPU milliseconds, the median of 164 frames a held pose (two flights), runs minutes apart
agreeing to 0.002 ms and runs an hour apart to 0.008. Every run under the GPU lock, and every run's `machine_state` the same: other processes
at 90 to 100% of the CPU (other agents' builds), the GPU 3 to 80% busy at the sample before the
flight, so these are upper bounds:

| Resolve, ms | 50 m | 500 m | valley |
|---|---|---|---|
| W85's tree, its authored table | 0.589 | 0.163 | 0.563 |
| W85's tree, no formation | 0.496 | 0.139 | 0.479 |
| W94, the authored table | 0.725 | 0.200 | 0.680 |
| W94, the drawn formation | 0.824 | 0.226 | 0.764 |
| W94, no formation | **0.579** | 0.164 | 0.557 |
| T94, the authored table | 0.593 | 0.173 | 0.572 |
| T94, the drawn formation | **0.590** | 0.168 | **0.566** |
| T94, no formation | **0.494** | 0.138 | 0.477 |

So the drawn formation is **within 0.001 ms of W85's own cost at 50 m, 0.003 in the valley and
0.005 at 500 m — over it, not under**. The table's rows were flown over two hours and differ by
up to 0.008 ms from one hour to the next, so the three binaries were flown again one after the
other, three times, each sample a lease of its own (CPU 32 to 55% busy with others' work): W85's
tree gave 0.588, 0.162 and 0.561 (each within 0.001 across the three samples), W94's drawn
formation 0.822, 0.225 and 0.765, and T94's drawn formation 0.589, 0.167 and 0.564. A banded pixel pays
0.096 ms a frame for the drawn formation at 50 m where W85's eight authored beds cost 0.093 and
W94's drawn section 0.33; and **a scene with no formation is 0.085 ms cheaper than W94 left it**,
which nobody had measured. What took it out, at 50 m on the drawn scene, in the order it was done
(each step's numbers are the shader at that step through the binary of the slice index, so the
last is 0.587 here and 0.590 above):

- **What a loop in the lookup cost.** W94's shader cost every terrain pixel of every scene, banded
  or not: 0.579 ms with no formation against 0.493 with the formation's code compiled out, on a
  scene where none of it runs. Compiling out any one of the lateral fields, the search or the
  filter's second lookup gave the 0.086 back, and so did writing the search's steps out with no
  `for`: it is what the driver's compile does with the shader once a loop of dependent loads with
  a data-dependent end is in it (W85's loop over eight beds did not cross it), not work done. So
  `formation_find` is nine halvings written out, each skipped by one compare once the run is one
  bed, and the header says why. **Anyone adding a loop over a table to the resolve should time a
  scene that never runs it.**
- **The slice index** (0.824 → 0.741 with the loop still in, 0.662 with it out). A lookup was a
  binary search over the whole table, nine loads each waiting on the one before, four times a
  pixel. Each table now carries 1,024 words, one a slice of its period: the first bed a coordinate
  in the slice can be in and how many, **wherever the tops stand** (a base ranges over its start
  plus the negative and the positive parts of its two amplitudes), with a margin of a millimetre
  and 2^-18 of the period for the float that picks the slice. The search runs over that run: 1.2
  beds a slice on a 264 m drawn section, 2.1 on 512 centimetre beds, so none or one step. It
  finds the bed the search of the whole table finds (`formation_tests.cpp`, "the slice index":
  3.8 million lookups over six tables at seven settings of the fields, none different). The table
  is still the definition; the index is derived from it by `pack_formation_index` and costs 4,096
  bytes a table (the block: 98,624 → 106,816 bytes).
- **A box inside one bed is that bed's value** (0.662 → 0.628). The filter looked both ends of
  its box up and differenced two integrals. Where the upper end is under the next bed's base in
  the same period — most pixels of a near face — the answer is the bed's value, which is what the
  difference gives to rounding, and nothing more is read. The twin keeps the difference always: it
  is the definition, and the probe holds the shader's band to it at 4e-3.
- **Division in 32 bits, and a member through its bed** (0.628 → 0.587). The remainders modulo the
  period, the fold's wavelength and the lateral lattices are of `whole millimetres << 24`, so they
  are the whole millimetres' by the modulus with the low 24 bits carried, and those fit 32 bits
  while the frame's cell is within 2,147 km of the origin along the direction; the 64-bit form
  stays for a frame further out and gives the same integers. A drawn formation's two periods are
  one, so one remainder serves both; a lateral field takes its cell and its remainder from one
  division where it took two. And a drawn formation's macro table **is** its members
  (`k_formation_drawn` in the block's flags): a bed's `member` is the macro's index and a member
  starts and ends where its first and last bed do, as the same floats, so where the box is inside
  one bed the macro's value is read through the bed and the macro's own lookup, which would return
  that number, is not made (`formation_tests.cpp`, "a drawn formation's macro table is its
  members"; the one place the two could differ is a float's step wide, where a lens that is a
  member's first bed has pinched out and the next bed's base, an f32 start plus an f32 amplitude,
  rounds a step under the member's own).

**What is left, feature by feature** (the shader before the last step, 50 m, one feature compiled
out): the lateral fields 0.042 ms, the macro's lookup 0.034, the four int64 divisions 0.028, the
fold 0.010, the fault 0.009; the band's two lookups 0.057 in all and the coordinate with its
fields 0.078. **Tried and not kept:** the remainders by a float reciprocal and two exact int64
corrections in place of `%` (no gain: 0.636 against 0.628). **Where the rest would come from:**
everything integer in `formation_coordinate` — the two dot products, their remainders, the lateral
lattices' cells — is a function of the frame's eye cell and the block, the same for every pixel of
the frame, and is recomputed a pixel because `formation.slang` is handed nothing a frame. A record
a frame beside `ResolveParams` would take it out; that is the resolve's file and not this row's.
**The picture moved by rounding and no more**: the drawn scene's captures from W94's binary and
this one, 1920 × 1080, differ by one step of 255 at most, in 1,452 pixels of 2,073,600 at 50 m,
42 at 500 m and 589 in the valley — the pixels whose box lies inside one bed, where the bed's
value now stands for the difference of two integrals that gave it to the last bit or two.

**Why the precision holds at 10 km — and at 10,000.** No absolute position is formed
(ADR-0053). The shader has the frame's eye cell and a float offset from its corner; the field's
origin is whole millimetres. It forms `D = cell * 64000 - origin_mm` in int64, dots it with the
normal and the dip direction **defined as integers over 2^24** (an exact int64 sum while
|D| < 2^37 mm, 137,000 km), and reduces the sum modulo each sequence's period — whole millimetres,
shifted by 24 bits — and modulo each fold's wavelength before anything is a float. What reaches
float is a remainder under one period plus the frame-local part dotted with the same directions as
floats (exact: a 24-bit integer over 2^24), so the error is a few micrometres whatever the distance
from the origin. The twin evaluates the same definition — the quantized directions, the millimetre
origin, thicknesses and wavelengths — in f64 without a reduction, which is why the two can be held
to 1e-3 m anywhere.

**What it costs.** Measured on the forest proof of concept's v31 terrain (`repro-terrain-hex/scene-norot.json` with a four-bed sequence and three macro beds, the bedrock, weathered-rock and gravel layers banded), `msvc-release`, RTX 5090, 1920 × 1080, `--raster hw --shadows csm --terrain-tiles --terrain-far 6`, the median of 35 frames a pose over three held poses, with and without the field (2026-11-05; the field run on a quiet machine, the control's harness saw the GPU 54% busy and calls its numbers upper bounds): the resolve **1.574 → 1.660 ms** on the fell slope, **0.883 → 0.928 ms** on the lakeside trail and **0.528 → 0.566 ms** looking 2.9 km across the lake at the granite summit — 0.04 to 0.09 ms, 5 to 7%, all of it on the pixels of a banded layer. A scene without a field pays nothing: the layers carry no bit and the branch returns first. The block is 928 bytes once per scene.

**What it looks like** (the same captures). On the fells the bands follow the ground's form: they
bend round every spur and gully as an outcrop pattern does (the rule of Vs where a dipping bed
crosses a valley), never a screen line and never a contour. Close, the metre beds read as regular
fine lines over the macro members' broad tones — more stripe than rock, because nothing yet ties a
bed to relief: the band is colour and roughness only, where a real resistant bed is also a ledge
(the exposed-bedrock solver's, W85's "Next"). At 2.9 km across the lake the macro members survive
as dipping bands on the granite summit while the beds have averaged out under the pixel. With a
one-pixel box a far hill kept a two-pixel period alternating row by row; the two-pixel box removed
most of it, and a faint row-to-row residue is left where the beds' period is near two pixels.

## Foliage lit from both sides

Roadmap R164 (2026-11-16); the sources, the derivation and the measurements are
[foliage, lit from both sides](../experiments/foliage-two-sided-light.md). Until it, the resolve
turned a two-sided card's shading normal to the eye's side of its plane and lit it by `n.l` alone,
so a card seen from its far side took no sun at all: 40 to 98 % of a conifer's needles seen from
1.7 m faced away from the sun ([conifer crowns](../experiments/conifer-crown-coverage.md#where-the-light-went-the-fourth-leg)).

**A property any asset can declare, never a generator's output.** A two-sided material carries
*foliage optics*, two shares in the flags word's top byte (`gfx::set_foliage_optics`, fifteenths):

- **`transmit`**, the diffuse transmittance as a share of the diffuse reflectance. Light from the
  sheet's far side comes through as Lambertian transmission of the albedo's colour (a leaf's
  reflectance and transmittance spectra have one shape in the visible). A broadleaf is about 0.8; a
  needle about half (a spruce needle's at 560 nm is 0.42 to 0.52 of its reflectance).
- **`spread`**, the share of the surface whose normals are a sphere's rather than the sheet's. A
  card of needles is opaque cylinders all round a twig: what it shows the eye is the visible half
  of a cloud of normals, whatever way the card faces. That share answers a light by the Lambert
  sphere's law, (2/3) phi(alpha) of a facet lit square on, alpha the angle between the light and
  the eye and phi Lambert's phase law: brightest with the sun behind the eye, dark against it, as a
  shoot is (backward scattering).

Where it comes from: the container's alpha word, bits 4..11 (`geometry::alpha_word_with_foliage`);
an imported glTF's `KHR_materials_diffuse_transmission` on a double-sided material (the extension
moves t of the diffuse into transmission, so the base colour factor takes `1 - t` and the share is
`t / (1 - t)`, at most 1: above t = 1/2 the leaf transmits what it reflects, less than glTF's t; its
transmission colour is not read, the base colour serves both sides; R164-3); a material pack role's `transmission` and
`normal_spread` keys (`materials::MaterialSet`, nonzero values replacing the part's own); and
flora's own parts (`k_leaf_transmission` 0.8 on every leaf and frond, `k_needle_transmission` 0.47
and `k_needle_spread` 0.8 on every needle card; [flora](flora.md#foliage-optics)). **A material
with none of it is drawn exactly as before**: every reader branches on the byte.

**A scene with none pays nothing** (R177, 2026-11-17). The branch alone cost a scene that never
takes it: the rock field's resolve was 1.462 ms on main before R164 and 1.488 after, at 3840 x
2160 traced (R164's second leg), the registers of code it never ran, which a build with the
branch forced off gave back (1.466). So `material_is_foliage` (`material.slang`) is ANDed with a
**specialization constant**, `k_scene_foliage` (`gfx::k_spec_scene_foliage`, true unless a
pipeline sets it), and every pipeline of the resolve's family — the resolve, its linear twin for
the frame passes, the split's class pipelines, the half-rate sun pass and the cache's sample pass —
is made with it false where no material row of the scene has the byte
(`GpuScene::has_foliage_materials`). The driver folds the constant before it allocates registers,
so such a pipeline is the module without foliage, from the same SPIR-V: not a fifth bit of
`resolve_module`, which would have doubled the resolve's sixteen modules to thirty-two and their
build. **A scene with a mesh room keeps the lines, whatever its generators declared** (review
finding A7): a tile may hand a foliage material at any frame, the constant is fixed when the
pipelines are made, and a picture must not depend on whether a generator remembered to say its
tiles may (the branch first kept them only behind `tile_meshes_masked`, and an undeclared world's
tile foliage was lit from the front alone where main lit it from both sides). Rebuilding the
family's pipelines when the first foliage material arrived was the other way, and was not taken:
a resolve family's build is long, and would land on the frame's thread or a frame late. So only a
**closed** scene with no foliage material drops them, which is where the saving was measured (the
rock field and the erg have no mesh room); a streamed world with tile meshes and no foliage pays
for the lines as it did on main. `mesh_texture_tests.cpp` ("a tile's foliage material arriving
after the first frame is two-sided") holds an undeclared scene's tile foliage to a declared
scene's picture and away from the same sheets with no optics.
`gfx::Specialization` (`pipeline.h`; [gfx](gfx.md#specialization-constants)) is how any pipeline
sets such a constant.

**The backlit sun's tier** (R177; `renderer.foliage.backlit_tier`, default 1). R164's lighting
cost the grove 0.25 ms of resolve at 3840 x 2160 traced, and 0.20 of it is the sun rays a sheet
lit from behind asks from the light's side of its card, which a turned-away sheet never asked.
The top tier (1) keeps them. The low tier (0) asks none: a foliage pixel whose sun is behind its
sheet holds the sun unshadowed, and once its ambient is known adds it at the share of the sky the
world-space cache measured reaching the point — what the scene let through of the front's raw
hemisphere, `scene_ambient` over it, its luminance, clamped to one. That is what shipped
shadow-mapped foliage does (Crysis's leaves, *GPU Gems 3* ch. 16: the back term is multiplied by
the shadow factor the front's lighting loop already took, no test of its own); a ray-traced
renderer has no such free answer, and the cache's is the nearest measured one. Only where the frame
reads the cache (`k_gi_read`): anywhere else the low tier traces as the top does, because the
cache's ratio is one there and the sun would come through every crown. Front-lit sheets trace as
they always did. **What a person loses**: the sun's pattern on the back of a crown. A backlit
needle the sun reaches through a gap and one a branch shades take the same mean of their cell,
so the glow of lit-through leaves against the sun is even where it was dappled. On the grove at
3840 x 2160 traced it gives back about 0.09 ms of resolve; the measured cost and the pictures are
on [the experiment's page](../experiments/foliage-two-sided-light.md#the-backlit-suns-tier-r177).

**What each reader does with it.** One model, in `brdf.slang` (`brdf_foliage_eval_cos`,
`brdf_foliage_direct`, `brdf_foliage_ambient`), mirrored in double in `brdf_reference.h`:

- the sheet's share is `brdf_eval` whole (its specular lobe included) on the eye-side normal, plus
  `transmit` times the Lambertian diffuse from behind it; the sphere's share is diffuse alone,
  `(1 - F0)` of the albedo over pi times (2/3)(phi(alpha) + transmit phi(pi - alpha));
- the resolve's sun, its analytic lights, and its hemisphere: the ambient its back sees through
  `transmit`, and for the sphere's share the n.v-weighted mean of a sphere's visible normals,
  (5/6) A(v) + (1/6) A(-v), each scaled by what the scene's cache let through the front;
- the traced hit shading (`hit_shade.slang`, the water's reflections) the sun term and the same
  hemisphere as the resolve (R164-3, review B7: it kept the sheet's ambient, so a leaf in a
  reflection was lit differently from the leaf beside it), and the reference path tracer the
  lights and the next direction, which samples the sheet's back half the time. Below the sheet
  either half can have drawn a direction (a grazing view's GGX reflection goes under the plane),
  so its density counts both (`ggx_vndf_pdf_below`; R164-3, review B5: the back lobe's alone read
  the mean of a uniform light 0.4 to 1.4 % high on a sheet and 121 % with the sphere's share at
  0.8, from 60 to 85 degrees; `foliage optics: the path tracer's draw is unbiased`).

**Reflected plus transmitted never passes one** (R164-3, review B4). The transmittance is
`transmit` times the albedo, but never more than what the albedo leaves, `1 - albedo`, channel by
channel (`brdf_foliage_share`). A share is the material's and the albedo a texel's, so no import
and no pack can hold the pair under one for every texel (a pack's albedo is an image); the response
holds it. Flora's leaves (albedo at most 0.36 under 0.8) and every glTF the importer splits sum to
less and are untouched. What it bounds is the diffuse: integrated over both hemispheres, the
response less the sheet's specular lobe stays under `1 - F0` for a white texel under a share of 1,
the pair that sums to one and the importer's split of a white base colour (`foliage optics:
reflected plus transmitted never passes one`). The specular lobe is the sheet's own, and the sheet
alone already returns more than one at a grazing eye (1.24 at 89 degrees and roughness 0.3, albedo
1: the single-scattering GGX with a Lambert under `1 - F`), which is not foliage's to mend.

**The shadow stays right.** A light behind the sheet is shadowed by a ray that leaves from the
light's side of the plane (`ray_side` in `material.slang`), not the eye's, or every ray would stop
on its own card. The half-rate sun pass (R126) asks a foliage block's ray from the light's side
too and takes it whichever side the sun is on (`resolve_half_sun.slang`; R164's second leg: the
first asked a lit-through pixel's own ray, so a surround's sides traced every such pixel at full
rate). The cascaded maps read the same flipped normal for their lift.

**The cache's bounce lights a foliage hit as the resolve does** (R177). `gi_update.slang`'s
`gi_bounce` takes the sun from behind the sheet through `transmit` and its sphere's share, its
shadow ray from the light's side, and the back's and the sphere's ambient scaled by what the cache
let through of the front's, so the light a bounce brings back from under a canopy is the leaves'
lit-through green rather than a dark sheet's back. `water reflect: a foliage card in the water is
shaded as the card on the screen` (systems/water) holds the reflected hit to the resolve: what the
optics multiply a backlit card by, in the sun and in a wall's shadow, agrees on the screen and in
the water within ln(1.05), against a sheet of the leaf's reflected part (the importer keeps 1 - t
of glTF's base colour, so a sheet of the whole would cancel the shadowed card's gain to the bit).

**Not done.** Water's flag-class mirror in `water.slang` does not name the byte (it checks only
that the classes stay apart, which they do).

## Alpha-tested geometry

Roadmap R65 (plan 04 §4.3). A material whose glTF `alphaMode` is `MASK` draws nothing where its base
colour's alpha (times the base colour factor's) is below its `alphaCutoff`: leaf cards, fronds, a
fence's wire. The importer has read the mode and the cutoff since the first glTF path, and the
container carries them; until R65 nothing honoured them, so every leaf card the flora solver emits
was an opaque parallelogram. Grounding: the practice every shipping engine follows — a masked
pipeline variant that interpolates the UV and discards below the cutoff, coverage kept down the mip
chain at build time (Castaño 2010; [texture](texture.md#alpha-tested-masks)), the colour dilated
under the mask so the filtered fringe is the leaf's, and in ray tracing a test of each non-opaque
candidate against the mask (the any-hit shader of a pipeline, a `RayQuery` loop here), accelerated
where the hardware has them by opacity micromaps (`VK_EXT_opacity_micromap`; Indiana Jones'
vegetation trace went from 7.90 to 3.58 ms on an RTX 5080 with them, NVIDIA's "Path Tracing
Optimizations in Indiana Jones", 2025). What the engine's visibility buffer allows is narrower than
a forward renderer's: **no MSAA, so no alpha-to-coverage** (Golus, "Anti-aliased Alpha Test", 2017):
the cut is hard at the cutoff, and an id is either a whole pair's triangle or nothing, which is what
keeps the resolve, the tie rule and the ray path's word-for-word match exact.

**The data.** The mask is the base colour's alpha, built with its coverage kept and its colour
dilated ([texture](texture.md#alpha-tested-masks) says why not a slot of its own).
`gfx::set_alpha_mask` flags the material (`k_material_alpha_mask`) with the cutoff and the factor's
alpha in `uv_offset.zw`; `GpuScene::has_masked()` says the table has one. A scene with none builds,
draws and traces exactly what it did: no masked pipeline is made, the mask tables stay zero, and
every pass takes the branch it always took.

**The classification.** What says a pair is masked is its material (`materials[cluster_materials
[cluster] + material_base]`), read through `gfx::MaskTables` — in the cull block right after the
eye, so the rasterizers reach it through the eye they already read (`FrameEye::masks` says the
tables follow; gfx.md). The material and not an instance bit, because a tree is one mesh of bark and
leaf clusters, and a bit per cluster would be a table of its own to keep beside the one that exists.
The cull pass sends **a masked pair to the hardware rasterizers only, never to the software one**: a
thread a triangle walking its box in compute would pay a UV interpolation and a texture fetch per
covered pixel with no quad to take a mip from, a few times the software path's whole per-pixel cost,
for clusters that are by definition a few pixels across. Only a pair that would have gone software
pays the two reads. `--raster sw` (everything software, a debugging mode) has no hardware draw and
draws a masked pair solid.

**The variants.** Each rasterizer draws twice where a scene has a masked material: its opaque entry
point, which now collapses a masked pair (the mesh stage emits no primitives for it, the vertex
stages a degenerate corner), then its masked variant **over the same run of the visible list**,
which keeps only the masked pairs, emits the UV per vertex and the material flat, and in the
fragment stage samples the mask with the quad's derivatives, discards below the cutoff and writes
exactly the opaque stage's word. **The mask's sample is one trilinear tap at the level of the
footprint's shorter axis, never the material's anisotropic one** (`mask_keeps`, G203): the
anisotropic tap averages up to sixteen taps along the longer axis, an average the texture build
never held to anything, and a thin mask on a card at a slant fell under the cutoff whole — with
the chain's texel-count rule that was the hardware rasterizer drawing a conifer 27 to 31 % thinner
than the rays at 300 m; one tap is a point sample of a level the build holds to level 0's coverage
([texture](texture.md#alpha-tested-masks)), and what is left after it is the far form's atlases
([the measurement](../experiments/conifer-crown-coverage.md)). A second run per pass would have kept the masked pairs out of the
opaque draw's work, but it is a run more of the list per view and pass, every per-entry table
(the pool's blocks, the indexed draw's records, the CLAS records) sized and indexed by one more,
and the classification would have had to happen before the vertex path's allocation; a second draw
over one run keeps the index space as it was, and costs the masked draw an empty workgroup or a
collapsed triangle per opaque pair (measured below). The variants: `mesh_main_masked` +
`fs_visibility_masked`, `vs_cluster_masked`, `vs_cluster_indexed_masked` +
`fs_visibility_indexed_masked`, `vs_cluster_fallback_masked` + `fs_visibility_fallback_masked`, and
for the cascades the same vertex or mesh stages with `fs_mask_depth*`, a fragment stage that only
discards, so a masked caster writes the atlas only where its mask keeps the pixel.

**The rays.** A masked pair is built **non-opaque** into the frame's structures, drawn or caster
(`clas_records.slang`), as the shadow casters already are, and the template path is not taken in a
masked scene (a template is built once, opaque, and an instantiation cannot clear the flag). Every
ray then decides its non-opaque candidates in its `RayQuery` loop by one rule
(`alpha_mask.slang`, `candidate_keeps`): **a pair whose material is masked is kept where its mask
keeps the hit** — the hit's barycentrics give the UV, the material's transform applies, the mask is
sampled at level 0 — **and anything else non-opaque is a shadow caster**. The primary ray of the
ray path cannot cull non-opaque geometry any more in such a frame; it traces with no flag, leaves a
caster out by its entry (`caster_base`, as its tie scan always did) and commits a masked candidate
the mask keeps; the tie scan skips a masked candidate the mask cuts. The resolve's shadow ray
(`k_shadow_alpha_masks`) and the path tracer's rays (`k_pt_alpha_masks`) drop `FORCE_OPAQUE` and
commit a caster or a kept masked candidate, the first one ending the search. A caster and a masked
cluster are told apart by the material, not by an instance mask bit: the TLAS's instance is the
scene instance, and a tree's instance holds both. **Opacity micromaps are not built**: they would
classify most of a leaf card's micro-triangles as wholly opaque or wholly transparent in the
traversal hardware and leave the loop only the boundary ones — the loop's whole cost below, less
what the boundary keeps.
### Impostors are masked clusters

**A tree's impostor chain draws through what R65 built and adds no shader** (R89, 2026-10-21;
[flora](flora.md#the-impostor-chain)). Its branch-group cards and its whole-tree star are clusters of
authored DAG levels ([geometry](geometry.md#authored-levels)) whose materials are alpha-tested,
two-sided, and sample a baked colour atlas (alpha the coverage the leaves cut) and a baked
tangent-space normal atlas: the cull pass chooses them by their errors like any cluster, the masked
variants rasterize them, the ray loops and the shadow maps test the same mask, and the resolve shades
the baked normal through the triangle's own tangent frame (`tangent_frame`, `material.slang`) with
the frame's lights as it shades any normal-mapped surface — so a card's leaves are lit by the sun
and the sky they face, not the flat card's normal. What a dedicated material kind would add, and is
not built: **view-chosen frames** (an octahedral atlas blended by the view direction, R92; the coverage
would then depend on the view, which every rasterizer's masked variant, every ray loop and the
cascades would have to compute alike to keep the visibility buffer and the ray path word for word),
and the baked depth offsetting a shadow ray's origin to where the leaf was.

### The foliage threshold

R91 (2026-10-21; [tree allometry](../experiments/tree-allometry.md#r91-foliage-lod-that-takes-over-2026-10-21)
has the sources). A card standing for a bough is judged by its coverage and its colour at the pixel,
not by the parallax of a point off its plane, so the cut holds a foliage level's **coverage error**
([flora](flora.md#the-impostor-chain) measures it, [geometry](geometry.md#two-errors-the-geometric-and-the-coverage)
has the formula) to its own threshold: `RenderSettings::foliage_px`, the tunable
`renderer.lod.foliage_px`, `engine-view --foliage-lod <px>`; `--lod` stays the geometric one. A
frame's override of the geometric threshold (`FrameDesc::lod_px`) moves the foliage threshold in
proportion, so the finest cut is the finest foliage and the chain's root its root; a view's
`lod_scale` and the cascades' `shadow_lod_scale` multiply both. **The default, 5 px**, is fitted to
the owner's observation that the 12 m oak's first cards hold the picture at 28 m (R89's capture at
`--lod 60`): its first level's coverage error is 0.15 m (a 0.17 m leaf times the measured difference
0.90), which projects to 5 px at 28 m at 1080p — where the leaf itself is 5.6 px. The switch
distances that follow, from a card group's near side at 1080p (a group's sphere is its sub-trees',
0.7 to 7 m on the oak, 0.7 to 46 m on the ancient tree): the oak's four card levels at 28, 172, 288 and
421 m and its star at 434 m from the tree's centre (R89: 589 m to 7.9 km); the default ancient tree's
five at 37, 189, 305, 434 and 582 m and its star at 691 m (R89: 832 m to 67 km). Both scenes' camera
paths now draw cards. A scene with no coverage errors reads none of it and draws byte-identically: the
cull pass's test with a coverage of +inf is the one-threshold test bit for bit.

### The cross-fade

A foliage switch is hidden by a dithered cross-fade across a band of projected error, 0.9 to 1.1 times
the threshold by default (`RenderSettings::lod_fade` half band, tunable `renderer.lod.fade` 0.1,
`engine-view --lod-fade`; 0 switches at once), about 10 % of the distance. Across it both levels are
drawn and **each pixel keeps one**: the cull pass computes each drawn pair's two splits
(`geometry::lod_fade_split`) and writes them and the pair's instance's seed to the view's fade table
(`MaskTables::fade`; gfx.md), and every masked reader keeps the pixel where its stable hash of the
pixel and the seed lies between them (`fade_keeps`, `alpha_mask.slang`) — screen-door transparency
through the masked variants' discard, so the visibility buffer keeps one id a pixel and the tie rule
stands. Both sides of a transition hash the same pixels with the same seed (the instance's, never the
pair's), so they are complementary: no holes, no doubles. The hash has nothing of the frame in it, so a
still view does not shimmer; only under the accumulation are the splits turned with the phase, so
that the frames blend the two levels ([leg 3](#leg-3-the-sharper-read-reactive-surfaces-and-the-fade-turned-with-the-phase)). **The seed is the instance's placement, never its index**
(`fade_seed` in `scene.slang`: the bits of its offset into its cell and of its rotation and scale,
hashed; not the cell, so a scene moved by whole cells draws the same bytes). Until R170
(2026-11-16) it was the instance's index, which is its place in the scene's layout and so the order
the instances reached the renderer: the same placements handed over in another order — the near
hand-off cells of `b65-G205`, or a tile's run arriving before its neighbour's — drew a different
screen door on every masked pair inside a band, which on the engine meadow's eye-down view was 0.03 to
0.38 % of a 4K frame, dotted lines along the blades within 2 m of the eye, each one instance changing
which of its own two levels kept a pixel (the capture's ids: one instance, its clusters 641 and 673
swapping pixel by pixel). A whole read and a streamed one place an instance at the same bits, so they
draw one dither. Two placements at the same offset in different cells, with the same rotation, share
a screen door; they are a cell apart, which is the price of the rule above. `impostor_view_tests.cpp`
("the dither follows the placement") hands the fade case's oak and a second one out of view over in
both orders across the band, ten frames at 480 × 480: with the index for a seed 55,694 of 379,695
covered pixels differed in id and colour on the mesh path, the vertex path and the ray path alike
(none switched at once), and with the placement none on any path. The ray path's loops hash the dispatch's pixel, the resolve's shadow rays
the resolved pixel, and the cascades the shadow map's texel against a table of their own (their LOD
can be scaled), so every path sees one of the two levels per sample. With the chain the finest leaves
are alpha-tested even with no pack's image (flora.md), because an opaque side cannot dither: an
opaque cluster of a fading mesh — the bark under the star — switches at the band's fine end, so its
masked replacement is whole before it goes. The reference tracer's frames take no fade
(`FrameDesc::lod_fade`), since its rays have no table. **Nor does a frame drawn with culling off**
(`RenderSettings::cull` false, the capacity draw of one mesh): the table is the cull pass's output and
such a frame has no cut to fade between, so `resolve_settings` sets its `lod_fade` to zero, its masked
readers are given no table and keep every pixel the mask keeps. Until an imported alpha-tested mesh
carried coverage errors (T147) no scene with them could be drawn that way; the first that could, the
masked quad of `alpha_mask_tests.cpp`, read an unwritten table and drew nothing, which is how the
rule came to be written down.

**What holds** (`impostor_view_tests.cpp`, the 8 m oak at 480 × 480, the camera 15 m off while the
threshold sweeps from 0.8 to 1.25 times the settings' over 20 frames, so only the switch moves): the
first cards' share of the tree's pixels moves at most 3.8 % a frame faded against 9.5 % switched at
once; the largest frame-to-frame mean change of an 8 × 8 block is 0.28 of 255 faded against 0.42; 2 × 2
blocks holding both leaves and cards number 11,346 faded against 3,105 (the screen door). The vertex
path's ids equal the mesh path's in every one of the 4.6 million pixels, faded or not; the ray path's
differ in 2,475 faded and 2,372 at once, the masks' level-0 sampling the ray loops always had. **Not
tested**: the cascades' masked depth against a reference inside the band (they run, keyed by texel).

**What it costs** (msvc-debug, RTX 5090, 1080p, each scene's camera path with traced shadows,
`--offscreen --repeat 1 --warmup 60 --wait-quiet 60`, 2026-10-21; neither run found a quiet machine —
before, others held 97–100 % of the CPU, after 21–50 % — so every number is an upper bound):

| | Elder grove, before → after | Grove, before → after |
|---|---|---|
| GPU total ms, median / p95 / p99 | 2.06 / 2.51 / 2.89 → 1.59 / 2.20 / 2.36 | 0.67 / 0.81 / 0.97 → 0.85 / 1.01 / 1.14 |
| rt, CLAS, raster, resolve (median ms) | 1.29, 0.99, 0.092, 0.36 → 0.68, 0.45, 0.055, 0.70 | 0.31, 0.13, 0.041, 0.26 → 0.29, 0.11, 0.042, 0.46 |
| Visible pairs, shadow casters (median) | 22,692, 20,005 → 7,429, 10,286 | 4,021, 88 → 3,154, 88 |
| Scene clusters | 129,403 → 74,823 | 5,465 → 4,328 |
| GPU memory the engine used | 1,143 → 875 MiB | 423 → 393 MiB |
| Frames that allocated | 0 → 0 | 0 → 0 |

The cards take over: a third of the elder grove's visible pairs, half its ray-tracing chain and 268
MiB less memory, and its GPU total back from 2.06 toward the 0.78 ms it took before G73's leaves (the
cut no longer pays for every leaf of the far crown). **The resolve went the other way**, 0.36 to
0.70 ms and 0.26 to 0.46: the leaves are alpha-tested now, so every shadow ray that meets a leaf
decides it in the ray loop instead of forcing it opaque, and that is the band's price on every frame,
not only inside it. Building an always-kept mask opaque into the structures outside the band (an
opacity micromap's job, or a per-entry opacity bit in the CLAS records) would take most of it back;
not built. The cull pass writes one 8-byte table entry per drawn pair and the masked fragments read
one (`cull` 0.023 → 0.019 ms, `hw` 0.092 → 0.055: the band's cost is inside the noise of fewer pairs).
The fade's tables are a `u32x2` per pair per view and one for the cascades (2.2 MB at the elder
grove's 136,464 pairs).

### Occlusion-aware LOD

R118 (2026-11-02; [the measurements](../experiments/occlusion-lod-2026-11-02.md)). **The owner's idea**:
a crown in a ring that does not lower its LOD, mostly hidden behind nearer leaves, gains nothing
the eye can see from keeping its polygons — the few pixels it still shows would not tell its parent
from it — while the trunk in front should keep them. The occlusion test was a yes or no, so a cluster
with one visible pixel drew at the LOD its projected error earned, as if whole. The literature has
the same move: Andújar, Saona-Vázquez, Navazo and Brunet's *hardly-visible sets* (Eurographics 2000,
CGF 19(3)) lower an object's LOD by how much of it the occluders leave visible, and Zhang et al.'s
hierarchical occlusion maps (SIGGRAPH 1997) cull approximately by an opacity threshold.

**The rule.** Each transition's two thresholds — `lod.y` and `foliage_px` — are multiplied by
`1 + k h`, where k is `renderer.lod.occluded_scale` and h is the **hidden share of the transition's own
sphere**: the share of the texels of its screen rectangle in the Hi-Z (`occluded_bias` mips finer
than the occlusion test reads, so at most 9 × 9 at the default 1) whose farthest depth is nearer than
the sphere's nearest point (`hidden_fraction`, `cluster_cull.slang`). It is conservative as the test
is: a texel holding one pixel of sky, of the crown itself or of anything farther is not hidden, so a
crown seen through a nearer one's gaps reads only the blocks the nearer one covers whole. A wholly
hidden transition's thresholds are `1 + k` times the plain ones, which bounds how far the term moves
any cut: at most log2(1 + k) levels on a DAG whose error doubles a level. Past the root of a tree's
DAG is its star ([Impostors are masked clusters](#impostors-are-masked-clusters)), so a crown far
enough behind others falls to the star while the trunk in front keeps its polygons.

**Why per transition and not per pair.** The cut is crack-free because the two clusters that test one
transition — the finer side as its parent, the coarser side as its own — compute the same answer
from the same sphere and error. A factor taken from each *cluster's* rectangle would break that and
open holes. A factor that is any function of the transition's sphere keeps it: a transition is
accepted or not, whoever asks, so a region is always covered by its finer side or its coarser side
(`cluster_lod_tests.cpp` covers a terrain's ground plan cell by cell under a hash standing in for an
arbitrary pyramid). What it gives up is the **monotone** cut: a parent sphere more hidden than its
child's by more than the errors grow may accept a coarser level while the finer one still draws, and
both cover that region — an overlap, never a hole, and only where the Hi-Z says the region is
hidden. The CPU mirror is `geometry::lod_selects(lod, view, coverage, own_scale, parent_scale)`;
scales of 1 are the rule bit for bit, and the cull pass's every threshold is the same float at k 0.

**Only a transition the factor could decide reads the Hi-Z**: one whose smaller ratio of projected
error to threshold lies in (1 − fade, (1 + k)(1 + fade)]. Below it the transition is accepted at any
factor of at least 1, above it refused at any factor of at most 1 + k, and the skip is a function of
the same inputs as the factor, so every pair that tests a transition skips or reads it alike.

**Where the Hi-Z comes from.** Under two-pass occlusion culling (`--raster hw`/`vertex` without
traced shadows) pass 1 reads last frame's pyramid and pass 2 pass 1's, the ones the culling reads;
a pair pass 1 drew under last frame's factor is not tested again, so in motion the two passes may
overlap a transition for a frame. **A frame without it — the ray path, and every frame with traced
shadows, which is the owner's — had no Hi-Z at all** (`resolve_settings` turns occlusion culling off
there, because the structures are built from one visible list). With the term on, such a frame builds
one at the end of its visibility writes (after the trace, the rasterizers, or both), and the next
frame's one cull pass reads it **for the term alone** (`gfx::k_cull_hiz_lod_only`): culling against
last frame's depth there would drop a pair that came into view since, and a pair hidden from the eye
must still be built, drawn or casting. So on the ray path the gain is the cut's level, not its pair
count. In a frame that builds acceleration structures every view reads the cut view's pyramid
through its projection, so one sphere has one hidden share in every view and [one cut for every
view](#one-cut-for-every-view) holds. A frame whose last one built none starts from an empty pyramid
(nothing hidden). The build costs `hiz`'s zone; k 0 with the counters off builds nothing and changes
nothing.

**What it changes, stated** (subjective fidelity, the owner 2026-11-01): pixels where a mostly hidden
transition shows — a crown's slivers between nearer leaves, a crown's far side at its silhouette —
are drawn from a coarser level. **Shadows follow the cut**: under traced shadows the structures are
the frame's cut, so a hidden crown casts its coarser level's shadow, which falls on visible ground; the
captures count those pixels with the rest. The cascaded maps keep the camera's plain cut (their
blocks have no Hi-Z). The Hi-Z is last frame's, so a cut follows a camera move one frame late; a still
scene's cut settles (`occlusion_lod_tests.cpp` holds its last two frames equal).

**Foliage only, by default.** The hidden share is the bounding *rectangle's*, and a trunk is a thin
thing in a large one: in a forest the rectangle of a trunk 20 m off is mostly nearer trees' leaves, so
on both thresholds the term coarsened visible mid-distance trunks — the opposite of the owner's ask.
`renderer.lod.occluded_foliage_only` (true; `gfx::k_cull_hiz_term_foliage`) moves the coverage
threshold alone, so a transition with no coverage error — a trunk's, the ground's — keeps its own, and
only foliage goes coarser; a tree whose next level is its star still switches whole, trunk included,
because the star is the whole tree.

**Off by default, measured.** On the owner's v25 walk (`--raster rt --shadows rt`, 1080p) the term
returned 0.2–0.5 ms of an 11.6 ms frame on the foliage threshold at k 4–8 and 0.7–1.0 ms on both
(1.6–2.1 ms of 46 ms at 11520 × 2160), all of it in the CLAS build of hidden swaying crowns, for 2–7 %
of the pixels changed at the markers on foliage alone and 8–16 % on both. **81 % of the drawn pairs
were wholly hidden**, but of those at least half hidden 63 % were already at their DAG's root and 36 %
more than five times from their next level: a threshold factor reaches about one in a hundred. So
`k_lod_occluded_scale` is 0 and the frame is the one it was; [the measurements](../experiments/occlusion-lod-2026-11-02.md)
name the two levers that would return the hidden forest (a pair's own visible pixels from last
frame's ids instead of its rectangle, and a shadow-only representation for what the eye never sees).

**Knobs.** `renderer.lod.occluded_scale` (k; default `k_lod_occluded_scale`, 0),
`renderer.lod.occluded_foliage_only` (true), `renderer.lod.occluded_bias` (1), and two measurement
switches: `renderer.lod.occluded_cycle` n (frame f takes k × ((f / n) mod 3) / 2,
so one flight measures 0, k/2 and k) and `renderer.lod.occluded_histogram` (the drawn pairs' hidden
shares by tenths and what the term changed, one log line a frame, counted by the GPU into the cull
blocks' host-visible buffer — `gfx::k_hidden_*`).

**What holds.** `occlusion_lod_tests.cpp`: a bumpy sphere's DAG behind a screen pierced by holes, one
cull pass a frame against last frame's pyramid — at k 0 the crown's cut is the same behind the screen
and alone; at k 4 it is coarser than at k 0 and than alone, the screen's cut does not move, every
changed pixel is one where the crown shows in one picture or the other, the last two frames draw
the same pairs, and on the foliage threshold alone this crown, which has no coverage error, keeps its
cut and its picture byte for byte. `cluster_lod_tests.cpp`: the CPU rule's factors, and no hole under any per-transition
factor. The two-pass occlusion test, the cull test's GPU-against-CPU cut and the cone test run with
the term off and are unchanged.

### The opaque shadow proxy

Roadmap R109, stage 1 (2026-10-28; [the measurement](../experiments/shadow-proxy-2026-10-28.md)). Under ray-traced shadows an alpha-tested caster is built non-opaque, and the resolve's shadow query decides each of its candidates itself (`shadow_ray_blocked` in `visibility_resolve.slang`): the candidate's entry, its instance, its cluster's material, the triangle's three UVs, and a level-0 sample of the base colour's alpha — and a candidate the mask rejects lets the traversal go on to the next one. On the forest that loop is most of the rays' cost: 34.3 ms of the resolve at 11520×2160 on the expanded forest, against 11.6 with every caster forced solid (`renderer.shadow.opaque_rays`, a measurement switch that draws the wrong picture).

**The proxy**: a masked cluster whose **alpha coverage** — the share of its surface its mask keeps — is at or above `renderer.shadow.opaque_coverage` is solid to a shadow ray: its candidate is committed without the material, the UVs or the mask, and the search ends there. Below the threshold, and for every cluster with no byte, the mask decides exactly as before; a fading pair still keeps only the pixels its band gives it (`fade_keeps`). The primary rays, the rasterizers, the cascades and the reference path tracer never read it.

**Where the coverage comes from.** Nothing carried it: the foliage's "coverage" words are coverage *errors* of a LOD transition (geometry.md, "Two errors"), not how much of a cluster is leaf. So it is **baked on the GPU when a renderer is first made over a scene** (`GpuScene::bake_shadow_coverage`, `alpha_coverage.slang`): the material upload lists every cluster whose material is alpha-tested (with its material — an instance's material base is always its mesh's), and one workgroup a cluster samples each triangle at the centroids of its n×n equal-area sub-triangles (at least 256 samples a cluster, at most 64 a triangle), asks each sample exactly what a shadow ray's candidate asks (`mask_keeps_level0`), weights a triangle by its area on the mesh's 16-bit grid, and writes the kept fraction in 255ths, **one byte per cluster**, four to a word. The table is the scene's cluster count long and stays resident (1.37 MB on the v20 forest, 319,484 masked clusters, baked in 11.7 ms at load); a cluster the bake never wrote reads 0, which is "ask the mask". It is baked only when the tunable is above 0 when the scene is made, the scene has a masked material, and it is read whole: a streamed scene's clusters live in a page pool whose slots change under any table made at load, so it gets none. `ResolveParams` carries the table, its length and the threshold byte (`shadow_coverage`, `shadow_coverage_count`, `shadow_opaque_coverage`, a new 16-byte row: 448 → 464 bytes); with no table the shader's loop is the one before R109.

**The default is off** (`k_shadow_opaque_coverage` 0), because the measurement says the proxy cannot buy the masks' cost at a threshold that leaves the picture alone. Read off the curve (the bytes themselves were not histogrammed), the clusters the rays spend their time in — the canopy near the eye — keep less than a third of their surface: on the expanded forest at 1600×900 a threshold of 0.5 or more saves nothing measurable (FLIP mean 0.0014 against the full masks), 0.3 saves 0.40 ms of the resolve's 3.04 (and 4.6 ms of 34.3 at 11520×2160) for FLIP 0.015 mean and 0.099 at the 95th percentile, and 0.2 saves 0.94 ms for 0.064 — and what changes is the dappled sunlight on the ground under the canopy, the flecks the proxy closes, which is the forest's light. None of the five budgeted runs draws an alpha-tested material under the rays (the overlook's shadows are off, the erg and the endless desert are terrain alone), so the frame budgets cannot move. The lever that keeps the flecks is a per-micro-triangle answer the traversal resolves itself — opacity micromaps, R109's stage 2, written up in the experiment.

The case: `alpha mask: a dense masked cluster is solid to a shadow ray at the proxy's threshold` (`alpha_mask_tests.cpp`) bakes the checker quad's coverage (a half), and at 0.45 the masked quad casts the opaque quad's shadow on every ground pixel the two pictures share (0 of 11,346 differ; 1,216 the mask had lit are shadowed), at 0.55 its mask still decides and the picture is the tunable at 0's, byte for byte.
## The sky above, the ground below

**The resolve's whole indirect term is a hemisphere of two uniform halves** (2026-09-25): the sky
above the horizon, at 0.35 of `k_sky` (`sky_radiance` in `material.slang`), and below it the
**ground** — the scene's ground albedo lit by the frame's sun and sky, `ρ (E_sun / π + L_sky)`, where
`E_sun` is the sun's intensity times the sine of its elevation, its irradiance on a horizontal
surface (`brdf_ground_radiance` in `brdf.slang`). A surface of normal n takes the two blended by the
share of its cosine lobe each half fills, `lerp(ground, sky, (1 + n.y) / 2)`
(`brdf_hemisphere_ambient`) — the sky view factor of a tilted plane, which makes the blend exact for
two uniform halves — and, as before, the diffuse albedo takes that and the specular lobe the share
`brdf_env_specular` gives it. The ground is **not shadowed**: it stands for the ground *around* the
point, which the sun lights whether or not the point is in shade, so a sun-shadowed pixel keeps the
ground's bounce of the sun (the shading tests' shadowed pixels are the model with the sun's direct
term removed and nothing else). Before, the lower half was the sky's own ramp run on past the
horizon — 0.15 of the sky colour facing straight down — so a surface turned towards the ground saw a
dim blue sky under it, which is what the third owner session's dunes asked about
([its write-up](../experiments/third-interactive-session-2026-09-25.md#the-grounds-bounce-measured-2026-09-25-evening)).
A real bounce is Phase 4's; this is the smallest term that lets the ground's colour reach a surface
facing it.

**The ground's albedo is a scene value.** `SceneData::ground_albedo`: `load_scene` makes it **the
mean base colour of what the scene's terrain draws** (R185, `terrain_ground_albedo` in
`terrain_materials.h`) and leaves the neutral grey `gfx::k_neutral_ground_albedo`, 0.2, without a
terrain. The root — the desert's four surfaces, the baked maps every terrain carries — is
`terrain_surface` averaged over the maps' square on a 64 by 64 grid (`terrain_surface_mean_albedo`),
which is the sand (0.84, 0.69, 0.47) to the bit for a ground with no ridge or basin, so a sand scene
draws what it drew. A palette with masks ("Ground materials by place") is its layers' means — the
colour each fades to far away, carried in the layer entry's emissive by the content build — by
each layer's share of the mask level (`terrain_mask_cover`: a point's weights over their sum times
its cover, the root where the cover falls short or no tile is, over mip 0 of at most 256 present
tiles strided in page order), measured by the scene reader beside its masks check and kept in
`TerrainDesc::mask_cover`; a description built in code that was never measured takes the layers
unweighted. W68's layers without masks composite over the root in array order by weight times
their coverage map's mean, as the resolve does. A snow layer's grain, a formation's tints and
wetness are left out. Until R185 any terrain was the desert's sand, which R182 found to be four
fifths of the light on a shaded wall, trunk or needle with the bounce off on ground that is not
sand ([its page](../experiments/sun-and-sky-on-level-ground.md#the-mend-designed)). **It is computed
once at load from what the scene already holds and adds nothing resident**: a mask tile's words
and a decoded coverage map are held only while they are summed, and what stays is a float per
palette layer. The rule reads the scene's own materials and never a generator's name; the sky's
`local_albedo` and the region's hue follow it with no shader change. `frame_lighting` hands it to
both integrators as `FrameLighting::ground`, which becomes `gfx::ResolveParams::ground` and
`gfx::PathTraceParams::ground` (each block 16 bytes larger, 320 and 272). No scene-file field or
flag sets it yet. **Why 0.2:** under the stand-in sun and sky a face turned straight down then
receives about the light it did before the ground existed — 0.2 × 0.49 = 0.099 in luminance against
the old lower end's 0.15 × the sky's 0.68 = 0.102 — so a scene without a terrain changes the hue of
its undersides, a neutral ground under them instead of a blue sky, and hardly their brightness.

**The reference sees the same two halves** (`environment_radiance`): an escaped secondary ray
returns the sky's uniform radiance above the horizon and the ground below it, computed from the
same three numbers. **Uniform, not the ramp the sky used to be, and that choice is measured.** The
old environment was one ramp over the whole sphere, `sky · lerp(0.15, 0.35, d.y / 2 + 1/2)`, which
the resolve evaluated at the normal; its cosine-weighted mean is `sky · (0.25 + 0.067 n.y)`, so the
resolve had been 10% bright facing up and 18% dark facing down against its own reference, and exact
only at the horizon. Keeping that ramp above the horizon and putting the ground below it — the first
