  0.1 %, the median pixel moves 0.57 % (p95 6 %, p99 12 %) and the map of the change is the grain
  removed — noise everywhere, strongest under the eaves and in the walls' shade, no structure along
  the dry-stone courses' shadows or the eaves' line.
- **No bounce, no change**: with `renderer.gi.mode` off the village and the cave draw the bytes
  main draws (the EXRs' hashes equal).

**What it costs** (the same flights, alternated in one lease, medians of 331 frames; the GPU's
timestamps, the GPU otherwise idle under the lock, 7 to 43 % of the CPU busy with other agents'
builds and this branch's tests):

| GPU ms | before | the mend | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| village house 0: resolve / sample pass / frame | 2.21 / 1.19 / 6.38 | 2.90 / 0.98 / 6.86 | **+0.70 / −0.21 / +0.48** |
| the cave | 2.03 / 1.01 / 4.15 | 2.52 / 1.00 / 4.62 | **+0.48 / −0.01 / +0.47** |
| the lane (outdoors) | 4.29 / 0.80 / 7.04 | 5.12 / 0.91 / 7.95 | **+0.84 / +0.11 / +0.91** |

Above the first leg's 0.3 to 0.5 ms: the last level's eight lookups are paid on every faced pixel
whose walk stopped at its own level — on the lane that is nearly every pixel, and on a face's edge
twice (the second face). What would bring it down: reading the last level once for both faces
(its cells are a sixteenth as many and the faces blend by weight), skipping the shrinkage where the
own level's cells hold no measured spread above the model's (tame open ground, where the grain is
under the surface's texture), or keeping the last level's mean in the own cell at the fold (one
more half, which the cell does not have). The sample pass's change is the bounce's hits reading
the last level too and the machine's noise (the before pair moved 0.18 ms between leases).

**Off by default** (third leg, 2026-11-16). Performance comes first: a read that costs open ground
nearly a millisecond for a mend that helps indoors only and reaches 2.5 % stays off until it costs
nothing there. What stays on is the fold's measurement, which the resolve does not pay for and
which leaves the cell at 32 bytes: with `renderer.gi.spread` off the read is stage 8's, arithmetic
for arithmetic, and the fold's only change is where the bucket's pressure is kept (the high half of
the first word, a test against the same frame), so the picture is main's. `gi cache: a turn shows
no fill` passes again at the defaults, as on main (the furthest frame 1.18 of a luma step against
its bound of 1.23 on the RTX 5090). Where a case runs the shrinkage, its bounds stay those of the
features off (below). Off is not quite free: on the lane, held 690 frames in one lease, main's
build drew 6.39 ms of GPU twice and this branch with both features off 6.46 (the resolve +0.04, the
sample pass +0.03), the read's struct carrying the shrinkage's fields whether or not they are
used; the picture's mean is main's to 0.01 % and the change against main (median 0.4 %, p95 5.7 %)
is the size of main against itself under the bounce (p95 4.6 %), whose rays are not repeatable.

### R171: a cell's memory by its own spread

Third leg (2026-11-16; `renderer.gi.memory`, off by default for the four failures under "Why
it is off" below, **on since the fourth leg mended them**, [below](#r171-the-memory-made-right); `gfx::gi_memory_fold`, `gi_memory_cap`,
`k_gi_memory`, `k_gi_change_sigmas`, `k_gi_memory_back` in `gi_cache.h`, the same arithmetic in
`gi_update.slang`'s fold and its sample pass). The lever at the source: noise falls with the square
root of a cell's memory, and the fold now measures each cell's spread, which is what an adaptive
memory needs. A face's cell whose light holds still remembers up to sixteen times today's history
(`gi_memory_cap`: 4,096 samples for an own cell at the trickle's eleven a frame, 372 frames; 256
frames for one taking sixteen or more; never past 0xfff0, under the count's full mark), and lets
go at once when its light changes. Foliage cells keep stage 8's rule.

**The rule, and where it comes from.** A-SVGF (Schied, Peters and Dachsbacher 2018, "Gradient
Estimation for Real-Time Adaptive Temporal Filtering", read in its preprint, §3 and §5) replaces
SVGF's constant exponential factor α with α_i(p) = (1 − λ)·α + λ, where λ = min(1, |δ̂| / Δ̂) is a
temporal gradient — one sample per 3×3 stratum re-shaded with last frame's random numbers, so that
noise does not count as change — reconstructed over the screen and normalised by the brighter of
the two frames; α is 0.1 for A-SVGF and 0.2 for SVGF in its evaluation. It blends continuously
from the long history to none, and "must not drop history information solely due to changes in
random numbers" (§3). SVGF (Schied et al. 2017) and DDGI (Majercik et al. 2019, whose probes lower
their hysteresis on a change) could not be read tonight (both PDFs past the fetcher's size limit),
so nothing here is taken from them. **The constants here are this page's, not the paper's**: the
cache cannot re-shade last frame's sample, so its gradient is the difference between two histories
of one cell, its noise is the cell's measured spread, and its pooling is up the ladder rather than
over the screen; the cut is a step rather than A-SVGF's blend, because the cell has one bit to hand
down.

- **Two means of one cell.** The long mean is the one the read shows; it averages every frame since
  the light last changed, plainly while the count grows and exponentially at the ceiling. A short
  mean at today's history (`gi_history_cap`) is kept beside it as a half in the high 16 bits of the
  cell's second word, whose low 16 keep the stamp: fifteen bits of the frame and the foliage bit
  (the age is the frame less the stamp modulo 2^15, exact because the fold frees a cell 240 frames
  after its last sample). **The cell is still 32 bytes.** While the light is still the two hold the
  same light; after a change the short one follows within today's frames and the long one does not.
- **The test** is their difference against the band the short mean's own noise makes: a sample's
  variance from the measured spread (at the ceiling, the spread times (2T − n)/T) over the short
  mean's effective count 2·cap − n. Out of it by four deviations (`k_gi_change_sigmas`) the cell
  sets its changed bit (the half's sign, never otherwise set) and lets go.
- **Tested on the cell and up its ladder.** A fine cell's short mean is a 16-frame average of eleven
  samples a frame, 10 % of its light at one deviation indoors, so a 13 % change is far inside its own
  band; a coarse cell three levels up pools sixty-four of them, 1.6 %, and sees it. So the sample
  pass, which holds the slots of a sample's whole ladder, hands a coarser cell's changed bit to
  every finer cell of that ladder the next frame (word 2's top bit, beside the frame's count), and
  a cell told so lets go too. A single heavy sample moves a coarse cell a sixty-fourth as far.
- **Letting go** takes the long mean to the short one's level (its colour scaled to the short
  luminance) and the count to a quarter of today's history (`k_gi_memory_back`, 64 samples for an
  own cell), so the part of a change the short mean had already followed is taken whole and the
  rest is followed four times as fast as today, which makes up the frames the detection took.

**Why four deviations and a quarter**, by a simulation of the fold (sixteen coarse cells over 1,024
own cells, the plain wall's heavy samples, Python in the row's scratch; the CPU case below runs the
same fold in the tree): at five deviations the moved sun's 13 % was never seen, because a coarse
cell's long mean (93 frames at 704 samples a frame, the count's ceiling) and its short one (16)
stand at most 0.58 of a step apart, under five deviations of 1.6 %, and the own cells took 333
frames to settle against today's 50; at four it is seen, and they settle in 49. Letting go to
today's history whole left the remaining part of the change to a count that grows again from 256,
slower than today.

**What it does** (3840×2160, `--raster rt --shadows rt`, `bounce`, the first leg's held views and
metric, held 690 frames; main's copied-out build b299cce2 against this branch, one lease):

| grain, % of the indirect term, frames 180 / 320 / 600 / 690 | main | memory off | **memory on** |
|---|---|---|---|
| village house 0, near wall | 4.19 / 3.98 / 4.03 / 4.12 | 4.29 / 4.00 / 4.04 / 4.05 | **1.34 / 1.36 / 1.64 / 1.45** |
| village house 0, far wall | 4.03 / 3.98 / 3.94 / 3.94 | 3.99 / 4.09 / 4.06 / 4.03 | **1.40 / 1.45 / 1.70 / 1.56** |
| the cave (over level +3's picture) | 9.88 / 9.83 / 9.83 / 10.03 | 9.96 / 9.91 / 9.84 / 9.92 | **4.14 / 4.11 / 4.22 / 4.19** |

A third of the grain indoors and two-fifths in the cave, by frame 180 already, without the read's

count takes to regrow.

- **Corners** (as the second leg measured them, frames 180, 600, 690): the back wall at the floor
  0.993 main, 0.995 with the memory; at the side wall 1.015 and 1.024; the right wall under the
  ceiling 0.837 and 0.843. A longer memory averages a cell longer and moves no light between cells.
- **The light's level moves a little**: the village's walls' mean +0.5 % and +0.7 % over the frame,

  the ratio's cap of 16) and a half's rounding of a long mean's small steps.
- **Open ground** (the lane): the change against main is main's against itself (median 0.45 %,

**What it costs** (the same flights; GPU timestamps, medians of 690 frames, the GPU otherwise idle
under the lock, 8 to 34 % of the CPU busy with others): the fold 0.075 / 0.034 / 0.052 ms on lane,
village and cave either way; the frame's GPU total with the memory against without it 6.39 / 6.46
on the lane, 6.05 / 5.97 in the village, 3.96 / 3.95 in the cave: no measurable change.

**In the tree** (`gi cache key: a cell remembers longer while its light holds still, and lets go`,
the fold on the CPU; the box's GPU cases, RTX 5090, msvc-debug, 2026-11-16): the box's plain wall
goes from 1.76 % to **0.84 %**, under the owner's 1 %, with its next-frame correlation 0.99; after
the sun moves two hours the wall settles within a tenth of its change in 98 frames against stage
8's 114, after it is switched off (twelve hours, −37 %) in 39 against 57, after one hour (−9 %) in
104 against 117; `gi cache: a turn shows no fill` with the memory on stands at 1.05 of a luma step
against the features-off bound of 1.22 (its own still floor is 0.15 against 0.61, a quarter). The
CPU fold: an own cell's mean's variance 0.076 of today's, the moved sun settled in 42 frames
against today's 81, a light switched on or off in 46 and 42 against 52.

**Why it is off.** Every item the leg was held to holds but one, and two more were found:

- **A change the coarse cells cannot see trails.** A coarse cell's two means stand at most 0.58 of
  a step apart, so a change under about 11 % of its light never leaves four deviations of 1.6 %, and
  the own cells follow it at their long memory's rate: on the CPU a 10 % step settles in 258 frames
  against today's 84. On the GPU the frames-to-settle counts above look no slower because they
  count to where each run itself settles, and the memory's runs had not got there: 160 frames after
  the move the wall had moved −12.1 % against stage 8's −13.1 % for two hours and −7.3 % against
  −9.3 % for one, a fifth of a small change still to come. A sun that moves through a day is a
  stream of such changes. A longer memory that trails a changed light is the rule failing.
- **Cells that let go by chance show as blobs.** An own cell tests itself too, and leaves its band
  by chance about once in 90,000 frames: across a 4K view's fifty thousand own cells that is one
  every two frames, each a bright or dark round blob a cell wide that regrows over a hundred
  frames (the crops show them; the CPU case sends back 3 of 1,024 cells in 500 still frames, as
  the model expects). A cell taking under 64 samples a frame should not test itself — its parents
  see what it would — and that is the next step, not built.
- **The box's corner** (`gi cache: the grain on a plain wall`) rises 0.013 towards the wall's middle
  where the bound is 0.011 (half of level +2's lift), and **the indirect light's level** rises 0.2
  to 1.8 %. Neither is isolated: a long mean's half-precision steps losing the small ones of a skewed
  sample, or the bounce's hits reading quieter cells, would do both.

What would bring it on: a cell's own test only at 64 samples a frame or more; a finer change test
than two histories of one cell (A-SVGF's re-shaded sample is the published one; a coarse cell's
short mean handed to its children as a scale each frame is the cache's own); and the level's rise
found.

### The change between frames, as the eye sees it

Roadmap R171, fourth leg (2026-11-16). The owner, on the bounce indoors, in the cave and "anywhere
with lower light too": "it changes every single frame, and that's noticeable more than the pattern
itself". The three legs before measured the grain — the spread of the indirect term across a wall
in one frame — and a change from frame to frame is another quantity: a cell whose mean moves a
sixteenth of the way to each frame's samples shows a still pattern's grain and a pattern that
crawls. So the row's judge is measured where the eye takes it: **on the displayed picture**, after
the exposure, the curve, the dither and the 8-bit store, between consecutive frames of a held view.

**The measure** (`renderer::TemporalChange`, `temporal_change.h`; `engine-view --temporal <file>
--temporal-from <n>`, [apps](apps.md)): every pixel of every consecutive pair from frame n on,
its change of displayed luma in code steps (Y′ = 0.2126 R′ + 0.7152 G′ + 0.0722 B′ of the codes)
and of its light relative to its level (each channel through the encode's 2.2 power, Rec. 709's
weights, |L₁ − L₀| over their mean; a pixel black in both frames has none), as histograms over all
pixels and by the pixel's displayed luma in six bands (0–7, 8–15, 16–31, 32–63, 64–127, 128–255
codes), with each frame's mean level over the picture and its centre for a moving case. Beside
them (the sixth leg) **the forest session's own measure**, so that the engine and the forest quote
one number: the share of pixels of which *any one channel* moved a whole code or more, and three
or more (`Stats::any_channel_one`, `any_channel_three`; `channels` in the report). It is always
the larger of the two shares: a grey step moves all three channels and the luma by one, and a step
of one channel alone moves the luma by 0.07 to 0.72 of a code, which the luma's share does not
count. The
display's dither is a function of the pixel's place and nothing else, so a picture that does not
change does not change a code: with the bounce off, a held view of the cave or the village moves
no pixel at all (below), and every step the measure counts under the bounce is the cache's.

**What an eye sees, and the threshold.** Temporal sensitivity follows Weber's law in bright light —
a threshold that is a fixed fraction of the level — and the DeVries–Rose law in dim light, where
sensitivity grows only as the square root of the light, so the threshold fraction rises as the
light falls (Cai, Bozorgian, Ashraf, Wanat and Mantiuk, "elaTCSF: A Temporal Contrast Sensitivity
Function for Flicker Detection and Modeling Variable Refresh Rate Flicker", SIGGRAPH Asia 2024,
§4.1, read tonight; its transient channel is fitted to de Lange's and Kelly's classic flicker
data). A change between frames at sixty a second is a temporal frequency up to 30 Hz, on the
falling side of the curve's peak at 10 to 20 Hz, and the pattern the cache draws is the size of a
cell (13 px at 4K), a small area, which raises the threshold again. **No threshold is pinned from
those papers' numbers here** (the figures sit in plots this session could not read); the
threshold is the display's own quantum instead, which is stricter than any of them where it
matters: a whole step of an 8-bit code is 0.4 to 1.7 % of the light from the top band to the
middle ones (2.2 / V of it at code V), near the Weber threshold at the curve's peak, and 9 to 30 %
in the two darkest bands, where even the DeVries–Rose regime's raised threshold is passed. A
change under a step moves no code but by the dither's fixed noise, so it shows at most as a pixel
that flips one step now and then. **The bounce is held to this: at a held view, the share of
pixel-frames whose displayed luma moves a whole step is under 0.1 % in every band, and the 99.9th
percentile of the change under one step** — the picture changing no more than its own quantum does
by chance, in the band where a step is most visible (the dark ones) as in the rest.

**The scenes**: `content/test-scenes/cave/` (G213: one passage under a 4 m shaft at noon, a held
view and a walk in from under the shaft) and the village's house 0 (`interior-held.json`, and
`interior-door.json`, the flight's last metres through the door and held there); both READMEs say
how to fly them.

### R171: the memory made right

Fourth leg (2026-11-16; `renderer.gi.memory` **on by default**, and off again since batch 67's
fixes: "Off again: the pre-roll's promise", below). Leg 3's four reasons, each found
at its cause and mended there, with the bar above as the judge:

- **The level's rise was the half's rounding.** The long mean is three halves, eleven bits of
  mantissa, and at 4,096 samples an own cell moves it a 372nd of the way to each frame's mean: a
  step of one to two units of the half. Indoors a frame's mean is mostly a little under the light
  and now and then far over it (a few heavy samples), so rounded to nearest the many small steps
  down are lost and the rare large ones up kept: +8.9 % in the CPU case
  (`gi cache key: a long mean in halves holds its level when rounded without a bias`, the plain
  wall's samples), +0.02 % with the mean in float. The fold now rounds the long mean to the half
  below or above with the chance its distance from each says (`gfx::gi_half_unbiased`), so the half
  is the float in expectation (−0.02 % in the same case); the chance is drawn from a hash of the
  cell's own words (`gi_round_hash` of its frame's sums, count and old mean), which the same samples
  make the same wherever the scene stands. It is rounding noise of a unit of the half a frame, a
  twentieth of a display step, and only under the memory. The box's corner, which leg 3's memory
  lifted 0.013 against a bound of 0.011, is held to that bound again by its case.
- **The blobs were own cells testing themselves.** An own cell's short mean averages eleven samples
  a frame and carries 10 % noise; across fifty thousand of them one left four deviations every
  frame or two and showed today's noise again for a hundred frames. Only a cell taking
  `k_gi_test_samples` (64) a frame tests itself now — the third level of a ladder at the trickle —
  and the own cells hear of a change from their coarser cells, which pool 16 and 64 times their
  samples. The CPU case sends no cell back while still (leg 3's: 3 of 1,024).
- **The small change that trailed now follows at today's pace.** A tested cell whose two means
  stand between 2.5 (`k_gi_follow_sigmas`) and four of the short mean's deviations apart lets go of
  nothing, but sets a second flag (the short mean half's lowest bit, `k_gi_cell_following`), which
  the sample pass hands down its ladders like the change (`k_gi_frame_follow`, word 2's next bit),
  and the finer cells fold that frame at today's rate. A 10 % step, which leg 3's rule never saw,
  is crossed within a few frames: in the CPU case it settles within a tenth in 120 frames against
  today's 84 (leg 3's: past the run's 500). From a simulation of the fold (sixteen coarse cells over
  1,024 own ones, the plain wall's samples, Python in the row's scratch):

  | rule | still variance | change a frame, mean / p99 | 10 % step settles | 13 % | 30 % |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | today (memory off) | 6.7e-4 | 2.44 / 9.07 % | 50 | 50 | 51 |
  | leg 3 | 5.0e-5 | 0.149 / 0.564 % | over 600 | 60 | 47 |
  | following at 3 | 5.0e-5 | 0.149 / 0.564 % | 303 | 50 | 47 |
  | **following at 2.5** | 5.7e-5 | 0.151 / 0.565 % | 122 | 47 | 47 |
  | following only, no let-go handed down | 5.7e-5 | 0.151 % | 413 | — | 600 (the children never catch up) |

- **The settle after a cut was the plain mean's ramp.** Leg 3's long mean was the plain mean of
  every frame since its cell was made, up to its ceiling, so a cut's or a walk-in's first frames —
  the bounce still converging, each wall reaching the others through their cells — weighed in it as
  much as the settled ones, and their error decayed as one over the frames since: six seconds
  after the village's door the room stood 3.2 % over the memory off, and the cave's held view 4.5 %
  at six seconds and still falling. Past today's history the count now grows by half a frame's
  samples (`k_gi_memory_ramp`), so a frame's weight falls as the square of its age's share. In a
  simulation of a light starting 10 % high and settling with a 60-frame time constant, the gap at
  3, 6 and 12 s is 0.9, −0.1, −0.6 % with the memory off, 3.8, 1.8, 0.7 % with leg 3's, **2.4, 0.4,
  0.2 %** growing by half (the grain while the count grows 2.81 % against 2.73 %) and 1.5, −0.1, 0.0
  % growing by a quarter (3.87 %, the count growing four times slower). The ceiling is reached
  in 770 frames at the trickle's eleven a frame, against 350.

**What it does on the screen** (3840×2160, `--raster rt --shadows rt`, `bounce`, the RTX 5090,

**The final rule** (the ramp in; the same flights, the session locked, which leaves the temporal

### Off again: the pre-roll's promise

Batch 67's fixes (2026-11-17) set `renderer.gi.memory` back to **off by default**, and leave the
fourth leg's rules in place behind it, for the owner to decide. On, it breaks the pre-roll's
promise (stage 5, `gi cache: the pre-roll runs on the first frame and on a cut`): every frame after
a cut within twice the still picture's floor, and every frame from the twenty-fourth after a load
— on the RTX 5090 the cut's worst frame stood 0.577 from the long-held picture against a bound of
0.397, and the load's 0.551 against 0.391, on the fourth leg's branch alone as on the stack. The
cause, read in `gi_fold_main`: **the pre-roll seeds the long mean.** The pre-roll's sixteen steps
and the first frames after them are the bounce's first rounds, short of the light its later rounds
bring (in the case's white box those still arrive past the thirty-second frame); with the memory
off they leave the cell's plain mean once today's history has passed, but with it on the count
grows past today's history (by half a frame's samples a frame, the ramp) towards sixteen times it,
so the long mean keeps those unsettled samples in its average and lags the still picture for a
second and more. The `following` hand-down does not catch it here; read, not measured, a
converging cell's long and short means part by a drift under the 2.5 deviations it tests for, and
only a cell taking 64 samples a frame tests at all. The ways
open: hold a cell's count at today's history until its light has settled (its short mean steady
over its own history), or let a cut's or a load's cells start the memory only after the pre-roll's
window; either moves every picture the fourth leg measured, so it is a leg of its own, not a fix.

### R171: where a dark room's light comes from

Fifth leg (2026-11-17). The owner walked the forest's village with `renderer.gi.memory` on and the
grain "is still there". The forest session held their five marks (4K traced, four consecutive
frames 2.5 s into each hold): in the two dark rooms, walls at display code 27 to 30, **75 to 80 %
of pixels move a code or more every frame with or without the memory** (three codes or more: 11.0
% plain, 5.6 % with it; the light's change a pixel 5.9 and 4.8 % plain, 4.7 and 4.1 % with it),
where the brighter marks fall to 0.3 to 0.5 % with it. Four legs mended the cache's averaging; the
fault that is left is in what a dark room's cells are given to average.

**The arithmetic of one sample.** At 3840×2160 an own cell covers about a hundred pixels and the
trickle samples one in nine, eleven samples a frame, into a history of 256. One sample of value x
therefore moves the cell's mean by (x / m − 1) / 256 of itself, and a frame's eleven by
CV · √11 / 256, where CV² is a sample's variance over its mean squared. A display code at 28 is
2.2 / 28 = 7.9 % of the light. Where a cosine ray finds the room's light one time in thirty — a
doorway or a shaft seen from a wall across the room — x / m is thirty and **one sample moves the
cell 11 %: more than a code, from one ray's luck**; the frame's change is 5.5 · 3.3 / 256 = 7 % of
the light at CV² = 30, which is the forest's 5.9 %. That is the cause the measurements below
single out, among the five the row weighed:

| candidate | verdict | by what |
|---|---|---|
| too few samples a cell | part of it | eleven a frame into 256: a frame is 4 % of the mean's weight |
| samples that rarely find the opening | **the cause** | the heaviest hundredth of a wall's samples carry two fifths of its light (`gi cache key: a guided sample keeps the mean and loses its heavy tail`, the cave's and the box's numbers below); the change a frame follows CV, and CV² is 5 on a lit room's walls and 20 to 30 where the opening is small |
| the fold's weight | where the memory is off or let go | n / 256 a frame; sixteen times less under the memory, which is the brighter marks' 0.3 to 0.5 % |
| the read's interpolation | no | eight cells' shares average the change down, never up |
| quantization with no dither in time | no | with the bounce off no pixel of a held view changes at all (leg 4); a change under a code flips a pixel that sits at a rounding edge, which is the 0.69-code tail of every table here |

**The village's interior paths were stale**, which is why the engine's own dark room had stopped
showing the fault: batch 67's plan version 5 moved house 0's door 1.8 m and re-pasted
`camera-path.json`, not `interior-held.json` and `interior-door.json`, whose pose then stood at a
level of 5.6 codes where nothing in the picture moves. Both follow the flight's keys again.

**What the research says to do about it** (read where marked; the rest is named and marked unread):
- *Path guiding.* Mueller, Gross and Novak, "Practical Path Guiding for Efficient Light-Transport
  Simulation" (EGSR 2017; read from the authors' PDF: the abstract, §3 and §5.3): the incident
  radiance field is learned as an adaptively refined piecewise-constant function, a binary tree
  over space with a quadtree over directions in **world-space cylindrical coordinates, which
  preserve area ratios**; a leaf is refined until it holds no more than 1 % of the flux; each
  pass is guided by the one before and combined with BSDF sampling **by multiple importance
  sampling**, and stays unbiased because a pass's samples are independent given the distribution
  it draws from. Vorba et al., "On-line Learning of Parametric Mixture Models for Light Transport
  Simulation" (SIGGRAPH 2014; only the project page's abstract could be read: mixture models
  trained on-line from a stream of particles, for scenes "featuring difficult visibility").
- *Reservoir resampling.* Ouyang et al., "ReSTIR GI: Path Resampling for Real-Time Path Tracing"
  (HPG 2021; **abstract only**, the paper's PDF is over the fetch limit: resampling of multi-bounce
  indirect paths in space and time, MSE improvements of 9.3 to 166 times at one sample a pixel).
  It reuses a neighbour's sample point with a visibility ray and a Jacobian, and is the heavier
  road: stage 2 of the plan's GI (R68) is where it belongs.
- *Probes.* Majercik et al., "Dynamic Diffuse Global Illumination with Ray-Traced Irradiance
  Fields" (JCGT 2019): **not read** (the journal's page came back empty and its PDF is over the
  limit); nothing here is taken from it.
- *Fireflies.* Zirr, Hanika and Dachsbacher, "Reweighting Firefly Samples for Improved
  Finite-Sample Monte Carlo Estimates" (CGF 2018; read from the preprint's abstract, §2 and §3):
  rejecting outliers gives estimates that are too low, clamping bounds the variance by biasing,
  and their reweighting trades bias for variance by design. So the control that does not bias the
  mean is not a filter on the samples; it is sampling the heavy part often enough that it is not
  heavy, which is what a guide does.
- *What the eye sees* is the fourth leg's source and bar, above.

**What is built: a guide** (`gfx::k_gi_guide`, `renderer.gi.guide`, **off**: "Why both are off",
below; `gi_cache.h` and `gi_guide.slang`). The samples of a coarse cell learn where their light comes from, and half the
samples are drawn there:
- **A guide is a coarse cell's**: three levels above a surface's own, the ladder's top, on the
  surface's face, which on a flat wall pools sixty-four own cells and seven hundred samples a
  frame. It holds the share of the cell's light that arrived through each of 128 **equal solid
  angles of the sphere** — eight bands of the world's y by sixteen sectors of longitude about it,
  the cylinder's equal-area map as in Mueller's quadtree, fixed where they refine: a cell's 32
  bytes have no room for a tree, and a bin of a tenth of a steradian is the size of a doorway at
  three metres.
- **A sample is drawn from the mixture** of its cosine lobe and its guide, half each
  (`k_gi_guide_alpha`), and counts for the lobe's density at its direction over the mixture's
  (`gfx::gi_guide_weight`: the one-sample form of multiple importance sampling). Its expectation
  is the cosine ray's own whatever the guide holds — mirror through the triangle's plane and
  all — so the cells average what they averaged; no sample counts for more than twice what it
  counted alone, and one through an opening the guide knows counts for a small part of it and is
  drawn that many times more often. A guided direction the surface's own plane hides is not
  traced and counts for nothing.
- **It learns from every sample of its cell**, guided or not: the sample's weighted light into the
  bin of its direction, folded a frame at a time into a history of sixteen frames
  (`gfx::gi_guide_fold`), by the fold pass's first threads. **A guide is not drawn from until it
  is trained, and then by degrees** (the sixth leg, `gfx::gi_guide_alpha`): the fifth leg drew
  half of a frame's samples from any guide holding 256 samples, which a coarse cell at 4K takes
  in the one frame it is first seen. Mueller's practice, read from §3 and "Exponential sample
  count" of the paper above: the first distribution is learned with BSDF sampling alone, the tree
  being written is never the one drawn from, and each distribution has twice the samples of the
  one before so that it "does not become noisier". Here a frame is an iteration: a guide's first
  frame is cosine rays and no one draws from it, from its second fold its share of the mixture
  grows by a seventh of the half a fold, and it is whole at the eighth, half its history; a
  sample never weighs more than 1 / (1 − share) of what it weighed alone, so a guide two frames
  old can cost a sample 8 % where one frame old it could cost it twice. The pre-roll's steps are
  folds, so a cut's or a load's first picture has whole guides. One nothing sampled for 64 frames
  is freed. The picture's own samples make
  guides; a sample round the eye only finds one, and adds to it only once a fold has trained it
  (whether it finds one a pixel's sample is making in the same pass is the order of two threads).
- **Where it lives**: a table of one guide to 256 cells behind the cells in the cache's buffer
  (16,384 guides of 800 bytes, 12.5 MiB beside the cells' 144 MiB at the default size), found by
  the guide cell's hash; nothing in `ResolveParams` or the resolve's shaders changed (the flag is
  bit 25 of `gi_shell_word`), so the resolve reads what it read and costs what it cost.
- **General**: it keys on a surface's place and face and learns from what the rays bring back. An
  imported room with one window gets it as a generated one does; a scene in open air pays the
  guide's lookup and draws its samples about as it did, since the sky's light is nearly the lobe.

**The memory holds after a cold start** (`gfx::k_gi_step_hold`, `gi_memory_holds`; the memory
itself stays **off** with the guide, below). "Off again", above, found the pre-roll seeding the
long mean. Every fold of a cold frame's steps and of the 48 frames after it now leaves no count
past today's history (a cell that already remembered longer keeps its count), so the bounce's
first rounds are forgotten at today's pace and never enter a long mean. And the pre-roll's case
holds its frames to **today's history's floor**, measured in its own first run with the memory
off: with the memory on the long-held picture's floor is that of a history several times longer,
which no frame within a second and a half of a cut can have, whatever folds it; the bound in
absolute terms is the one the case held before the memory. With the guide and the memory both on
the case passes (the cut's furthest frame 0.43 of an 8-bit step, 1.2 floors of today's history
and 2.3 of its own; the load's frames from the twenty-fourth 0.56 against twice 0.40).

**Whether the memory is engaged** is counted now: `Stats::gi.let_go` (face cells whose fold gave
up a long history this frame), `.followed` (those folded at today's rate because a coarser cell
saw its light moving) and `.guided` (samples drawn with a trained guide), in `renderer.gi.log`'s
line.

**What it does on the screen** (3840×2160, `--raster rt --shadows rt`, `bounce`, the RTX 5090, the
session unlocked; `engine-view --temporal --temporal-from 150 --frames 186`: the forest session's
protocol, the 36 frames from 2.5 s after the view is first held, which is the first seconds a
person walking in sees and before a long memory has filled; the light's change is the measure's
`light.mean`, each pixel's change relative to its level):

| held view, frames 150 to 186 | the light's change a frame | pixel-frames stepping a whole code | the same in the 16–31 band |
|---|---|---|---|
| house 0 (level 20.9 codes), cosine rays, today's history | 1.46 % | 2.06 % | 2.41 % |
| house 0, the memory alone | 0.38 % | 0.098 % | 0.108 % |
| house 0, the guide alone | 0.86 % | 0.51 % | 0.60 % |
| house 0, **the guide and the memory** | **0.24 %** | **0.019 %** | **0.020 %** |
| cave (level 10.1), cosine rays, today's history | 1.60 % | 1.01 % | — |
| cave, the memory alone | 0.29 % | 0.020 % | — |
| cave, the guide alone | 0.55 % | 0.047 % | — |
| cave, **the guide and the memory** | **0.15 %** | **0.003 %** | — |

The guide alone takes the whole-code steps to a quarter in the house and a twentieth in the cave,
whose light comes down one shaft; under the memory the two leave a fifth of what the memory alone
leaves at 2.5 s, and the fourth leg's bar (under 0.1 % in every band) holds in every band of both
by then (the house's 32–63 band, 1 % of its pixels, stands at 0.089 %; the memory alone had it at
0.35 %). 99.99 % of the samples have a trained guide behind them by frame 150. The flora's motion
and a wind of 0.7, the forest's flags, change no number of the house's (0.238 % and 0.019 % with
them): nothing outside its door moves its light.

With the sun at a 24-minute day (sixty times real time) the house holds the same over frames 150
to 330: 0.015 % of pixel-frames step a code, the light changes 0.18 % a frame. Walking in at the
door the picture's level stands at 23.6 codes at the stop, 21.9 a second on and 21.3 three seconds
on, within 0.5 % of where it is six seconds on (the same walk with the two off was not flown
beside it, so how much of that is the memory's lag is not said).

**What it costs** (medians of the GPU's timestamps over frames 120 to 780 of held flights and the
lane's, main's copied-out build against the branch with both on, one lease, alternated, the
session locked on both sides): the cave 3.93 → 4.06 ms (`gi_trace` 0.871 → 0.949, the fold 0.094 →
0.112), house 0 5.62 → 5.76 (0.798 → 0.907, 0.085 → 0.108), the lane outdoors 6.67 → 6.85 (0.902 →
0.985, 0.138 → 0.169; the resolve 3.70 → 3.68, untouched). So **0.12 to 0.18 ms at 4K**, in the
sample pass (the guide's lookup, its draw over 64 words and its two adds a sample) and the fold
(sixteen thousand guides of 128 bins); indoors and outdoors alike, since an open scene pays the
lookup too. It is the device's memory traffic, so it scales with the samples a frame and not with
the scene. Ways down, not tried: a guide's shares as bytes, the draw by rows then columns.

**Why both are off.** (The fifth leg's account, kept as it was written; the sixth leg's, "R171:
the cases, each by its cause" below, took each of the five to its cause and corrects the first,
the second, the third's last part and the fourth.) With both on by default every `gi cache:` case
ran once (msvc-release, the RTX 5090): fourteen passed and five failed, and a default that fails
a case is not a default.
1. *The grain's law* (four times the rays, half the grain): the guide halves the base run's grain
   (0.89 % against 1.76 %) and what is left is no longer the cosine rays' sampling noise, so four
   times the rays take it to 0.83 of itself. The case now asks for cosine rays by name; its law is
   theirs.
2. *A scene moved by whole cells draws the same bytes*: two to four thousand pixels differed. A
   sample round the eye found, or missed, a guide a pixel's sample was making in the same pass.
   Mended as the bullet above says; **not run again**.
3. *A turn shows no fill*: the furthest frame 1.13 against a bound of 0.95, the largest change in
   the first seven frames 1.01 against 0.44. Two things: the case's run "with the features off"
   left the guide on, so its floor was 0.475 where main's is 0.61 (it must turn both off: the bound
   is main's absolute one); and frame 1 after the turn changes by 1.01 where main's changes by
   0.53, which is a guide trained on one frame's samples steering half of the next frame's. A
   guide should have several frames behind it before a sample is drawn from it
   (`k_gi_guide_trained`, 256 samples now).
4. *A turn to a stand of solid crowns*: with the crown's prior the first frame after the turn
   stands 28 steps under the long-held picture (it must stand nearer than without the prior, 8.8),
   and 17 under on the leaf cards. **Not explained**: foliage takes no guide and its cells no
   memory, so it is in what the crowns' samples read at their hits, or in the hold; it is the
   first thing the next leg runs with each of the two on alone.
5. The row's own case held the guide under the memory to less than the memory alone, which in the
   box is a difference of a few thousandths of a percent either way; that check is a message now.

With both off a frame draws what main draws: no sample reads or writes a guide and the buffer has
none, and the hold changes nothing without the memory. **That configuration was not run on the GPU
after these changes** (the sixth leg ran it, below); the cases above were run with both on, and the row's own case and the
pre-roll's passed in msvc-debug with both asked for (the pre-roll's against the fifth leg's own
restated bound: the sixth leg put main's back, and against it the case fails with the memory on).

**What this does not show, said plainly.** The forest's two dark rooms change 5.9 and 4.8 % a
frame with cosine rays, three to four times the engine's house at a *brighter* level, so their
light is carried by rarer and heavier samples than any room the engine's own scenes have; and
there the memory bought a fifth where the ramp's arithmetic and the house both say a factor of
3.8 at 2.5 s (1.46 to 0.38 %). The engine's scenes do not reproduce that: in the house the memory's
cells follow at today's rate on 190 cells a frame of 146,000 and let none go, in the cave on 660
and five. The reading left, **not verified**, is that those rooms' light really moves — the sun
through swaying crowns onto the ground outside their openings — so their coarse cells see it move
and their fine cells follow at today's pace, as the fourth leg built them to; the counters above
say so in one flight of the forest (`renderer.gi.log`, `--log info`). If that is it, the guide is
the half of the mend that applies there (a followed cell shows today's change, which the guide
halves or better where the light comes through an opening), and the other half is a fine cell
following its coarse cell's change as a ratio instead of re-averaging its own few samples, which
is not built. **A person in such a room would still see the walls' grain crawl, at about half its
amplitude or less; in a room whose light holds still they would see it settle under a display
step within three seconds of walking in.**

### Main's three: the cache's passes read what they declared only to write

Found the same morning (2026-11-18, a diagnosis row of batch 68), and **mended: the three pass
again, with the figures they had.** They had passed in batch 67's stack and gate on 2026-11-17
(06:49 and about 12:40) and failed in every run after 16:41 that day, when the display driver
went from **617.42** (the gate's own adapter line) to **621.24**; main's code had not moved.

**The cause is the engine's.** The cache's passes — `gi clear`, each `gi preroll sample` and
`gi sample`, each fold, and `gi stats` — declared the cache buffer as written only
(`Access::ComputeWrite`, and `TransferWrite` for the copy), so the barrier the render graph puts
between two of them named storage *write* as the only access behind it. Every one of them also
**reads** what the pass before wrote: the sample pass a bucket's keys and a cell's mean, the fold
the keys and the frame's sums, the copy the header's counts. A barrier orders an earlier write
before the accesses its destination mask names and no others (Vulkan's memory dependency: a write
is made visible to the access types of the second scope), so by the specification's letter those
reads were never ordered behind the writes. 617.42 ran one pass after the other anyway; 621.24
does not, and is entitled to. Nothing in the acceleration structures, the traversal or the
rays' arithmetic changed: with the mode off the same field draws the same bytes twice and moved.

**The evidence** (msvc-debug on the joined tree d2697bcf, the RTX 5090, 621.24; a scratch case
that drew the translation case's field several times in one process and compared pictures and
the passes' counts frame by frame):
- **The same scene drawn twice, not moved, differed**: 2,394 pixels of 16,384 under the sky alone
  (2,960 colour steps, the worst 4), 206 under the bounce (every one by a single code); moved by
  6,548 cells 3,050 and 283. Identifiers and depths never differed, and with the mode off nothing
  did. So the translation case was never measuring a move.
- **One frame, no pre-roll, no samples round the eye**: after one sample pass and one fold the
  cells held were **4,967, 4,612 and 4,927** in three renders of one scene, where the same frame
  holds **20,061** every time once the passes are ordered — three quarters of a first frame's
  inserts were cleared under it or folded before they landed (which, was not told apart). With
  the pre-roll's sixteen steps
  the counts agreed by the frame's end and the pictures still differed (802 pixels), the sums
  having been folded at different steps.
- The three cases fail the same way run by name and in the gate's whole part (`renderer.3`
  through CTest, 132 cases: 129 pass and these three fail, 4,097 / 3,992 / 198 / 308 colour
  steps; 0.975 against 0.633; 28.42 steps under), so no earlier case's state was in it.
- **With the three declarations made true** (below) every figure above is 0 and the cases draw
  what they drew on the old driver: 0 colour steps in all four; the first seven frames' change
  **0.534** against 0.633 (the gate's 0.534); a crown's first frame after a turn **3.23** steps
  under (the stack's 3.24).

The turn's two cases were the same fault seen from the other side: a first frame after a turn
reads cells the samples round the eye filled, and a fold that runs beside its sample pass folds
part of them a frame late or not at all, so the crowns stood 28 steps dark for a frame and the
turn showed its fill. Read, not measured: the figure repeated to a few hundredths (28.41 to
28.46 over the runs) because a mean over 8,000 crown pixels of that many lost samples does, not
because the passes ran in a fixed order.

**What a person saw of it: nothing in a held view, a dark first frame on a turn.** The joined
tree's msvc-release with and without the mend, 3840×2160, `--raster rt --shadows rt`, the
bounce, frame 186 of a held view, each flown twice (the session locked, the card otherwise
idle):

| held view | unmended, two runs | mended, two runs | unmended against mended | mean code, unmended and mended |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| the village's house 0 (`interior-held.json`) | 129,863 pixels apart (1.57 %), 129,461 of them by one code, none by more than two | 721 (0.01 %), every one by one code | 164,054 and 157,967 (2.0 and 1.9 %), none by more than four | 20.838 and 20.837 |
| the grove (its path's first key held, the flora's motion off) | 122,872 (1.48 %), every one by one code | **0** | 114,172 and 114,165 (1.38 %), every one by one code | 131.919 and 131.917 |

The change between frames is the same too (the house: 2.06 % of pixel-frames step a code
unmended and 2.05 % mended; the grove 0.081 and 0.080 %). So on a held view the fault moved one
pixel in sixty by a single display code and the level not at all, which no eye takes; what
showed was the frame after a turn or a load, where a cell's first samples are what the picture
reads: the crowns of the turn's case a ninth of the range dark for a frame (28 codes of 255,
where 3), and the first frames' change nearly twice the still picture's allowance. The house's
721 pixels between two mended runs are not explained here; the young rays' claim on their half
of the budget is by the order waves reach it, as the sample pass says, and is the candidate.
(An `engine-view` copied out of its tree finds no generated material sets, since the pack is
found from the executable's directory: the first pair flown here, from copies, differed in 99.8 %
of the house's pixels for that reason alone. A pair is flown from inside a tree, or with
`--materials`.)

**The mend** (`SceneRenderer::record_frame`'s cache block): the clear, the sample passes and the
folds declare `Access::ComputeReadWrite`, and `gi stats` declares the copy's read
(`TransferRead`) before its write, so each barrier names the reads too. The graph emitted a
barrier at each of these places already; only its masks change, and a frame's passes and their
count are the same. [gfx](gfx.md) has the rule ("A pass that reads back what it writes says
so").

**Not done.** Twenty-one of `record_frame`'s passes declare a compute access as written only
(the two culls, the pool's passes, the records chain, `tlas instances`, `trace`, `motion`,
`half sun` and others). Most write and never read back; none of their tests fail on this
driver; and none was read against its shader here for an atomic or a read of what an earlier
pass left. That audit, or the graph naming the read with every storage write — a shader that
can write through an address can read through it, an atomic is both, and the barrier is emitted
either way — is a row of its own.

### R171: on an ordered cache, and in the forest's own room

Seventh leg (2026-11-18, on the base with the passes ordered, above). The fifth and sixth legs
took every figure on a cache whose passes the new driver ran out of order, and never stood in
the room the owner saw the grain in. Both are done here. **Nothing is mended and no default
moves in this leg**: it is the tables again, and the forest's room found and measured.

**The tables stand.** Held views, 3840×2160, `--raster rt --shadows rt`, the bounce, frames 150

**The sixth leg's three unexplained findings.**
- *The guided wall under the cosine rays' under the sky alone*: the figure stands, 0.40 % under

  under with the guide, where the five differences scatter by 0.015 % among themselves. So a

  instead of its fourth to sixth) the same five eyes stand 0.33, 0.31, 0.24, 0.28 and 0.25 %
  under. A change of which numbers of one sample's stream feed which draw is not allowed to
  move an unbiased estimate by a quarter of its bias, so the suspect is the joint distribution
  of a sample's successive numbers (`rng_next` is a 32-bit generator stepped from a hashed
  state; the sixth leg's check looked at the choice against the direction's two numbers at two
  parts in a thousand a bin, and four in the opening's bins is all it takes). The next step
  needs no GPU: a census on the CPU of the shader's own stream over its states, for the box's
  bins.
- *The memory failing the pre-roll's bound after a cut*: **it stands, and it is now the only

**What a person sees.** At the defaults (both off) a dark room's walls crawl as they did: a
third of the pixels flip a code every frame. With `renderer.gi.memory` and `renderer.gi.guide`
on, in the engine's rooms and in the forest's room alike, one pixel in twenty flips in any
channel and three in a hundred thousand step a whole luma code: the wall holds still two and a
half seconds after walking in. That is the same answer the fifth leg gave for the engine's
rooms, now with the forest's room in it and on a cache whose passes run in order.

**For whoever flies a cut of someone's world.** A scene cut from a larger one needs the
`formation` block where a terrain material asks for it, and loses every mask region that names
a water body with the water. A first load with a resolve variant the pipeline cache does not
hold compiles one pipeline on one thread (565 s here for the variant with water and terrain),
and a run ended before it exits saves none of it: without the water the cut drew the village
scene's variant, which the slot's cache already held, and loaded in 70 s.

## The sun's day

*A scene that names a sky takes its sun, its moon and its sky from it instead, on the world's clock ([The sky](#the-sky)); everything in this section is the stand-in's, which every other scene still draws, to the bit.*

The stand-in sun has a day (2026-09-27, lighting.h; engine-view's `--sun-rate` and `[` / `]`, [apps](apps.md#--interactive-a-camera-somebody-flies)). **A day that has not moved is the sun every frame had, to the bit**, which is the rule the rest follows from: a frame is told how far into the day it is — `FrameDesc::sky_time_s`, game seconds past the scene's epoch, 0 by default — and at 0 `sun_on_arc` returns `sun_direction(azimuth, elevation)` of the start (`--sun`, `RenderSettings::sun_*` or the `renderer.sun.*` tunables) and `lighting_options` lets it shine at 1, so every caller that never heard of the day draws what it drew. The time is the host's to keep, not the frame index's, because the rate the day runs at changes while it runs: engine-view integrates it (`view::SunDay`, the rate times each frame's simulated seconds), and a flight takes `FlightOptions::sun_rate` and lights path frame f at `sun_rate · f / 60`, which is what engine-view's plain offscreen run lights frame f with. The reference path tracer takes the same number (`ReferenceSettings::sky_time_s`, and `world_time_s` beside it), so the two integrators still light a comparison alike.

**The arc is the start's own diurnal circle.** The sun turns once a game day (`k_sun_day_s`) about the celestial pole, which stands `renderer.sun.arc_tilt_deg` above the northern horizon — north is −z, the camera paths' and `--start`'s "looking north", so east is +x and south +z — westward, a morning sun climbing towards the south and an evening one sinking towards the west. It is the circle about the pole **through the start**, so the start is on the arc whatever it is, and the season is whatever the start implies: the circle's angle from the pole is the declination. The tilt is the latitude — 0 the equator, where the circle stands upright and an equinox sun crosses the zenith, 90 a pole, where it circles at one elevation — and its default of 40° is a mid-latitude. The default start (south-east, 53° up) at 40° is a mid-morning in April (declination 9.75°): the sun culminates due south at 59.75°, is above the horizon for 13.1 hours, and sets 12.8° north of west. Fitting a circle through the start, rather than placing a sun by a date and an hour, is what keeps the still day exact; a scene that wants a date and a latitude is a scene format's question when there are authored lights. `sun_on_arc` evaluates the turn in `f64` (Rodrigues about the pole, the day reduced to a fraction of a turn first so a year of game time stays exact) and is continuous in the time.

**Below the horizon the sun fades, and only its strength follows the day.** `sun_intensity` is 1 at and above the horizon and fades to nothing `k_sun_twilight_deg` (6°) below it, a smoothstep in the direction's y; a frame of a running day shines by it, so night is the sky's ambient and the ground hemisphere alone, and the sun no longer lights a slip face from underneath. At time 0 the start shines at 1 wherever it stands — a `--sun` below the horizon is lit as it always was until the day moves it and by the rule after, which is a step once, at the day's first frame; a start at or above the horizon has none. **The colour is left alone**: the sun is white, the sky is `k_sky` and the two point lights are what they were. The sun has no colour in `ResolveParams` or `PathTraceParams` to redden at dusk without a shader change, and the sky is the resolve's clear value and the reference's background as well as the hemisphere's upper half ([Reference renderer](#reference-renderer) says why those are one constant), so a darkening sky is three changes in step — a night sky is not built. A moving sun also turns the cascaded maps' light frame, which a still sun kept fixed, so their texel grid rotates with the day; nothing snaps it.

**What holds it.** `sun_arc_tests.cpp`, with no device: at time 0 the arc is `normalize(0.4, 0.8, 0.45)` to the bit at the defaults and `sun_direction` of any start — four of them, one below the horizon, at three tilts — to the bit, shining at 1, and `frame_lighting` hands the resolve and the reference the same sun as before; over a day at a game minute a step the direction is a unit vector the same angle from the pole throughout (to 10⁻⁶), turns no more than a minute of the day between steps, is back at the start after a day and after 365, moves a second's worth of a turn in a second, climbs towards the south from the default morning, culminates due south at 90 − tilt + declination, and is 30° below the horizon and dark twelve hours on; at the equator an east sun is overhead six hours later and at a pole the elevation holds all day; and the fade is 1 above the horizon, 0 past twilight, about a half at −3° and never rises as the sun sinks, with a setting sun's frames shining by it.

## The sky

**A scene that names a sky is drawn under a physical atmosphere; one that names none draws exactly what it drew** (2026-09-30; `sky.h`, `SkyPass`; [ADR-0048](../adr/0048-the-sky-is-a-providers-model-drawn-by-the-renderer.md)). The *model* — the air, where the sun and the moon are, the stars — is a sky provider's, looked up by the name the scene's `sky` entry gives (`engine.scene.Sky`, "earth" by default: the sky capability's, [sky](sky.md); the registry is [scene_gen](scene_gen.md#sky-providers)'s). The *drawing* is `domain/gfx`'s functions and tables ([gfx](gfx.md#the-sky)) and this module's passes. Nothing here names a capability: `SkyPass::create` makes the provider through the registry, and a build without one refuses a scene with a sky when it is read.

**What a scene says** (`engine.scene.Sky`, `Scene` version 6, absent by default): `latitude_deg` (30), `day_of_year` the world's epoch begins on (80, the March equinox), `moon_age_days` at the epoch (0, new; 14.8 is full), `turbidity` (2: very clear; a desert is 2.5–4), `ground_albedo` of the region the sky sees below its horizon (0.3; its hue is the scene's own ground's, its brightness this), `moon` and `stars` (on), and the exposure: `exposure` `Auto` or `Fixed`, `exposure_compensation_ev` (0), `exposure_ev100` (15). The erg and the storm erg name one; their READMEs say what to look at.

### What a frame does with it

**Four passes under one timer zone, `sky`, before the resolve** (`record_frame`): the transmittance and multiple-scattering tables on the scene's first frame (they depend on the air alone), then every frame the sky-view table (the sky from the eye's height, the sun and the moon both scattering), the aerial-perspective volume (the air between the eye and anything up to 32 km, by direction and distance, so one table serves every view of a surround or Panini frame) and one workgroup that sums the frame: the ambient term's nine harmonics, the ground's radiance, the sun's and the moon's light at the eye, and the exposure. Everything is a buffer read through a device address, so the passes add no binding. The frame's `gfx::SkyParams` block rides in the resolve's per-slot buffer behind the ground's detail, and the frame's sums are copied into the statistics block, read one frame late like every count (`Stats::sky`).

**What the resolve does with a sky** (`visibility_resolve.slang`, [gfx](gfx.md#the-sky)):

- **An uncovered pixel is written** with the sky along its direction (`sky_background`: the sky-view table, the night's glow, the sun's disc with its limb darkening, the moon's lit disc and the stars, dimmed and reddened through the air), where the stand-in's clear-and-discard wrote nothing. A Panini view's pixel takes its source direction. **The direction is the view's rotation and projection and nothing else**: `SkyView::clip_to_ray` is `View::clip_to_ray`, the inverse of the projection times the rotation with the eye at the origin, and the pixel's clip-space point at infinity through it is the direction, the same bits wherever the camera stands. It was the inverse view-projection, a point a decimetre ahead less the eye in world coordinates, and two kilometres out that difference was a few pixels wrong and differently wrong at every step, which is the sky the owner saw shaking behind the endless desert ([gfx](gfx.md#the-sky), the fifth lesson); the ray path's primary rays and the reference's camera rays take their directions through the same function.
- **The sun's light at a surface is the sky's**: its illuminance outside the air through the transmittance from the surface's own height towards it, so it reddens and dims through the air mass and is gone below the planet's horizon; a directional light of the array (the moon) the same.
- **The ambient term is the sky's hemisphere**: the nine harmonics at the shading normal in place of the two uniform halves, the lower half the local ground (the scene's ground albedo, a terrain's sand) lit by the sun, the moon and the sky.
- **The air to the surface** from the aerial-perspective table: every covered pixel is its colour times the air's transmittance plus the light the air scatters in. Past 32 km the lookup continues from the last two slices (F3): the transmittance as an exponential of the table's own slope at its end (the last two slices' difference times d slice/d d = depth/2D = 0.5 per km), the in-scatter by that slope falling away at the same rate (floored at 0.001 /km) towards a finite limit, so value and slope are continuous where the table ends (across it: a value step of 3e-6 of the value, a slope change of 0.4%) and a far ridge at 60 km is hazier than at 32 rather than the same; nearer than 32 km nothing changes, the lookup being the old one, `sky_reference.h` mirrors it, and the one extra table fetch is made only past the end.
- **Exposed and shown**: times the frame's exposure, through the display's shoulder, then the output encode — the transfer curve and the dither ([below](#the-output-encode)).

**The moon is a light**: the array's light 0, directional (`gfx::k_light_directional`, `ResolveLight::position_radius` the direction towards it), at its illuminance outside the air (its phase and distance, the provider's), dimmed through the air like the sun. It is **shadowed as the sun is where the shadow mode allows**: `--shadows rt` traces it like every light of the array, and `--shadows csm` draws the cascaded maps **from the moon** when the sun is below the horizon and the moon above it (`FrameSky::moon_key`; `gfx::ShadowMapParams::light` says which light the maps are, 0 the sun, i + 1 light i, and the resolve asks the maps only for that light). The stand-in's two orbiting point lights are not lit under a sky.

**The ray path and the reference draw the same sky.** The ray path's uncovered pixels are the resolve's. The reference path tracer's primary misses are `sky_background`, its next-event estimate of the sun and the moon goes through the same transmittance, an escaped ray sees the scattered sky above the horizon and the ground below it (never the discs, which next-event estimation reaches), the air is applied at the first hit, and the picture is exposed and shouldered by the frame's own numbers; `ReferenceSettings::sky_time_s` is the frame's sky seconds past the epoch.

### The discs' sizes

**The sun's and the moon's discs are their real angular sizes** (`gfx::SkyParams::sun.w` and `moon.w`, radians, the provider's `SkyState::sun_radius`, `moon_radius`): the earth provider gives the sun 695,700 km over its distance, 4.65 mrad (0.2665°) at 1 AU and within the orbit's 1.7 % of it all year, and the moon 1,737.4 km over the ephemeris's distance, 4.52 mrad (0.259°) at the mean 384,400 km and from 0.245° to 0.279° as its orbit swings. Measured on the erg's sky three years and a hundred days in (an April day): the sun 4.644 mrad (0.2661°), the moon 4.440 mrad (0.2544°) (`sky_scene_tests.cpp` holds both to the real values). **`Sky.disc_scale`** (scene version of `Sky` 2, default 1, physical; [1, 20]; engine-view's `--sky-disc-scale` for looking) multiplies both radii for a game that wants larger discs, **without changing the sky's light**: the sun's disc spreads its illuminance over its own solid angle (`sky_sun_disc`), so a disc k times wider is k² dimmer by construction; the moon's is a Lambertian sphere whose radiance does not depend on its size, so its albedo in the block (`moon_illuminance.w`, read by the disc alone) is divided by k² (`SkyPass::fill`). What the sun and the moon give the sky, the ground and the shadows — `sun_illuminance`, the `rgb` of `moon_illuminance`, the directions — is untouched, and at 1 the block is the bytes it was.

### One world clock, and the day's length

**Until 2026-10-20 everything that moved ran on one clock, the sky's** — the sky at the ground's surface time plus `FrameDesc::sun_time_s`, the water at `water_clock` of the same sum, the medium's drift, the fire's flicker and the flora's gust on it too — chosen so the sun's hour, the wind's day and the moon's month could never disagree. What the owner saw was its cost: with the proof-of-concept game's sun at 60× the smoke, the waves, the sway and the cloud drift ran at 60× too; raising the dunes' time-lapse turned the screen into a day-night strobe, because the sky stood on the moving ground's surface time; and a production game that wants a sixty-minute day with every animation at real speed could not have one. **Now a session has three times, each a function of its ticks** (`renderer::WorldClocks`, `systems/renderer/clocks.h`; [ADR-0056](../adr/0056-one-world-clock-and-the-days-length.md); roadmap R88). With `session_s = ticks / tick_hz`, real seconds and never scaled:

| clock | what | sum |
|---|---|---|
| **world** | real time scaled by the **world rate**: what every surface and medium that moves reads | `world_start + Σ dt · world_rate` |
| **sky** | the sky's hour: absolute game seconds since the world's midnight epoch | `epoch + sky_start + Σ dt · sun_rate` |
| **ground** | the dunes' time-lapse (geology), riding the world clock | `epoch + time_rate · (world − world_start)` |

`epoch` is the scene's `Terrain.time` (0 without a terrain; `GpuScene::epoch_s`, `scene_epoch_s`), so the storm erg still opens at 12:50 under a 12:50 sun. `sky_start` is `--time-of-day`'s offset from it. **The day's length is the knob, in real seconds**: `sun_rate = 86,400 / day_length_s`, so a sixty-minute day is `day_length_s` 3,600 (`sun_rate` 24), a real day 86,400; 0 holds the sky. The rate is what is stored — every flag, key, request and state file before the day length spoke it, and a rate round-tripped through a length would not come back to its own bits — and `--day-length`, `RenderClock.day_length_s` and the state file's `day_length_s` say it the other way. **The world rate** (1 by default, real time; `--world-rate`, `RenderClock.world_rate`, engine-view's `,` and `.`) scales the world clock and, through it, the dunes, and never the sky: the owner inspects the sand moving, a fire's smoke or the waves at any speed, from a pause to a fast-forward, while the sky keeps the pace its day length gives it. That the day is in real seconds rather than world seconds is the choice that keeps a replay and the state file simplest: the two rates are independent sums of the same ticks, a world rate of 0 is well defined (everything on the world clock pauses, the sun keeps moving), and "scaling the day with the world" is the same statement for a day measured in world seconds.

**The rule a reader follows: a light source is on the sky's clock, a surface or a medium that moves is on world time, the ground's geology is on its own time-lapse.** Every reader, and which clock it reads:

| reader | clock | where |
|---|---|---|
| the sun and the moon (place, light, the moon's phase), the sky's light, the stars, the exposure | sky | `SkyPass::evaluate(epoch + FrameDesc::sky_time_s)` |
| the stand-in sun (a scene with no sky) | sky, as seconds past the epoch along its arc | `lighting_options(settings, sky_time_s)` |
| the wind the weather feels — the trees' gust direction and strength, the medium's wind (dust, smoke bend), the crest plumes' hour | the record's hour at the **sky** time (weather follows the day) | `flora_frame`, `MediumPass::record`, `build_plumes` |
| what that wind moves — the sway, the smoke's and the clouds' drift distance, a flame's noise | world | `flora_part_poses`, `CloudDrift::offset_m`, `medium_fire` |
| the water's waves | world, `water_clock(world_time_s)` | `ResolveParams::water_time_s` |
| the sun's glitter on the water | the sun's place from the sky, the waves from the world | the resolve, as it already decomposed |
| a fire's flicker and its light | world | `FireSet::burn(world_time_s)` |
| the dunes' fields, saltation, the ripples' wind | ground (the surface time) | `TerrainMotion`, `GpuScene::ground_time_s` |

**What a frame carries**: `FrameDesc::world_time_s` (world seconds) and `FrameDesc::sky_time_s` — the sky's game seconds **past the epoch**, so the sky's hour is `epoch_s() + sky_time_s`. It replaces `sun_time_s`, which was an offset on the ground's *moving* surface time: the same number wherever the ground stands still — so every frame lit at a held or real day draws the bytes it drew — and the sky's own wherever a time-lapse moves the ground. 0 is the scene's own hour; a host with no day of its own leaves both at 0. `FramePassContext` carries `world_time_s` and the sky's hour, absolute. The CPU sums are in the order the one clock added them (`epoch + (start + rate · ticks / hz)`), so a frame at a still or real day draws the bytes it drew. **What moved**: the water, a fire's flicker and the medium's flames and drift now stand at the world time, which starts at 0 — they stood at the ground's time plus the sun's offset, which was the scene's `Terrain.time` for a scene with a sky or a detailed terrain, and they no longer freeze when the sun is held (engine-view's default sun rate is 0, and its default world rate 1); the flora's sway is the same number it was (`frame_index / 60` for a host at 60 frames, now through `world_time_s`), and its gust, the medium's wind and the plumes stand at the sky's hour, which is the old sum wherever the ground does not move. A dune time-lapse at any rate leaves the sun where the sky's hour says (`sky_scene_tests.cpp`, "a dune time-lapse leaves the sun alone": 10,000× for a minute, the sun to the bit). The crest plumes' brinks are the ones of the sky's hour, so under a fast time-lapse they lag the drawn brinks by however far the sand moved in the hour — metres a year — which costs nothing visible and keeps the plume cache on the sky's hour instead of rebuilding it every ground hour.

**Who sets the clocks.** A host passes the frames' clocks through `frame_clock` (request.h): frame f of a run at `f / 60` real seconds, its world at `world_rate · f / 60`, its sky at `sky_start + sun_rate · f / 60` past the epoch (`FrameClock::world_at`, `sky_offset_at`), and a flight the same (`FlightOptions::sun_rate`, `world_rate`, `sky_start_s`; `sky_start_s` was missing at first, and a benchmark asked for 16:00 flew at the ground's midnight). The dunes' motion runs at `time_rate · world_rate` per real second (`settings_for` multiplies a request's `time_rate` by its `world_rate`; engine-view's `settle_world_rate`). engine-view's window keeps two sums a frame's ticks advance — `view::SunDay` and `view::WorldDay` (time_controls.h) — and its keys change their rates, never where they stand ([apps](apps.md#the-two-rates-on-four-keys)). A `--game` session's frames take both from the game runner's clocks, stepped a tick at a time at the rates the keys had set by each tick, in the window, in an offscreen replay and in a `--capture` alike, so a replay draws the sky and the world the live session drew ([apps](apps.md#the-game-contract), roadmap P44); a session without `--game` is drawn from the frame index offscreen, as before. The game's hour is apparent solar time (the sun is due south at 12:00). A terrain whose ground time nothing else sets — no detail block, no time-lapse — still has its surface time set to the scene's when the renderer is made, for whoever reports it.

### Exposure

**Before this, there was none.** The resolve wrote `pow(radiance, 1/2.2)` into a UNORM target and the stand-in's radiances were chosen to land in [0, 1]; the sky was `k_sky` cleared into the target and the resolve discarded the pixel (`sky_is_clear`). That is still what a scene without a sky gets.

**With a sky, a declared rule** (`gfx::sky_exposure_ev100`, the same in `sky.slang`): **incident-light metering at ISO 100**, `EV100 = log2(E / 2.5)`, whose intent is that a white Lambertian surface lit by E is shown at 1.0 and an 18% card at middle grey. E is the sun's and the moon's illuminance on a level surface at the eye plus **π times the sky's mean radiance** over its dome — not the sky's own level illuminance, which weighs the horizon by its elevation's sine and so read a dusk whose light is all at the horizon as darker than it is, and exposed it until the glow and the sand were white. A photograph's rule is right for noon and wrong for a sunset or a night, which an eye does not compensate for fully, so **below a knee each further stop of darkness is compensated by only a share of a stop**: `renderer.sky.exposure_knee_lux` (40,000 lux, a clear sun about 20° up) and `renderer.sky.exposure_slope` (0.75). Chosen by eye on the erg's captures ([the experiment](../experiments/sky-2026-09-30.md)): noon and a late afternoon expose like a photograph, a sunset about a stop under one, civil twilight two and a half, a full-moon night four and a half, and a moonless one nearly six. Then the scene's `exposure_compensation_ev`, the run's (`RenderSettings::exposure_ev`, engine-view's `--exposure`), the frame's (`FrameDesc::exposure`, engine-view's `-` and `=`) and `renderer.sky.exposure_compensation_ev` add; a fixed EV100 — the scene's `Fixed`, `--exposure-ev100`, or `0` in engine-view, which holds the current one — replaces the rule. **The rule alone has no eye adaptation**: the exposure is the sky's light at the eye with no history, indoors as out; the eye's adaptation is a pass of its own, off by default ([below](#exposure-the-eyes-adaptation)). The meter's reading, the EV100 and the exposure are in `Stats::sky` and engine-view's summary.

**The meter is a function of the frame, to the bit.** `sky_frame_main` (`sky_luts.slang`) is one workgroup of 256 threads: each sums its strided share of the 2,048 directions in a fixed order, then a tree over shared memory adds the 256 partial sums in a fixed order, and one thread meters from the total. No atomics, no reduction across workgroups, no CPU sum, no history: the same frame gives the same `SkyFrame` in any renderer and any process on one device (`sky_scene_tests.cpp`, "the same frame meters the same exposure in fresh renderers"). What it is a function *of* includes the eye's altitude to its last bit — every table of the sky is built from it — so two hosts agree on the exposure exactly when they agree on the camera exactly. On 2026-10-03 they did not: engine-view's `--orbit 22` stood 0.8 mm above the protocol's `orbit {distance: 22}`, the metered sum differed in its seventh digit, and a channel byte moved at a pixel or two; the meter was suspected and was not the cause ([One request, two hosts](#one-request-two-hosts)).

**The display's shoulder** (`gfx::k_sky_shoulder`, `renderer.sky.shoulder`, 0.6): an exposed channel at or below 0.6 is shown as it is, one above rolls off towards 1 with the line's slope where they meet. A sky puts the sun's aureole and a sunset's horizon several times above the ground it is metered from, and a clip turned them into white bands; per channel, so a bright orange stays orange until it is very bright. The stand-in keeps its clip.

### Exposure: the eye's adaptation

**The frame exposed for what the eye is looking at** (2026-11-17, roadmap R168 and R57's first leg; `exposure.h`, `src/exposure_pass.h`, `shaders/exposure.slang`; the sources and every constant's origin in [the experiment](../experiments/eye-adaptation.md)). The rule above meters the sky's light at the eye, so a room at noon is exposed for noon: the village's rooms at 20 to 38 of 255 with the bounce ([village](village.md#what-was-measured)). With adaptation on, a frame pass of the renderer's own at `FramePassStage::Exposure` — after every pass that composites light, before a reconstruction — meters the picture the resolve drew and the encode multiplies it by the difference:

- **The meter**: one pixel in each 2 × 2 tile of the **metered view** — the one whose rectangle holds the target's centre: the single view, a surround's centre monitor (the side monitors are the periphery, plan 04 §4.6, and are not metered, so a window at the edge of one never pumps the frame), the whole of a Panini view — taken back to cd/m² through the exposure the resolve drew at and counted into 128 quarter-stop bins from 2^-10 to 2^22 cd/m², **centre-weighted** (a disc a third of the view's width across weighs 16 against 1: 74.6% of the weight on 16:9, a camera's centre-weighted meter). The bins are integers added in workgroup memory and then by atomics, so the count is the same whatever order the threads ran in.
- **The reading**: the log mean of the weight between the 10th and the 90th percentile (`renderer.exposure.low`, `high`): the field's level with the doorway, the sun and the darkest jamb left out.
- **The target**: the exposure that shows that luminance where Reinhard's operator shows it at the **eye's key** (Krawczyk's `a(L) = 1.03 − 2 / (2 + log10(L + 1))`: 0.03 on a moonless ground, 0.42 in a room lit to 100 lux, 0.72 on sunlit sand; the operator scales the adapting luminance to the key and maps it through `Y / (1 + Y)`, so it is shown at `a / (1 + a)`), `EV100 = log2(π L (1 + a) / (2.5 a))`, less the compensation the rule takes (the scene's `exposure_compensation_ev`, the run's, the frame's and the tunable's, as the sky block carries them), held within `renderer.exposure.min_ev100` and `max_ev100` (−6 and 18). On sunlit sand it is three quarters of a stop under the rule (the rule shows the sand at its albedo, near white; the eye at 0.42); in a room at 19 cd/m² it is 6.3, nine stops up from noon's 15.4.
- **The speed**: an exponential in stops each frame, `ev += (target − ev)(1 − e^(−dt/τ))`, so a step is the same however time is cut into frames. Darkening the picture is light adaptation, τ 0.1 s by day (the cones) to 0.4 s at night (the rods), blended by the rods' share `0.04 / (0.04 + L)`; brightening it is dark adaptation, **1.5 s, a game's choice** (the eye's takes minutes; the sources leave it out): a room still reads dark a frame after the door and is within a quarter stop of its exposure 5.4 s after a nine-stop step (the eye: "after several seconds the silhouettes of objects start to appear", Krawczyk 2007 §3.1.5). `dt` is `FrameDesc::dt_s`, or where a host gives none (engine-view, the protocol) the frame index's at 60 Hz, the clock a path and a capture advance by; the first frame metered, and a frame whose index went back, take the target at once.
- **Applied in the encode**: the state's scale, `2^(base − ev)`, is one float the encode multiplies the linear picture by before the display's curve (`FramePassReport::exposure`, `FrameEncodePush::exposure`). The resolve still draws at the rule's exposure, so a dim room's values sit low in the half-float image (19 cd/m² at noon is 7 × 10^-4, a normal half; 0.05 cd/m² is a subnormal one, steps of 3%), which is the reason a second leg should hand the resolve last frame's exposure instead (pre-exposure). **With the accumulation on as well** (both are off by default), the accumulation blends what it holds as the display shows it, through the display's knee and ceiling on the *unexposed* picture, while this scale is applied after it in the encode, so its clip boxes and its blend are taken at the wrong level whenever the exposure is far from 1 (review A4, batch 68; noted, not mended: the fix is to hand the accumulation the frame's exposure).

**Off unless a scene or a tunable turns it on**: `Sky.exposure: Adapted` (scene.schema; the rule's knee and compensation otherwise as `Auto`) or `renderer.exposure.adapt`. Without either nothing is made and no frame pass is registered, so every picture is the bytes it was. **A fixed exposure value pins it** — the scene's `Fixed`, `--exposure-ev100`, a frame's fixed request, `0` in engine-view — the pass then reports itself pinned, its scale is 1, and the frame is the rule-pinned picture through the linear image (a code apart at most, the frame passes' half). So a capture, a test and a benchmark hold exposure by naming one. Whether the default should flip: not yet — measured, it draws the village's rooms and the cave where main drew them black, and lifts a shaded street front about two stops until its sky burns ([the experiment](../experiments/eye-adaptation.md#what-it-looks-like)); a cap under the open sky and pre-exposure come first, then the owner's walk. A scene that wants it says `Adapted`.

**Deterministic along a path**: integer bins, one thread's loop in bin order, the frame index's clock: frame *n* of a path is the same exposure and the same picture in every run on one device (`exposure_tests.cpp`). The view a surround meters is the centre monitor's, so its exposure is the single view's of that monitor where the picture is.
