Verdicts (2026-11-21): all six cases on the RTX 5090; on the Titan X profile (`ENGINE_GFX_TEST_DEVICE=titanxp`) the CPU cases and `csm`, the `rt` case skipped there (no ray queries); 3,771 floor pixels held, 40 of them in the slab's shadow, the worst at 0.12 of the allowance; the globe with no radius moved the floor by at most 0.00054 of its light under `rt`. **A scene with no lamp**: the lamp room with none under `rt` and `csm` and the stand-in heightfield under `rt` are the bytes main's binary draws; so is the campfire (one fire, `csm`), **once both binaries read the same derived data**. The first comparison put it 31 of 518,400 pixels apart by one code round the fire, and that was not the branch (2026-11-22, R86-2): main's code built in the same tree, with the compiler cache and without it, draws the branch's bytes, and putting back the shaders' `spot.z` or the array's old six lights moves nothing; the 31 pixels are the textures. A binary copied out of the repository finds no `ddc/` root above it, so it decodes the campfire's images and samples them as RGBA8, where one inside a checkout samples the block-compressed `.tex` its derived data holds (main's copied-out binary with `--ddc` at the checkout's root draws the branch's bytes; the branch's with `--no-cache` draws main's copied-out bytes). A comparison of two binaries names one derived-data root for both, or `--no-cache` for both. Every `ResolveLight` but a lamp's has `spot.z` 0: the stand-in's two and a sky's moon start from `FrameLighting{}` (`frame_lighting`, `lighting.cpp`), a fire's from `ResolveLight{}` (`add_fire_lights`), the path tracer reads the same array (`reference.cpp`), and the tests' hand-built tables are default-constructed (`shading_tests.cpp`); the sun is not in the array.

## Picking

`SceneRenderer::read_last_frame` reads the ids (and depth) of **the frame last submitted, without drawing another**: it waits for the device, reads the one visibility buffer every frame writes, and decodes it exactly as `capture` does (the pair through `GpuScene::pair_cluster` to instance and cluster, per view rectangle, Panini resampled). It exists because a window's renderer owns no target of its own, so `capture` — which draws a new frame into that target — cannot answer a click in a presented picture; and because a click is answered from what the person saw. Colour, light and normals are refused (a presented frame's colour is the swapchain's), as are `--raster direct` (no visibility buffer) and a renderer that has drawn nothing yet. A click's cost, not a frame's: the whole buffer is read back. engine-editor turns the instance into its document record through [`doc_scene`](doc_scene.md).

## Moving an instance

`SceneRenderer::move_instances(indices, placements)` places **loaded** instances again: instance `indices[i]` takes `placements[i]`'s transform and origin through its mesh's fit, exactly as the load placed it (`GpuScene::place_instances`, `gfx::set_instance_placement`). **A move changes the placement and nothing else**: of the instance's flags only the uniform-scale bit is the new placement's, and the species' caster policy and the static-structure bit are kept (until 2026-10-31 `set_instance_placement` wrote the flags from the scale alone and a moved instance lost both — found by R111; `untraced_tests.cpp`, "a moved instance keeps its caster policy"). It keeps its mesh, its pairs, its material base and its deformation, so nothing laid out per pair or per instance moves. **It waits for nothing** (2026-10-22, roadmap R93): the CPU's table takes the new placement at once, and the next frame draws the instances where they now stand while the frames in flight draw them where they stood. In a **scene read whole** the moved entries ride the next frame's **record upload**: `GpuScene::prepare_records`, which every frame runs after `terrain_prepare`, copies each moved record (each once, with the placement it ends in, however often it moved since the last frame) into the frame slot's own host-visible record staging, and a transfer pass, "record upload", copies them into the one instance table, a region per run of consecutive instances. In a **dynamic scene** (2026-10-19) they ride the next frame's flip to a table set no frame in flight reads, as a tail block's change does ([Instances that come and go](#instances-that-come-and-go), "A loaded instance moves through the flip"). The scene's bounds stay the load's. Refused, with nothing moved, for an index past the instances, a dynamic scene's tail slot (the tail is `set_dynamic_instances`'), a placement of another mesh, or a translation off the world grid. A placement that changes the mesh or the instance count is a reload ([doc_scene](doc_scene.md#changes)).

**Until 2026-10-22 a move in a scene read whole waited for the device** (`FrameContext::wait_idle`) and wrote the entries with a blocking submission, because the one table is read by every frame in flight. For an editor's edit that was one wait; for a host that moves actors every frame it threw away all overlap between the CPU and the GPU, so each frame cost its CPU time plus its GPU time: the forest PoC's 208 animals at 1280×720 ran 2.36 ms a frame against 0.68 ms of CPU and 1.29 ms of GPU ([the measurements](../experiments/forest-cpu-2026-10-21.md)). The scene was not made dynamic instead, which would have changed its table layout and refused `--rt-templates`; the ring slots' records already went through the command stream, and the record upload is that path made general — with its own staging per frame slot rather than the terrain's ring, because a record has to land in the very next frame and can never be left for a later one when a ring is full, and the frames in flight are free to number more than the ring's three regions.

**Why the copy is safe without a wait.** Four things have to hold, and each is checked:

1. **The copy writes only after the frames in flight have read.** Every frame, upload and readback is submitted to the graphics queue; the compute and transfer queues the device fetches are never used ([gfx](gfx.md)). On a frame with records, `record_frame` imports the instance table (and the mesh table, for a ring slot's records) into the render graph as last used at `AllCommands` by `MemoryRead`, so the graph emits a memory barrier in front of the copy whose first scope is every command submitted earlier on the queue at every stage — the frames in flight included, in submission order — and whose second is the copy's transfer write. That is the write-after-read the copy has against the frames that read the old records, ordered on the GPU; the CPU does not wait. (It is the barrier the ring slots' chunk copies have always had.)
2. **Every reader of the frame reads after the copy.** The graph turns the copy's write into a barrier before the first pass that declares a read of the table, and every pass that reads the instance table declares it through `read_pool`: the cull pass (and the shadow cull), the deformed-vertex pool's allocation, the static shape cache and the pool pass, the vertex path's expansion, the hardware and vertex rasterizers, the direct path, the software rasterizer, the CLAS records, `tlas_instances` (which writes every top-level transform from the frame's table), the ray-traced visibility and the resolve. The deform cache and the direct path did not declare it before this date and do now. Later readers are reached through the frame's chain of barriers, as every buffer the graph tracks is.
3. **The staging is not rewritten while a frame copies from it.** A frame slot's record staging is written only by the frame recorded in that slot, after `begin_frame` has waited for the frame that last had the slot — the only one that could still be copying from it — and is made again larger only then (by half as much again as asked for, in 64 KiB steps; `reserve_record_staging` makes each slot's at the scene's 64 KiB minimum, or two ring swaps of every slot's records, when the renderer is made, and touches it once). So a steady stream of moves makes no buffer and allocates nothing after warm-up: the lists keep what they grew to.
4. **Every reader sees one placement per frame.** The device's table changes only inside a frame's own command stream, before any of that frame's readers, so a frame reads either the placements of the moves made before it was recorded or, if it was recorded first, the ones before — never a mix. The CPU's copy of the table (`instance_table_`), which a move writes at once, is read at record time only: by the trees' pose stage (`FloraPoser`'s `placed`, for the frame about to be recorded), `pair_cluster` and picking (the pair numbering, which a move keeps), and the top-level records' first write at load (whose transform no frame reads). Nothing a frame in flight reads is written by a move: the deformed-vertex pool, the static-shape caches and the joint matrices are in mesh space, the bottom-level structures are built every frame from the frame's cut, and the pair table and the per-pair buffers are functions of the slot and its mesh. A capture, a `read_last_frame` after it and the reference renderer all go through a frame (the reference draws one real-time frame first), so the first picture after a move shows it.

`systems/renderer/tests/dynamic_instances_tests.cpp` ("moving instances: a scene read whole …") holds all four to the picture: three instances of a scene read whole — the skinned bar, a box beside it and a box of a tile, two copy regions — walk a step for six steps, moved again before each of `frames_in_flight + 1` frames submitted and not waited for, and the frame after each step's last move is the scene loaded with those placements, id for id, depth for depth and colour for colour, on the mesh path with occlusion, the vertex path, the cascaded maps with three frames in flight, and the ray-traced raster with traced shadows; and over those frames the thread made no device wait (`gfx::device_waits_on_thread`, which counts `submit_immediate` and `FrameContext::wait_idle`) but the ray tracing chain's own resizes, and a move alone none at all.


**The capture: a picture's light, in an EXR** (roadmap R79; `capture.h`'s `CaptureChannels::light` and `capture_light`). A PNG holds 8 bits of an SDR picture; an HDR picture is read back as its **light**: RGB floats a pixel, linear Rec. 709, with **1.0 at the picture's white** — paper white for HDR10 and scRGB, the SDR picture's own white for SDR. `capture_light` inverts each encoding exactly as `display.h` wrote it: an SDR target's codes through the 1/2.2 power (`sdr_decode`), HDR10's PQ codes through ST 2084 to nits, back from BT.2020 with the inverse of the encode's own matrix (`gfx::bt2020_to_bt709`, computed from `k_bt709_to_bt2020` in double, so a colour outside Rec. 709 comes back negative as scRGB would hold it) and over paper white, scRGB's halves times 80 nits over paper white. **Why the picture's white and not scRGB's 80 nits**: so an SDR, an HDR and a linear capture of one frame are in one unit, an EXR viewer shows 1.0 as white, and below the curve's knee an HDR capture's light *is* the SDR picture's — the curve's whole promise, now checkable on a file; the nits are not lost, since `write_capture` puts paper white in the EXR's standard `whiteLuminance` attribute. `write_capture` writes the light as `<stem>.exr` (halves through `foundation/image`'s `exr.h`) and **`<stem>.codes.json`, the histogram of the codes the picture was stored in** (`CodeHistogram`): an SDR target's own 8 or 10 bits, HDR10's PQ codes, and for scRGB and the linear radiance the 10-bit PQ codes an HDR10 signal of that light would carry — what says how many steps a sky's gradient really spans. An HDR picture has no 8-bit `color` channel; `capture` refuses one.

**"The resolve's linear radiance"** is a fourth encoding, **`gfx::DisplayEncoding::Linear`**: the exposed radiance itself, before the shoulder, the transfer and the dither, into `R16G16B16A16Sfloat`, clamped at a half's largest value (65504, because the sun's disc exposed for the ground is larger and a half store of it would be infinity). It was chosen over reading the radiance out of the resolve beside the picture because it is one branch at the top of `display_output` and one more value of a field the resolve already reads — a second colour target would have been a second write of every pixel in the bandwidth-bound pass, on every frame, for a capture taken once. Its light is the radiance as it is (1.0 a white Lambertian surface under the metered light, the curve's input unit), so a linear capture beside an HDR one is the curve itself: equal below the knee, rolled off above it. engine-view draws it offscreen only (`--present-format linear`; no display takes it).

**The ramp** (`gfx::ResolveMode::Ramp`, `--view ramp`): every pixel of the view is `gfx::display_ramp` — grey from black to white evenly in the SDR signal, the darkest eighth of that, four stops past white — through `display_output` with a knee of 1 and the frame's dither, in place of the scene, at the top of `fs_resolve`. It is E39's 10-bit ramp: the encode, its quantizer and the display behind it with nothing upstream. `hdr_output_tests.cpp` holds it undithered to `display_ramp` rounded at 8 bits, HDR10's light to `display_tone` of it within PQ's step, and HDR10's 10-bit codes, dithered and not, to the CPU mirror's (`display_pq_codes`), each off by at most one code and only within 0.02 of an edge ([above](#the-output-encode), "HDR10's PQ codes are the encode's too").

**What it costs** (measured 2026-10-09 at the batch 12 merge gate, `msvc-release`, the erg walk at 1920×1080 offscreen with `--terrain-rings --shadows rt`, 30 warm-up frames, under the GPU lock with `--wait-quiet 300`, GPU timers; the machine had 8 to 17% of other CPU load, so these are upper bounds): the resolve pass, which holds the encode, is **0.200 ms** at the median through the SDR path (the frame budget's own quiet run of the same scene and path), **0.203 ms** through HDR10 (BT.2020, PQ, dither), **0.200 ms** through scRGB and **0.199 ms** through the linear capture encoding; the whole frame is 0.725 to 0.728 ms in every case. The HDR encode costs about three microseconds a frame at 1080p, inside the run-to-run noise of the resolve; the two formats' swapchain bytes at 11520×2160 (199 MB against 100 MB for scRGB) remain the measurable difference and are the proposal's to weigh ([the proposal](../experiments/hdr-output-proposal.md#what-is-built)).

**What holds it**: `domain/gfx`'s `display_tests.cpp` holds the CPU side to `display_reference.h`, the same in double — PQ's round trip to 1e-13 in double and the float encode within a hundredth of a 10-bit code, the matrix derived from the two sets of primaries to 1e-6 with every row summing to 1, the curve monotonic, never past its ceiling, the identity below the knee and never below the SDR picture above it, the headroom, and one pixel of each encoding (a white below the knee at exactly paper white). `hdr_output_tests.cpp` draws the same frame as SDR into a 10-bit target, as HDR10 and as scRGB, decodes all three to light relative to paper white, and holds the HDR pictures to the SDR one wherever the SDR picture shows a channel below the knee, within one code of each encoding (the dither both carry); nothing past the peak; HDR10 and scRGB the same light; the same frame twice the same bytes; for the stand-in, and under the sky capability's sky at 16:00 (measured: at worst 0.56 and 0.88 of the allowance under the sky; 0.57 and 0.89 with HDR10 rounded by the encode, RTX 5090 on 621.24, R187-1). An HDR encoding over an 8-bit target is refused.

## A shading normal is not the surface

Two ways a shading normal — an interpolation of vertex normals, or a normal map's texel — parts
from the surface it shades, and what the resolve does about each (2026-09-25, the change after the
ground's):

- **It leans away from the eye on the camera's side of its triangle.** n·v is negative for a point
  the camera plainly sees. `brdf_eval` used to return nothing there, so the pixel lost every light
  and kept only the ambient; it now **clamps n·v to 10⁻⁴** (`k_min_n_dot_v`, Filament's
  `clampNoV`), so the diffuse lobe takes a light by n·l alone and the specular lobe's visibility term
  stays finite. That was the whole of the dunes' grey seams ([above](#the-sky-above-the-ground-below)):
  at the third session's three markers the seam pixels go from 13,093, 7,212 and 6,653 to **0, 0 and
  0**, the slabs of the first marker and the crest dashes of the other two alike, and FLIP against
  the pictures before either change is 0.011, 0.012 and 0.010, its maxima of 0.72 to 0.83 on the
  seams themselves. `brdf_eval` is the path tracer's too, so its next-event estimate at such a
  vertex takes the sun as well; it still ends the path there, because a direction cannot be sampled
  about a normal the ray arrived from behind.
- **It is behind the surface** — the far side of thin two-sided geometry, whose vertex normals are the
  near side's, seen from the far side. The resolve now **turns it to the camera's side**
  (`dot(shading_normal, geometric) < 0` flips it, `geometric` being the triangle's own normal turned
  towards the camera), which is what the reference path tracer always did with the side its ray came
  from. Before the clamp this mattered less, because such a normal usually faced away from the eye
  and so took no light at all; with the clamp, left alone, it would take the lights on the far side
  of the surface through it.

The CPU reference (`brdf_reference.h`, `eval`) clamps the same way. The attributes test holds both:
a normal map tilted 80° faces away from the camera over 3,850 of the quad's 12,100 pixels while it
faces the sun, and every one of them is the reference within 1 of 255 and lit by the sun; and the
quad seen from below, whose vertex normals point up through it at the sun, is the reference for a
normal of (0, −1, 0) — lit by the ground alone — to 0 of 255 on every covered pixel. Against the
reference path tracer the corpus moved by at most 0.0003 either way (`heightfield` 0.0235 →
0.0238, `flighthelmet` 0.0132 → 0.0131, `helmet-grid` 0.0037 → 0.0034, `thin-geometry` 0.0035 →
0.0034, `wide-frustum` 0.0010 → 0.0009, `shredded-atlas` unchanged), and PSNR rose on every helmet
scene (34.5 → 34.7, 36.7 → 37.2, 40.1 → 40.7, 42.1 → 42.5 dB), which is the normal maps' texels
turned from the camera getting their light back in both pictures.

## Geometry streaming: the GPU half of pages and residency

[04 §4.3](../plan/04-renderer.md#43-geometry) step 3 and [§4.9](../plan/04-renderer.md#49-streaming-and-residency) ask for clusters in fixed-size pages, GPU feedback that requests them, a CPU that streams them, and a residency budget that evicts by last use. [geometry](geometry.md) built the CPU half — the layout, `select_lod_streaming`'s drawing rule, and `PageResidencyManager`'s priority heap and ancestor-closed eviction. `systems/renderer/streaming.h` is the half that runs beside a frame, and `--stream` on either host turns it on.

**What is paged and what is not.** The descriptors stay resident whatever the budget: `geometry::ClusterDesc`, `geometry::ClusterLodDesc`, the material index, the page table, `page_of_cluster` and the per-cluster child ranges — 112 bytes a cluster plus 48 a page. Everything a cluster costs *in bytes* is paged: six bytes of quantized position and eight of attributes a vertex, four bytes a triangle, and — when the frame builds acceleration structures — twelve more bytes of float position and three more of 8-bit index. That is about 7% held to stream the other 93%, and the split is not a compromise: the cull pass tests **every pair of every frame** and has to be able to say "not that one" about a cluster whose payload is not here, so its inputs cannot themselves be streamed without a second level of the same problem.

**The drawing rule, on the GPU.** `cluster_cull.slang` implements `select_lod_streaming` exactly: draw a cluster when its page is resident **and** its projected parent error is over the threshold **and** (its own error is at or under it **or** the pages holding its children are not all resident). The last clause is the fallback that makes a starved budget coarse rather than holey. Both residency tests are over a whole *group* in the CPU model, and the GPU tests one cluster's page instead — which is the same thing, because `build_cluster_pages` never splits a group across pages (it closes the open page before a group that would not fit and gives a group that fits in no page one of its own). `GpuScene::create_streaming` checks that before it uploads a page table, because the rule is crack-free only while it holds.

**Feedback.** A cluster that wanted to refine and could not appends a `geometry::PageRequest` — the page, the projected diameter in pixels of the requesting cluster's sphere, and the distance to it — to a bounded buffer under an atomic, **deduplicated behind a per-page mask word** that the first lane exchanges, so a page a thousand clusters want costs one twelve-byte entry and not a thousand. A cluster that is drawn sets a "used this frame" word for its page, which is what gives the manager's LRU something to order by. All three arrays are cleared by the frame's reset pass and copied into a per-frame-slot host-visible buffer at the end of it; the CPU reads them when the slot comes around, which is `frames_in_flight` frames later and is the same deferred pattern the visible-pair counts already use. **The frame never waits on the device**, and the price of that is that a page a camera jump asks for arrives two or three frames after it was wanted — which is exactly what the fallback clause is for.

One thing the GPU does not reproduce: the CPU reference keeps the *best* priority of every cluster that asked for a page, and the GPU keeps the **winning lane's**. A lock-free best-of would be two more atomics on every losing lane and it buys nothing over a frame or two, because `PageResidencyManager::request` keeps the best of every request it sees and a queued page's key can only improve.

**The page pool, and why the offsets are patched.** The paged streams are a pool of fixed-size slots, each sized for the largest page's vertex and triangle counts. When a page lands in slot *s* the host rewrites that page's `ClusterDesc::vertex_offset` and `triangle_offset` to point into slot *s* and uploads the 48-byte records with the payload. **Nothing in any shader changes.** The alternative — leaving the offsets page-relative and having the shader add `slot_base[page_of_cluster[c]]` — would need two more addresses in every pass that reads geometry, and `gfx::ClusterDrawParams` is full at its 128-byte push limit while `gfx::MeshDesc` is full at 64: the indirection has nowhere to put them without restructuring the rasterizers', the resolve's and the CLAS records' blocks. It would also cost two dependent loads on every position read, where patching costs one memcpy of 48 bytes a cluster on a page that is being copied anyway. See [gfx](gfx.md) for the measurement.

**How many slots, and what an eviction is.** The budget is in page bytes and the pool is in slots, and the two have to agree on the worst case or a frame would admit a page with nowhere to put it. The bound is exact and cheap: sort the pages by size and take them smallest first until the budget is spent — no set of pages within the budget can be larger than that count. Real pages are 85–95% full, so the pool is about a tenth larger than the budget it serves, which is the price of a fixed-size slot and is what makes an eviction *a slot handed back* rather than a compaction. Two consequences are worth knowing. The pool can run out of slots while the byte budget still has room, and then the slot is the budget: one eviction is forced by lowering the manager's own budget for the length of the call, which takes the least recently used page with nothing under it exactly as a byte-driven eviction would. And **a freed slot retires for `frames_in_flight` frames** before it is filled again, because the frames still on the queue carry residency words that say the page is resident and their draws read that slot.

**Uploads.** A staging ring with one region per frame slot and a per-frame byte budget (`--upload-budget`, 256 KiB by default; a value under the largest page's payload is raised to it, because a budget no page fits in never converges). A frame copies what it staged in one transfer pass before the cull pass, so a page that arrives is drawn in the frame it arrives in. Nothing is allocated in steady state: the ring, the scratch for a page's patched descriptors, and the heap the manager queues in are all sized once.

**Two invariants, and the one that cost an afternoon.** The manager keeps residency ancestor-closed: requests only ever come from a resident parent, and eviction only ever takes a page with no resident child. The renderer has to keep a *second* copy of that on the pool, because the pool lags the manager by an upload budget — a page the manager holds but whose bytes are still in the queue is invisible to the cull pass. Two rules do it: pages are staged in **page order**, which is coarse first and therefore parent before child, and **nothing new is admitted while the pool is behind the manager**.

That was not enough, and the case that broke it is the one [04 §4.9](../plan/04-renderer.md#49-streaming-and-residency) calls "cancellation of requests that became stale". A request arrives with a resident parent, by construction. But a queue is not served in the frame it was filled in, and by the time a page reaches the front of the heap the parent that asked for it may have been evicted — and admitting it then puts the fine geometry back under a hole, which is precisely the grandparent case the invariant exists to prevent. It showed up as one page in sixty, resident with nothing above it, and only under a budget tight enough to evict every frame. `PageResidencyManager::drop` is the removal the fix needed and `GeometryStreamer::may_admit` is the test: a page is still loadable if it is pinned, if it spans two DAG levels (such a page holds its own parents, and the child list leaves it out of its own run — which is a second thing worth knowing before it looks like a bug), or if any page holding its clusters' parents is still resident. A dropped request costs nothing: a view that still wants the page is still drawing its parent and asks again next frame.

**What streaming refuses, and why each refusal is a refusal.** `resolve_settings` turns `--stream` off, with the reason logged, for a scene with no page table. It forces culling on, because the drawing rule's fallback clause *is* the LOD cut. It drops `--rt-templates`, because a template is built once at load from every cluster's float positions, which a streamed scene does not hold — a template has to be built when its page arrives and dropped when it leaves, which is a second residency problem with its own budget. And it refuses **a deformed or skinned scene** outright, because `gfx::DeformDesc::pool_offset` indexes the deformed-vertex pool by the *scene-wide* vertex index while a streamed scene's vertices live at slot-relative ones; joining the two is a change to the pool's allocation, which is E25's open suballocation item.

### Admission never waits on a read it cannot start

**The stall the desert flythrough found, and the rule that ends it** (2026-09-24). One streamed run of the flythrough — the first, at 1080p with occlusion culling off and a 5% budget — made 60,034 page requests over the path and uploaded nothing; three reruns of the same command were normal ([the write-up](../experiments/flythrough-desert-overlook.md#the-streaming-run-that-uploaded-nothing)). It was not bad luck and not the disk. It was a **circular wait** between three rules above, each right on its own:

- a page's load slot is given back when the page is **staged**, and a pool slot is held from the moment its read starts;
- pages are staged strictly in **page order** — coarse first, which is parent before child — and the walk goes on past a page still waiting for its read only to *start* the reads behind it;
- admission, and the reads it starts, go in **priority order**, the manager's heap by projected size.

So when reads take longer than frames, the eight load slots (`k_page_loads`) fill with pages behind the walk's head. If a page is then admitted with a lower index than every one of them — a coarser page some cluster asked for a little later — while no slot is free, admission makes it resident in the manager with no read, and on the next frame it *is* the head of the walk. It cannot start its read: every slot is held. None of those can be staged: they are behind it. So none is ever given back, the pool stops at what it had, `blocked` keeps admission shut, and the requests pile up for the rest of the run. Nothing in the loop ever leaves that state. What it needs is reads slower than a frame — the first run after a build reads the containers off a cold file cache, and the reruns found them in memory — and a priority order that puts a low page after the slots have filled, which a fly-in toward a terrain does almost at once.

**The rule: the head of the walk always gets a load** (`GeometryStreamer::steal_load_for`). When the page at the head of the page-order walk has no read and no free load or pool slot, the streamer gives up the load of another page — one the manager no longer holds if there is one, otherwise the one furthest behind the head, which the walk would reach last — and starts the head's. Every load belongs to a page at or behind the head, since the pages before it are in the pool and a pool page has no load, so when the head has none there is always one to take. The page it was taken from reads again when the walk reaches it; `StreamStats::steals` counts every read that is done twice, and a run that counts many has too few load slots for its read latency. With the rule the head waits for its own read and nothing else, so the pool gains a page at least every few read latencies whatever order the requests came in.

**A read that fails is read again.** A short or failed read already dropped the page rather than staging it; the case below makes sure dropping it does not strand it — the walk reaches it again, starts it again, and the pages behind it follow once it lands. A page whose read fails *every* time still holds the pages behind it in page order, since staging past it would break the ancestor-closure the order exists for; a container that cannot be read is a load-time failure the source should refuse, not a frame-time one, and it is a follow-up.

**How often, before and after.** The stuck run's own command — the landmarks overlay at 1080p, occlusion off, shadows off, a 5% budget, pages from the containers — each run over a cold file cache: on the RTX 5090 the old streamer stalled in **7 of 10** runs, six from the warm-up and one 33 s into the path, and the new one in **0 of 10**; with the substitute set, **4 of 10** against **0 of 10**. The TITAN Xp's runs, and every stalled run's state, are in [the write-up](../experiments/flythrough-desert-overlook.md#the-streaming-run-that-uploaded-nothing).

**What holds it.** `streaming_tests.cpp` serves the pages from `SlowPageSource`, a `PageSource` whose loads land a fixed number of frames after they begin, over the scene's own host streams — which is what a cold cache does to a real run, and what a container the test just wrote never does, because it is in the file cache. `PageSource` is the interface `GeometryStreamer` reads pages through, and `FilePageSource` is the one the hosts use. **`admission never waits on a read it cannot start`** flies the 129-grid heightfield in 16 KB pages toward the camera under a 32 KiB upload budget with a six-frame source. Against the streamer before the rule it stalls on every run — the pool frozen at 12 of the 21 pages the manager admitted from the 48th frame to the 1,200th, all eight loads out — and with the rule it converges in 89 frames, 27 pages of 27, having given up one load, with no stretch longer than 12 frames without a page landing (the test allows four latencies and eight frames of feedback, 32). That is the RTX 5090. Whether the slots fill behind the head depends on the order the cut asks for pages in, which differs by device, and on the TITAN Xp the same fly-in never filled them — no load given up, converged in 83 frames — so there the case holds convergence and nothing more; its message says which. A case that builds the wait on every device would drive admission directly rather than through a cut, and is a follow-up. **`a read that fails is read again, and the rest of the queue goes on`** fails the first page past the roots four times with a three-frame source: the page is read five times and the run converges in 82 frames, 26 of 26, longest stall 19 frames. That one passes against the old streamer too — dropping a failed read was already right — and is there so the rule cannot break it. `FrameStats` and the flythrough's `.jsonl` carry `pending`, `loads_in_flight` and `pool_pages` beside the manager's `pages_resident` on every frame, which is the trace that says a run is in this state — the pool flat, the queue full, eight loads out — rather than leaving it to be inferred from a summary with no uploads in it.

### A page's 8-bit indices are its own

**The defect this section used to record — a starved budget and the ray chain together losing the device — was a host-side buffer overrun in the staging path, and it is fixed.** It is written up rather than deleted because the shape of it is worth keeping: nothing about it was on the GPU, nothing about it was a barrier, and every suspect the symptom suggested was innocent.

**What it was.** `GeometryStreamer::pack_indices` turns a staged page's packed triangles into the tightly packed 8-bit indices a cluster acceleration structure build reads, into the reused scratch vector `indices8_`. `gfx::pack_cluster_indices` **appends** — which is what `GpuScene::create_ray_tracing`'s one-shot pack of a whole mesh wants — and the per-page caller never cleared the vector between pages. So the *k*-th page staged in a run wrote the concatenation of all *k* pages' indices, starting at this page's 8-bit index block. Two things followed from one missing line:

- **The pool got the wrong page's triangles.** Page 0 was correct; every page after it was staged with page 0's indices at the front of its block, so a CLAS build record for one of its clusters described triangles that are not in that cluster — local indices past the cluster's `vertexCount`, addressing vertices outside the cluster's run of the pool.
- **The write ran off the end of the page's region of the staging ring**, by one page's indices for every page staged before it. The ring is `k_stream_slots` regions of one upload budget, so the spill first landed on the *other frame slot's* staged page — whose copy into the pool may not have executed yet, since a frame's staging is written on the host after `begin_frame()` and its transfer is recorded into that frame's command buffer — and, once long enough, off the end of the mapped ring entirely, into whatever host-visible allocation VMA had placed behind it. `GpuScene::rt_instances` and `ClusterSet::addresses` are both host-visible and both hold device addresses that a build or a traversal dereferences; a spill onto either is a wild address in an acceleration structure, which is exactly the `vkQueueSubmit2` device loss that was recorded.

**Why only that configuration.** The 8-bit index block is staged **only when the frame builds acceleration structures** — `GpuScene::page_stage_layout` sets `ray_tracing` from `ResolvedSettings::rt_chain` — so `--shadows off` never called the packer and never overran anything. And the overrun grows with the number of pages staged in a run, so it takes a budget tight enough to keep re-uploading: a budget that holds the working set stages a dozen pages once and stops. Reproduced on the RTX 5090 with `--mesh FlightHelmet.gltf --grid-instances 8 --stream --page-budget-pct 25 --page-source host --orbit 4 --frames 150` at 1920×1080 in `msvc-release` — three runs of three lost the device, and the same command with the fix runs 300 frames and 125 uploads clean.

**The invariant, as a rule a future change must keep.** *A page's staged bytes are a function of that page alone, and every one of them lands inside that page's own region of the staging ring.* Concretely: a block written into a staged page is sized from the page's `geometry::ClusterPageDesc` and placed at its offset in `GpuScene::page_stage_layout`, never sized from a buffer that outlives the page. `pack_indices` now clears the scratch, copies exactly `triangle_count * 3` bytes, and asserts both halves of the rule in debug; `patch_clusters` already obeyed it. The wider statement for anyone adding a stream to a page: **a scratch buffer shared across pages is a hazard unless the copy out of it is sized by the page**, because the staging ring has no guard band and the frame slot next to it is live.

**What holds it.** `systems/renderer/tests/streaming_tests.cpp`, "a page's 8-bit indices are its own, under a budget that evicts every frame": the heightfield with 16 KB pages, `ShadowMode::RayTraced`, a tenth-of-the-page-bytes budget and a camera that moves, so the pool recycles its slots (28 uploads, 23 evictions in 48 frames). It then reads both pool streams back — `GeometryStreamer::slot_of_page` is the accessor that says where a page's payload actually is, so the check walks the pool rather than re-deriving the mapping and getting it wrong the same way twice — and requires `indices8[3t .. 3t+3)` to be `pack_cluster_indices` of `triangles[t]` for every triangle of every page the pool holds. The two are written by the same upload from the same staged bytes, so nothing but the right bytes can make them agree. Before the fix, 4,121 of 5,078 pool triangles disagreed, the first on page 1; after it, none. **Every other case in that file runs with shadows off**, which is why the defect lived: the stream it corrupts does not exist without the ray chain.

**What a validation layer would still have to say.** None of this needed one — it is a host-side overrun of a mapped buffer, which `VK_EXT_debug_utils` and the standard layers would not have flagged either. What a layer *would* settle, and what is still owed, is the cross-frame question this investigation raised and did not resolve: the render graph is reset per frame and an imported buffer starts each frame with no recorded producer, so the first use of a buffer in frame N is barriered against nothing in frame N−1. The pool's slot-retirement rule (`frames_in_flight` frames before a freed slot is refilled) makes that safe for the payload streams, and the scene-wide `ClusterDesc` array is rewritten in place with identical bytes for every field the cull pass reads — but "identical bytes" is an argument, not a check, and `VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_synchronization2`'s hazard tracking is what would turn it into one. The SDK is not installed on this machine.

**Where a page's bytes come from, and why that decides whether streaming saves host memory.** There are two sources and `GeometryStreamer::copy_page` is the seam between them (`systems/renderer/page_source.h`).

*In memory* is what the first streaming change had: a page's payload is copied out of the `SceneData` the load produced. It is what the procedural heightfield and a glTF loaded with `--no-cache` have to use, because there is no file behind them — and it means the whole scene's geometry stays in the process whatever the budget is, so streaming saved **device** memory and not host memory.

*From the container* is `FilePageSource`, one implementation of `PageSource` — the interface `GeometryStreamer` reads every page through: begin a load into one of `capacity()` slots, ask whether it is `done` and `complete`, read its `bytes`, `release` it (the tests' `SlowPageSource` is the other, and lands its loads a set number of frames late). Every mesh of a scene came out of a `.clusters` container — one named outright, a derived-data cache hit, or the entry the load just wrote (`SourceMesh::container`) — and `geometry::ClusterFileReader` addresses that container's sections by byte range ([geometry](geometry.md), "The container read by range"). A page's payload is then **three ranged reads, or four when the frame builds acceleration structures**: the quantized positions, the attributes, the packed triangles, and the float positions. The other two blocks of a staged page are the host's either way — the cluster descriptors, which have to carry *this* slot's offsets, and the 8-bit indices, which are packed from the triangles that just landed rather than read a second time, so the two can never disagree about a triangle. Before either block is written, **the landed triangles are checked against their clusters** (`geometry::check_page_triangles`, T194): a container's bytes are a client's, the load reads no page, and the rasterizers add a triangle's locals to its cluster's offset on the GPU, so a page whose triangle names a vertex outside its cluster is logged as refused, dropped as a failed read is, and never staged. That a page's slice of each stream is one contiguous run is not luck: `build_cluster_pages` reordered the streams so that it would be.

`attach_page_source` opens the containers **and releases the merged host streams** — quantized, attributes, triangles, float positions, vertex sources, bindings — which is the point of the whole thing and is why the two are one call rather than two. What it does *not* release is the cluster and LOD descriptor arrays: they are 96 bytes a cluster against the ~1.5 KB a cluster a page carries, the streamer patches a page's descriptors out of them on the way past, and the cull pass needs them for every pair of every frame anyway.

**All or nothing, per scene.** A scene whose meshes are not *all* backed by a container is refused with the reason and keeps the in-memory source. A partial source would be worse than none: the caller's next act is to release the streams, and the pages the source could not answer for would then have nowhere to read from.

**What is bounded is the steady state, not the peak.** `load_scene` still materializes the merged streams and `attach_page_source` releases them afterwards, so the working set falls after the load and the *peak* does not. Making the load never read them needs `geometry::merge_paged_cluster_meshes` to stop deriving the merged bases from `mesh.vertices.size()` — the counts are in the page table, which tiles the vertices and the triangles — and that is a change to the merge's signature rather than to this seam. Both numbers are in engine-view's summary (`host_memory.bytes` and `peak_bytes`) so the distinction is measurable rather than assumed.

**The scene's host copy after the upload** (T129, 2026-11-14; [the measurement](../experiments/memory-commit-accounting.md#the-second-cuts)). A scene uploaded whole keeps its merged `SceneData::lod` for the session, because some of it is read after the upload. `release_uploaded_streams` (`page_source.h`) gives back the three streams nothing reads again — the 16-bit positions, the vertex attributes and the canonical vertex ids — and engine-view calls it once every `GpuScene::create` of its run is done (both scenes of `--verify-occlusion`), unless a streamed scene copies its pages from host memory. What stays, and why: the float positions and the packed triangles (the crown priors in `SceneRenderer::create`, a swaying tail tree's padding the first time its mesh appears, the collision's cut proxies on a walk), the per-vertex source indices (the cut proxies), the cluster and LOD descriptors (the cull's tables, the static forms rebuilt after the micromaps, the collision, the census, the summary), and the skin and morph streams, whose emptiness says whether the scene is skinned or morphed. engine-host never calls it: it rebuilds its GPU scene from the same `SceneData` on a settings change. After it, `mesh_vertex_ids` answers empty.

**A mesh's leaves, measured at the load for its sound** (S112, 2026-11-21; [world_sound](world_sound.md#the-wind-in-the-trees-and-at-the-ears-s112)). `load_scene` ends with `measure_mesh_leaves` **when the desc asks for it** (`SceneDesc::measure_leaves`, S112-2: engine-view sets it only when the world is heard, so engine-host, `--audio off` and a build without `world_sound` pay nothing; a mesh a job on the load's pool, timed as `SceneLoadReport::leaves_ms` and the startup trace's `mesh leaves`), one pass over each mesh's finest-level foliage triangles — a cluster whose material is alpha-tested (the test the crowns' priors take leaves by) or two-sided and translucent (a flora's own leaves with no image) — into `SceneData::mesh_leaves`: the cards' one-sided area, how high they stand in mesh space, and where (their centroid by area and the farthest leaf's horizontal distance from it: S112-2, so a stand flattened into one mesh is the size of the stand), a distance form taking its source's. No mask is decoded and no grid built, so every load affords it whether or not the indirect light builds its priors, and it is kept through every release of the floats below. A card's cut-outs count as leaf (the masks' fill is the priors' measure, not this one's). A mesh handed in by a tile after the load has none, and is not heard.

**The float geometry goes too where no collision reads it** (T138, 2026-11-15). `release_uploaded_streams(data, HostReaders::none)` also gives back the float positions, the packed triangles and the per-vertex source indices — about 2.1 GB on the forest's staging, and the only cut of the host copy that lowers the working set, since the crowns and the collision touch them. It can because `GpuScene::create` now measures, before it returns, everything the renderer used to read from them later: every swaying mesh's sway bound (`flora_padding_of` read the positions the first time a tail tree appeared, which on a walk is long after the load), the crowns' priors where the settings' indirect light reads them (`crown_priors_built`, `crown_priors`), and the meshes that face the sky (`sky_facing`). `SceneRenderer::create` takes the last two from the scene, so a renderer made after a release — or over a streamed scene whose `attach_page_source` released the same streams before the renderer was made — has them; until this change such a scene silently had no crowns and no sky-facing meshes, and its first tail tree read an empty array. **The walker's collision reads a copy of its own** (T138's second leg): `SceneCollision::cut_proxy` cuts every proxy from the scene's DAG at `walk.collision.mesh_error_m` over the instance's scale, and it now does so from `scene_collision::ProxySource`, which engine-view builds before anything releases (`view::copy_collision_geometry`) when a walker or `--collision-draw` will cut — the clusters a cut can select and a tree's wood alone ([scene_collision](scene_collision.md#the-collisions-own-copy)) — so engine-view passes `HostReaders::none` in every session (`view::release_host_geometry`, `apps/engine_view/walk.h`). `HostReaders::collision` stays for a host that cuts proxies from the scene's own floats after the upload; nothing in the tree does now (the streaming tests' harness uses it for the partial release T129 landed). The other readers, checked by reading: the acceleration-structure builders (`create_ray_tracing`'s 8-bit indices and the float positions' upload) and the micromap bake run inside `create` or from device buffers; the static forms and the structure cache rebuild from device buffers and the descriptors; the captures read the GPU's targets (and `render.compare` is engine-host's, which never releases); nothing in engine-view picks against the host copy; a tile's mesh (`GpuScene::admit_mesh`) and a terrain chunk read their own `SceneData`, not the scene's; the animation's skinned bounds are measured before `GpuScene::create`. How it scales down: the release is proportional to the load's geometry (16 bytes a vertex and 4 a triangle), so a 16 GB machine running a smaller world gives back the same share, a walk included; a walk keeps the collision's copy instead, 3.3% of them on the streamed forest.

**The upload-only streams go inside `create`** (W51-3 stage 4, 2026-11-18; [the measurements](../experiments/start-commit-by-owner-2026-11-18.md#w51-3-what-the-stages-returned)). Released after `create`, the whole host copy stood beside the whole device copy at the end of `gpu scene`, which is where a load peaked: the textures, the working set and the traced chain's first capacity are made after the geometry's upload. A host that releases after `create` anyway passes its `SceneData` as `create`'s `release`, and `create` gives back, right after `upload_geometry` and the measurements that read them (`measure_host_reads`, moved up from the end of `create`: the crowns read the UVs), what only the upload read — the 16-bit grid, the attributes and the vertex ids (`release_uploaded_streams` with `HostReaders::collision`, which keeps the floats). The floats stayed for the chain's 8-bit indices and the collision's copy until W51-4 (below). engine-view passes it in both loops unless the scene streams (the page source uploads from the host streams) or `--verify-occlusion` builds its second scene from them; engine-host, which rebuilds its scene from the same `SceneData`, never does.

**The floats go inside `create`** (W51-4, 2026-11-19; [the measurements](../experiments/start-commit-by-owner-2026-11-18.md#w51-4-a-launch-standing-and-the-next-stages)). Of what stage 4 kept, nothing inside `create` read the floats after `measure_host_reads`: `create_ray_tracing` packs the chain's 8-bit indices from the *triangles* and builds every structure from the device's float buffer, and the collision's copy came after `create` only because engine-view made it there. So engine-view makes the collision's copy first (`copy_collision_geometry`, both loops), and `create`, handed `release`, gives back the float positions and the per-vertex source indices with the upload-only streams (`release_uploaded_streams` with `HostReaders::chain` when the chain will pack, `none` when it will not), and the triangles right after `create_ray_tracing` has packed them: all of the merged host copy but its descriptors is gone before `create` returns, where it used to stand beside the whole device copy at the load's peak. **Who reads them later, and what each does**: the collision's proxies read the copy made before; a scene that streams or a `--verify-occlusion` run passes no `release` and keeps them as before; engine-host never passes one. A reader added inside `create` after the release reads an empty stream, and `streaming: a whole scene draws the same bytes when create gives its host geometry back` holds the cascaded and the traced pictures to the bytes of a scene that kept everything; the walk's case in `walk_ruins_view_tests.cpp` holds the collision to the copy made first.

**What a place holds** (T138; [the design's row a](../experiments/streaming-by-travel.md#the-build-in-stages)). `GpuScene::place_bytes` sums the device bytes of every buffer the scene owns where the eye stands into the kinds a budget's pools would hold: **geometry** (the load's cluster and LOD tables, positions, attributes, triangles, mesh records: the geometry buffers less the arenas a world's tiles arrive into), **companions** (8-bit indices, skin, morphs, the motion contract, coverage, the shadow proxy's table, the deform cache, the field's parts, cluster templates), **micromaps**, **materials** (the table, a material a cluster, the terrain's masks and formation), **textures**, **structures** (the traced chain's chunks, bottom-level set, scratch, top level, records and tables, the structure cache, the static forms; split again by what sizes each part in `PlaceBytes::structure`, since R81: `frame_sets` and `frame_tables` by the capacity, `bottom_level`, `top_level`, `scratch`, `per_instance`, `cache` with its `cache_slots`, `static_forms`), **tiles** (the mesh room, the terrain's ring arenas, its fields, the staging ring), **frame** (the instance and pair tables, visible lists, indirect blocks, the vertex path's records, the deform pool and its tables, the flora's poses), **pages** (a paged scene's pool and tables), and the **host geometry** the scene's `SceneData` still keeps. Counters only, no device call: `engine-view --memory-report` puts the block in each snapshot as `place` and logs `what the place holds`. What it does not split yet: the frame's own targets and the indirect light's cache (the renderer's, not the scene's), and the driver's own pools; the walk's device owners beside it say how far the sum is from the allocator's.

**Nothing blocks, and the pipeline is what makes that affordable.** `begin` issues a page's reads on the Efficiency pool and returns; `prepare` polls one counter per load. Three rules keep it correct and fast:

- **Staging is in page order**, which is coarse first and therefore parent before child, which is what keeps the pool ancestor-closed. Unchanged from the in-memory path, and it is what makes an out-of-order completion harmless.
- **Past a gap, the walk goes on but only starts reads.** Without that the disk would work on one page at a time and a scene would converge at one page per read latency; with it the queue is being read while the frame waits for the page at its head. Nothing behind the gap is staged, so the order holds.
- **Pending is not blocked.** A page whose reads are on their way stops *that* page being staged and nothing else, because what keeps the pool ancestor-closed is the staging order and not what the manager holds. No upload budget, no pool slot and no load capacity do still stop admission. A frame's upload budget bounds both what it copies and what it newly asks for, so it can neither move nor request more than one budget's worth.

A page evicted while its reads are in flight is cancelled in a pass of its own, because `apply_evictions` walks what the *pool* holds and a load is not that yet; without it a load slot and a pool slot would leak one per eviction. A read that fails or comes back short drops the page rather than staging it, since the pool would otherwise hold that page's descriptors over whatever was in the buffer.

Eight loads may be outstanding (`k_page_loads`), which is more than the default 256 KiB upload budget can stage in a frame, so the reads are never what holds a convergence up; their buffers are one largest page each and are sized once, like everything else in the frame path.

**The fly-in, and the guarantee it holds.** `renderer::fly_camera` and engine-view's `--fly <from> <to> <steps>` are a scripted path in mesh radii, interpolated **geometrically** — halving the distance doubles every projected error whether it is 50 radii to 25 or 2 to 1, so equal steps in log distance are equal steps in refinement, and a linearly sampled path would spend nine tenths of its steps on the outer half where a mesh draws out of one page and asks for nothing. The streaming test walks 24 steps of the heightfield from 8 to 0.9 radii under a **quarter budget and a 32 KiB upload budget** and compares every step against the fully resident picture *of that step*.

What it asserts is on the reference coverage **eroded by two pixels**: every surviving pixel must be covered, which says "no region of the surface is missing" with no tolerance to calibrate. Counting silhouette pixels against an area-scaled tolerance measures the shape of the object instead — at 8 radii the terrain covers 2,494 pixels of 76,800 and its jagged horizon is a sizeable fraction of that, while at 0.9 radii it covers most of the frame and the same edge is a rounding error. **Zero interior misses at all 24 steps.** The single-frame starved case (`a starved budget is coarser and never has a hole`) asks its question the same way since 2026-09-23. It used to count holes against a tenth of a percent of the covered pixels plus eight, and that was a calibration of one GPU: at a quarter budget the manager never settles (one of eight pages resident, 86 uploads and 85 evictions to the 256-frame cap), and the RTX 5090 left 65 edge pixels against an allowance of 66 on the mesh and the vertex path alike, while the TITAN Xp's cut of the same frame left 70 and failed. Both leave 0 interior pixels. The whole-frame counts, which are the honest picture of what a coarser cut does to a silhouette:

| step | radii | covered | holes | extra | interior misses |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 8.00 | 1,134 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 4 | 4.56 | 2,494 | 18 | 14 | 0 |
| 8 | 2.60 | 5,629 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 12 | 1.48 | 13,682 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 14 | 1.12 | 22,455 | 7 | 17 | 0 |
| 16 | 0.85 | 36,007 | 29 | 20 | 0 |
| 18 | 0.64 | 47,497 | 15 | 11 | 0 |
| 20 | 0.49 | 50,718 | 18 | 9 | 0 |
| 22 | 0.37 | 53,117 | 23 | 16 | 0 |
| 23 | 0.32 | 54,191 | 31 | 13 | 0 |

(The steps left out are 0 holes and 0 extra; the run ends with 13 of 44 pages resident, 23 uploads and 10 evictions. `holes` never exceeds 0.06% of the covered pixels and every one of them is on an edge.)

**What it costs on the FlightHelmet.** `msvc-release` on the RTX 5090, 1920×1080, `--raster hw --shadows off`, `--mesh FlightHelmet.gltf --grid-instances 8` (64 instances of one 2,348-cluster mesh, 25 pages, 2.85 MB of page bytes), 120 frames, container-backed source, **every row run twice with the figures below reproduced to the digit unless a range is given**. The card was shared with the owner's other work throughout: `nvidia-smi` read 4,062–4,087 MiB used and 5–8% utilization across the batch, and the per-run `machine_state` recorded 5–25% GPU utilization and 6.8–18.7% CPU from other processes, so **every millisecond here is an upper bound**.

| budget | slots | pool bytes | resident | visible pairs | uploads (MB) | evictions | stale | cull ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| streaming off | — | — | 2.85 MB whole | 1,545 | — | — | — | 0.029–0.031 |
| 100% (2.85 MB) | 25 | **3.73 MB** | 16/25 pages, 1.84 MB | 1,545 | 1.77 | 0 | 0 | 0.029–0.032 |
| 50% (1.43 MB) | 13 | 2.32 MB | 12/25 pages, 1.39 MB | 1,506 | 3.67–3.90 | 99 | 75–77 | 0.029 |
| 25% (0.71 MB) | 6 | 1.49 MB | 4–5/25 pages, 0.44–0.58 MB | 1,080–1,298 | 4.32–5.08 | 110–111 | 91–97 | 0.030 |

Four things in that table are worth reading carefully.

**The cull pass's streaming cost is not measurable here.** The extra work is one residency-word load per pair and, for a cluster that wants to refine and cannot, a masked atomic append — and against 150,272 pairs a frame it is inside the run-to-run spread of the same scene with streaming off (0.029–0.031 ms either way, on a card another process was using). That is the honest statement: not "free", but smaller than this machine can resolve.

**A 100% budget costs more device memory than not streaming at all** — 3.73 MB of pool, ring and tables against 2.85 MB uploaded whole. That is not a defect, it is the price of a fixed-size slot: the pool is 25 slots each sized for the *largest* page, plus two 256 KiB staging regions, plus the always-resident descriptors. Streaming is a way to hold *less than the scene*, and a budget that holds all of it is the configuration where it has nothing to trade. The benefit starts at 50% (2.32 MB) and the quarter budget holds half of what the whole scene costs.

**A camera jump converges in the same two frames a cold start does**, at every budget: the interval is bounded by the feedback latency (`frames_in_flight` = 2) and not by the bytes, because two 128 KB pages a frame is more than this cut asks for. `frames_to_converge` is the *last* interval, so under a tight budget — where eviction restarts an interval every few frames — it reports a few frames and not the whole run; the uploads and eviction counts are what say how much churn there was.

**A tight budget churns, and the stale-request rule is what makes that safe rather than wrong.** At 25% the run evicts 110 pages, drops 91–97 requests as stale, and uploads 4.3–5.1 MB — nearly twice the whole scene — to hold 0.5 MB at a time. The picture degrades as designed (1,080–1,298 visible pairs against 1,545) and never holes, which is what the fly-in case asserts.

**And the row the table could not hold before: the quarter budget with the ray chain on.** The table above is `--shadows off` because the shadowed run used to lose the device; it does not any more, so here is the same scene with shadows on. Same machine, `msvc-release`, 1920×1080, 120 frames, container-backed source, `--orbit 4` — which is the camera that reproduces the table's own 1,545 visible pairs, so the two sets of rows are the same cut. **Run twice, and every figure below was identical to the digit across the pair unless a range is given.** The card was shared throughout: `nvidia-smi` read 6,049–6,750 MiB used and 5–9% utilization around the batch, and the per-run `machine_state` recorded 4–20% GPU utilization and 9.5–34.4% CPU from other processes, so **every millisecond here is an upper bound**.

| 25% budget (0.71 MB) | shadows off | shadows rt |
|---|---|---|
| pool bytes | 1,530,540 | **2,145,330** |
| pages resident | 6/25, 721,568 B | 6/25, 721,568 B |
| visible pairs | 1,538 (max 1,545) | 1,553 (max 1,562) |
| uploads | 15 (1.72 MB) | 13 (2.65 MB) |
| evictions / stale | 72–73 / 63–64 | 54 / 47 |
| frames to converge | 75–76 | 72 |
| `gpu_ms.cull` | 0.0362–0.0363 | 0.0155–0.0157 |
| `gpu_ms.rt` | — | 1.594–1.622 |
| `gpu_ms.clas` | — | 0.077–0.080 |
| `gpu_memory.used_mib` | 662 | 1,712 |

Four things in it are worth saying out loud. **The ray chain costs the pool 40% more bytes** — 1.53 MB against 2.15 MB for the same six slots — because a slot then also holds the float positions (12 bytes a vertex) and the 8-bit indices (3 a triangle) the CLAS builds read, on top of the quantized positions, attributes and triangles the rasterizers do. That is the paged half of what [gfx](gfx.md) calls "a mesh that is ray traced uploads both streams", and it is the ratio a budget has to be set against: **a page costs about 1.4× as much resident with shadows on**. **The same six slots hold the same pages**, so the budget buys the same cut either way; what the ray chain adds is bytes per page, not pages. **`gpu_ms.cull` halves with shadows on**, which is not the cull pass getting faster: shadows turn two-pass occlusion culling off (`resolve_settings`), so the frame runs one cull dispatch instead of two and the zone is summed over one. And **device memory is dominated by the CLAS set, not by streaming**: 1,712 MiB against 662 MiB, because `create_cluster_set` is sized for `views * pair_count` = 150,272 clusters while the frame builds about 1,550 of them. Streaming bounds the *geometry* and does nothing about that; a CLAS set sized for the cut rather than for the scene was the open item beside it, and is closed ([The ray tracing chain's memory](#the-ray-tracing-chains-memory): this scene's chain now holds a few thousand clusters).

**A quarter budget is only pressure under a camera that wants more than six pages.** The same command at the default breathing camera — `--orbit` unset, so 8 to 36 radius-tenths — holds **one** page of 25, uploads once, evicts nothing and converges in two frames, at 486–547 visible pairs. That is the same demand-paging point the 100% row makes from the other end, and it is why the rows above name their camera: a budget stated as a percentage of the page bytes says nothing about whether it binds.

**Host memory: the number this change is about.** Same scene, same 25% budget, cold camera, the only difference being where a page's bytes come from:

| source | host working set | peak | released | ranged reads | read |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--page-source host` | 307.4–307.5 MB | 338.2–338.3 MB | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `--page-source file` | **303.2–304.7 MB** | 338.0–338.2 MB | 4.83 MB | 342–348 | 11.9–12.3 MB |

The working set falls by about the 4.83 MB the release reports, and **the peak does not move at all** — which is exactly the caveat above, stated as a measurement rather than as a promise: the load materializes the merged streams and `attach_page_source` frees them afterwards. On a 2.85 MB mesh the absolute numbers are small; what they establish is that the mechanism works and where its remaining cost is. (The read total is larger than the scene because a churning budget re-reads a page it evicted — three ranged reads a page against a memcpy, which is the trade a budget under the working set makes whichever source it has.)

**And on a scene large enough for the budget to matter.** The procedural heightfield at `--grid 2048` (8.4 M triangles, 2,052 pages, **235 MB of page bytes**), same machine, same settings, camera at 0.6 scene radii, 120 frames, run twice. This is the case the FlightHelmet is too small to show, and it is also the case that has **no container behind it** — the heightfield is built in the process, so it keeps the in-memory source, which is exactly the refusal working as designed.

| budget | slots | pool bytes | resident | uploads | `gpu_memory.used_mib` | cull ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| streaming off | — | 235 MB uploaded whole | all of it | — | **461** | 0.0293–0.0294 |
| 100% (235 MB) | 2,052 | 244.9 MB | 75 pages, 8.6 MB | 75 (8.3 MB) | 485 | 0.0306–0.0313 |
| 50% (117.5 MB) | 1,074 | 129.6 MB | 74 pages, 8.5 MB | 74 (8.2 MB) | 369 | 0.0306–0.0326 |
| 25% (58.8 MB) | 553 | **68.2 MB** | 74–75 pages, 8.5 MB | 74 (8.2 MB) | **339** | 0.0306–0.0308 |

The quarter budget draws the same picture — 1,136 visible pairs at every row — out of **68 MB of pool against 235 MB uploaded whole**, and the driver's own figure agrees to the mebibyte across both runs: 339 MiB against 461 MiB for the process. Nothing is evicted and nothing goes stale at any budget, because this camera's cut wants 74 of 2,052 pages and even a quarter budget is four times that: a budget is only pressure when it is under the working set, which is what the FlightHelmet rows show and this one deliberately does not. Convergence is one frame at every budget.

The cull pass is the one place streaming's shipped cost is visible at all here: **0.0293 ms off against 0.0306–0.0326 streamed**, over 2,052 pairs — about 4%, and larger than the FlightHelmet's spread only because this scene's pair count is small enough (2,052 against 150,272) that the per-page residency read is a bigger share of a short pass. Read the two together: the extra work is one load per pair and a masked append, it does not scale with the scene, and on the larger pair count it disappears into the noise.

**Costs, at a glance.** `Stats::stream` carries what a run did — pages total, resident and pinned, slots, pending requests, requests, uploads and their bytes, evictions, stale drops, request-buffer overflows, frames to converge, the resident and total page bytes, and — for a container-backed source — which source it was, the ranged reads and their bytes, the host bytes released, and how many frames a page was wanted before its reads had landed — and the pool's own page count (`pool_pages`, on every frame of a flythrough's `.jsonl` too, beside `pending` and `loads_in_flight`) and the loads given up for the walk's head (`steals`, [above](#admission-never-waits-on-a-read-it-cannot-start)). Both hosts report all of it.

## Reference renderer

[04 §4.8](../plan/04-renderer.md#48-reference-renderer-and-objective-optimization) asks for *a GPU path tracer in Slang sharing material/BSDF, light, and camera code with the real-time path*, converged to a noise floor, against which the real-time path is measured. `systems/renderer/reference.h` is that: `ReferenceRenderer::render(camera, settings)` gives back a linear HDR buffer and an RGBA8 picture through **the same display transform the resolve ends on**, so a reference image and a real-time image are in one space and FLIP compares pictures rather than transfer curves.

**It uses a `SceneRenderer`; it is not one.** A reference render is one ordinary frame followed by N compute dispatches. The frame is what matters: it runs the cull pass, fills the visible list, and builds the cluster acceleration structures and the top-level structure over them — and *those* are what the path tracer traces. There is no second scene, no second geometry path and no second material table, so a reference ray shades the material the resolve would have shaded on that pixel, and a disagreement between the two pictures is a disagreement about **transport** rather than about two different scenes. The one thing the reference changes about the frame is `FrameDesc::lod_px`.

**What the reference is a reference *for*.** On this engine the geometry under the acceleration structures is the frame's **LOD cut**, so a converged path trace of it is the right answer *for the geometry the renderer chose*, not for the source mesh. Both questions are worth asking and a capture says which it answered:

| `finest` | The structures hold | The comparison measures |
|---|---|---|
| false (default) | the frame's own LOD cut | shading, lighting and transport — everything but the cut |
| true | the finest clusters (`FrameDesc::lod_px` = 0) | those **plus** what the LOD cut costs |

Measured on the FlightHelmet at 640×480, `--orbit 22`, 1024 samples, three bounces, `msvc-release` on the RTX 5090, twice with identical numbers: the frame's cut is **189 pairs** and the finest **1031**, 5.5× as much geometry for 45.4 ms of tracing against 40.5. The real-time picture is 0.0190 FLIP from the reference of its own cut and **0.0214** from the reference of the source geometry, and the two references are **0.0106** apart from each other. So at a 1-pixel threshold the LOD selection costs about a tenth of a FLIP percent of the real-time path's total error against the truth — small, but the only way to see it at all is to render both, which is why the flag exists and why a capture records which one it used.

**What is shared, and why each piece had to be.** `brdf.slang` was already shared. That was not enough: two integrators that agree on `brdf_eval` and disagree about how a triangle's UVs are interpolated, what a metallic-roughness texture multiplies, where a light's falloff reaches zero, or what the display transform is would produce a comparison of their material layers. So everything between the geometry and the BSDF moved into `material.slang` ([gfx](gfx.md)) and the resolve now calls it — the move is behaviour-preserving and was checked as such, byte for byte, on five FlightHelmet configurations. The lights moved too, into `renderer::frame_lighting` (`systems/renderer/lighting.h`): the sun, the sky, the two orbiting point lights and the ray bias are one function that both `record_frame` and `ReferenceRenderer::render` call with the same frame index, because "the same scene at the same moment" has to include the lights.

| Shared | Separate, and why |
|---|---|
| the scene, its materials and textures, the acceleration structures the frame built | the integrator: rasterize-and-resolve against trace-and-accumulate |
| `brdf.slang`: the BSDF, the falloffs, the roughness clamp | `sampling.slang`: densities and a random stream, which the resolve has no use for |
| `material.slang`: the triangle fetch, the attributes, the tangent frame, the textures, `light_sample`, the environment (`sky_radiance`, `ground_radiance`, `environment_radiance`) | the resolve's screen-space reconstruction, which exists because a rasterized pixel carries no barycentrics and a ray-traced one does |
| `display.slang`: the output encode, `display_output` — the transfer curve and the dither, the same noise at the same pixel ([below](#the-output-encode)) | the target: the resolve's is the renderer's colour target, 8 or 10 bits; the reference's tonemap writes packed 8-bit bytes, dithered at 8 |
| `frame_lighting`: sun, sky, the ground's albedo, the two point lights, the ray bias | the shadow ray's *shape* is the same; the reference traces one per light per **path vertex**, the resolve one per light per pixel |

**The sky has two roles and the reference mirrors both, deliberately.** In the real-time path `ResolveParams::sky` is written straight out for an uncovered pixel *and* used, with the ground, as the entire indirect term. Those are two different functions of one number, which is a property of a renderer that has no sky model yet. The reference copies it rather than fixing it: a **primary** miss returns `sky^2.2` in linear, so the display transform gives back exactly the bytes the resolve writes, and a **secondary** miss returns `environment_radiance` — the sky's uniform radiance above the horizon and the lit ground below it — the environment whose cosine-weighted mean the resolve's hemisphere term is ([The sky above, the ground below](#the-sky-above-the-ground-below)). Copying it is what makes the two comparable at all; fixing it belongs with the atmosphere of §4.2 step 5.

**Where the two still disagree, in order of size.** No indirect light in the real-time path at all — the resolve has one ambient term where the reference integrates a hemisphere, and at more than one bounce the reference carries light that bounced off the rest of the scene, which is most of the FLIP on any scene with interiors or close-standing geometry. The ambient model itself: since 2026-09-25 the diffuse half is exact in open space — the resolve's `albedo * lerp(ground, sky, (1 + n.y) / 2)` *is* the cosine-weighted mean of the reference's two uniform halves — and what is left is the specular lobe's share (`brdf_env_specular`, an analytic fit of the lobe integrated against a uniform environment, evaluated with the environment at the normal rather than along the reflection) and the Fresnel the reference's diffuse lobe loses and the ambient does not. Until that day the environment was a ramp the resolve read at the normal, 10% bright facing up and 18% dark facing down against its own integral. Antialiasing: the reference box-filters a pixel and the rasterizer point-samples one, which shows at every silhouette — `ReferenceSettings::pixel_center` turns the jitter off when a comparison is about shading rather than about edges. A shading normal that ended up behind the surface used to be one honest divergence — the reference turned it into the geometric hemisphere and the resolve let the BSDF return nothing — and since 2026-09-25 the resolve turns it too ([A shading normal is not the surface](#a-shading-normal-is-not-the-surface)). What is left of it: at a vertex whose shading normal leans away from the ray the reference takes the lights and then ends the path, where the resolve adds its ambient.

**Accumulation, batches, and what "deterministic" means.** `accum` is one `float4` per pixel — radiance sum in rgb, sample count in w — and a dispatch adds `batch` samples starting at `sample_base`. A pixel's Nth sample is a function of (pixel, N, seed) and nothing else, so the *samples* do not depend on how the render was split; batching exists so progress can be reported, a render can be stopped and still produce a valid (noisier) picture, and no single submission runs long enough to meet the display driver's watchdog. The guarantee is therefore precise: **the same seed and the same batch size is the same bytes**, which the tests check. Across batch sizes the samples are identical and only the order the partial sums are added in differs, and float addition is not associative — measured at 64 spp that is under `4.5e-7` of linear radiance, which after the display transform moves **no byte at all**.

**The finding that cost the most, and the reason a background pixel is not tonemapped.** The first corpus run came back with FLIP means of 0.04 to 0.07 on every scene and a p95 *below* the mean, which is the signature of a flat difference rather than a rendering one. It was: the real-time path writes `sky` for an uncovered pixel as a **display-space** colour straight into a UNORM target, while the reference carried linear radiance and had to round-trip it through `pow(sky, 2.2)` and back. Two things then went wrong at once. The round trip is exact to about a part in ten million, but `sky.g` = 0.70 lands at 178.4999969 of 255 — three millionths under a byte boundary — so the trip moved it to 179. And the shader's own quantization could not have saved it either: `0.699999988 * 255` is 178.4999969 in exact arithmetic, and **rounding that product to float32 gives exactly 178.5**, because the spacing of float32 there is 1.5e-5 and the error is 3e-6. The fixed-function UNORM conversion the resolve's colour target performs does not have that problem; it converts the float exactly and writes 178. So the reference does two things: it keeps a one-bit **coverage** buffer saying whether any sample's primary ray hit geometry, and it writes the background for an uncovered pixel from a value **quantized on the CPU in double precision** (`gfx::pack_unorm_rgba8`). A pixel something did cover is tonemapped as before, including a silhouette pixel whose box filter mixed sky and surface, which is what that pixel should be. Removing the flat one-byte offset took the corpus from 0.019–0.063 FLIP to **0.0014–0.035**: between 45% and 96% of what the gate was measuring was a rounding artefact. The lesson is general enough to write down: *whenever two paths have to agree to the byte, the last quantization must happen once, in the place with precision to spare.*

**The integrator.** Unidirectional paths; next-event estimation to the sun and to the analytic lights, one terminate-on-first-hit ray each, offset along the geometric normal by the same bias the resolve uses; the two-lobe BSDF importance-sampled with a Fresnel-weighted lobe pick, GGX by visible normals and Lambert by cosine, the estimator dividing by the *mixture* density; Russian roulette after three scattering events; emissive — the factor times the emissive texture, through the same `sample_material` the resolve calls — added where a ray lands on it, with weight 1, and never sampled as a light, which is v1's stance on emitters ([texture](texture.md#emissive)); no occlusion map, ever. Every light the engine has today is a **delta** light, so nothing a BSDF ray can hit is also sampled directly and every multiple-importance-sampling weight is 1 — the power heuristic is written and tested in `sampling.slang` for the area and environment sampling that will change that, and is not called here. `max_bounces` counts **scattering events after the primary hit**, so 1 is direct lighting plus one bounce, which is exactly what the resolve approximates with its ambient term.

**What the tests hold it to** (`systems/renderer/tests/reference_tests.cpp`, all headless, all skipping with a message on a device without cluster acceleration structures, since there are then no structures to trace). A **furnace**: a white cube in a closed environment of one radiance with the sun and the lights off — a furnace with a sun in it is not a furnace — where an uncovered pixel returns the environment to 1e-5 and a covered one returns the surface's directional albedo. Measured over ~3,300 covered pixels at 512 spp: a white dielectric at roughness 1 returns **0.9746** of the environment (the CPU quadrature in `domain/gfx/tests/sampling_tests.cpp` says 0.9726 at `n·v` = 0.95) and a white metal at roughness 1 returns **0.3870** (the CPU says 0.3168 head-on; a cube shows grazing angles too, where Fresnel is higher).
