The metal row is the energy single-scatter GGX loses, and it is a property of the model the two integrators *share*, so it cancels in a comparison. **Determinism**: same seed, byte-identical; different seed, different picture. **Convergence**: the root-mean-square linear error of a 32×32 block against a 4096-spp picture at 16, 64, 256 and 1024 spp falls by 2.08×, 2.06× and 1.64× per quadrupling, against the 2× that 1/√n predicts — the last step is short because the picture it is measured against is itself only 4096 samples converged, which is the honest reading and the reason the bound is a range rather than a number. **Agreement with the resolve** at one bounce, jitter off, 512 spp, 128×128, on four scenes the engine can build with no content at all:

| Scene | FLIP mean | FLIP p95 | PSNR | SSIM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| diffuse plane, sun and two point lights | 0.0051 | 0.042 | 55.5 dB | 0.9996 |
| diffuse plane, sun only | 0.0055 | 0.045 | 54.5 dB | 0.9996 |
| a cube over the plane, shadows traced | 0.0157 | 0.106 | 39.5 dB | 0.9922 |
| emissive: a dark plane lit by its own texture | 0.0015 | 0.011 | 64.6 dB | 0.9999 |

FLIP calls about 0.1 the threshold at which a person starts to notice a difference, so all four are comfortably "the same picture", and what is left is the ambient model and the one bounce of real indirect light the resolve does not have. The shadowed case is the largest because a shadow edge is where a one-ray-per-pixel test and a converged integral differ most. **The table moved twice on 2026-09-25.** In the evening the environment became two uniform halves with a ground below ([The sky above, the ground below](#the-sky-above-the-ground-below)), which made the resolve's diffuse ambient the reference's integral exactly: the four read 0.0131, 0.0140, 0.0215 and 0.0034 the same day before that change (44.7, 43.7, 37.7 and 59.3 dB). Earlier, when the resolve's sky term stopped weighting its specular share by bare Schlick at n·v — a mirror's curve at every roughness — and took the GGX lobe's own reflectance of a uniform sky (`brdf_env_specular`, [gfx](gfx.md)): the same four cases measured the same day before the change read 0.0206, 0.0218, 0.0281 and 0.0144 FLIP (39.5, 38.8, 35.3 and 43.1 dB), so the path tracer, which integrates that sky, agrees with the resolve better by a quarter to three quarters. That change is what made the ashlar ruins matte ([the second owner session](../experiments/second-interactive-session-2026-09-25.md)).

**The noise floor, and how many samples a scene needs.** A reference is only a reference once its own noise is well under the difference it is being used to measure. Measured on the RTX 5090 in `msvc-release` at 640×480, three bounces, against a **different-seeded** 8192-sample picture of the same frame, taken twice with identical results (GPU 1–3% busy, 3.6 GiB of 32 GiB held by other processes, CPU 12% — quiet enough that the times are close to a cost rather than an upper bound):

| spp | heightfield FLIP / PSNR / time | FlightHelmet FLIP / PSNR / time |
|---|---|---|
| 16 | 0.0073 / 44.4 dB / 0.01 s | 0.0034 / 44.6 dB / 0.01 s |
| 64 | 0.0048 / 50.1 dB / 0.01 s | 0.0022 / 50.3 dB / 0.01 s |
| 256 | 0.0035 / 55.2 dB / 0.02 s | 0.0015 / 55.7 dB / 0.03 s |
| 1024 | 0.0027 / 59.2 dB / 0.04 s | 0.0011 / 60.4 dB / 0.05 s |
| 4096 | 0.0022 / 62.0 dB / 0.14 s | 0.0008 / 63.9 dB / 0.18 s |
| 8192 (the picture the rest are measured against) | — / — / 0.31 s | — / — / 0.39 s |

PSNR is the honest convergence indicator here and it climbs by **5.7, 5.1, 4.0 and 2.8 dB per quadrupling** where 1/√n predicts a flat 6 dB; the shortfall at the top is the 8192-sample picture's own noise, not the estimator's. FLIP flattens sooner because most of these frames are exactly-matching background, which no amount of sampling improves. **The corpus runs at 1024 samples**, where the noise floor is 0.0027 and 0.0011 against a real signal of 0.035 and 0.019 — an order of magnitude of headroom — and a scene costs a twentieth of a second. These are small scenes seen from a distance, so most rays miss; a frame that fills the screen with geometry costs far more, and the corpus's own report carries the time per scene.

**Today's corpus** (`content/test-scenes/`, `tools/ci/reference-compare.ps1`, same machine and preset; the numbers as of the evening of 2026-09-25, after the environment gained its ground, below the table). `direct` is the same real-time picture against the reference at **one bounce**, so `full` − `direct` is the indirect light the real-time path does not have:

| Scene | FLIP mean | FLIP p95 | direct-only FLIP | PSNR | SSIM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| heightfield, 640×480 | 0.0238 | 0.1338 | 0.0209 | 39.1 dB | 0.9903 |
| flighthelmet, 640×480 | 0.0131 | 0.0900 | 0.0133 | 34.7 dB | 0.9830 |
| helmet-grid (3×3), 640×480 | 0.0034 | 0.0023 | 0.0035 | 37.2 dB | 0.9952 |
| thin-geometry (Lantern), 640×480 | 0.0034 † | 0.0000 | 0.0035 | 40.7 dB | 0.9960 |
| wide-frustum, 1920×360 | 0.0009 | 0.0000 | 0.0010 | 42.5 dB | 0.9988 |
| shredded-atlas, 512×512 ‡ | 0.0389 | 0.1137 | 0.0389 | 34.2 dB | 0.9846 |

**The table moved three times on 2026-09-25.** In the evening the environment gained its ground and became two uniform halves: heightfield 0.0268 → 0.0235 (direct-only 0.0281 → 0.0209), shredded-atlas 0.0424 → 0.0390, thin-geometry 0.0036 → 0.0035, flighthelmet 0.0128 → 0.0132 (under the reference's own noise), helmet-grid and wide-frustum unchanged ([The sky above, the ground below](#the-sky-above-the-ground-below) has the table and why uniform); and then, by no more than 0.0003 a row, when `brdf_eval` stopped rejecting a shading normal turned from the camera ([A shading normal is not the surface](#a-shading-normal-is-not-the-surface)), which is the table above. The first time, every row by a quarter to a third, when the resolve's sky term stopped weighting its specular share by bare Schlick at n·v and took the lobe's own reflectance of the sky (`brdf_env_specular`, [gfx](gfx.md)). The same corpus the same day, one build apart (the older one an engine-host with the Schlick term and no shader manifest beside it — a build directory's manifest recompiles an edited `.slang` at start-up, so a before-and-after by editing the source and rebuilding measures the source on disk, not the binary): flighthelmet 0.0168 → 0.0128, heightfield 0.0348 → 0.0268, helmet-grid 0.0050 → 0.0037, thin-geometry 0.0053 → 0.0036, wide-frustum 0.0014 → 0.0010, shredded-atlas 0.0575 → 0.0424. The reference integrates the same sky the resolve's ambient term approximates, so a term closer to that integral moves every scene towards it; the thresholds were left where they were. (The [second owner session](../experiments/second-interactive-session-2026-09-25.md) is why the term changed.)

† **The thin-geometry row used to have two values, and finding out why was worth the gate's whole cost.** It read 0.0116 (PSNR 33.6) when the Lantern came out of the derived-data cache and 0.0051 (PSNR 37.4) when it was built from the glTF — reproducibly, and with the *same* 15-pair cut either way, which is what made it look like noise rather than a defect. It was neither the renderer nor the reference. Measured directly, three `--no-cache` renders of the Lantern were byte-identical to each other and to the first cached run (the one that missed and built in memory), three cached renders were byte-identical to each other, and the two groups differed by 0.019 FLIP with a worst pixel of 0.97. The Lantern is a GLB, so its four textures live in buffer views and have no paths — and a `.clusters` container recorded image *paths* and nothing else, so from the cache the mesh drew untextured. Containers carry the encoded bytes of the images their source embedded since 2026-09-18 ([geometry](geometry.md#embedded-images-the-container-carries-them)), and the corpus now gives **identical numbers cold and warm**: the row above is both, run twice from an empty `ddc/` and twice from a full one.

Two things about how that was caught are worth keeping. The gate found a bug it was not looking for — it is a *picture* comparison, so a picture that changed for a reason nobody had modelled still moved a number — and it only became legible because the report records `mesh_cache` per scene, which is why that field is in the report and why anything else whose provenance could vary belongs there too. And the threshold had been set to clear **both** states (0.03 against 0.0116), which is the mistake to avoid repeating: a margin sized around a symptom hides the symptom. It is **0.01** now, about twice the measured mean, in line with flighthelmet's and heightfield's margins — and deliberately *below* the 0.0116 the defect produced, so the same regression fails the gate instead of passing it.

**Where a paged mesh's leaves are, and the measurement that found out they were not there.** `ClusterMeshPart::first_leaf_cluster` exists because a `.clusters` container is in **page order** — coarse first, leaves last ([geometry](geometry.md#pages-and-streaming)) — and every container is, whether or not anyone will stream from it, because the page layout is part of the derived-data cache key. The single-mesh load path built its part by hand and left that field at zero, so everything that asked a part where its leaves are got the **coarsest** clusters instead. The visible consequence was the camera: it frames the leaves' bounds, a coarse cluster's sphere is looser than the surface it stands for, and how loose depends on how far the simplifier got — so two builds of one mesh that differed only in their *coarse* levels were drawn at two different sizes. It surfaced while measuring the atlas-seam fix: the two builds' pictures disagreed by **0.23 FLIP at the finest threshold**, where they draw exactly the same triangles. With the field right they are **byte-identical** (FLIP 0, SSIM 1) on all four test models, which is what made the rest of that measurement trustworthy. The lesson is the one the field's own comment already gave and nobody applied: a convention that is true for half the meshes is worse than no convention, and the test that pins it now (`atlas_lod_tests.cpp`) writes a paged container and asserts the leaves are a contiguous run at `first_leaf_cluster` and that nothing before it is one.

‡ **This row is the odd one out and is meant to be.** Its number is not the shading gap the other five measure but **what LOD costs the picture**, because its reference is traced from the finest geometry while the real-time path draws a 16-pixel-threshold cut of it — the only comparison in the corpus that renders two different cuts. Its thresholds are therefore set from both ends rather than from one: the measured 0.0575 / 0.1870 below (0.0424 / 0.1339 since the sky term changed on 2026-09-25), and **0.1231 / 0.6481** above, which is what the same scene gives with the LOD builder's seam rule turned off (`engine-view --procedural shredded-atlas --uv-seams none --uv-weight 0`, the same camera, the same reference). 0.09 and 0.30 sit between the two, so the regression this scene exists for fails the gate instead of passing it — which is the rule the thin-geometry row learned the hard way, applied at the time rather than afterwards.

**A sixth scene, and the blind spot it closes.** Every row above compares the real-time path and the reference at the **same** LOD threshold — the reference traces the structures the frame built, which is what makes the comparison about shading rather than about geometry. That is also a blind spot the size of the whole LOD system: a defect in simplification puts the same wrong triangles into both pictures and the gate reports that they agree. It hid one for months ([geometry](geometry.md#what-the-simplifier-is-given-and-why)): the LOD builder was collapsing across UV atlas islands, and no picture test in the tree could see it because none of them ever rendered two different cuts. `shredded-atlas` is the row that does — the procedural atlas fixture at a coarse threshold against `"reference": {"finest": true}`, which traces the source geometry — so the number it carries is *what LOD costs the picture* rather than what shading does. Measured through the renderer's own test at 384×384, coarse (63 pairs) against finest (140 pairs) on the same camera: **FLIP 0.0092, PSNR 39.0 dB** with the seam rule, and **FLIP 0.140, PSNR 18.8 dB** without it, from cuts of the same size — 63 pairs against 64. The whole of that difference is texture, not geometry, which is the clearest statement of the defect there is.

Two things are worth reading out of that. **The indirect share is near zero on the isolated objects**, which is not a claim that the real-time path has global illumination — it is that these are isolated objects under an open sky, where a second bounce almost always escapes and the resolve's hemisphere ambient is a fair approximation of it. The heightfield is the one scene where it shows (0.0235 full against 0.0209 direct): its hills light each other, and once the ambient model's own error stopped being larger than that light, the column could see it. A scene with interiors, a mirror room or a foliage wall would separate the two columns, and none of those is in the corpus yet; that is the gap the pathological scenes of §4.8 fill. **The p95 is below the mean on three scenes** because most of those frames is background the two agree on exactly, so the error is concentrated in the few percent of pixels the object covers — which is why the thresholds carry both numbers.

**An animated instance.** A reference render is one frame, so what it draws is **one pose**, and getting that right needed a pass-through and nothing else: `ReferenceSettings::joints` and `instance_joints` are the same two spans `FrameDesc` takes, the preliminary frame writes the deformed-vertex pool from them, the cluster acceleration structures are built from the pool, and the reference traces those. The reference therefore path traces a character where the tick put it without this module learning what a clip is — which is the same "nothing had to change" that [Skinned instances](#skinned-instances) reports for the ray path, for the same reason. Measured on the Khronos Fox at 320×240, 64 samples: the posed reference is **0.0275** FLIP from the posed real-time frame and **0.0675** from a reference of the same scene at rest, so the pose is demonstrably in the picture rather than assumed to be. What the reference cannot do is *play* the clip: `engine-view --reference --animate` ticks the world once and draws the pose the windowed path's first frame would draw, `--frames` means nothing to it, and it says so on stderr when a caller passes one anyway. A sequence — which is what §4.8's temporal-stability metric will need — is a loop over frame indices that does not exist yet.

**The fixed-cost work the resolve gained, and the gate it sits behind.** The resolve skips a 32×32 tile the Hi-Z build called empty (`ResolveParams::coverage`) and discards an empty pixel rather than writing the sky the clear already wrote (`sky_is_clear`). The tile mask is exact **only** while nothing writes the visibility buffer after the last Hi-Z build, which is exactly when two-pass occlusion culling is on — and a reference render is never in that case, because `reference_available` demands `rt_chain` and `resolve_settings` turns occlusion off whenever the chain runs. So the preliminary frame carries no mask and reads every word, which is correct and costs a fraction of a millisecond on a render measured in seconds. `FrameDesc::lod_px` cannot disturb it either: it changes the cull pass's threshold, which runs before every raster and every Hi-Z build in the frame, so it moves *which* clusters are drawn and not *when* anything is written.

The `sky_is_clear` path is also why the reference's background is now written from a CPU-quantized constant rather than tonemapped (above): the bytes an empty pixel carries come from the **clear**, one fixed-function conversion of `renderer::k_sky`, and the reference's `gfx::pack_unorm_rgba8(k_sky)` is the CPU's answer to the same conversion. There is one spelling of that colour in the tree (`lighting.h`), and three things read it — the clear, `ResolveParams::sky`, and the reference's background. A second spelling would be a one-byte difference on every empty pixel of every comparison, which is exactly the bug this section already records.

**Availability.** `reference_available(resolved, device, &why)` refuses three things before anything is created, the way `check_availability` does for the renderer: a device without cluster acceleration structures or ray queries — said in the device's verdict's own sentence, which names the one it lacks (on the TITAN Xp, both) —, settings that build no structures at all (`--shadows rt` or `--raster rt` is what turns the chain on), and more than one view — the reference renders one view, and a surround reference is open work.

**Cost.** The reference is not a frame path and the rules that keep readbacks and driver queries out of one do not reach it: `render()` blocks per batch, reads two buffers back, and is measured in wall seconds. `ReferenceFrame::trace_ms` is the integrator's own GPU milliseconds from a `gfx::GpuTimer`, summed over the batches; `seconds` is what a caller waits, including the real-time frame and the readbacks.

## Capture channels, and the id encoding

`CaptureChannels` asks for any of four, and `CapturedFrame` carries what came back.

| Channel | Form | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `color` | RGBA8 | the picture, as `engine-view --capture` writes it |
| `ids` | three `u32` per pixel | instance, cluster, triangle; `0xFFFFFFFF` in all three where the scene did not cover the pixel |
| `depth` | `f32` per pixel | reversed-Z clip depth, 0 where nothing covered it, plus the covered range as `depth_min`/`depth_max` |
| `normals` | RGB8 | the world normal encoded `n * 0.5 + 0.5` |

A capture is always in the **target's** pixels, whatever the layout: the walk is per view, a pixel inside a view's rectangle reads that view's region of the visibility buffer, a pixel no view covers is empty, and a Panini view's pixels go through the same map the resolve used (`panini_source_pixel`, the CPU mirror of the shader's), so an id names what is under that pixel of the picture rather than of the source.

**The id channel is the plan's entity-ID buffer** ([04 §4.2](../plan/04-renderer.md#42-frame-architecture), [10 §10.2](../plan/10-roadmap-risks.md#102-phases) Phase 1), and it is resolved rather than raw on purpose. The visibility buffer holds `depth << 32 | (pair << 8 | triangle)`, where `pair` is the scene's (instance, cluster) pair index ([gfx](gfx.md), "The tie rule"; it was the frame's visible-list entry until 2026-09-24, which a capture had to read the list back to decode). A capture decodes it with the scene alone — `GpuScene::pair_cluster`, a binary search over the instances' `first_pair` and the mesh's `first_cluster`, the inverse of the cull pass's arithmetic — and writes the (instance, cluster, triangle). That is the number an agent can act on ("which instance is under this pixel"), and it is stable across rasterizers, runs, frames and LOD cuts. The no-cull case, where the list is null and the rasterizers draw instance 0's clusters in index order, names cluster *i* as pair *i* and decodes it that way.

`--raster direct` writes no visibility buffer — it draws mesh shaders straight to color with a depth buffer — so asking it for `ids` or `depth` is an **error with a message**, not a buffer of nothing.

`normals` costs a second frame: the normal is what the resolve reconstructs, and only the resolve knows it, so the renderer renders again in the normals view mode and reads the color back. `ids` and `depth` come out of the visibility buffer of the first frame and cost one blocking readback each.

**On disk** (`write_capture`, which engine-host calls and the module's tests check) the channels are `<base>.png`, `<base>.ids.bin` + `<base>.ids.json`, `<base>.depth.png`, and `<base>.normals.png`. The id buffer is a raw little-endian `u32` array with a JSON header beside it rather than an image, because it is data to be indexed (`(y * width + x) * 3`) and any lossy or reordered image form would make a pixel's instance number unreadable:

```json
{"format":"engine.renderer.ids.v1","file":"shot.ids.bin","width":400,"height":300,
 "type":"u32","byte_order":"little","words_per_pixel":3,
 "channels":["instance","cluster","triangle"],"order":"row_major_top_first",
 "empty":4294967295,"covered":47213}
```

Depth is an 8-bit gray PNG normalized over the frame's own covered range (black is both "not covered" and the far end), because the engine's own encoder writes 8 bits per channel and a depth channel is looked at far more often than it is measured — a measurement takes the ids beside it or the `f32` array in `CapturedFrame`. Adding a 16-bit path to `foundation/image` is the obvious next step if that stops being true.

## The frame capture

While a host has [core/profiling](profiling.md#the-frame-capture)'s frame capture on (`profile.start`, [protocol](protocol.md#profile-the-frame-capture-over-the-protocol)), every `SceneRenderer` frame records itself into it (roadmap A10): `begin_frame` marks the frame's start — before its wait for the slot — under a number from one process-wide sequence (so two renderers' frames in one capture never share one), kept with the slot (`slot_capture_`), and the end of `submit_frame` marks its end. When the slot comes around, `collect_slot` (`record_capture`) records **every GPU timer zone of that frame under the timer's own name** — the passes as `gfx::GpuTimer` names them, finer than `FrameStats`' buckets, one per view where the zone is per view — and its eight CPU spans (`FrameCpu`: `renderer.wait`, `renderer.begin`, `renderer.tables`, `renderer.terrain`, `renderer.passes`, `renderer.compile`, `renderer.record`, `renderer.submit`) against that number, which is how a GPU time measured `frames_in_flight` frames later lands on the frame that drew it. Off, it is a relaxed load at each of the three points; on, it allocates nothing. Nothing about a frame changes.

## Statistics

`Stats` carries exactly the fields engine-view's JSON summary prints and engine-host's `render.benchmark` returns: frames, timed frames, the three visible-pair counts and their running minimum and maximum, the shadow casters the frame built beside them ([Shadows](#shadows)), the pairs the cascaded shadow maps drew and their fallback count, with `gpu_shadow` and `gpu_shadow_cull` beside the passes' milliseconds ([Cascaded shadow maps](#cascaded-shadow-maps)), the vertex path's indexed-draw counts — `triangles_hw`, the triangles the cull pass allocated in both hardware runs, which is 0 on every other draw, and `vertex_fallback`, the survivors the index budget sent to the capacity draw, which logs one warning per renderer the first time it is not 0 because it is a frame that got slower with nothing else saying so — the GPU milliseconds of each pass (cull, hw, sw, hiz, resolve, rt, clas, deform, deform_alloc, trace, total) as sums with `*_ms()` accessors that divide by the timed frames, the deformed-vertex pool's suballocation for the frame (vertices used, the run's peak, the entries given a block and the entries refused), the CPU nanoseconds spent inside `submit_frame`, and one `ViewStats` per view (above). The per-view rectangles and tiers are filled when the layout is laid out rather than when a frame completes, because a capture is one or two frames and would otherwise report a run of zeros. The visible counts are read one frame late from a per-slot copy of the indirect argument blocks; `collect_visible()` is how a caller that waited for a specific frame (engine-view's last, before it captures) folds that frame's counts in without waiting for the slot to come around. The GPU timings of that frame are *not* in it, because a timestamp pool is read when its slot is reused.

**`Stats::gpu_memory` says who else was using the card.** `budget_mib`, `used_mib` and `device_local_total_mib` come from `gfx::MemoryBudget` ([gfx](gfx.md)) through `sample_gpu_memory()`, which `create()` and `reset_stats()` call so a summary always has a figure and which a host that measures calls again at the end of a run. It is a driver query and so is **not** in the frame path, which is the same rule as the one that keeps buffer readbacks out of it. The reason it is here at all: this project's development machine renders beside GPU jobs that hold most of its memory, and a frame time measured against a contended card is a measurement of the contention. Read it together with the `machine_state` block both hosts print — the Vulkan budget under-reports a CUDA tenant, and `nvidia-smi`'s number does not ([bench](bench.md#measuring-on-a-shared-machine) says how far apart the two were, measured).

**`Stats::last` is one frame on its own**, beside the sums (`FrameStats`): which frame it was — its own `FrameDesc::frame_index` and its `submission` since the last `reset_stats()`, both **carried** from the submit rather than inferred, because the fold lags the submission by the frames in flight and a caller counting that lag would be wrong the day it changed — its visible pairs by draw, its shadow casters, every pass's GPU milliseconds from that frame's own timer zones (the bottom-level build, `gpu_blas`, beside `gpu_clas` inside `gpu_rt`), what streaming did while it was the latest frame folded (pages uploaded and their bytes, evictions, requests, pages resident) and the state it left (`pending`, `loads_in_flight`, and `pool_pages`, what the pool holds as against what the manager has admitted), and what the ray tracing chain built, wanted and had room for (`rt_built`, `rt_wanted`, `rt_capacity`). **`Stats::rt`** (`RtStats`) is the chain's run: its capacity and bytes now and at their peak, the budget as a capacity, the scene's union, the resizes, and every frame that dropped instances' structures ([The ray tracing chain's memory](#the-ray-tracing-chains-memory)). `Stats::folded` counts the folds, so a caller reads `last` after each `begin_frame()` that moved it. It is the only per-frame number the renderer exposes and it costs a struct copy per frame; the flythrough below is built on it.

**`Stats::tiles`** (`TileStats`) is a streamed world's run ([Instances that come and go](#instances-that-come-and-go)): the changes the scene took and the CPU nanoseconds they cost in `set_dynamic_instances` (summed, and the worst), the blocks kept, rewritten in place, reused, appended and freed, the compactions and the changes that grew the per-pair buffers, and the frames that brought a table set up to date with the slots, pairs and GPU milliseconds they wrote (`gpu_tables`, the copy and the expansion; `gpu_pair_expand`, the expansion alone). `Stats::last` carries the same frame by frame, with the frame's `hole_pairs`. The renderer logs the run's totals once when it is destroyed (`tile changes`), since no per-frame record says them whole.

**`Stats::tiles`** (`TileStats`) is a streamed world's run ([Instances that come and go](#instances-that-come-and-go)): the changes the scene took and the CPU nanoseconds they cost in `set_dynamic_instances` (summed and the worst), the blocks kept, rewritten in place, reused, appended and freed, the compactions and the changes that grew the per-pair buffers, and the frames that brought a table set up to date with the slots, pairs and GPU milliseconds they wrote (`gpu_tables`, the copy and the expansion; `gpu_pair_expand`, the expansion alone). `Stats::last` carries the same frame by frame, with the frame's `hole_pairs`. The renderer logs the run's once when it is destroyed (`tile changes`), since no per-frame record says it whole.

## Scenes, camera paths and flythroughs

The benchmark corpus of [plan 09 §9.4](../plan/09-testing-profiling.md#94-benchmark-scene-corpus) starts with a **flythrough**: a scene, a scripted camera path over it, and per-frame numbers along the path, so the same scene and path give a comparable number across builds and machines. Everything the two hosts need for it is in this module — the scene file, the terrain, the path, the timed flight, the census and the summary — so `engine-view --benchmark` and `render.benchmark` with a `camera_path` fly the same frames through the same function and report the same shape. The first scene is [desert-overlook](../../content/test-scenes/desert-overlook/README.md); its measurements are in [flythrough-desert-overlook](../experiments/flythrough-desert-overlook.md).

**The formats are schema types** (`schemas/scene.schema`, namespace `engine.scene`), so `schemac` generates them and `engine-cli schema.describe '{"type":"engine.scene.Scene"}'` explains any of them: `Scene` (meshes with a name, a content `hash`, an `overlay` hash and a `Fit`; instances with a translation, rotation, `yaw_deg`, scale and `ground`; seeded `Scatter`s; `ruins`, the `RuinScatter`s below; an optional `Terrain` with `Ridge`s and `Basin`s; since version 2, an optional `camera_path` naming the path the scene is flown along, which `read_scene_file` resolves against the scene file into `SceneDesc::camera_path` and which a host with no path of its own starts a camera at — engine-view's `--interactive` ([apps](apps.md#--interactive-a-camera-somebody-flies)); and, since version 3, in a fragment the ruin assembler wrote, a `RuinTag` on each instance with `ruin_sites` and `sand_drifts` beside them, which the reader accepts and does not interpret), `Overlay` (a local manifest from content hash to file), `CameraPath` (`CameraKey`s and `CameraMarker`s), and what a run writes — `FrameRecord` per frame and `FlythroughSummary` at the end. **Why a JSON file keyed to schema types and not a `doc::Document` layer**, which is how the plan stores a world ([03 §3.2](../plan/03-data-model.md#32-the-authoring-document-world-document)): the renderer reads scenes and must not depend on the document model's journal and ids to do it; a corpus scene is a fixture whose identity is its bytes, so one committed file that diffs as text and hashes as a unit is the honest unit; and the types are chosen to map one-to-one onto a layer's placement objects, so the move is an export and not a redesign. `read_scene_file` reads the **oldest spelling too** — `{"meshes":[{"path"}],"instances":[{"mesh","translation","rotation","scale","animation"}]}` is a valid `Scene` — and is stricter than it was: an unknown field is refused with its path, because a misspelt `ground` that quietly did nothing would float a building.

**A generated mesh in the mesh table.** A mesh path ending in `.<generator>.json` — `content/flora/date-palm.flora.json` — is built by that mesh generator ([assets](assets.md#generated-meshes)) instead of being imported: `load_source_mesh` hands it to `load_generated_mesh` (`src/scene_flora.cpp`, the one call site), which finds the generator by the name in the file's name, takes the source hash over what the file says, looks in the derived-data cache under `assets::generated_mesh_build_key(source hash, the inputs, the scene's LOD options, the default page target)` — `cluster_cache_key` with no weld and the material pack's key when there is one, the key `engine-content flora` writes under — and on a miss builds the container with the generator and writes it there, then adopts it exactly as a `.clusters` named outright is adopted, so everything downstream is the container path. **The material pack** the generator's parts fall back to is `SceneDesc::materials` ([materials](materials.md)): a directory, or empty and the repository's `content/materials` **whatever the derived-data root** (T103; until then only when the cache root was looked up too, so every run with `--ddc` drew flat), except in a test, whose main switches the default off for itself and every child (`SceneLoadReport::materials` says which pack the load used; [materials](materials.md), "Where the hosts find it"). **The images a generated mesh's parts sample are built into the cache's textures** (`build_cache_textures`, the same texture step as a glTF's, run beside the container on a hit or a miss when the scene reads the cache), so a palm's bark draws block-compressed and mipmapped from `<ddc>/textures/`; without a cache they draw through the decode, as a glTF's images always could. On a hit the container's source path is set to the path the scene names, since a recipe's image paths are relative to the recipe and another host may have written the entry from another spelling of it. `cache` reads `hit`, `miss` or `none`; a `hash` in the scene file is checked against the generated mesh's source hash. **The renderer names no generator**: a build without the flora capability compiles the same file and refuses the path with the registry's sentence, which names the capability (`ENGINE_WITH_FLORA`), and a host carries a generator by linking its capability, as it carries the scene generators. `flora_scene_tests.cpp` builds one through the cache, reads it back as a hit and built in memory, refuses a file the solver refuses, and draws [oasis-palms](../../content/test-scenes/oasis-palms/README.md) offscreen ([flora](flora.md#in-a-scene)).

**Content addressing.** A mesh's `hash` is the hash of the file's bytes and buffers, `assets::source_bytes_hash`; the load computes it beside the cache's key from one read (`source_mesh_hash(path, key, bytes)`) and refuses other bytes, naming both hashes. The key is not the pin: it folds in a tag for every importer change that reads some files differently, so a pin compared with it refused the desert overlook's Lantern after G2 although its bytes had not moved (2026-11-18, `scene file: a pin names the bytes, not the importer's key`). An overlay's and a prop's `hash` are the same pin. A generated mesh's is its generator's source hash, which has no such split: it is the canonical parameters with the generator's version, so a version bump moves it. The terrain's is `terrain_hash`, over every field and `k_terrain_version`. **An authored tile set (`TerrainDesc::tiles`, the `tiles` provider) enters it by its content, never its paths** (2026-10-18): a built set by its manifest's build key, set hash and recorded lattice (`key`, `source_hash`, `hash`, `cells`, `spacing_mm`, `origin_mm`, `width`, `height`, `vertical_scale`, `offset_y_mm`, `chain`), a set built on load by its heightfield header's `data_hash` and lattice plus the block's `origin`, `vertical_scale` and build options — the fields the set's build key is made of ([tileset](tileset.md#the-set)). Until then the hash named the provider and nothing of the set, so a heightfield rewritten behind the same path drew the old cached render mesh under the new heights. The renderer reads those fields as JSON and does not link the capability (ADR-0027); a file that is not JSON enters by its bytes, and the block's `ddc` (where, not what) never. Only a terrain with a tile set reads them, so every waves and dunes terrain keeps its hash and its cache entry, pinned in `scene_gen_scene_tests.cpp` ("a tile set enters the terrain hash by its content"). A run's summary carries the scene file's hash, the path file's hash, every mesh's hash and where it came from (`scene`, `overlay` or `terrain`), and one `identity` over all of them: the number that names what was measured.

**The overlay.** A mesh may name, in `overlay`, the content hash of a file that should stand in its place; `SceneFileOptions::overlay` (`engine-view --overlay`, `render.load`'s `overlay`) is a local `engine.scene.Overlay` manifest from hashes to paths. A mesh the manifest names is loaded from there and checked against the hash; one it does not name keeps the scene's file, with a warning. That is how the owner's paid-plan landmarks — never committed — replace a committed scene's Khronos placeholders by their bytes alone.

**Fit.** `MeshFit` scales a mesh uniformly to a height or a longest extent and puts its bounding box's bottom centre (or its centre) at its origin, before any instance transform: a fitted slot occupies the same volume whichever file fills it, which is what lets a 2 cm sample and a 2-million-triangle landmark share one set of placements and one camera path's occlusion. The box is read from the mesh's float positions during `load_scene`, while they exist, and it is the box of the **source's surface, the level 0 clusters' vertices** (`fit_parts`): a level that grows a loose island holds corners no source vertex has ([geometry](geometry.md#loose-islands-removed-whole-the-rest-grown)), and fitted by every level's box the static world's lantern stood shorter than its file says once its parts were islands (T147).

**The terrain** (`terrain.h`) is the classic heightfield's generalization, built **beside** it rather than into it, because the classic one is a fixed 20-unit fixture whose ids and cuts the tests pin: seeded dunes — a handful of transverse waves around one prevailing wind, normalized so their peak-to-trough is about `dune_height` (the first normalization made a 5 m field 2 m high, and the LOD builder rightly turned the ground in front of the camera into clusters a few hundred metres across) — plus hand-placed ridges (a cosine profile around a segment, roughened by a seeded value noise) and basins. `terrain_height` is analytic, so an instance can stand on the ground (`ground`) and a camera key can hold a height above it before the mesh exists. **A caller that asks more than a handful of times holds a `TerrainSampler`**: `terrain_height` draws the dune field from the seed on every call (six waves' worth of trigonometry and a `pow` each, more than the height itself costs), and the scene read asks for every grounded instance and scatter and a ruins entry's dozens of heights per building — reading 1,000 ruins over the desert overlook spent 43–59 ms in the scene read with the field drawn per call and 23–28 ms with one sampler for the read (2026-09-24, seven runs each, [ruins](ruins.md#performance-notes)). The sampler **is** the object `terrain_height` and `build_terrain_mesh` build, not a cache of it, so its heights are the direct function's and the mesh's to the bit; the flythrough test compares all three on a grid across a ridge, a basin and plain dunes. `read_scene_file` builds one per read and `parse_camera_path` one per path. The mesh gets **the grid's own normals** as an attribute rather than normals recomputed per LOD level — recomputed ones made every LOD boundary a visible change of shade — and **one material whose colour and roughness are two maps over the terrain's UVs** (`bake_terrain_maps`: one texel per grid cell, `terrain_surface` at the texel's centre — sand, ridge rock, basin sand and the basin's green floor, blended across a band of 0.1 of the feature's weight around each threshold of `terrain_material`, ten to twenty metres on the desert). The maps travel as PNG bytes in the mesh's images, so the cache entry carries them and the texture step builds them into mipmapped BC7 beside it like a GLB's embedded textures (two 2048² maps for the 2049 grid: the bake and the PNG encode 646 ms of a 42 s cold load, the texture build 410 ms, `msvc-release` on the i9-10980XE beside other agents' builds, so upper bounds). **Why not per cluster, as it was until 2026-09-25**: the terrain carried the four materials and drew each cluster with the one most of its vertices were. A coarser cluster votes over a larger patch and comes out differently near every border, so as the camera moved and the cut changed, patches of rock and of the green floor grew, shrank and jumped by whole clusters — the "green and grey ground textures that shift at position thresholds" of the second owner session ([its write-up](../experiments/second-interactive-session-2026-09-25.md): at the owner's six markers a cut change alone moved the ground's colour on 2.6–4.3% of its pixels, and moves it on 0.009–0.027% now, all of that the cut's own geometric error across a blend). The UVs every level interpolates come from the same source vertices, so a point of the ground is one colour whichever cluster draws it; `flythrough_tests.cpp`'s "the ground's colour does not move when the LOD cut does" draws the owner's terrain at his six marker cameras from two cuts and holds it to that. It is laid out in pages exactly as a glTF's cache entry is and cached in the derived-data root under `cluster_cache_key(terrain_hash, …)`, so a 2049 × 2049 terrain costs its clustering once per machine (`k_terrain_version` 5 is the maps; an entry of 4 is simply not found).

**Ground providers** (`engine.scene.Terrain.provider`, version 4; [scene_gen](scene_gen.md), [ADR-0046](../adr/0046-scene-generators-register-themselves.md)). What a terrain's height is comes from the **ground provider** it names, found in the scene-generator registry by name and made from the terrain entry: `TerrainSampler` is the reader's view of one (`provider()`), and everything that asks the terrain anything — the scene read's grounded instances and ruins, `build_terrain_mesh` (the provider's `grid` on the scene's lattice, the mesh's own points), the time-lapse (its `evaluate` and `travel_m`) and the rings (its `make_rings`) — asks it through the provider. **The waves are the renderer's own provider**, registered by `src/terrain.cpp` itself, so the default goes down the same path as a capability's ground; the terrain capability's dunes are another, registered from their own module, which the renderer does not link (a host does: engine-view and engine-host, where the configuration has it). A terrain names its provider by `provider` (`"waves"`, `"dunes"`), or by the older `generator` enum, which reads as the provider it always meant — the same terrain and the same `terrain_hash` either way; a `provider` other than `dunes` beside `generator: Dunes` is refused, and so is a name the executable does not carry, with the registry's sentence ("… names the ground provider "snow", which this build does not have: its capability is switched off or not linked into this executable (it has dunes, waves)"). **The ridges and basins are the scene's**, not a provider's: their arithmetic (`scene_gen::terrain_features`, the renderer's own until the dunes moved out) is added by every provider the same way, and the surface map is chosen from them (`TerrainSampler::ridge_weight`, `basin_weight`). A provider that cannot be made leaves the sampler drawing the waves over the same description, with `ok()` false and the sentence in `error()`, which is what the scene reader refuses the file with (`terrain_moves`, `terrain_has_rings` and `terrain_provider_known` answer from the registry without making one). `terrain_generator_tests.cpp` reads a terrain naming its provider both ways, and refuses the two answers and the unknown name.

**The dune generator** (`"generator": "Dunes"` or `"provider": "dunes"`, `engine.scene.Terrain` version 2; the terrain capability, [terrain](terrain.md), [ADR-0043](../adr/0043-dunes-as-a-function-of-time.md), proposed). A terrain may hand its dunes to the terrain capability's generator instead of drawing the waves: parametric dune primitives the seeded wind has carried to the terrain's game `time` (seconds since the world's epoch) at its mean `sand_flux` (m² a year), integer and the same bits on every toolchain. Since `Terrain` version 3 it may also carry the generator's **band table** (`bands`, `engine.scene.TerrainBand`: per band its kind, heights, cell, share, crest shape, sinuosity, sharpness, slip-face windows, coupling (`couple_width`, metres inside the taller dunes' footprints) and far flag; [terrain](terrain.md#the-band-table)) — absent is the default three bands from `dune_height` and `dune_wavelength`, an empty or invalid table is refused naming the band (the provider refuses it when it is made) — which is how `desert-dunes` and `desert-erg` draw an erg; the table enters `terrain_hash` only when present. `terrain_hash` names the generator's version as a number (2 since the [repose limiter](terrain.md#the-repose-limiter) changed every dune field's heights), so a mesh cached from an older generator is rebuilt rather than drawn. **Only the dunes change.** The ridges and basins are this module's in both fields and added the same way — the generator knows where they are, thins its sand over rock, flattens it in a basin and bows its crests round a ridge, but the rock and the bowls are the scene's (`scene_gen::terrain_features`, `TerrainSampler::features`), the waves' own arithmetic. The waves stay the default and their arithmetic is untouched, statement for statement, so every existing terrain keeps its heights, its `terrain_hash` (the generator's fields enter the hash only when the generator is named) and its cache entry; the owner's fly-through decides when the generator becomes the default. With the generator the sampler holds the generator's field and a point query gathers the primitives near the point — a few microseconds, and thread-safe, since the scene reader grounds a large ruins entry on a job pool through one sampler — while `build_terrain_mesh` gathers once per 64 × 64 block of vertices: the same heights to the bit (a test compares every vertex of a mesh with the sampler and the direct function), and 1.34 s for the desert overlook's 2049 × 2049 grid where the waves take 0.72 (GCC release, once per machine, since the mesh is cached by its hash). **`TerrainSampler::ground` is what buildings stand on**: with the waves the surface, as before; with the generator the interdune floor plus the ridges and basins, which never moves, so a ruin is the same building at any `time` and the dunes migrate over it and bury what stands there (the scene reader hands it to every placement generator as the ground's floor; the world's placements consumer too). [`content/test-scenes/desert-dunes/`](../../content/test-scenes/desert-dunes/README.md) is the overlook's terrain with the generator three years in, for the owner's fly-through. A build without the terrain capability builds the renderer, draws every waves terrain, and refuses a terrain that names the generator with the registry's sentence; a generator time outside [0, 3·10¹¹) s or a flux outside [0, 100,000] is refused too. `terrain_generator_tests.cpp` holds all of it with no device, including a ruins scene read a year apart to the same instances.

**The dunes in time-lapse** (`terrain_time.h`; `engine-view --time-rate <r>`, `RenderSettings::time_rate`, `render.load`'s `settings.time_rate`): the generator's terrain moving while someone watches, blended between evaluated fields a little every frame so that no dune ever changes height in an instant. It has a section of its own, [below](#the-dunes-in-time-lapse).

**Ruins** (`ruins`, `engine.scene.RuinScatter`; the ruins capability, [ruins](ruins.md)), **and placement generators by name** (`placements`, `engine.scene.PlacementEntry`, `Scene` version 5: `{"generator": "<name>", "params": {...}}`; [scene_gen](scene_gen.md), [ADR-0046](../adr/0046-scene-generators-register-themselves.md)). **The reader names no generator**: every placement entry — a `ruins` entry is the generator `ruins` with the entry as its parameters, and the `ruins` entries come before `placements` — is looked up in the scene-generator registry by name, opened on its parameters, and expanded standing on the terrain's ground (the ground provider's floor, `TerrainSampler::provider().view()`: ground first, then the entries in the file's order), its meshes appended after the file's own and each earlier entry's (a mesh an earlier entry appended under the same name is shared), and its placements become plain instances (`expand_placements` in `src/scene.cpp`); a name the executable does not carry is refused with the registry's sentence, after where the entry is (`scene.json: ruins 0 names the placement generator "ruins", which this build does not have: …`). `SceneDesc::placed_buildings` and `placed_instances` say what the entries made. The ruins, as their generator reads them: a scene may ask for ruined buildings over the terrain's tiles instead of placing them: a kit file (relative to the scene), a world seed, a tile size, a square of tiles, and either a `count` — the tiles of the square the seed ranks first — or a `density`, the endless desert's share of tiles with a building, and the wind's direction. The generator reads each kit, and the reader appends its meshes **after the file's own** (so every index the file used still names what it named) and **before the terrain** (which stays the last mesh, its index now the count of meshes before it rather than the file's mesh count — the first draft kept the old index and gave the terrain's instance a kit mesh, which the scene test caught), assembles every building standing on the terrain (through the read's one `TerrainSampler`), and hands the renderer plain instances of kit meshes: nothing downstream knows a ruin from a scatter. An entry with `"representation": "Blocks"` and a `block_kit` (`engine.scene.RuinBlockKit`, relative to the scene) draws the same buildings **laid block by block** ([ruins](ruins.md#the-block-layer)): the kit is read for the footprint, and only the block kit's meshes are appended, since nothing would instance the kit's members and E33's are hundreds of megabytes on the GPU; every block is a plain instance, standing or fallen. An entry of more than 32 tiles is assembled on the job system's performance pool the reader offers the generators (`scene_gen::Context::jobs`, made the first time one asks, as `build_cache_textures` makes one for textures) because a thousand buildings laid block by block are hundreds of milliseconds on one thread; the buildings are joined in tile order, so the instances are the single thread's (the renderer's ruins test reads forty buildings pooled and compares them with the layer's own single-threaded output), and the `ruins assembled` line says how many threads it used. `load_scene` ends with a `scene loaded` line (`ms`, `meshes`, `instances`, `pairs`, `clusters`): an offscreen run had no other record of what the load cost, and a scene of hundreds of thousands of instances spends its time there. The renderer links no capability for any of it: engine-view and engine-host link the ruins where the configuration has them, for the generator's registrar, and a build without them refuses a scene that names ruins with the registry's sentence and reads every other scene as before (the renderer's conditional link, ADR-0037's interim, is gone). A scene fragment `engine-content ruins` wrote is an ordinary scene of instances and reads the same with or without the capability. **Island City** is the generator `city` the same way ([city](city.md#where-it-attaches)): a `placements` entry naming a plan (and a district or a tile, or neither) expands to the proxy instances `engine-content city fragment` writes, with the twelve proxy boxes as its meshes, and a streamed one is the plan's per-tile query at each ring's detail; the renderer links nothing of it either.

**A sky** (`sky`, `engine.scene.Sky`, `Scene` version 6; [The sky](#the-sky), [ADR-0048](../adr/0048-the-sky-is-a-providers-model-drawn-by-the-renderer.md)). **The reader names no sky provider either**: the entry's `provider` (empty is "earth") is looked up in the registry and made once to check the entry, and a name the executable does not carry or an entry the provider refuses is refused with its sentence after the file's path (`scene.json: the sky names the sky provider "mars", which this build does not have: …`, `scene.json: sky.turbidity must be within [1, 10]`); the entry is kept as it was read (`SceneDesc::sky`, `SceneData::sky`) and the renderer makes the provider again for its frames. A scene without the entry draws the stand-in's sky, to the bit. A flight's per-pass milliseconds gain `sky`, the passes' zone (`PassMs` and `PassPercentiles` version 5).

**The camera path** (`camera_path.h`) is keys of time, position, a look-at point or an orientation, and a vertical field of view, flown `Linear` or `Smooth` — a cubic Hermite through every key with tangents averaged from its neighbours, except that a key beside a segment that does not move gets none, so a hold is a stop and not a wobble; the field of view eases rather than following the cubic, because an overshooting zoom would be the one wobble nobody could explain. A key may hold its height above the terrain, and an orientation becomes a point 100 m ahead so both forms interpolate alike; both are resolved once, when the file is read against the loaded scene, so sampling is arithmetic. `camera_path_frame(path, f, frames)` spreads `frames` over the path, both ends included: at the path's own `frame_count()` it is time `f / fps`, and any other count resamples it. Markers name frames at the path's own rate; `marker_frame` maps them onto a resampled run.

**The timed flight** (`fly_camera_path`, `flythrough.h`) is the loop both hosts ran already, with the path in it: frames kept in flight, never waited on, `Stats::last` read after every `begin_frame()`, each path frame's record (`frame_record`) kept against the submission that drew it, and `frames_in_flight` extra frames at the end so the last path frames fold in. Each of `repeats` flights starts with `warmup` frames **and** `warmup_seconds` of them at the first camera: the frames give every repeat the same occlusion history, the seconds bring a fast card's clocks up (240 frames of a 0.1 ms scene is 24 ms of work). `summarize_frames` takes each frame's **median over its repeats**, then the median, p95 and p99 over the path, per pass and for the frame's sum of passes; it also says whether every repeat drew the same visible pairs at every frame (`deterministic`), which holds for an unstreamed scene and does not for a streamed one, whose pages land when their reads do.

**The CPU's side of a frame, and an interactive session's ticks** (2026-09-24, `FrameRecord` version 4, `FlythroughSummary` version 4). A record now carries `cpu_ms` — the CPU's own milliseconds for the frame, which in the timed flight is `submit_frame` and the camera sample, never the wait in `begin_frame` for a free slot — and `frame_ms`, the wall time since the previous submission began, which is the frame time a player sees. `frame_record` leaves both at zero and the loop that runs the frames fills them, because the renderer does not see the loop around it. The summary gains their percentiles beside the passes' (`cpu_ms`, `frame_ms`), `ticks`, and `interactive`: engine-view's `--interactive` and `--replay-input` write this same JSONL with a **`ticks`** count on every record — the fixed camera ticks the frame consumed — and the session's header and trajectory in `interactive` (null for a path). The additions are `@since(4)` with defaults, so an older reader of either line sees what it saw, and `render.benchmark`'s `flythrough` result carries the two new percentiles through the same `summarize_frames` ([apps](apps.md#--interactive-a-camera-somebody-flies)).

**The census is a second, untimed pass** (`VisibleCensus`): the same warm-up, then one frame at a time, the frame's visible list read back and counted by DAG level and by scene mesh (and, with pixels, the id channel counted by mesh). It cannot be inline, because the renderer never reads a buffer back inside a frame and a wait between timed frames would let the clocks fall and measure that; it compares its visible pairs with the timed pass's frame by frame, which is a second determinism check. `engine-view --verify-occlusion` goes further: every frame of the path drawn with and without occlusion culling, from two uploads of the scene in lockstep, and the (instance, cluster) under every pixel and every colour byte compared — [the occlusion invariant](#invariants) held over a real path instead of one frame. **What it first found on desert-overlook was a tie-break, not a culling bug**: over 2,401 frames at 1080p no pixel ever lost a nearer surface to occlusion culling, and yet 64 frames (Khronos set) and 1,118 frames (the owner's landmarks) differed, every differing pixel a pair of surfaces at **exactly the same depth** — overwhelmingly the palms, whose fronds are coincident back-to-back faces — because the visibility word's id was then the visible-list entry and the list's order is the cull pass's append order, which culling changes and nothing made repeatable (two identical checks of one build disagreed by 9 and 13 tied pixels). The id has been the scene's pair since 2026-09-24 ([gfx](gfx.md), "The tie rule"), and the same check now finds **nothing**: 0 frames, 0 pixels and 0 colour bytes differ over the whole path, on both sets and on both the mesh and the vertex path ([flythrough](../experiments/flythrough-desert-overlook.md)). So the invariant is the strict one again — occlusion culling does not change the picture — and the check keeps classifying a differing pixel by depth (`lost_nearer`, `gained_nearer`, `tied`, and `frames_culled_visible` for a frame with a nearer surface lost or gained), so that if a difference ever comes back it says at once whether it is a culling bug or a tie.

**What the flythrough found in the renderer, and fixed.** The occlusion history's ping-pong buffers were indexed by the **caller's frame number** (`FrameDesc::frame_index % 2`). That number drives the lights, and a caller may repeat it — a benchmark's warm-up holds frame 0, `render.capture` may ask for one frame twice — and a repeated parity made pass 1 read the flags written two frames earlier, or never: the first frame after a warm-up drew with no history at all (pass 1 empty, every pair through pass 2). The picture was right either way, because pass 2 catches what pass 1 missed, but the visible pairs and the timings were not the frame's, and repeats of one path disagreed at their first frame. The parity is now the renderer's own count of frames recorded (`recorded_`), which alternates whatever the caller passes; every picture is unchanged, and the flythrough's repeats agree frame for frame.

**Shadows are `auto` in both hosts**: traced wherever the device has cluster acceleration structures and ray queries (the RTX 5090), cascaded maps where it has not (the TITAN Xp; off there until 2026-09-24). A flythrough that measures occlusion culling passes `--shadows off`, because a frame that traces shadows runs one visible list and turns occlusion culling off ([Invariants](#invariants)); the maps leave it on. `FrameRecord::shadow_casters` counts the casters the ray chain adds when it is on, `FrameRecord::shadow_pairs` the pairs the maps draw, and `PassMs::shadow` what the maps cost.

**A flight's host may change the scene between frames** (2026-09-25, `FrameRecord` version 5, `FlythroughSummary` version 5). `FlightOptions::before_frame` is a function pointer and a context called before every submission — warm-ups and the drain included — with the repeat, the path frame, its place in the warm-up and the camera the frame will be drawn from (`FlightStep`): where a streamed world updates its ring and hands the renderer its instances ([Instances that come and go](#instances-that-come-and-go)). It runs before `begin_frame`, so it is in the frame's `frame_ms` and not in its `cpu_ms`, which stay the renderer's own. A record now carries the scene the frame culled, `instances` and `pairs` (`FrameStats::instances`/`pairs`, captured per slot at the submission like the frame index), which are constant for a scene read whole and are the number E34 said a streamed world's ring bounds; the summary carries a streamed world's own block, `world` (`engine.world.TileWorldSummary`, [world](world.md#the-world-log)), null otherwise. Since `FrameRecord` version 6 a record also carries what a streamed world's tables cost that frame — `table_slots` and `table_pairs`, the instance slots it copied into the table set it flipped to and the pairs it expanded for them (zero on a frame with no change behind it), and `hole_pairs`, the pairs of its dispatch no instance holds — and `PassMs` (version 4) and `PassPercentiles` (version 4) carry `tables`, the copy and the expansion's GPU milliseconds ([Instances that come and go](#instances-that-come-and-go)); all of them default to zero, so an older reader sees what it saw.

**A windowed frame's waits, and when it was shown** (2026-09-25, `FrameRecord` version 6, `FlythroughSummary` version 7). A record gains `wait_ms`, `acquire_ms`, `present_ms` and `pace_ms` — the CPU milliseconds a window's frame spent waiting for its frame slot, a swapchain image, the present call and the pacer, which `cpu_ms` leaves out — `pace_depth`, how far back the pacer waited, `submit_ms`, the part of `cpu_ms` inside `submit_frame` (where a driver can hide a presentation wait), and `shown_ms` and `latency_ms`, from the previous present reaching the display to this one's and from the frame sampling its input to its reaching the display, where the swapchain can say, and `pose_position`, `pose_yaw`, `pose_pitch` and `pose_time`, the camera an interactive frame drew and the simulated time it stands for. The summary gains `presentation` (`FlythroughPresentation`): the present mode asked for and got, the images, the frames in flight, the pacer with its misses and changes of depth, whether the window was borderless, the refresh the driver reports, the recreations and suboptimal presents, and the percentiles of every wait and display time. engine-view's window fills them ([apps](apps.md#pacing)); a flight fills none of them, since nothing in it presents, and `render.benchmark`'s `flythrough` carries `presentation` as null. Everything is `@since` with a default, so an older reader of either line sees what it saw.

**Where a frame's CPU time went** (2026-10-04, `FrameRecord` version 8, `FlythroughSummary` version 11). A record gains `cpu` (`CpuMs`): the renderer's own stages of that frame — `wait` and `begin` for `begin_frame`, then `tables`, `terrain`, `passes`, `compile`, `record` and `submit` — and the pass whose recording took longest (`slowest_pass`, `slowest_pass_ms`), from `FrameStats::cpu` ([What a frame waits for](#what-a-frame-waits-for)). The summary gains `cpu` (`CpuPercentiles`): each stage's percentiles over the path, of each frame's median across the repeats as `cpu_ms` is, and `over_8ms` and `over_16ms`, the frames whose `cpu_ms` passed 8 and 16 ms. Both are filled by `frame_record` and `summarize_frames`, so a window's records, a flythrough's and `render.benchmark`'s summary carry them alike.

**The pose is the world's, in f64** (2026-10-05, `FrameRecord` version 9, [ADR-0053](../adr/0053-world-positions-are-f64-and-the-gpu-sees-none.md)). `pose_position` is a `worldpos`: the interactive session's camera as it drew it, three doubles, where version 8 wrote a float32 that 420 km out stood on a 3.1 cm grid. The JSON is the same three numbers, so a version 8 record reads as the same position; engine-host's records leave it at zero as they always did ([apps](apps.md#far-from-the-origin)).

**A streamed world's scene file** (`"world": {...}`, `engine.scene.WorldRings`, or `SceneFileOptions::world` — engine-view's `--world` — on a file with none). The block is carried and never interpreted, like an instance's `animation` (`WorldDesc` on `SceneDesc` and `SceneData`): the tile ring is the world capability's ([world](world.md)). What the reader does differently is the placement entries: each entry's generator is opened on it against the world's block — so a bad kit is refused with the scene, not when the first tile asks for it — and asked for the meshes it holds resident (`meshes`: for the ruins **both** kits', the section kit's always and the block kit's when the entry is drawn in blocks, because the rings draw both), which are appended; **nothing is expanded**, and the entry becomes a `StreamedPlacements` with everything the world's placements consumer needs to open the generator again and ask it for a tile exactly as a whole read would have expanded it (the generator's name, the entry's parameters, the scene's directory, and which scene mesh each resident mesh is). A generator with no `tile` cannot be streamed and is refused; so is a ruins entry whose `tile_size` is not the world's: a ring tile has to be the entry's tile. `SceneData::dynamic` is set, which is what tells the GPU scene and `resolve_settings` that instances will come and go. **A block that asks for `ground`** (`WorldRings` version 2, with each ring's `ground_cells`) draws the terrain from the world's tiles ([The ground from the world's tiles](#the-ground-from-the-worlds-tiles)); a scene whose block streams only its ground is not dynamic, since tiles are terrain levels in fixed slots and not instances of the tail, and one that also streams placement entries is refused with a sentence, since those would make it dynamic and a dynamic scene has no pool.

**A participating medium** (`medium`, `Scene` version 8; 2026-10-17, roadmap R47). The scene's `medium` block — `engine.scene.Medium`: `clouds` {`base_m`, `top_m`, `coverage`, `type`, `seed`}, `dust` {`enabled`, `scale`, `height_m`}, `plumes` {`enabled`, `strength`} — is **carried uninterpreted**, a `json` field read by nothing here (`SceneDesc::medium`, `SceneData::medium`), as `world` is carried for the world capability: the types are the volumetrics capability's, which reads the block and draws it through a frame pass ([Frame passes](#frame-passes), [volumetrics](volumetrics.md)). Absent (null) is no medium, and a host registers no pass, so the frame is what it was. A flight's per-frame milliseconds gain `frame_passes` (`PassMs` version 6) and its summary a `medium` block (`FlythroughSummary` version 13).

**Props** (`props`, `engine.scene.Prop`, `Scene` version 7; 2026-10-17, roadmap P43). A scene may declare meshes it places nowhere — `{"name": "can", "mesh": "can.glb", "hash": "", "fit": {...}}`, the same mesh fields as `meshes` — for a game module running over the scene to place, move and remove instances of between frames ([apps](apps.md#the-game-contract)). The reader appends them **after the file's own meshes and before every placement generator's** (so every index the file's instances use still names what it named, and each generator still counts the meshes before it), with `SceneMeshInfo::origin` `prop`, refuses a prop with no name or mesh and two props of one name, and lists them in `SceneDesc::props` and `SceneData::props` (`SceneProp`: the name and the scene mesh it became); no instance of a prop exists after the load. The renderer knows nothing else about them: a module's instances reach it as a block of the tail ([Instances that come and go](#instances-that-come-and-go)), which is the rule that made them a scene-file block in the first place — the meshes stay, only instances change, so what a module may place has to have been loaded with the scene. A scene with props is **not dynamic by itself**: engine-view makes it so when a game runs over it, and a scene with none reads and draws exactly as it did. `read_scene_props` reads the names alone — one schema read, no generator opened, no mesh loaded — for a host that has to know them before it loads the scene (engine-view's game runner, whose module loads before any device).
**Water** (`water`, `engine.scene.WaterBody`, `Scene` version 8; 2026-10-17, roadmap S63). A scene may name water bodies — a circle or a star-shaped polygon at a level, with its colours, fade, waves and roughness ([water](water.md#the-block)). The reader hands the block to the placement generator `"water"` (`src/scene_water.cpp`, one call after the placement entries), which the water capability registers; each body becomes one mesh — written once into `<ddc>/water` and clustered by the cache like any mesh — and one unrotated instance at its centre and level, after every placement entry's meshes and before the terrain, which stays last. A build without the capability refuses the block with a sentence; a scene without it reads exactly as before. The meshes carry the water class ([Materials](#materials)). A body marked `open` (`WaterBody` version 3, 2026-10-31, roadmap S93) is a sea whose water goes on past its outline to the horizon, drawn by the resolve's water modules as a plane at its level ([water](water.md#to-the-horizon)); at most one a scene.

### The targets a frame reads

**The Hi-Z pyramid and the depth image are made only where a frame reads them** (batch 69, roadmap R4 stage 1; [the design](../experiments/render-graph-aliasing.md#7-stages-in-build-order)). The pyramid is read by two-pass occlusion culling and by the occlusion term of the LOD threshold ([Occlusion-aware LOD](#occlusion-aware-lod), `renderer.lod.occluded_scale` above 0 or the histogram); the depth image is the direct path's depth buffer and the target the resolve by pixel class writes its classes into ([The resolve by pixel class](#the-resolve-by-pixel-class)). Under traced shadows occlusion is off and the term is off by default, so on the owner's frame neither was ever written or read, and each was made at every create and resize: 18.5 MiB at 1920×1080, 73.8 at 3840×2160 and 221.6 at 11520×2160 together, by the design's formulas, and 10, 75 and 224 MiB given back by the device's own count on the grove (at 1080p VMA places them inside blocks it already holds; [the table](../experiments/render-graph-aliasing.md#7-stages-in-build-order)). A target not made costs no frame time, so no pair was flown for it. Now `Targets::create` lays both out and makes them only when the renderer's settings read them (`targets_hiz_wanted`, `targets_depth_wanted`: two-pass occlusion or the term's tunables; the direct path, or the split resolve's tunable naming a mode with its pipelines made), and `record_frame` asks `Targets::ensure` for what *this* frame reads before it imports anything: the pyramid when it culls against it or builds it for the term, the depth image when it draws direct or plans pixel classes (the class plan is made there now, before the imports, and the resolve's block reads it). A target a setting asks for mid-session is made at that frame and cleared by it as a new one is (a new pyramid is marked dirty, so its first frame reads everything far), and kept until the next resize, so a tunable flipped back and forth allocates once and the steady state allocates nothing ([The frame loop allocates nothing](#the-frame-loop-allocates-nothing)); a resize makes again what the settings then read. A frame that reads neither imports neither: the graph sees no "hiz" or "depth" on the traced defaults, and its barrier counts do not move, since an import nobody declares makes no barrier. `hiz_bytes()` and `depth_bytes()` say what the renderer holds. `frame_targets_tests.cpp` holds the matrix — the traced frame, the hardware rasterizer with the cascades (occlusion on and off) and with traced shadows, the direct path — to the rule, a renderer made to hold both (the term's histogram, the split resolve) to the colour and ids of one that holds neither, and the term at k = 4 and the split resolve turned on mid-session to the bytes of a session started with them.

### The frame loop allocates nothing

**Streamed tile changes are steady state too** (2026-10-26, W73). The streamed-trees case now
requires zero allocations and zero device buffers in both its rigid and swaying second flights;
equality between two nonzero counts is not a pass. The authored reader records each tile's exact
instance count in `StreamedPlacements::tile_instances`. The world's consumer uses those counts
at load to size its placement scratch, per-tile instance/tag storage and combined tail, exchanging
the per-tile storage with a kept pool on arrival and departure. Ring changes and re-standing
rebuild into the held storage. Distance forms change meshes without changing these counts.
No instance, pair, motion key or rendered byte changes. See the
[allocation hunt](../experiments/streamed-tree-allocations-2026-10-26.md).

In debug builds, every counted submission captures up to 64 distinct allocation stacks (16 return
addresses, count and requested bytes per stack) in caller-owned storage. `FlightBookkeeping`
pauses capture as it excludes its allocations from the metric; submission-list and frame-record
bookkeeping is outside capture too. An allocating recorded frame prints its repeat/frame and
sites to stderr, which the test prints on failure. Overflow is explicit. Use that executable's
matching debug symbols to resolve addresses; Windows output includes its load base and Linux
output includes module-relative offsets. Capture and diagnostic output are absent in release.

**What a frame allocated is part of its record** (2026-10-07, `FrameRecord` version 10, `FlythroughSummary` version 12; roadmap T48). AGENTS.md's rule is that the frame loop allocates nothing in steady state, and plan 11 §11.2 makes the count a CI metric; until this date only the world tiles' long-flight test (`terrain_tiles_gpu_tests.cpp`) counted, for one scene. Now every flight does: `fly_camera_path` snapshots, on the frame's thread, the engine's allocations (`mem::allocations_on_thread`, a thread-local count kept in every build, tracking or not) and the device buffers made (`gfx::buffers_created_on_thread`) around the host's turn (`FlightOptions::before_frame`: a streamed world's update, the ground's frame), `begin_frame` and `submit_frame`, and writes the sum into the frame's record as `allocations` and `buffers`. The flight's own bookkeeping between those calls — the list of submissions, the records — is outside the windows, and **what a host's hook records for the benchmark is left out by the host**: it holds a `renderer::FlightBookkeeping` round that recording (engine-view's time-lapse state for the record, its world log's line and ring times), and what is made inside one is subtracted. A job worker's allocations are its own thread's and not counted: the rule is the frame thread's. The summary's `frame_loop` block (`FrameLoopAllocations`) has the totals over the recorded frames, the frames with any, and the last path frame that had any; `device` beside it names the adapter. Both hosts fill them (`render.benchmark` returns the same summary); a window's loop does not count yet, and its records say zero.

**Steady state is the second flight over the path.** `engine_view`'s `frame_loop_tests.cpp` flies the three path scenes — the overlook, the erg's walk on its rings and the endless desert over its tiles, each made small enough for a debug build and its path resampled to 96 frames — twice each after 12 warm-up frames, and asserts that the second flight's records are all zero. The first is the warm-up: lists that grow with what a frame holds reach the most the path needs during it. **What the first run found** (2026-10-07, `msvc-release`, RTX 5090): **one allocation in every frame of every scene**, `gfx::GpuTimer::begin_frame`'s read-back of the frame's timestamps into a vector made per frame — now sized once in `GpuTimer::create`; two more a frame on the erg and the endless desert that were engine-view's own measurement (the time-lapse record and the world log's line), now inside a `FlightBookkeeping`; and on the endless desert's first flight 57 allocations and 6 device buffers over its first 57 frames — the world's tile ring and tier lists (`world::TileRing::update`, `sim::TierAssignment::assign_tiers`) and the terrain's staging records (`GpuScene::stage_chunk`, `terrain_prepare`) growing to the path's high-water mark, and the staging ring's overflow buffers while the first rings fill — and none in its second. The long-flight test's note that the renderer's half "made one engine allocation a frame" was the timer.

## The dunes in time-lapse

**Its clock is the ground's, riding the world's** (since 2026-10-20, [One world clock](#one-world-clock-and-the-days-length)): `RenderSettings::time_rate` is game seconds of sand a *world* second, so the motion runs at `time_rate` times the world rate per real second (engine-view's `,` and `.` step the world rate and the dunes with it; `--time-rate` has no key of its own any more), and **the sky never follows it**: the sky stands at its own hour, so a time-lapse at any rate leaves the sun, the moon and the exposure where the day's length puts them, where it used to drag them round with the sand.

ADR-0043's own revisit question — do the migrating lattices read as dunes advancing, or as a texture sliding? — needs the dunes to move while someone watches. The field is a closed-form function of game time ([terrain](terrain.md#the-time-function)), so moving it is only asking it for another t; what the renderer has to add is getting a new t onto the GPU without the picture noticing. **The owner's one hard requirement is that the height change be smooth**: a dune must never change height in an instant; at a normal clock the change between two frames must be imperceptible, and at a time-lapse rate it must read as motion, not as steps. So a re-evaluated field is never swapped in whole.

**Two fields and a blend, in the deformed-vertex pool.** With a time rate above zero (`engine-view --time-rate`, `RenderSettings::time_rate`), or one that may become so (`RenderSettings::time_rate_live`, [Changing the rate while it runs](#changing-the-rate-while-it-runs)), the scene's terrain is drawn as a **terrain level** (`ResolvedSettings::terrain_levels`): its instance is a deformed instance whose `gfx::DeformDesc` runs one stage, `gfx::k_deform_stage_terrain` ([gfx](gfx.md#the-deform-chain)). The pool pass finds each vertex of the frame's cut on the level's lattice from its rest position — which every copy of the vertex on every LOD level shares bit for bit, so the stage keeps the deform chain's crack rule — and writes it at that lattice point with the height `a (1 − t) + b t` of the level's two evaluated fields and the normal of the blended field's central differences (the arithmetic `load_terrain` gives the rest mesh its normals with, one-sided at the grid's edge like it), into the pool and the deformed normal pool. Everything downstream already reads a deformed instance through the pool: the three rasterizers, the resolve's reconstruction and tangent frame, and the ray path's CLAS records — so a moving terrain needed nothing new in any of them, and the cone test is off for it by the rule every deformed instance follows. `a (1 − t) + b t` rather than `a + (b − a) t` because it is exactly `a` at t = 0 and exactly `b` at t = 1: a level that has reached its next field draws that field's heights to the bit, which is what lets one pair hand over to the next without a trace.

**What a frame draws is a table, not an upload.** Each level has a `gfx::TerrainLevelDesc` per frame slot in a host-visible table (`GpuScene::terrain_prepare`): its lattice (origin and spacing), its two fields (a device address and the window of the lattice each covers), the blend, the padding its spheres take, a ring's skirt depth, and the square of a finer level it leaves out ([The rings in the scene](#the-rings-in-the-scene)). The cull pass and the pool pass read it through one address each (`CullParams::terrain`, `DeformParams::terrain`), and `InstanceDesc::terrain` (the record's last pad word) names an instance's level.
