So the per-frame cost of the motion on the CPU is writing a 96-byte record a level; the fields are uploaded once each, into three device buffers for the scene's grid — the pair being drawn and the next one — and four for a ring, whose re-centre carries its pair over to a new window beside the one drawn, and which between re-centres holds two fields after its b (`GpuScene::terrain_field_slots`; [A clock that never stops](#a-clock-that-never-stops)), from a host-visible staging buffer the frame copies from in a `terrain upload` transfer pass before the cull, and then retires to the frame context. A field slot is only written once no table still to be recorded names it, and it is imported into the render graph as last read by every stage, so the copy's barrier orders it after the frames in flight that may still read the old contents; nothing waits for the device. **A field goes over a budget a frame, and is shown only once all of it has** (`GpuScene::terrain_prepare`, `terrain_slot_uploaded`). The erg's grid is 67 MB a field, and copied whole it cost the frame that took it 7 ms of GPU on a quiet RTX 5090 and 13–22 ms beside other work — a hitch every few frames at a game day a second. The next field is ready well before the surface needs it, so the frames copy `renderer.terrain.upload_mib` (8) of fields each, a field in as many pieces as that cuts it into, and the motion takes it as b only from the frame after its last piece was recorded (`Next::uploading`). The first fields, which the first frame shows, go over whole (`urgent`), and an offscreen run, which waits for its fields, copies everything the next frame (budget 0). The rule that a frame shows no slot whose copy is not in it is older than the budget, and was found broken by the rings test: a frame recorded at most eight copies and left the rest for the next, and an offscreen frame that catches the surface up installs several fields a level, each into the slot the one before freed — so a ring drew for a frame whatever its slot had held, a frame's worth of sand behind the model, which a scene grid alone had never been caught at. A copy that a later one into the same slot replaces is dropped and its staging retired, since two copies into one buffer in one pass would race.

**Why the pool, and not re-uploading the mesh.** The requirement is a small change every frame, and the pool already produces, every frame, exactly the vertices the frame draws: a moving terrain costs the cut and not the grid. The alternatives cost the grid. Re-quantizing and re-uploading the erg's 4,097 grid every frame is 16.8 million vertices of six bytes, 100 MB a frame over the bus, and the CPU work of blending them; doing it a 64 × 64 tile at a time at the evaluation's cadence swaps a tile's heights whole — a step — unless the tile is blended too, which is the per-frame upload again. Blending in every position reader instead of in a pass would leave the ray path out: a cluster acceleration structure is built from positions in memory, which is why the pool exists at all (E25). The pool's price is its budget and its allocator, both of which a terrain's cut is the largest tenant of (the costs, below): a scene with terrain levels takes at least `renderer.terrain.pool_mib` (768) of pool, because an entry the budget has no room for draws its rest pose, and for a terrain that would be a jump.

**The bound, and a late field.** Every frame each level's *surface time* moves towards the game time (`TerrainMotion::frame`, `terrain_blend_frame`), no further than b's time and no faster than moves any vertex by `renderer.terrain.move_fraction` of the level's spacing — a quarter by default: a vertex changes by `|b − a|` times the change of the blend, so a pair whose largest difference is `delta` may advance the blend by at most `fraction × spacing / delta` a frame (`terrain_blend_step`). When the surface reaches b exactly, b becomes the next pair's a — the same heights to the bit — and the next field becomes b, with what is left of the frame's budget. If the next field is not there yet the surface cannot pass b — offscreen it waits for it; in a window the surface clock has already slowed it ([below](#a-clock-that-never-stops)). **Offscreen, a field that is already there is taken in the same frame, however many are** (2026-10-07): a pass of `terrain_surface_frame` offers each level one field and a ring holds two after its b, so when the pass stops on a level whose next field is ready, the waiting loop in `TerrainMotion::frame` goes round again rather than giving up. It gave up until then, and the frame stood short of game time by up to a pair — but only in a run whose field worker had got two fields ahead of its frames, which is a matter of how busy the machine is, so offscreen pictures were not a function of their frames: the rings' culling case, which draws five rigs and compares them frame by frame, found one rig a frame's worth of sand behind the others under a merge gate's load and read it as a tenth to a quarter of its ids differing (roadmap F1, [the experiment](../experiments/load-sensitive-tests-2026-10-07.md)). A window never ran that loop and is unchanged. The per-frame change of any vertex is at most `fraction × spacing` whatever the rate and however late a field is — which `terrain_generator_tests.cpp` holds sample by sample on a travelling dune profile at a real clock, a day, a week and a month a second, with fields on time, 20 and 45 frames late and none for 400 frames; and `terrain_motion_tests.cpp` holds on the GPU, against the pool's own output. **Measured in a window on 2026-09-27, that was not enough**: at a week and at a day a second on the erg, where every whole-grid field is late, the surface held at b and then caught up at the capped speed, which read as a step about once a second (the displacement bound held; the velocity was not continuous), while 8,640 was smooth ([third session](../experiments/third-interactive-session-2026-09-25.md#the-owners-flight-in-time-lapse-2026-09-27)). The surface clock below is the fix.

**The owner's jump at 600, which was not the drawing** (2026-09-29, [the experiment](../experiments/walk-in-time-lapse-2026-09-29.md)). Walking the erg with the dunes at 600 game seconds a real second, the owner saw the ground round him change smoothly for about a second and then jump in height, over and over for about 20,000 ticks, and then stop. His frame records rule the drawing out: the largest vertex move a frame was 0.2–1.3 mm and no frame's was more than 1.8 times its neighbours' in 14,934 frames at 600; every pair was the displacement cadence's, 4,112 to 24,708 game seconds apart, so the one-second floor of `min_step_s` decided none and the keep-up rule pushed none; every handover was exact; the rate changed once, and the steps kept their beat long after; and the sand's detail turns its wind over two game hours. What jumped was the camera: it is the walker's eye, which stood on a collision ground that followed the drawn sand in 5 cm steps and dropped 4.65 cm in one frame at each, 45 times in 65 s ([scene_collision](scene_collision.md#the-walker-goes-with-the-ground) has the rule that fixed it: the ground under the walker follows the drawn sand to a millimetre and carries him with it). What changed after 20,000 ticks was the wind: the record's days 1,096 and 1,097 are calm and the waves travel nothing in them, so the pair his grid took at frame 6,814 spans 193,353 game seconds, 2.2 days, the sand's largest move fell from 0.42 to 0.015 mm a frame, and a 5 cm step would have taken minutes. `terrain_clock_tests.cpp` holds his run (below).

**One surface time for every level** (`terrain_surface_frame`). With the rings in the scene there are several levels — the scene's grid and the rings, the same function of time at different spacings, each with its own pair on its own cadence — and where two meet they must draw the same sand. Each level blending towards the game time on its own would not: a ring whose next field came late would hold while the grid round it moved on, and at a week a second the waves would stand a step proud of each other along the border, which no skirt hides. So the levels **share the surface time**: it moves no further than the nearest of their b's and no faster than any level's own bound allows (each level still moves no vertex more than `fraction` of *its* spacing a frame), a level standing at its b takes its next field and the surface moves on, and a level whose next field is late holds them all. The finer levels have the shorter cadences (a quarter of 50 cm of travel is a quarter of 1.5 m's) and the smaller windows, so they are asked for first — the worker takes the level whose b the surface reaches soonest — and cost little: the inner ring's field over its 500 m square is 1 million samples, a sixteenth of the erg's grid. A single level is exactly the one-level blend; the CPU test drives two levels a metre and 25 cm apart, the finer one's every third field 40 frames late, and holds the surfaces equal, each level to its own bound, and the grid held by the ring when it waits.

**The cadence is by displacement, not the calendar** (`terrain_next_time`). The generator knows how far each band travels between two times — the wind's flux path over the band's height, Bagnold's rule, storms included (`terrain_band_travel_m`, along the path rather than between its ends, so a reversal inside the interval is not a short move) — so the next field is timed for when the **fastest band** will have travelled `fraction × spacing`: the blend then crosses at most a fraction of a sample, where a straight line between two fields is the motion rather than a cross-fade. It is found by bisection on the closed form and clamped to `[renderer.terrain.min_step_s, renderer.terrain.max_step_s]` (a second and thirty days). **The travel is the gained one**: the flux integral the cadence reads is the one the dunes move by, so a storm with a transport gain ([terrain](terrain.md#a-storm-scales-transport)) shortens the cadence exactly as much as it speeds the sand, and its pairs stay slides. In `terrain_clock_tests.cpp`'s model, a storm of forty seconds at the game's own rate (sixteen mean hours' flux times the gain) keeps every pair within a quarter of a sample at gains 1, 10 and 50, where a cadence reading a calm day's travel put 0.92 of a sample between two fields at 50, and the old one-minute floor of `min_step_s` 0.50 — which is why the floor is a second since 2026-09-28 (it only matters at slow rates, where the cadence is hours). On the erg at a real clock that is hours to days of game time between fields and the field is effectively still; the waves, 0.3–0.8 m on 10 m cells and the fastest band by far (Bagnold: the lowest band moves fastest), set it at about three game hours for a 0.5 m spacing. At a game day a real second that is several fields a second, which no evaluation of a whole grid keeps up with, so in a window the next field is also timed at least `renderer.terrain.lead` (1.5) times the level's worst recent turnaround ahead at the rate ([A clock that never stops](#a-clock-that-never-stops); `LevelStats::late` counts the fields that rule timed): the blend then crosses more than a fraction of a sample and the waves cross-fade rather than slide, still without a single step. Offscreen (`TimeLapseConfig::wait`, which engine-view sets for every offscreen run) fields are timed by displacement alone and a late one is waited for instead of held at, so the pictures of a run are a function of its frames however fast the machine evaluates, and two runs of `--frames N --time-rate r` capture the same bytes.

**The rest pose's bounds and LOD errors, and how far the field may move before they matter.** The cluster spheres and the LOD DAG's errors are the rest pose's — the mesh built at the scene's `time`. The spheres are padded by the level's `padding`, the largest distance any vertex of either field is from its rest height (`terrain_field_delta` against the rest heights, computed on the worker for every field), which the cull pass takes from the table in place of `InstanceDesc::bounds_padding` and adds to every sphere of the level alike, so the cut stays crack-free and culling stays conservative however far the sand has gone. The errors cannot be padded the same way: a coarse cluster's vertices are a subset of the grid's, so against the moved surface its error is at most its rest error plus twice the largest height change since the rest pose. That bound is the padding, and it grows with the time-lapse, not with the cadence — the cadence bounds one step, the padding the distance from the rest. The padding enters the LOD spheres as well, and a larger sphere projects a larger error, so the cut errs finer as the field moves away. On the erg the waves stop mattering first — after a few game weeks they are a different wave pattern, a height change of their own amplitude, under a metre — and the crests and barchans after months (several metres); the mega-draa, at about a metre and a half a year, take decades. A time-lapse of the erg at a week a second is a year of sand in a minute of flight, and the scene's grid is then drawn with the rest pose's coarse clusters over sand up to about ten metres from where they were fit. Re-basing the grid — rebuilding its DAG at the current time in the background and swapping it at a field boundary, where the surface is exactly a field — is not built ([Not yet](#not-yet)).

**What it costs** (the erg along its own path, 600 frames of it flown three times offscreen at a game day a second, RTX 5090, `msvc-release`, the machine quiet but for one reading; [the write-up](../experiments/third-interactive-session-2026-09-25.md#the-dunes-in-time-lapse-looked-at-2026-09-26) has the table). **The pool pass** is 0.016 ms at the median at 1080p and 0.058 at 11520×2160 over three views (0.024 and 0.53 at the 95th percentile), and the allocator's one serial workgroup 0.008 and 0.018, for a cut of about 1,100 and 2,800 pairs: a frame's median GPU time goes from 0.42 to 0.48 ms and from 1.65 to 2.03. **An evaluation** of the erg's whole 4,097 grid takes 750–775 ms on the job pool, a middle ring's field 190 ms and an inner ring's 72, and **a field's copy** 7.1 ms of GPU for the grid's 67 MB taken whole (9.4 GB/s) — the frames that took one are the whole of the 95th percentile, 7.6 ms at 1080p, which is why a window copies `renderer.terrain.upload_mib` (8) a frame. **The padding** reached 15.6 m on the grid after six weeks of game time — the time-lapse's own rest-pose problem ([Not yet](#not-yet)) — and stayed under 0.8 m on the rings, which a re-centre re-bases. **The rings** ([The rings in the scene](#the-rings-in-the-scene)) cost what their clusters cost: the median frame 1.17 ms at 1080p and 3.28 ms over three views, 1,540 and 3,520 pairs, 1.46 GB of slots and arenas on the device, and 3.3–3.9 s on a load. A re-centre's chunks took 0.5 s on the ring worker at the median and 3.4 s at worst (a middle ring's), carrying the pairs over 0.23–0.29 s (0.53 s at worst), and 107 re-centres in the three flights built 8,111 chunks and kept 26,496, 91 MB of chunks each; the arenas were at most 69% full. Offscreen a re-centre's chunks and fields go over in the frame that asks, which is the rings' 99th percentile (38 and 50 ms); in a window they go over `renderer.terrain.ring_upload_mib` and `upload_mib` a frame.

**What it hands a summary.** engine-view's summary line gains a `time_lapse` block: the rate — the one the run ended at, the one it started at and how often the keys changed it (`start_rate`, `rate_changes`) — and the rules (`fraction`, `min_step_s`, `max_step_s`, `lead`, `wait`), the game time reached, the clock's latency now and at most, the lag the run ended on, and the frames the sand stood still or was braked, the uploads' bytes and GPU milliseconds (`FrameStats::terrain_upload_bytes`, `gpu_terrain_upload`, the `terrain upload` timer zone), and per level its spacing, the surface's time and its pair's, the blend, the padding, the fields evaluated and installed, the frames held, capped and waited, the fields timed late, the largest per-frame move, pair difference, step and lag, the evaluation's last and mean wall time, the last and largest turnaround, and the hash of the last field's bytes; and with `--benchmark` every frame's record carries a `terrain` object with the same frame's rate (`FrameTerrain` version 2), surface, pair, blend, largest move and whether a late field held or braked it; and a `sun` block beside it, the sun's day (`FlythroughSummary` version 9, [The sun's day](#the-suns-day)) ([apps](apps.md#--time-rate-the-dunes-in-time-lapse)).

**The lights stand still.** The stand-in lighting's two point lights orbited the scene with the frame index (lighting.h), a warm one a scene's radius away going round in eight seconds, which over a time-lapse of the erg read as a sun racing across the sky while the sand crawled; since 2026-09-27 they stand where frame 0 put them unless `orbit_lights` (`--orbit-lights`) asks, and the sun starts where `RenderSettings::sun_*` (`--sun`) or the `renderer.sun.*` tunables put it, by default the direction it always had, to the bit. It moves only on its own day, whose clock is the host's and independent of the sand's ([The sun's day](#the-suns-day)): the owner watches the sand move under a still sun, and the sun move over still sand.

**What holds it.** `terrain_clock_tests.cpp`, with no device: the erg's three levels on one worker at their evaluation times, 900–1,200 frames at 8,640, 86,400 and 604,800 — the code before the clock stands and sprints at the two high rates (a window ratio above 10), the clock never stands after its start, never runs above 1.5 times the rate, keeps every one-second window's speeds within 1.25 of each other, keeps every sample within its level's bound, hands every pair over exactly and every level one surface time, and two runs are the same run; a worker that stops for five seconds brakes the sand to a stop and sets it off without a sprint; the clock's latency and braking and the keep-up rule on their own; and the highest rate at which the one worker keeps every level on the displacement cadence (about 7,200 game seconds a second at the owner's times); and **the owner's walk at 600 on the committed erg** (2026-09-29) — his window's grid level with the clock, the keep-up rule and one worker at 59 frames an evaluation, his rate changes at his frames and the erg's own fields round his start — takes his seven pairs (the shortest 4,112 game seconds, none timed late), hands each over exactly, moves the sand at most 1.13 mm a frame until the pair over the calm days at frame 6,798 (his was 6,814) and 0.015 mm after it, and never moves it more than three times both its neighbouring frames. `terrain_generator_tests.cpp`, with no device: a field evaluated on the scene's lattice is the mesh's heights at that time to the bit and the same bytes on no pool, one worker and three, and a ring lattice's window is the point function's; the cadence rule keeps the fastest band within the fraction of a sample and is the longest step that does, to a second, shortens with the fraction, clamps, and takes more fields through a stormy stretch of the record than a calm one; the blend never moves a sample more than its bound in a frame in the six cases above and never more than it says it moved; and a blend step is exact at its ends and never goes past b. `terrain_motion_tests.cpp`, on a GPU: a 64 m terrain at a game week a real second, fields arriving when the worker has them, 150 frames at the finest cut, every covered pixel's depth unprojected and held to the CPU's model of the pool — the two fields at the motion's times, blended in floats, interpolated over the grid's own triangles — within 2 mm (0.9 mm at worst over 2.5 million pixels on the RTX 5090, with 69 fields installed, 2 frames held and a largest vertex move of 0.21 m a frame against a bound of 0.25); and on the same terrain moving, occlusion culling and the cone test change no pixel and no depth (the cone test does not run on it, and a rigid copy shows it would have culled), the software rasterizer agrees with the hardware one as it does on a rigid mesh (10 and 15 ids of 12,500 pixels, depth to 2 × 10⁻⁷), and the ray path draws the same coverage and 14–17 differing ids of 12,500, which is what a silhouette costs a rigid mesh too.

### A clock that never stops

In a window the surface does not chase game time; it runs at **game time minus a latency L**, at the rate while it is there, and its speed changes smoothly (`TerrainClock`, `terrain_time.h`; [the experiment](../experiments/time-lapse-smoothness-2026-09-27.md)). **The picture lags game time by L**: a few frames' worth at a slow rate, about 1.5 s of real time (90 frames) at a day or a week a second on the erg with the owner's evaluation times, reported as the summary's `latency_s` and every `--benchmark` record's `terrain.latency_s`. Offscreen (`wait`) there is no clock: the surface keeps game time and waits for its fields, as before, so offscreen pictures are a function of their frames.

- **L is how long a field takes to come, at the rate**: `margin` (1.2) times the worst of each level's last eight **turnarounds** — real seconds from the level wanting its next field (its b installed, or room for one more) to that field being ready to draw, which is the evaluation *and* the wait behind the other levels' on the one field worker — times the rate, the largest over the levels, because they share one surface. Not the interval between arrivals, which the brief suggested: at a slow rate that is the displacement cadence, hours of game time between fields that were ready in milliseconds, and a latency that large holds the sand back for nothing. And not the game time the clock had run past the newest field when the next arrived, which was the first thing tried: fields are asked for when the surface reaches b, so a lagging surface asks later, the newest field falls further behind game time, and that measure of L grew without bound in the model (8 s of lag at a week a second).
- **The speed** moves towards `rate + (game − L − surface) / settle_s` (2 s) within `[0, 1.5 × rate]` and changes by at most the rate every `response_s` (0.5 s): a gap closes over seconds, never faster than half again the true speed.
- **It brakes for the horizon** — the newest field every level has ready — at the same deceleration, never faster than it could stop at it (`√(2 a d)`), so a field later than L allowed slows the sand to what the worker delivers and sets it off again gently; it stops only when the worker stops, and then without a sprint after. `terrain_surface_frame` and its per-frame bound still apply after it: the clock chooses a target, the blend's rule decides how far the surface goes towards it.
- **A ring holds two fields after b** (its four slots are a, b and these), so it asks for the one after next while the next waits to be drawn, and a wait behind the grid's evaluation does not make it late. The scene's grid has three slots (`GpuScene::terrain_field_slots`, not changed here) and so one field after b; it times its fields with **twice** `renderer.terrain.lead`, because it has no second field to cover a wait.
- **The keep-up rule times a field by the turnaround, not the evaluation** (`terrain_keep_up_time`): `from + lead × rate × turnaround` — the worst recent turnaround, since a field timed by a typical one is late whenever it waits behind a longer evaluation — and no shorter than the span over which a pair as different as the level's last crosses at the rate within the per-frame bound, a quarter to spare.

Measured on the CPU model of the erg's three levels on one worker (45, 11 and 4 frames of evaluation), over a second's window of frames, as the largest over the smallest per-frame advance of the surface: the code before the clock stood still 93% of the frames at a day a second and sprinted at up to 8.3 times the true speed after each stand (a window ratio of 833), and 60% at a week a second (143); with the clock the ratio is 1.0 at 8,640, 86,400 and 604,800, the speed stays within 0.91–1.00 of the true one, and no frame stands. `terrain_clock_tests.cpp` holds it.

### Changing the rate while it runs

engine-view's `,` and `.` step the world's rate, and with it the rate of a running time-lapse (`time_rate × world_rate`) ([apps](apps.md#--interactive-a-camera-somebody-flies)), through **`TerrainMotion::set_rate`** and nothing else, because every rule above has to keep holding across the change. A change moves nothing the surface stands on — not the surface time, not a pair, not a blend — so it cannot step the sand, and every frame after it goes through `terrain_surface_frame`'s per-frame bound like every frame before. What it changes:

- **Game time runs on at the new rate** from the next frame (it integrates the rate, so it never jumps).
- **The surface clock takes the rate** (`TerrainClock::set_rate`): L is the new rate's at once — the same turnarounds, which are real seconds, at the new rate — and the speed the surface had carries over and changes at **the acceleration of that speed** for a latency's worth of real time, and after that while it is still above the new rate's reach. Slowing down, that is the faster change: a week a second slowed to an hour decelerates in under a second, as it set off, where the new rate's own deceleration would take hours, and a rate of zero brings the sand to rest the same way rather than dead in a frame (with the old rule of chasing game time at a rate of zero, the surface would have run L ahead to where game time stopped, at the per-frame bound). Speeding up, it is the slower one, and that is the point: the fields on their way were timed at the old rate and hold about a latency of it, so a surface that took the new rate's acceleration at once outran them and braked to a stand before the first field timed at the new rate could come — five frames of standing, a second after the key, from a tenth of a day to a day in the CPU model. It is the speed the sand had and not the old rate because keys come faster than the clock settles: taken from the old rate, a week a second slowed to an hour and then at once to zero would have crept down at an hour's deceleration for minutes. From rest the new rate's own acceleration starts it, as at the start. At a constant rate nothing differs from the clock above.
- **The next field is timed at the new rate.** A level with nothing on its way comes to want its next field now — the time before, at a rate of zero when nothing is asked for or at a rate whose field it had already been given, is no field's turnaround — and whatever it asks for next is timed by the cadence rule and the keep-up rule at the new rate. Fields already evaluated or on their way keep their times: they are the same function of time, and a pair of them is crossed within the bound whatever it spans — after a slow-down, by a cross-fade over the span the faster rate chose, until the fields timed at the new one arrive.

**A still terrain that may move.** The motion has to exist, standing still, for a key to set it going, so `RenderSettings::time_rate_live` draws a dune terrain as terrain levels at a `time_rate` of zero ([below](#the-dunes-in-time-lapse)); engine-view sets it for an interactive window. It costs what a still terrain's levels cost — the pool's `renderer.terrain.pool_mib` floor, the rest pose evaluated once at load, no cone test on the terrain — and draws the same picture. Offscreen (`wait`) the fields are timed by displacement alone as ever, so a run that changed its rate at the same frames would draw the same pictures; engine-view's offscreen runs never change it.

**What holds it.** `terrain_clock_tests.cpp`, on the CPU model of the erg with the rate changed between frames exactly as `set_rate` changes it, read in the sand's own units (the surface's game seconds per real second, since across a change "the true speed" is ten times something else in a frame): **up the dune ladder a rung every six seconds from a standing start to a week a second, down to zero and to a day again** — 13 changes, no frame standing while the rate runs, no stand followed by a sprint, the speed changing from frame to frame by at most 1.10 of what the clock allows (the brake's last discrete steps), within 1.5 of the rate a second after each change, every one-second window three seconds after a change within 1.11, every sample within its level's bound (0.27 of it at worst), every handover exact, one surface time, and two runs the same run; **three presses a second** down the ladder from a week to zero, up it again and back and forth — the bound, the handovers and the single surface hold, no sprint, rest within the second at zero, but not "never stands": a week reached from an hour in one press leaves the surface far behind game time, it catches up at half again the rate, and one worker's fields, timed for the rate, run out under the catch-up, so it brakes to a stand for about half a second as it does for a stalled worker; and the clock alone across a change up, down, and to zero, a second change before the first has settled included. `terrain_motion_tests.cpp`, on a GPU: the 64 m terrain with `time_rate_live` at a rate of zero, then a day, a week, an hour, zero and a week a second, fields arriving when the worker has them — 190 frames, 12 fields installed, the largest vertex move 0.118 m a frame against a bound of 0.25, the pool within 1.1 mm of the motion's own pair and blend at 466,000 pixels, the surface never backwards and at rest at zero (RTX 5090, 2026-09-27); and without `time_rate_live` a still terrain is drawn rigid, as it always was.

## The rings in the scene

The scene's grid is 4,097 vertices a side at most — 1.5 m a sample over the erg, where a slip face is five samples wide: the faceted crest of the owner's first flight ([third session](../experiments/third-interactive-session-2026-09-25.md)). The terrain capability builds finer grids near the camera as square **rings** of chunked cluster meshes ([terrain](terrain.md#rings)), which the renderer asks of the ground provider (`scene_gen::GroundRings`: the dunes have them, the waves do not) and links nothing of the capability for; with `--terrain-rings` (`RenderSettings::terrain_rings`, `ResolvedSettings::terrain_rings`) the renderer draws them as terrain levels beside the scene's grid, moved by the same pool stage at the same surface time, and re-centres them under a moving camera a changed chunk at a time (`terrain_rings.h`, `TerrainRingSet`). They are off by default: a ring set is built at load round the camera's first position, a few seconds on the erg, and its slots hold device memory whether the camera is near the ground or not ([what they cost](#the-dunes-in-time-lapse)).

**Levels, coarsest first.** Level 0 is the scene's grid, the cached mesh; level 1 the middle ring (1 m, a kilometre either side by default) and level 2 the inner one (50 cm, 250 m either side), from `terrain.rings.*`. Each level leaves out the square of the level inside it. A ring does so by its geometry: the capability builds it with a hole and hangs a skirt from both its borders. The scene's grid is one cached mesh and cannot be rebuilt round a hole that moves, so its table's `hole` does it: the pool pass moves its vertices strictly inside the middle ring's square onto the square's nearest edge — a lattice line of the grid, which `terrain::ring_snap_mm` makes it — and down by as far as each was moved, and the cull pass drops its clusters wholly inside. The sinking is for the square's corners: a map of a square's inside onto its edge folds along the diagonals, so a grid triangle whose corners went to two different edges spans the corner at the edges' heights, and unsunk it stood up to 1.3 m proud of the middle ring's ground in the rings test and drew over it ([gfx](gfx.md#the-deform-chain) has the bound). The price is a notch at most one grid triangle wide just outside the middle ring's border, which its skirt stands in. A ring's skirt vertices carry a rest normal turned straight down (`GpuScene::stage_chunk`), which the terrain stage reads to hang them `TerrainLevelDesc::skirt` under the blended field, so a skirt follows the sand ([gfx](gfx.md#the-deform-chain)).

**A ring is chunks, and a chunk is a slot.** The GPU scene lays the rings out once, beside the scene's own meshes, when it is made with the `TerrainRingSet` built round the camera (`GpuScene::create`'s last argument): per ring a fixed set of **slots** — a mesh and an instance each (placed at its chunk's corner when it is turned on, ["The ground's tiles are placed at their corners"](#the-grounds-tiles-are-placed-at-their-corners)), owning a fixed run of the cluster array and of the pairs, `clusters_per_slot` long — and **arenas** of vertices and triangles in the scene's global buffers, all sized from the chunks the load built (`TerrainRingSet::capacity`): twice the most chunks a ring can be cut into, each slot the largest chunk's clusters with `renderer.terrain.ring_slack` (1.15) on top, and arenas for two rings — the one drawn and the one replacing it — each the larger of the ring built at load scaled to its most chunks and the most chunks each as large as the largest built, with the same slack. (Scaling alone left a small ring cut four ways in the test 2.3 times its size, and a re-centre that cut it differently found no room; the peak a swap has seen since is 55%.) So nothing about the scene's layout ever moves for a ring: a slot's pairs are always the same numbers, the visibility ids mean what they meant, and the cull drops a pair past a slot's chunk's own clusters as it drops a streamed world's hole (the slot's `MeshDesc` names its chunk's count, and none when it draws nothing). A chunk goes into a free slot as copies out of one staging buffer — its clusters with their vertex and triangle offsets moved to the arenas', its LOD records, its 16-bit positions on its own grid, its attributes and triangles, and with ray tracing its float positions and 8-bit indices — which the next frame's `terrain upload` pass records; that frame imports the geometry buffers as last read everywhere and every pass that reads geometry declares them, so the copies wait for the frames in flight and nothing reads a slot before its copy lands. A frame with no chunk declares nothing, as a scene read whole never has. A slot's host copy of its DAG is dropped once it is staged.

**A re-centre, from its asking to its swap** (`TerrainMotion`). When the camera leaves a ring's middle half — the capability's rule, asked of `TerrainRingSet::next_layout` — the chunks the move changes are rebuilt on a **ring worker** of their own (`TerrainRingSet::update`), from the field at the surface's time, while the sand goes on moving; a chunk whose cells, hole and borders are unchanged is kept with its slot. Its new chunks are then uploaded into free slots, `renderer.terrain.ring_upload_mib` (16) a frame and at least one. When all of them are on the device the rings **freeze their pairs**, and the field worker carries each moved ring's drawn pair over to the new layout's window — the same two times, so at the same blend the same sand: the lattice points the old window held are copied from the kept fields (the evaluation is a function of the point; `TerrainMotion::field_over`) and only the strip the ring moved into is evaluated — and measures the pair's padding against the new chunks and the old. Then, in one frame, the new chunks' slots are turned on and the replaced ones off (`GpuScene::terrain_chunk_show`), the rings draw their carried pairs, and the grid's hole moves with the middle ring. **A change costs the chunks it changed**: a kept chunk keeps its slot and is never copied again, and a turned-off slot's arena ranges are free for the next upload, whose copy the frame orders after the frames in flight. Offscreen (`TimeLapseConfig::wait`) a re-centre is completed in the frame that asks for it, so the pictures of a run are a function of its frames.

**Why a swap is not a step.** Every level is the same function of the same game time at its own spacing, and a ring's pair over its new window is the old pair at the same lattice points, copied. So a swap changes which triangles draw the sand — a chunk rebuilt round a moved hole simplifies differently, and ground the middle ring drew at a metre is now the inner ring's at 50 cm — and never the height of a lattice point: what changes is the tessellation, which the cluster LOD changes every frame anyway. The freeze costs a moment of stillness when a ring reaches its b before the swap (the surface holds for it, as for any late field); it lasts the carrying over, a strip of each moved ring (0.23–0.29 s on the erg), and the frames that copy the carried pairs over at `renderer.terrain.upload_mib` a frame (two 16 MB fields for a middle ring: four frames). The chunks' own rebuild, the long part, runs before it with the sand moving.

**The padding across a re-centre.** A ring's spheres and LOD errors are its chunks' rest pose — the field at the time each chunk was built — so a field's padding is measured against the rest heights of the chunks it is drawn over (`TerrainRingSet::padding`, from a per-chunk grid of rest heights taken off the chunk's DAG). Between a rebuild and its swap a ring's fields are drawn over the old chunks and will be over the new ones, so the padding is the largest over both (`previous_` keeps the replaced chunks' rests until the next rebuild), and the pair a swap carries over is measured again against both. The field worker asks for it while the ring worker may be swapping the chunk lists, which a lock in the set covers.

**What is refused.** The rings are more meshes in the scene's load: not for a streamed scene, whose clusters live in pages, and not with cluster templates — a scene whose instances come and go takes them as its prefix since 2026-10-12 ([Instances that come and go](#instances-that-come-and-go)) — which are built once per mesh from a rest pose a slot does not have (`resolve_settings` turns `--rt-templates` off with a warning). A re-centre that finds no free slot or no arena room is dropped with a sentence: whatever it uploaded is freed, the rings stay where they are drawn and no further re-centre is asked for — fine ground where the rings stand and the grid past them, which is a picture, where a half-swapped ring would be a hole. `renderer.terrain.ring_slack` is the knob.

**What holds it.** `terrain_motion_tests.cpp`, on a GPU, with the rings shrunk to a 128 m terrain at a metre (an inner ring 6 m either side at 25 cm, a middle one 20 m either side at 50 cm): a camera high over the sand slides 24 m in 60 frames at a game week a real second, and every frame the levels' surface times are equal, every covered pixel's depth is unprojected and held to the level that draws it there — between the lowest and highest of the four lattice points round it of that level's blended field at the motion's times — away from the borders, every pixel is drawn by the level whose square it is in (the grid's instance, the middle ring's slots or the inner ring's), each level's lattice points move no more than its own bound in a frame, re-centre frames included, and the re-centres are all swapped and none dropped. It is the case that found the copy cap (a ring a frame's worth of sand behind, 7–16 mm off at 25 cm) and the corners of the grid's hole (1.3 m proud); with both fixed it holds every level to its model within 0.2 mm over 2.4 million pixels, with 9 re-centres swapped in 60 frames (RTX 5090, `msvc-debug`). And the visibility invariants of the moving terrain hold over the rings as over the grid alone, with the camera walking along the sand at a metre and the rings re-centring under it: occlusion culling and the cone test change no pixel and no depth, the software rasterizer agrees with the hardware one as on a rigid mesh, and the ray path draws the same coverage. Those comparisons are between five rigs, so the case first checks that they rest on the same sand: every rig's levels at the same surface, pair, blend and padding and its rings at the same place, frame by frame, failing at the first frame that differs and printing both — the check that named the waiting loop's give-up (above, "The bound, and a late field") when the comparisons below it only said that ids differed. **An offscreen frame takes every ready field**: frames of no time first fill each level's room after b with ready fields (`LevelStats::ready`: one for the grid, two for a ring), and the next sixtieth of a second at a week a second then stands every level at game time, uncapped, the inner ring taking four fields; before the fix it stood at the inner ring's first field, 2,693 of 10,080 game seconds in, on every machine.

## The ground from the world's tiles

**Status, 2026-09-30:** the mechanism, its seams, the grid's picture and the time-lapse across tiles are built and held by the tests below; engine-view draws a world's ground from the world's own ring (`--terrain-tiles`, or a world block's `"ground"`; [world](world.md#the-consumers)) and its walker stands on the same tiles; `content/test-scenes/desert-endless` is the scene to fly, and [the flight's measurement](../experiments/world-tiles-flight-2026-09-30.md) what it costs. [ADR-0050](../adr/0050-the-ground-is-drawn-from-the-worlds-tiles.md) (accepted, 2026-10-07) records the decisions and the alternatives.

The scene's grid ends at the terrain's `extent`, and the rings move round the camera only inside it. **The world's tiles** are the ground a world streams round its observers ([world](world.md)): with them the desert does not end, and the tiles are the same ones the walker's collision stands on.

**One mechanism, two layouts.** A tile is drawn the way a ring's chunk is: **a chunk of a terrain level**, in a slot of the level's, through the pool's terrain stage, blended between the level's two fields at the one surface time every level shares. Everything above in this section and the last two — the slots and arenas, the uploads a budget a frame, the freeze and the carry-over of a pair to a new window, the swap in one frame, the padding measured against the rest heights of the chunks drawn and replaced — is the tiles' too, unchanged. What differs is who says which chunks exist: `TerrainRingSet` lays them out as squares round the camera by the terrain capability's rules, `TerrainTileSet` (`terrain_tiles.h`) as the world's tile grid, and `GpuScene` and `TerrainMotion` take either through `TerrainLevelSet`. **The scene's grid stays level 0 and draws nothing**: its hole covers the world, so the cull drops every one of its clusters, and it stays for what it carries — the terrain's one material and the UV frame its maps are baked over, which every tile's material lookup puts its UVs back in (a tile's UVs are from its corner, [above](#the-grounds-tiles-are-placed-at-their-corners); so a tile samples the map a grid vertex at the same point samples, and past the grid's extent the maps' edge) — and as the reference a tile is held to. A scene built for tiles gives its grid a few samples; the old extent is then only the maps'.

**Levels.** One tile level per ring of the world's (`engine.scene.WorldRings`, innermost first), each at the tile's edge over its `ground_cells` (0 takes the rule: 64 a side in the inner ring, halving outwards to 8; 50 cm, 1 m, 2 m and then 4 m on 32 m tiles). The levels are counted coarsest first as the rings' are: level 1 is the outermost ring's, and the grid is level 0. A level's tiles are the ones the world's ring holds in that ring, so its tiles are a band, not a square with a hole, and no two levels hold one tile.

**A tile is heights, and the renderer meshes it** (ADR-0050 decision 2). The mesh is the tile's lattice points at the level's spacing, two counter-clockwise triangles a cell with the grid's diagonal, its border locked (`geometry::AttributeSource::locked`), and its cluster DAG is built on the ring worker from the heights at the surface's time, like a ring's chunk. Its UVs are from its corner at the grid's UV scale, and its material adds the corner's place in the grid's frame ([above](#the-grounds-tiles-are-placed-at-their-corners)). A tile's mesh is a function of its **key**: its coordinates, its level, and the levels of the eight tiles round it (below), so a tile is rebuilt when it changes ring or a neighbour does, and kept, slot and all, otherwise.

**A terrain's holes are in the tile's mesh** (2026-11-07, W87; [terrain](terrain.md#holes)): a cell wholly inside one of the terrain's `holes` has no triangles and its corners are locked, as a far tile's hole over the finer rings is; the tile's key adds its hole cells only when it has some (`TerrainTileMeshSpec::ground_holes`, `terrain_tile_key`), so a tile no hole reaches keeps its key, its slot and its bytes; a far level whose cells are larger than the hole closes it. The scene's grid does the same (`build_terrain_mesh`, `terrain_grid_cell_is_hole`, its hash moving only with holes). The pool's terrain stage needs nothing: it moves vertices and the opening is the absence of triangles, so every rasterizer, the ray path, the cascades and the structures agree (`terrain_holes_tests.cpp`: on a GPU, a 6 m hole over the grid seen from 9 m above opens 9,151 of 49,152 pixels on the hardware and vertex paths and under either shadow mode, the vertex path's ids the hardware's to the word, and the software and ray paths within two pixels of the opening. **Found on the way, not the hole's**: on this flat grid with no hole the software rasterizer and the ray path already differ from the hardware's by 8 and 37 id words at the default cut, at pixel centres on a triangle's edge in the ground, and where they differ moves with the mesh's DAG; the visibility and ray query tests hold them equal on their own meshes, so the flat grid is a case those tests do not cover). A ring's chunk of the dunes draws no hole yet.

**Seams, by construction** (ADR-0050 decision 3; each is a test below):

- **One level.** A border vertex is locked, so every level of the DAG keeps it, and it is a world lattice point that both tiles count in the same integers from the same origin; the pool writes it at `origin + (i, j) × spacing` from the level's one `TerrainLevelDesc`, with the height and normal of the level's blended field there. The two tiles' copies are the same floats. **How two tiles' 16-bit grids agree on a shared edge: they do not have to.** Each mesh keeps its own grid (`geometry::quantize_positions`, over its own bounds); a terrain vertex's rest position is read only to find its lattice point, by rounding, which needs a step under half the spacing — a 32 m tile's is about 0.5 mm, against 25 cm. The positions drawn come from the lattice, not the grid.
- **Two levels.** Where a tile meets a coarser one, its edge keeps only the coarser lattice's points: each of its other edge vertices is collapsed onto the nearer kept one (the lower on a tie) and the triangles that leaves degenerate are dropped, which turns the edge row into fans with no vertex on the coarser tile's edges that the coarser tile does not have. **And a vertex a tile shares with a coarser tile is drawn from the coarser tile's level**: the mesh names the level in the vertex's rest normal — a downward direction, at the level's number of sixteenths of a turn — and the pool's terrain stage reads that level's description for it instead of the tile's, so its lattice point, height and normal are the coarser tile's own. A corner is drawn from the coarsest of the four tiles round it. A shared vertex is then one computation on both sides, whatever pair and blend each level is at.
- **A time-lapse step apart.** Each level has one pair and one blend, and a vertex two levels share is drawn from one of them, so a border between two levels whose fields are at different steps is as exact as one between two tiles of one level.
- **Far from the origin.** A lattice point is `i × spacing`, the spacing a whole number of millimetres; at 25 cm or more every point is exact in f32 to 4,000 km, so 50 km from the origin is the same arithmetic as the origin.

**Fields.** A tile level's fields cover a square window of its lattice: every tile the level can hold, and a point of apron round them, while the camera stays within a margin of the window's centre (a quarter of the ring's radius, two tiles at least). The window moves only when the camera leaves that margin — the rings' re-centre rule, applied to the window — and its pair is then carried over by the rings' pair step. A tile arriving or leaving inside the window is a mesh and a slot and no field work.

**The time-lapse across tiles.** Every tile level is a terrain level like a ring: its own pair on its own cadence, every level at the one surface time, each within its own per-frame bound, a pair handed over to the bit — the promises of [The dunes in time-lapse](#the-dunes-in-time-lapse), which the tiles keep through the same code. What differs is how often the layout changes: a ring re-centres every hundred metres or so, a tile set with every tile a camera crosses. A ring's swap freezes every ring level — holds its pair and drops its fields after b — from the moment its new chunks are on the device to the swap, and that, at every tile a camera crosses, stutters the sand: `terrain_clock_tests.cpp`'s model, extended with the endless desert's four tile levels on one worker and a rebuild every half second (a camera at 60 m/s over 32 m tiles), every fourth moving a window, stood the sand still a frame in a hundred and more and swung its speed by a window ratio of 115–134 at a day an hour, a day a second and a week a second. So **a tile level is frozen only when its window moves** (`TerrainMotion::freeze_rings`); one whose window stays goes on taking fields while its tiles are swapped, and the pairs step measures every field it holds — its pair and the fields after it — against the new tiles and the replaced ones, which the swap applies to whichever it still holds, by time. The same model never stands the sand then, keeps a day an hour as smooth as with nothing changing (a window ratio of 1.1 against 1.0), and leaves a dip where a moved window's level waits for the field after its carried pair (4.9 at a day a second and 11 at a week, against 1.3 and 1.9 with nothing changing): the fields after b are not carried over a window's move ([Not yet](#not-yet)).

**Where heights come from: a tile source** (`scene_gen::TileSource`, [scene_gen](scene_gen.md#the-tile-source)). The tile levels ask a tile source for the heights of a window of the world's lattice at a spacing and a game time, and for how far its fastest feature travels (the cadence); nothing about how the heights were made. The scene's ground provider is one (`GroundProvider::tiles()`), a tile set built ahead and read back from the derived-data cache is another (the tests build one, and since 2026-10-17 the tile-set capability builds one from an authored heightfield with the far levels' mip chain and draws pixel for pixel what its heightfield is: [tileset](tileset.md)), and the collision asks the same source ([scene_collision](scene_collision.md)).

**Static authored terrain follows the camera too** (2026-10-23, W67, [ADR-0057](../adr/0057-ground-providers-expose-their-native-tile-source.md)). Tiles need a millimetre-capable provider and a valid tile source; they do not require `terrain_moves`. The provider's native `GroundOps::tile_source` preserves an authored set's filter refusals through the registry. The shared `MovingGround` owns that provider and builds the layout for engine-view, engine-host and the editor viewport. A still source keeps its surface time fixed and schedules no future fields, including after a nonzero rate request; camera movement and teleports still rebuild the resident layout. Its hidden grid is only a 17-point material/UV carrier when tile drawing was requested before scene loading. Its extent remains the material's UV frame. Source data and cache indices are bounded independently of source extent ([tileset](tileset.md#the-reader)). This is terrain streaming: it does not enable `RenderSettings::stream`, so flora motion and loaded skeletal/morph animation remain available.

Document-backed `render.load` forwards the same pre-load `terrain_tiles` hint as file-backed loads and the editor. A session reload changing that intent rebuilds its carrier under the existing scene id, even without a document edit; an unchanged intent keeps the ordinary change-feed reuse path. This keeps the initial load and a later switch to tiles bounded by the carrier rather than the authored source resolution.

**A refused field is never drawn.** Initial field refusal fails terrain setup with its spacing/filter. A refusal during a field evaluation stops surface time and logs the failed level; a refused moved window abandons that re-centre and keeps the last complete layout, reporting a failed rebuild. Empty rings' sizing samples obey the same refusal rule. This covers missing tiles and unavailable filtered levels rather than drawing zeros or silently using point samples.

**A steep face is a surface, never a stitch marker** (W67). Named-level rest normals point down 45 degrees, with their x/z direction encoding the level in sixteenths of a turn. The shader recognizes `y < -0.5`; a real heightfield's upward normal remains far above that threshold after octahedral packing, even when a cliff's y rounds near zero. The former horizontal test (`abs(y) < 0.25`) assumed sand no steeper than its repose angle, mistook authored cliffs for level indices, and could read past the terrain table and lose the device. Ring skirts never set the named-level flag, so their downward markers stay separate. The packing and mirrored types retain their sizes. `terrain_tiles_tests.cpp` checks all sixteen markers after packing and surfaces with slopes from 4 to 1e8; the stock authored GPU case crosses a steep ridge, LOD boundaries and teleports.

**Which grounds may be drawn from tiles** (2026-10-07, roadmap W62). The tiles go wherever the camera does, so the ground under them must be right wherever a cell reaches: `resolve_settings` draws the world's tiles only from a provider whose descriptor says so (`scene_gen::k_ground_millimetres`, `terrain_has_millimetres`: its point entries and its grids sample the ground at whole millimetres, never at a float32 metre of the world); otherwise it draws the scene's grid and says why (`the ground is not drawn from the world's tiles`, with the reason). The dunes say so. **The renderer's waves do not, and are refused rather than given millimetre entries**: they are the stand-in ground of a scene that names no generator, drawn as the scene's one grid round the origin — a few kilometres, where a float32 metre holds the millimetre to 16 km — and their arithmetic is float32 sines of absolute metres, so millimetre entries would have to recompute every wave's phase in f64, which moves the waves' heights by the origin (and their mesh cache key and every fixture's pinned number) for a ground nothing draws far out. They never reached the tiles before either (they do not move); the line is now the one that matters, stated and tested (`renderer: the world's tiles are drawn only from a ground with millimetre entries`, `scene_gen_scene_tests.cpp`: a moving ground of the test's own without the flag is refused tiles, by the setting and by a world block's `ground`, and the same ground with it gets them). What still asks the waves far out — a grounded instance, a camera key on the ground, a placement's ground, the walker, all through `height_mm` or `surface_mm` — gets the waves' own float32 answer there, consistent between them, over ground the waves never draw ([scene_gen](scene_gen.md#placements-far-from-the-origin)).

**Which tiles.** The world's ring decides ([world](world.md#the-consumers)): engine-view registers a consumer that hands the renderer what changed in the held tiles and their rings (`TerrainTileSet::change_tiles`; `set_tiles` takes a whole set and turns it into the same changes) after an update that changed them, and `TerrainMotion` takes a change as it takes a re-centre. The first layout, built before the scene is, is the ring's first-fill rule — a tile's ring is the band its centre's distance from the camera falls in (`terrain_tiles_round`) — which is what the world's first update, from nothing and with no budget, arrives at too. The renderer's tests use the same rule. **A camera that outruns the ring sees what the ring holds**: the windows follow the camera and a tile outside them is withheld, so a ring that falls behind — a budget of changes an update, a jump of kilometres — draws only the tiles it has round the camera. Two things found it on 2026-09-30. An offscreen smoke run spread the 12 km path of `desert-endless` over 41 frames, 300 m a frame, under the world's default budget of eight activations an update: every tile was withheld from the third frame on, and the whole ring was rebuilt — 12,863 tiles in 8–12 s on the worker — only by the last frame's capture, which asks for a whole update. And the path flown at its own 100 m/s wants about ten promotions a frame (six tiles into the outer ring, four moving inwards), two more than the budget: the ring fell behind by the difference, and after 12 km it held 8,971 of its 12,900 tiles, the horizon ahead thinning. **engine-view's drawn ground therefore takes no budget** when the world has nothing else to stream (`ViewWorld::create`): its events are a hash map's writes, and their cost is the renderer's rebuild, which runs on its own worker and takes whatever changed since the last one in one go. A jump then activates the whole ring at once and costs one whole rebuild — in a window, the old tiles drawn until it swaps in; offscreen, a frame that waits for it. A host that streams other consumers too keeps the budget and asks for a whole update on a cut, as engine-view does on its first frame, a flythrough on each repeat and a marker capture on each marker.

**Slots and room** (`TerrainTileSet::capacity`, `renderer.terrain.tile_slack`, 1.5). A level has two slots for every tile its ring can hold — counted with the camera anywhere in its tile, past the hysteresis — so a rebuild's new tiles always find free slots beside the ones drawn; a level holding more than half its slots (a world whose budget deferred the deactivations behind a fast camera) withholds its farthest tiles rather than failing a rebuild. A slot holds the largest tile the first layout built with the slack on top, and never fewer clusters than a tile that did not simplify at all could have, since a tile over rougher sand than any the first layout held must not find its slot too small, rounded up to four clusters — a slot's run is pairs the cull visits every frame, filled or not, and a coarse ring's tile is one or two clusters, so the sixteen it was first rounded to was eight times the pairs of the ring with the most slots; the arenas hold a slot's worth for every slot. Nothing about the layout moves after load: a tile's pairs are its slot's, whichever tile it is.

### What a frame waits for

**Offscreen, everything; in a window, nothing of the tiles' own.** An offscreen run (`TimeLapseConfig::wait`, which engine-view sets for every offscreen run) completes a rebuild in the frame that asks for it — the world's changes, the tiles built, uploaded, paired and swapped inside that frame's wall time — so the same path draws the same pairs frame by frame and the flythrough tests can assert it. A window never waits for a tile: the frame thread asks for a rebuild (`prepare`, a swap of two lists), and the rebuild runs on the ring worker over the terrain's job pool while the frames go on drawing the layout swapped in last. When it is done, its tiles are staged for upload `renderer.terrain.tile_upload_mib` (4) a frame — the host copy into staging is the frame thread's whole share of a tile — and swapped in in one frame once all of them are on the device, with the pairs carried over first if a level's window moved (on the field worker). What a frame thread spends on the ground in a window is that staging, the swap's slot records and the taking of finished fields; the `--benchmark` records carry it as `terrain.host_ms`.

**An offscreen flight's long frames are that wait, and the record says so** (T137, 2026-11-14). The forest staging's 360 m walk, flown offscreen, has **32 frames of 450 to 780 ms, six for every 64 m tile crossed**, on main and on every branch alike, and for a batch they were read as time "no section names". They are named: each is the frame's thread standing in `TerrainMotion::take_rings` for the ring worker's rebuild (`world.ground_ms` and `terrain.host_ms` 538 ms of frame 188's 542, `terrain.rebuild_ms` 533), and the rebuild is that long because a tile entering the first ring (256 cells of a 64 m tile, 131,072 triangles where the second ring's 64 cells are 8,192) is built whole — its heights, its mesh and its cluster DAG, one thread a tile — **with every first-ring neighbour whose key its arrival changed**, four to six tiles and 14 to 27 MB a rebuild (a tile's key names its neighbours' levels, which is the seam rule's price). What hid it is that a record's `frame_ms` is the interval *before* its frame: the 542 ms stood in frame 189's `frame_ms` beside frame 189's own parts, which were small. A record's own interval is `sections.wall_ms`, and since T137 the summary reads that one (`slow`: [apps](apps.md#flythroughs), "The summary's slow frames") and names each long frame's span — `host.ground.wait` for these — and `terrain.wait_ms` is the wait itself, beside the rebuild's CPU milliseconds by what its workers did (`rebuild_heights_cpu_ms`, `rebuild_mesh_cpu_ms`). **A window does not have these frames**: the same ground under `--terrain-async`, which steps an offscreen run as a window's, has none (engine's own heavy-ground stand-in, 64 m tiles of 256 cells: 7 frames of 647 to 1,166 ms waiting, none over 11 ms without the wait); what a window's walk does have at the same crossings is the tail's layout at the pair cap ([Instances that come and go](#instances-that-come-and-go), "At the cap the pairs are numbered again"). A flight meant to say what a player's frames cost is flown with `--terrain-async`; one meant to draw the same pictures twice is flown without and its `slow.ground_waits` says how many of its long frames were the wait. **Not built**: the rebuild itself is still half a second of four to six cores for one tile's change of level; building a tile and its neighbours' new keys ahead of the crossing, from where the camera is heading, would take the wait out of an offscreen flight and the half second of coarser ground out of a window's, and is a row of its own.

**The catch-up rule: the coarser ground, already resident, never nothing.** While a rebuild runs behind the frames the layout drawn is the last one swapped in, round where the camera was when it was asked for. Every level of it is resident and its seams are whole (a layout's keys are computed together and swapped together, so ADR-0050's seam rules hold at every moment): a camera that has moved on draws the finest ring behind it and, under it and ahead, the next level's tiles, which the old layout drew there at a metre or two — coarser ground, never a hole, until the swap brings the finer tiles in at once. Only a camera that outruns the whole outer ring (2 km on the endless desert) before a rebuild lands could see past the ground; that would take twenty seconds of rebuild at 100 m/s. A coarser level added past the outer ring (ground to the horizon) is what that edge would fall back to, by the same rule. Where a re-centre stands is `TerrainMotion::recentre_stage()` (none, rebuilding, uploading, pairs asked, pairing, swapping), which engine-view's walking records carry beside the walker's numbers ([apps](apps.md#walking)). How far behind the finest ring is, is measured every frame: the camera now against where it was when the drawn layout was asked for, metres on the ground and frames (`TerrainMotion::frame_layout`, the records' `terrain.layout_lag_m` and `layout_lag_frames`, the summary's `rings.max_lag_m` and `max_lag_frames`; zero offscreen).

**A rebuild costs what changed** (`TerrainTileSet::rebuild_changes`). The world hands over changes, not its set; the rebuild applies them to its own copy of the held tiles, and the tiles whose drawn level may change are those changes and, for a level whose field window moved (or with the finest far square, [Ground to the horizon](#ground-to-the-horizon)), that level's held tiles whose coverage by the window, or place inside the square, the move changed — one pass of arithmetic over the held tiles; until 2026-10-03 every held tile of the level was asked again, and while a whole rebuild has held tiles back for a level's slots they still are. The ones whose level did change, and their eight neighbours — a tile's key names its neighbours' levels — are the only tiles whose keys are derived again, and of those the ones whose key changed are built; the chunk lists are kept with a map from tile to place, a tile let go swapped out with its level's last, a new one appended. What the rebuild changed is handed on as lists (`TerrainLevelSet::changed_only`, `added`, `released`), so the motion uploads, swaps and measures those and nothing else: a swap turns off the released slots and on the added ones, and the padding a field takes over the new tiles is measured against the added chunks alone (`padding_added`) and kept with what the field had measured over the rest — a field is a function of the point and the time, so what it measured over a kept tile holds whatever the window. Until 2026-10-03 every rebuild derived the key of every held tile, searched every level's list twice and scanned every resident chunk's rest heights for each field the pairs step measured: 7.5 ms of a 27 ms rebuild at 100 m/s for the keys, 3.8 ms for the lists, on top of the 1.5 ms the world's whole-set hand-over took the frame. A level that would hold more than half its slots (a world whose budget deferred its deactivations) falls back to the whole rebuild, which withholds the farthest tiles, and the motion then reads the lists whole. The first fill is a whole rebuild. `next_layout`, asked every frame, looks at the changes since the last rebuild and at the tiles that rebuild withheld for their window, not at every tile held.

**The threads.** The terrain's job pool in a window has `renderer.terrain.workers` threads (0, the default: half the logical CPUs; `terrain_window_workers`, which a host reads when it makes the pool). A rebuild at 100 m/s fills every worker it is given for 20–60 ms, and a level's window move fills them again on the field worker; with a worker on every logical CPU the frame's thread lost its time slices to them, and the first windowed flight hitched to 50–65 ms every 2.2 s, at each move of the 2 m level's window ([the experiment](../experiments/world-tiles-window-2026-10-03.md)). An offscreen run's pool keeps every CPU but one: it waits for the work anyway.

**Every frame says where its CPU time went** (`FrameCpu`, `FrameStats::cpu`; 2026-10-04). The renderer times its own stages on the frame's thread, wall milliseconds, kept with the frame slot and folded into `Stats::last` with the frame's GPU numbers: `begin_frame`'s wait for the slot (`wait`, the GPU's time) and what follows it (`begin`: the slot's deferred frees, its timestamps, the fold, a step of the chain's capacity), and inside `submit_frame` the tables, the terrain's copies (`terrain_prepare`) and the record upload (`prepare_records`), declaring the passes, the graph's compile, its recording — with the pass whose recording took longest, from the graph's own per-pass clock (`RenderGraph::pass_cpu_ns`) — and the submission. Both hosts carry it: engine-view's frame records as `cpu` and both hosts' flythrough summaries as `cpu`, percentiles by stage with the frames whose `cpu_ms` passed 8 and 16 ms ([apps](apps.md#flythroughs)). A frame whose recording took more than 25 ms still logs a warning with the same parts, and a resize of the ray tracing chain that took as long says so too. **What it found** ([the experiment](../experiments/frame-thread-spikes-2026-10-04.md)): the "graph recording" of 26–97 ms that the flights of 2026-10-03 named was one command, the copy of every instance's bottom-level address into its top-level record as 47,849 eight-byte regions (above, "One bottom-level build"), which the driver encoded on this thread at 3 ms a frame and up to 287 ms when the machine was busy; a dispatch replaced it, and the 12 km flight at 11520×2160 with traced shadows went from 163 frames over 8 ms (17 over 25 ms, at most 288 ms) to none over 4 ms, 3.5 to 0.43 ms at the median. With the maps instead of traced shadows the offscreen flight had no frame over 8 ms before or after.

### What a slot wait was

**A slot wait is three different things, and the record says which** (W155, 2026-11-21). R195's 4K walk of the forest staging had 26 frames whose wait for their slot was two to five times what the GPU's zones added to, and the record could not say whether the rest was GPU work no zone named, another process on the card, or a frame thread that woke late on a machine at 79–100 % ([the page](../experiments/wide-frame-and-long-frames-2026-11-21.md#w155-the-walks-own-long-frames)). Now `gfx::GpuTimer` writes **a mark at the head and the tail of each frame's commands** ([gfx](gfx.md#the-frames-own-span)), and where the device calibrates its clock against the host's (`VK_KHR_calibrated_timestamps`, enabled wherever offered, presenting or not) the two marks come back on `time::monotonic_ns`'s clock. `begin_frame` splits its own wait by the frame it waited for (`FrameCpu::wait_gpu_ms`, `wait_before_ms`, `wait_late_ms`, which sum to `wait_ms`): the GPU inside that frame, the GPU not yet started on it (the card on something else, or work of ours submitted outside any frame), and the time after its last command until the thread woke. And each frame carries its own span (`FrameGpu`: first command to last, the part of it no zone names, how long after its submission the GPU began it, and how much of that came after the GPU had finished the frame before it). The frame record carries both as `gpu_frame` (`engine.scene.FrameRecord` version 25; [apps](apps.md#flythroughs), "The frame record's GPU clock"), and `slowest_span` names a long wait `slot_wait.gpu`, `slot_wait.before` or `slot_wait.late`. A device that cannot calibrate still gets the span; its wait is not split (`wait_split` false). The marks are two timestamp queries a frame in pools that were already there; the calibration is one call every half second. **And a frame that is not a wait says whether its thread was working**: a flight's sections (`FrameSections` version 2) carry the frame thread's own CPU time over the frame (`thread_cpu_ms`, `profiling::thread_cpu_ns`, good to a 15.6 ms clock tick on Windows) and the wall time beyond it (`off_cpu_ms`), so a 60 ms recording that held 10 ms of the CPU was the thread descheduled on a busy machine — R195's 21 "preempted" frames were inferred from a different pass being slow each time; now each says so.

**Staging allocates nothing in steady state** (2026-10-04). Every chunk staged for upload goes through **one staging ring** (a frame's slot records did too until 2026-10-22, and now go through the frame slot's record staging: [Moving an instance](#moving-an-instance)) (`GpuScene::terrain_chunk_fits`, `renderer.terrain.staging_mib`, 32): host-visible, mapped and touched once when the scene is made, a frame's share released when its slot comes round. A window's frame stages what fits and leaves the rest to the next frame; a frame that waits for its rebuild (offscreen) stages it all, and what does not fit makes a buffer of its own, counted (`terrain_staging_overflows`). The fields' staging buffers are **kept and handed out again** (`terrain_staging`): a buffer comes back once the frame that copied its last piece is done, and a new one, the level's field capacity long, is made only when none is free. Until then every chunk made a staging buffer of its own and `terrain_prepare` made one every frame that turned a slot on or off — a device allocation on the frame's thread, and every page staged into a buffer the system had just committed. The long flight (below, "A long flight") counts the device buffers the frame's thread makes, the renderer's half included, and holds 0.

**What is refused.** Tiles are terrain levels, so they need a ground that moves (the dunes) as the levels do and a scene not paged. **Streamed placements beside them are not refused since 2026-10-12**: until then a scene asking for ground tiles and streamed placements together was refused with a sentence (ADR-0050, consequences), because a scene whose instances come and go had no pool; it has the pool and the ray tracing chain over its tail now ([Instances that come and go](#instances-that-come-and-go), "The pool and the chain over the tail"), and `desert-endless`'s `scattered.json` streams its scatter layer beside the tiles. **A bounded placement entry is not streamed** (2026-10-11): a `placements` entry with `"stream": false` (`engine.scene.PlacementEntry` version 2) is expanded whole when the scene is read, even inside a world, opened as a generator is outside one (`Context::world` null), and its instances are the scene's own fixed ones — so the pool, the ray tracing chain and the tiles all keep them. That is how `desert-endless`'s bounded variant (`scattered-bounded.json`) carries its scatter layer over a polygon along its camera path ([scatter](scatter.md#where-it-enters-the-renderer)). With tiles, `--terrain-rings` is ignored with a warning (they take the rings' place) and so is `--rt-templates`, as with the rings.

**What holds it.** `terrain_tiles_tests.cpp`, with no device and a tile source of the test's own: the cells rule and every refusal of a description; the first fill against a brute-force count at four cameras (the origin, a tile's corner, 200 m out and 50 km out), in tile order; a tile's mesh covers its square once, face up, border locked, every vertex on the world's lattice at the source's height; a tile beside a coarser one has the coarser tile's boundary exactly — the same segments along the shared edge, so no vertex of one inside an edge of the other — keeps every vertex along a tile of its own level, and names the drawing level in every vertex it shares with a coarser tile, corners the coarsest round them; and the set — its first layout is the first fill's, its windows cover every tile it draws with a point of apron, the same set handed over again asks for nothing, a tile moving out a ring rebuilds it and at most its eight neighbours and keeps the rest, a tile no window can cover is withheld, and a window follows the camera past its margin. `terrain_tiles_gpu_tests.cpp`, on a GPU (RTX 5090, `msvc-debug`, 2026-09-30):

- **The erg's picture.** The committed erg's field (its five bands, wind and time) on a grid of 257 samples at its own 1.5 m, against the same field from 48 m tiles of 32 cells — the grid's lattice — in one ring, both drawn through the pool at the finest cut, from three cameras: **156,172 pixels inside the grid compared, 0 differ in depth and 0 in colour**, and 12,319 pixels of ground past the grid's edge; two kilometres past it, every pixel of a view down on the sand is ground. (The first run found 298 pixels "different": ground the grid drew beyond the one ring's reach from one camera, where the tiles, rightly, drew none; the ring now reaches every corner the views see.)
- **Seams, by the visibility buffer.** 8 m tiles in rings of 1.5, 3 and 6 tiles at 50 cm, 1 m and 2 m, at the origin and 50 km out, looking down and grazing, at the finest cut and a pixel's: every pixel of the view down is covered, no column of the grazing view has a hole under its ground, and every sampled pixel stands on the surface (within 12 µm); and the shading normal — read from the normal channel — steps across a border between tiles of one level (349–1,387 pixel pairs a view) and between two levels (181–776) no more than it does inside a tile, and **jumps** there (steps more than on either side of it) at most 0.008–0.023 radians against 0.019–0.17 inside a tile across a triangle's edge. What it fails on without each half of the seam rule, measured by switching it off: with no vertex drawn from another level, the normal jumps 0.08–0.12 radians across two levels' borders (a lighting seam of five to seven degrees) and, in time-lapse, the two levels' blends open a hole a pixel wide in a frame; with the edges not collapsed (T-junctions), 8–29 holes a view, 2–7 a frame in time-lapse, and jumps of 0.12–0.28 radians.
- **The time-lapse across tiles.** The same tiles at a game week a real second, the camera sliding 12 cm a frame for 90 frames so tiles change ring as the sand moves: 252 fields installed, the finest and the coarsest level at different pairs in every frame, the levels' surface times equal, no vertex moving more than its own level's bound (exactly 1.0 of it at worst), 41 rebuilds swapped in, and every sixth frame's view down covered, hole-free and seam-free as above.
- **A tile set built ahead.** 361 tiles of the dunes at 50 cm with their aprons, written into a derived-data cache as `<ddc>/terrain_tiles/<key>.tile` and read back through a tile source of the test's own (behind a lock: a source is asked from several jobs at once), draw the procedural source's picture: 80,950 pixels compared, 0 differ.
- **A long flight.** 520 m over 260 frames with the tiles following the camera: 260 rebuilds swapped, 4,469 tiles built and 24,945 kept, at most 87, 24 and 8 tiles a level (with the three far levels it carries since 2026-10-03, 12,641 built and 385,309 kept, and at most 432, 432 and 555 far tiles a level), none withheld, no rebuild dropped, and the device's slots and arenas the same 1.89 MB from the first frame to the last (2.46 MB while a slot was rounded to sixteen clusters, below; 5.14 MB with the far levels). **And the frame's half of it allocates nothing** over the flight's second half — the tiles handed over, the re-centres asked for, taken, uploaded, paired and swapped, 130 of them in 130 frames — counted on the frame's thread with a memory tag (the workers' builds are theirs). It found three lists made afresh every frame, all of them the rings' too: a swap built each moved level's list of slots and searched the old one for each (18 allocations a swap, and quadratic in a level's chunks, which is thousands for a tile level; now a byte a slot, sized at `start`, and linear), and `GpuScene::terrain_prepare` moved its lists of copies and staging out and started new ones, and made each level's list of what is left for later (now swapped, cleared and compacted in place). 2,343 allocations in those 130 frames before, 0 after; the world's half is `drawn_tiles_tests.cpp`'s ([world](world.md#the-consumers)).
