Since 2026-10-03 the flight runs on rebuilds of changes, and holds the same 0 — **with three far levels** too, whose squares move seven times in the counted half: their first version made 5 allocations there, every one an arena's free list (`GpuScene::give_range`) reaching a new length as a far square's move let a strip of tiles go at once and fragmented the arena; the free lists are reserved at `lay_out_rings` for the most they can hold (free ranges never touch, so there is a slot's range between any two: a level's slots and two), and the slot records' list for every slot off and on. Since 2026-10-04 each step is also drawn — begun and submitted in flight, as a host's frame is — and the flight counts the **device buffers** the frame's thread makes over both halves (`gfx::buffers_created_on_thread`), which the memory tags never see (the tag stays on the host's half: the renderer's half made one engine allocation a frame in this test, with its debug logging on, not traced yet): a staging buffer for every tile staged and one every frame for the slot records, before the staging ring and the fields' kept staging (above, "Staging allocates nothing in steady state"); 0 since, and the ring never overflowed.

And with no device: **a rebuild of changes draws what a whole build draws** (`terrain_tiles_tests.cpp`) — a camera flies a curve across 30 tiles in steps of a third of a tile, handing the set the first-fill rule's tiles as changes, and after each of the 90 rebuilds every tile a set built afresh round the same camera has is drawn at the same level with the same key, no other tile is, nothing is withheld, every chunk the rebuild says it added has no slot yet, and no rebuild builds more than 37 tiles, under half the set. And end to end (`apps/engine_view/tests/walk_view_tests.cpp`): **a flight started high over the tiles has them where it starts** — a session started in flight 1.5 km off the erg's window and 350 m up, replayed offscreen, draws from its first frame the tiles the world holds round it, with no rebuild; with the first layout built round the orbit camera, as it was until 2026-10-03, it rebuilt all 52.

## Ground to the horizon

**Optional error rule (2026-10-26, F20).** `terrain_far_error_px` is zero by default:
existing scenes retain their spacings, windows, tiles and bytes. Positive values derive the first
spacing from the view and a **measured per-scene error**. `terrain_far_error_per_m` supplies the
envelope `B(s) = c s` in metres; neither the tile-source interface nor the set's format currently
stores a range/error mip. The tunables are `renderer.terrain.far_error_px`, `.far_error_per_m` and
`.far_ratio`; zero settings take their defaults (all zero). `terrain_far_ratio` explicitly overrides
the rule, keeping the requested count. With neither rule nor override the ratio remains four.
engine-view exposes `--terrain-far-error-px`, `--terrain-far-error-per-m` and `--terrain-far-ratio`
beside `--terrain-far <count>`; protocol `RenderSettings` version 14 carries the same fields, and
the flag and the field take the same range, the ratio 0 to 128 with 0 the setting's "no override"
(until T78 the flag refused 0; `request_tests.cpp` and engine-view's usage case hold the two).
Hosts pass the actual pixel height and first camera's vertical FOV to `MovingGround::prepare`.
Selection happens at load: rebuilding after a resolution/FOV change retains the estimate.

**Define the error before using it.** For heights in `[m,M]` and box mean `mu`,
`E_box = max(M-mu, mu-m) <= M-m`. Half the range bounds deviation from the **midrange**,
not generally the mean (a narrow peak is a counterexample). A cell's slope range is also not
the reconstructed triangle mesh's error: a plane has a large range and zero residual. To bound
the mesh, measure its residual against the source over its interpolation/filter support, or use
the range of that whole support. A p95 is a quality estimate with a tail, not an everywhere bound.
Automatic certification would require spatially queryable per-spacing min/max or reconstruction
residual records in the set and `TileSource`; no such data is invented by this change.

The frozen forest mountain (0.5 m source, 64 m world tiles, outer ring 4 m, correcting the initial
brief's 1 m/32 m) was measured over world-aligned boxes centred on heights at least 200 m, north
of z = 1024 m, wholly inside the source. The histogram and separate triangle-residual census are
in [the dated experiment](../experiments/far-ground-2026-10-03.md#2026-10-26-f20-the-forest-mountains-error).

| spacing | boxes | range median / p95, m | deviation from box mean p95, m |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 16 m | 5,995 | 12.611 / 20.393 | 10.473 |
| 32 m | 1,492 | 25.440 / 40.789 | 21.182 |
| 64 m | 374 | 49.761 / 82.483 | 42.263 |

At vertical FOV 55°, `P = H / (2 tan(55°/2))`, so `t` pixels admit `t d / P` metres at
distance `d`. At 2 km, one pixel is **1.446 m at 2560×1440** and **0.964 m at 11520×2160**
in single-view perspective; width changes the horizontal FOV, not this projection. At 5 km the
values are 3.615 and 2.410 m. This mountain's literal range envelope cannot meet one or two
pixels without finer near rings; the rule refuses that request. It cannot repair authored ribs
or gullies, or distant colour (R96/R97).

**Derivation (`derive_terrain_far`).** Try every legal power-of-two multiple of the outermost
ring spacing, including one (the same lattice). Keep at least the old worst-camera reach by
adding finer levels; retaining the old coarsest spacing as well would needlessly extend the
ground and reserve an extra level. Require `B(s_k) P <= terrain_far_error_px d_k`
at **every** level; the largest admitted ratio wins. The CPU API accepts a measured table,
never extrapolating missing entries; settings build a table from the supplied linear envelope.
The first conservative start is `max(0, (R (1-hysteresis) - 0.75) tile_size)` (inward hysteresis
and an upward rounded tile half-diagonal); later starts are the inner square's
`half-margin-snap/2`. From the second start these double, but the first transition need not.
Withheld world tiles can expose fallback ground closer, so the estimate assumes a filled outer
ring. Coarser residuals need not grow linearly: this is why every level is checked. An excess is
refused with **"derived far ground needs N far levels; at most eight fit the sixteen-level layout
reserved for the grid, seven rings and eight far levels (k_max_terrain_levels)"**, never clamped.
Missing filtered heights retain W77's refusal: rebuild the set into the caller's DDC for that
chain. Near rings and their spacing are unchanged.

**Capacity.** A 16-cell far tile has at most 289 source lattice vertices and 512 triangles before
holes and collapsed edges. A square of half-side `h` at spacing `s` has `(2h/(16s))²` tiles,
or three quarters of that in a coarser annulus. Two slots per tile hold both layouts. A slot
reserves at least 16 cluster pairs, rounded to four above the largest measured DAG times
`tile_slack` (1.5); vertex/triangle arenas reserve the largest measured DAG times that slack,
times slots, plus 1024. Two field buffers each hold `(2h/s+3)²` floats. Halving spacing at fixed
reach therefore costs roughly four times the vertices, pairs and memory per level, before adding
a level. Actual DAG sizes and device bytes are reported per run: source vertices alone do not
account for them.

**Status, 2026-10-03:** built and held by the tests below; the captures from 2 m to 2,000 m, the far edge's hand-over and the offscreen cost (about 0.4 ms of GPU at 1080p and 0.5 ms at 11520×2160, 164 MiB of device memory) are in [the experiment](../experiments/far-ground-2026-10-03.md); the windowed lag is not measured yet. **The frame's thread allocates nothing when a far square moves** (2026-10-03): the 5 allocations the long flight first counted with far levels were the arenas' free lists growing as a far square's move let a strip of tiles go, not the upload lists; they are sized at load for the most they can hold, and the long flight holds its zero with three far levels ([The ground from the world's tiles](#the-ground-from-the-worlds-tiles), "A long flight"). [ADR-0051](../adr/0051-the-far-ground-is-the-renderers.md) (accepted, 2026-10-07) records the decisions.

The world's tiles end at the world's outermost ring — 64 tiles, 2 km, on the endless desert — and from a few hundred metres up that was a straight edge against the sky model's planet. **Far levels** carry the ground on past it (`TerrainTilesDesc::far_levels`, `RenderSettings::terrain_far_levels`, engine-view's `--terrain-far`, `render.*`'s `settings.terrain_far_levels`, the tunable `renderer.terrain.far_levels`, 6; both hosts lay them out through `MovingGround`, [One request, two hosts](#one-request-two-hosts), so a call that names no count draws engine-view's): coarser tile levels of the same mechanism, laid out by the renderer and not by the world, whose ring keeps one tile size and streams nothing past its rings ([ADR-0051](../adr/0051-the-far-ground-is-the-renderers.md) decision 1). A scene that does not ask for tiles is untouched; one that does gets far levels unless it asks for none.

**The arithmetic** (`terrain_far_level`). Far level *k* (1 the finest) has twice the spacing of the one inside it, the first `far_ratio` (4) times the outermost ring's; its tiles are `far_cells` (16) cells a side, so twice the tile too; and its window is a square twice the half-side of the one inside it, centred on a multiple of the next level's tile (its *snap*) and moved, like a ring's window, when the camera is more than a quarter of the half-side from the centre. The first half-side holds every tile the rings can hold — the outermost radius past its hysteresis, a tile's half-diagonal and a tile beyond — from a centre as far from the camera as a margin and half a snap, and is at least six of the next level's tiles: two centres are then never further apart than three quarters of the finer half-side and a tile and a half, which keeps every square inside the next whatever the camera does. On the endless desert: 16 m tiles of 256 m in a square 7.2 km across, then 32 m, 64 m, 128 m, 256 m and 512 m to a square 229 km across; the ground reaches 77.8 km from a camera at the worst place the windows let it stand (`terrain_far_reach_m`), 115 km from the last square's centre along the axes and 162 km to its corners (five levels: 38.9, 57 and 81 km). A `far_ratio` of 1 is legal and is not an accident (2026-10-27, roadmap F22): the first far level then sits at the outermost ring's own spacing, holds no finer lattice than the ring, and adds only reach past the ring's radius in larger tiles; the measured-error rule above chooses it where the picture's error allows the ring's spacing farther out (`terrain_tiles_tests.cpp` pins both the choice and the validation), and zero is the refusal. Why 4 and not 2 for the first: a far level's samples are its square over its spacing squared whatever its tiles, and the first square has to be 7 km across to hold the rings; at 8 m that is 800,000 samples a level, four times the device memory, for detail the outermost ring's own 4 m tiles at 2 km are already drawn coarser than by the LOD ([the experiment](../experiments/far-ground-2026-10-03.md) has the cost of both).

**The layout** (`TerrainTileSet`): levels count coarsest first, so the grid is 0, the far levels 1..`far_count()` and the rings after them, and the bound is sixteen levels (`k_max_terrain_levels`: the grid, seven rings, eight far levels; a vertex names the level it is drawn from in sixteenths of a turn, `gfx::terrain_level_normal`, where it was eighths). A far level draws its square less the next finer level's square; the finest draws its square less **the world tiles the rings draw**, each of its tiles carrying a 64-bit **hole mask** of the world tiles inside it that a ring draws (`TerrainTileMeshSpec::hole_mask`; so a far tile is at most eight world tiles a side). A ring's tile is drawn only a tile inside the finest far square (`inside_far`), so every tile round it is drawn by a ring or by that level. A far tile's key is its level, its coordinates in its own tiles, its hole mask and which of its edges lie on its square's border; a far level whose square moved, or whose hole did, is laid out again whole on the worker — its keys asked over the square, a millisecond, and the tiles whose key changed built: the new strip, the row whose border flag it cleared and the coarser level's tiles the strip uncovered, about 210 far tiles every quarter of its half-side the camera travels (about every 1.1 km for the finest on the endless desert) — and otherwise the finest far level rebuilds only the far tiles that hold a world tile whose drawn level changed (12 a rebuild at 100 m/s). **What a far square's move costs** (2026-10-03, [the experiment](../experiments/far-ground-2026-10-03.md#a-far-squares-move)): 33 ms of the worker's wall against 13 for an ordinary rebuild, 17 ms of the field worker carrying the moved level's pair over its new strip (28,864 samples; a ring's window moving in the same rebuild is the rest), and on the frame's thread 2.4 ms of staging and 0.18 ms of swap. A window's fields are evaluated a block a job when they have fewer than four blocks a worker (`blocks_per_job` in `terrain_time.cpp`; a strip at four a job ran on two of the pool's workers, 13 ms for the far strip and 23 for a ring window's), and a window or square's move asks again only the held tiles whose coverage or `inside_far` it changes (`rebuild_changes`; every held tile until 2026-10-03, most of a far move's 2.5 ms scan). **The far levels' extra building is the outer ring's**: with them the rings build 71 tiles a rebuild against 32, the outer ring's tiles re-keyed as the boundary passes because their edges and corners collapse onto the far level beside them. Each level reserves two slots for every tile its square can hold, as a ring's level does.

**Seams** are ADR-0050's rules, unchanged ([ADR-0051](../adr/0051-the-far-ground-is-the-renderers.md) decision 4): a ring's tile beside the finest far level collapses its edge onto that level's lattice and names it in the vertices it shares (the collapse ratio is now the two levels' spacings, `TerrainTileMeshSpec::level_spacing_mm`, since far tiles are larger than the world's); a far tile on its square's border does the same against the next coarser level; a far tile's hole border is locked and drawn from its own level, which the ring's tile beside it names. **A corner cell of two collapsed edges** took the other diagonal on 2026-10-03: its two collapsed corners and its own lie on one line, so the usual split left a triangle of no area and the cell's corner vertex on the other triangle's long edge — a T-junction the far levels' tiling test found at the corner of a far square, and which a ring's tile at a corner of coarser neighbours had too.

**A far level follows the outermost ring, and a tile set must too** (2026-10-24, roadmap W77). The first far level is `far_ratio` times the *outermost ring's* spacing, so a world of four rings of 32 m tiles at the default cells — the fourth at 8 cells, 4 m — asks its far levels for 16 to 512 m, where the stock three rings (outermost 2 m) ask 8 to 256 m. A procedural ground answers any filter; an authored tile set holds the chain it was built for (`ring_spacing_mm`, `far_ratio`, `far_levels`, [tileset](tileset.md#the-far-mip-chain-and-its-filter)) and refuses a filter it lacks. The forest POC's world of four rings over a set built for the stock 2 m therefore failed on its first far tile, seconds into the first build, as "a tile's heights or its cluster LOD could not be made" (`terrain_tiles.cpp`'s two failure sites, the rebuild's and the update's). **The build now asks the source for every far level's lattice once, at the camera's lattice point, before anything is built** (one point a level), and refuses with a sentence that names the far level, its spacing and filter, the outermost ring and cells it came from, and the `ring_spacing_mm` (`far_ratio`, `far_levels`) a set must be built with to answer it — "far level 6 of 6 asks the ground for heights every 512 m, filtered to 512 m (4 times ring 3's 4 m, …, doubled 5 times), and the tile source has none: … build it for this world's outermost ring (`ring_spacing_mm` 4000, …)". A tile that still fails later is named by its level and coordinates, and by whether its heights or its cluster LOD failed (`TerrainTileSet::refusal_of`). The fix for the scene is the set's: built with `ring_spacing_mm` 4000 the four-ring forest builds and draws. Why a refusal rather than the renderer choosing far levels the set has: a tile source cannot list its filters, and a far chain anchored anywhere but the outermost ring would break the seam the finest far level makes with it (its lattice must hold the ring's). `terrain_tiles_tests.cpp` ("four rings ask a tile set for the far levels of their outermost ring") holds the sentence and the build over a source that answers only a set's chain; `authored_ground_gpu_tests.cpp` ("four rings over a set built for their outermost ring draw") builds a real set both ways, draws the four-ring world over the right one with the fourth ring on its 4 m lattice, and holds the refusal over the other.

**Heights filtered to the spacing** ([scene_gen](scene_gen.md#the-tile-source)). A far level's lattice (`TerrainLattice::filter_mm`, its spacing) asks the tile source for what that lattice can carry: the dunes keep each band whose cell is at least two of its points and stand the rest in with their mean, flat and still, and a set built ahead answers from its mip chain. Its fields and its tiles' rest heights are the same filtered answer, and **its cadence is the fastest band it keeps** (`terrain_next_time`'s `filter_mm`): the erg's 256 m level keeps the mega-draa alone, which travels a metre and a half a year, so its next field is a quarter of 256 m away — decades — and the cadence's thirty-day ceiling (`renderer.terrain.max_step_s`) times it. **What that means in a time-lapse**: every far level shares the one surface time and its own bound (a quarter of its spacing a frame, 4 to 64 m on the endless desert, which its sand never comes near), and blends between pairs a month apart rather than standing still and stepping; a level whose next field is late holds the surface as any level does, but a far field is 200,000 samples of three or four bands, a fraction of the finest ring's evaluation. The time-lapse test asserts it with the far levels in: one surface time over every level, no vertex past its own level's bound, and the coarsest far level taking 2 fields where the finest ring took 143.

**What a frame waits for**: what the rings' rebuilds wait for, no more — the far levels are chunks of the same rebuild on the same worker, uploaded at the same budget and swapped in the same frame. A camera that climbs fast moves no window (the windows follow x and z); one that flies faster than a far window's margin before a rebuild lands draws the last layout's far squares, which are whole and seamed, round where it was. **The catch-up rule** is ADR-0050's with one more rung: what a ring falls back to past its own windows is now the finest far level, never nothing.

**What it does not change**: the rings' picture. A view that sees no far level and none of the outermost ring's tiles beside one draws the same depth and colour to the bit with the far levels as without them (`terrain_tiles_gpu_tests.cpp`, at the origin and 50 km out), since every ring tile not beside a far tile has the key it had.

**The far edge is the horizon** (2026-10-03, [the experiment](../experiments/far-ground-2026-10-03.md) has the captures and the rows). Past the last level the sky draws its planet ([The sky](#the-sky)), and the planet shows only where the ground ends below the planet's horizon line: flat ground meets that line √(Rh/2) away — 17.9 km from 100 m, 33.4 km from 350 m, 79.8 km from 2,000 m. Five far levels (38.9 km from the worst place) left a band of the planet's flat colour under the horizon from about 500 m up, a ruled line across the picture from 2,000 m. **Six reach 77.8 km**, past the line from every height up to 1.9 km and to within a pixel at 2,000 m, so the ground's last row stands above the planet's horizon and meets the sky, and no planet shows below it: that is the default. The two cheaper options did not remove the band: the planet at the sand's albedo (`sky.ground_albedo` 0.71 rather than the scene's 0.38) evened its luminance but not its hue, and lifted the whole sky by the brighter ground's bounce; ending the far levels where the aerial table ends (32 km) would widen the band from high up and open one from 350 m. The reason is the haze, not the albedo: the aerial-perspective table reaches 32 km, so ground beyond it keeps the 32 km transmittance (29% from 2,000 m) where the planet next to it is drawn at its own distance. **What remains** is that the horizon is a little clearer than real air would leave it — from 2,000 m at 10:00 the ground's last rows are 183 of 255 against the sky's 164 — which is the sky's to remove (an aerial table that reaches the last level, `sky.slang`, untouched here). A camera far above 2 km (a flight, not a walk) would want a seventh level, or a ground that curves with the planet.

**A sea to the horizon** (2026-10-31, roadmap S93; [water](water.md#to-the-horizon)): an `open` water body's water goes on past its outline wherever the ground is below its level, and it is not a far level: the resolve's water modules draw it as a plane at the level on every shaded pixel whose ray meets the plane before its surface, or that has none and looks down, so it reaches the eye's horizontal past the last far level and its coast is wherever the far levels' (or the rings') triangles cross the level. The far ground under it is drawn as before and is what the ids and depth channels show there.

**Shadows.** With traced shadows (the default on a card with ray queries) the far dunes cast their own shadows to the horizon: the rays go against the frame's own structures, which hold the far levels' cut. Two things show there. A few one-to-three-pixel dark **specks** on distant ridges, in dotted rows along far tiles' borders: a shadow ray leaves a point reconstructed on a far triangle's plane lifted by millimetres (`ray_offset`, the receiver's 16-bit grid) where a pixel is metres across, so at a crease the neighbouring triangle shadows it — covered pixels with their neighbours' triangle and normal, gone with `--shadows csm`; an offset that grows with the pixel's footprint, in the resolve, would remove them. And the shadows' edges are stepped by the far levels' 128–512 m triangles at a low sun. **Past the cascaded maps** (`--shadows csm`, and a card without ray queries) the far dunes are lit without their own shadows, so at a low sun their lee faces are lit by the sky alone only where they face away from the sun, and the long shadows a 150 m mega-draa throws across the interdune floor are missing — a far slope is shaded by its own normal and nothing else. The maps are not extended. The cheap option is a **horizon angle** from the far levels' own heights: per far lattice point, the elevation of the highest terrain towards the sun over a few kilometres, marched over the level's field once per field (it changes as slowly as the field) and stored beside it, which the resolve would compare with the sun's elevation. It would need a resolve change (`visibility_resolve.slang`, another agent's this week) and is not built.

**What holds it.** `terrain_tiles_tests.cpp`, with no device: the far levels' arithmetic (twice the spacing, tile and half-side each, the first square holding the rings' reach from its worst centre, the reach) and the descriptions refused; and **the far levels tile the ground**: every drawn chunk's mesh, rings' and far levels' alike, built again from the spec the set derives for it — its key the one it was built with, the meshes covering the coarsest far square exactly once and face up (twice their area is twice the square's, to the square millimetre), and **every edge a mesh's triangles use once is two meshes' edge** — so no crack and no T-junction anywhere — but the square's own border, which is one mesh's: at the first layout, every eleventh of 110 rebuilds of a flight 300 m east and 120 m north in which the far squares moved, and 50 km out. `terrain_tiles_gpu_tests.cpp`, on a GPU: the rings' picture to the bit (above); no hole in any column of four views at the origin and 50 km out — from 90 m up over the far levels' borders and from 6 m over the sand out to the last level's edge — at the finest cut and a pixel's, with dunes every far level carries all of; the shading normal's jump across two levels' borders no more than across a triangle's edge inside a tile; **a far level's tiles leave no mark** — far tiles of six cells draw what far tiles of four draw, pixel for pixel, wherever both draw one level clear of a ring and of a square's border (below, "Settled"); the time-lapse above; and a tile set built ahead with its mip chain, whose far levels and the rings beside them draw the procedural source's picture pixel for pixel, with no level's padding above zero while the sand stands still. `terrain_tests.cpp` in the terrain capability holds the filter ([terrain](terrain.md)). **Every level shares the surface**: `terrain_surface_frame` takes as many levels as a set can have (`k_max_surface_levels` is `k_max_terrain_levels`); it took eight until 2026-10-03, and the endless desert's ninth drawn level, its finest ring, crashed engine-view a frame after taking a field on an uninitialized word (`terrain_generator_tests.cpp` holds sixteen; [the experiment](../experiments/far-ground-2026-10-03.md)). **A far square's move allocates nothing on the frame's thread**: the long flight (`terrain_tiles_gpu_tests.cpp`) carries three far levels whose squares move seven times in its counted half, and holds the rings' zero with them.

**Settled on 2026-10-03**, the two things the first version reported and did not hold. *A far tile's rest heights are its level's filtered answer* (`TerrainTileSet::build_tile` asks the source with the level's `filter_mm`, as the fields do): they were the ground at each point, so a far tile's padding was the gap between the point-sampled and the filtered ground (a metre on the test's dunes) and its DAG was simplified over heights it never draws; and a set built ahead, which keeps its finest lattice only where it was built, answered zeros past it — flat rest meshes, three metres of padding, and a grazing view whose rings drew 10,733 pixels differently from the procedural source's (how a far level's rest meshes reached the rings' pixels was not traced further once the cause was gone). Both sources now draw every view to the pixel, and every level's padding is zero while the sand stands still. *Between two far tiles of one level there is no seam*: the census's 0.137 radians against the inside's 0.086 at one grazing view was a crease of the surface that a border pair happened to cross (its pairs out there are a 4 m cell apart), and the test now holds the seam by the picture instead — the same far levels cut into tiles of six cells rather than four draw the same depth, normal and colour on every pixel of far ground both layouts draw clear of a ring and of a square's border, some 1,900 to 31,500 pixels a view and 40% of them on a border of the four-cell layout.

## The far forest

Roadmap R111 (2026-10-31), [ADR-0059](../adr/0059-the-far-forest-is-the-renderers-per-world-tile.md)
(proposed). **A streamed world's own trees go on past its ring.** Inside the world's outer ring a
tile's authored trees are their distance forms ([Authored instances per tile](#authored-instances-per-tile));
past it nothing was drawn, so from the forest proof of concept's mountain top the forest ended in a
line 1,280 m out, and the tiles the pair cap withholds inside the ring (242 in the owner's v23 run)
were holes. The far forest draws every one of those tiles' trees as their coarsest form.

**What it is.** When the world streams its authored instances and the host asks
(`RenderSettings::far_forest`, which `authored_rules` copies into `AuthoredStreaming::far_forest`;
engine-view's `--far-forest on|off`, on by default; engine-host's `render.load` takes the default),
`stream_authored` takes every streamed instance and merges them **per world tile** into one rigid
mesh (`far_forest.cpp`, `build_far_forest`): each instance's **coarsest form** — the clusters of its
mesh's DAG whose parent error is terminal, which for a tree with an impostor chain is its whole-tree
star of at most 16 planes ([flora](flora.md#the-impostor-chain)) and for any other mesh the top of
its decimated chain — with the instance's fit and transform applied, the tile's corner its origin,
one part per (mesh, material) and the clusters two-sided (no cone). Each far tile is a mesh after
every other mesh and **an instance after the prefix**, at its corner: the far forest is its own run
of the prefix, laid out once, and the prefix never moves (`SceneData::far_forest`,
`FarForestData`, one `FarForestTile` a tile, sorted by key). What it takes is ruled by two tunables:
an instance shorter than `renderer.far_forest.min_height_m` (4 m: the fitted mesh's height times its
largest scale) takes none — **the understory does not fit**: a fern or a shrub is under 4 m and a
pixel at 1.3 km, and the proof of concept's ground cover alone is 115,629 grass instances — and a
mesh whose coarsest form passes `renderer.far_forest.max_triangles` (512) takes none: **a rock's
coarsest rung fits**, at a few dozen triangles, and is taken like a tree's when it is that tall.

**Why a star and not a sprite.** A camera-facing quad has no shader here, and the visibility buffer's
masked variants need geometry whose coverage every rasterizer, the ray loops and the cascades compute
alike ([Impostors are masked clusters](#impostors-are-masked-clusters)); a quad turned to the view
would make the coverage a function of the view, which is R92's question and not this one's. The
star is the engine's own far form, drawn by the masked variants with no new shader, its baked
colour and normal atlases shaded by the frame's lights.

**The hand-off: one world tile is one far tile.** A world tile is drawn by the ring's tail or by the
far forest, never both and never neither. The tail's blocks are named by the world's tile key
(`far_tile_key` mirrors `world::tile_key`), so `SceneRenderer::set_dynamic_instances`, after the
GPU scene took the tail, asks the hand-off (`FarForestHandOff`, `far_forest_handoff.h`) which far
tiles change: a far tile is drawn unless the tail holds a block of its key **with instances in it**.
A tile the ring does not hold, and one it holds but withholds for the pair cap, is therefore the far
forest's. The far instances that change move through `place_instances`, which marks them pending
for every table set, so they ride **the same flip as the tail's change** and no frame draws a tile
twice or not at all; a refused move is logged and leaves the far tiles as they were. The hand-off
allocates nothing after load (its lists are sized for every tile).

**Parked, not hidden.** A far tile the tail draws is moved a million kilometres below its corner
(`k_far_park_depth_m`): outside every view's frustum, every cascade's (which reach toward the light,
above) and every camera ray's, its pairs culled as any pair out of view is. The GPU scene has no
per-instance switch, and its slot records — the terrain levels' way of drawing nothing in a slot —
are another stage's file; parking needs neither.

**Why one world tile and not ADR-0051's squares** (the ADR has the rest). The far ground has
coarser levels because the ground is a lattice it can filter; the forest is a finite authored set,
and its coarsest form is already the tree's own. Its hand-off has to be by world tile because the
ring decides and withholds by world tile, so a far tile larger than a world tile would need its mesh
rebuilt round a hole mask whenever the ring moved. One world tile is a few clusters, so the whole
authored set fits in the prefix: below.

**The cut thins it by measured errors.** A star's part carries a second level, the **cross**: the
star's planes in two of its four directions a right angle apart (directions found from the planes'
own normals; every triangle vertical and at least three directions, else it is not a star), held to
the largest distance any vertex of a dropped plane lies from a kept plane — measured on the mesh,
times the fit and the instance's largest scale, the largest over the tile's trees — the error
flora.md holds the star itself to, measured the same way (`build_cluster_lod_hierarchy`, an
element a tree, so two or three trees share a cluster and a group's sphere is theirs). Every other
part is one level that never coarsens: what its mesh draws from that far. The cross is drawn where
its error projects under the threshold — a 5 m crown's cross (3.5 m) past 3.6 km at 1080p — so the
proof of concept's 2 km region draws stars; a world larger than its ring takes the cross. No
coarser stand-in is invented: a coverage-keeping coarser form is the flora capability's to bake (R92);
the conifers have had a star of their own since G120 ([flora](flora.md#the-conifers-chain-g120)).

**How it casts** (ADR-0059 decision 4). The far forest carries no caster policy and casts as any
rigid instance: under traced shadows its drawn clusters are in the ray tracing chain and cast, and
its trees shadow each other and the far ground; the cascades take it where their frusta reach it,
which past the ring is the two farthest (their light-space boxes reach past their far splits). **Untraced was the intent, and is not possible
today**: `GpuScene::place_instances` sets a moved instance's flags from its placement alone
(`set_instance_placement`), so a policy's bits — and `k_instance_static_rt` — would be gone after
the first hand-off and the far forest would be traced or not by when its tile last moved. The same
loses an untraced actor's policy when a game moves it; the fix is that file's (reported).

**The derived-data entry.** Each far tile is `<ddc>/far_forest/<key>.far` (`k_far_forest_version`), **A hit names only its tile's parts** (T194): every cluster's part index is compared with the tile's part count as it is; the count of parts used was `p + 1`, which wrapped to 0 for an index of 0xFFFFFFFF and took the entry as a hit ("far forest hostile: a cached tile naming a part past its tile's is rebuilt"). **And its clusters stay in its streams** (T198, the class T187 mended for `.clusters` files): a cluster whose vertex or triangle run leaves its stream, a triangle naming a vertex its cluster lacks, or a quantized stream that is not three coordinates a vertex (with its one pad word) makes the entry a miss, built again ("far forest hostile: a cached tile whose cluster leaves its streams is rebuilt").
its DAG's streams and the part of every cluster, keyed by the version, the tile, the world's tile
size and every merged instance's mesh form — its coarsest clusters' bytes and materials — fit and
placement, so a changed tree, scale or position rebuilds its tile and nothing else. The materials are
copied from the instances' meshes at every load, one per part, with their images' built-texture
records and **none of their bytes**: the GPU scene finds the textures the species' own meshes
uploaded, by key ([One upload per distinct image](#one-upload-per-distinct-image)), so a far tile
uploads no texture and holds no image; a load with no derived-data cache has no records, and then
the bytes go along. A tile is built by one job in a fixed order, so the entries are **the same bytes
at any job count**.

**The arithmetic.** A far tile's pairs are its clusters: a star is 16 quads, 32 triangles over 64
vertices, so a cluster holds one tree's star (or two trees' crosses), and a tile of *n* starred
trees is about *n* clusters at the finest and *n*/2 at the cross. On the renderer's test forest (120
trees of 6–10 m over 160 m, 32 m tiles) it is 25 tiles, 4,860 triangles and 189 clusters — 189
prefix pairs. **Over the proof of concept's v23 region** ([the measurement](../experiments/far-forest-2026-10-31.md)):
of 243,808 streamed instances it takes 59,178 (184,593 are under 4 m — the understory, saplings,
grass, litter and small deadwood — and 37 have a coarsest form past 512 triangles), from 251 meshes,
into **1,812 far tiles of 2,761,477 triangles and 93,454 clusters**: 46.7 triangles and 1.58 pairs
a tree (the conifers' decimated tops, before G120 gave them stars, are heavier than a star), 0.56% of the visibility id's 2^24,
where the same trees streamed are millions of pairs. The prefix grows from 64,011 to 157,465 pairs,
and the device memory by 110–190 MiB as measured device-wide. A frame draws what the hand-off left
at the corners — 771 to 1,136 far tiles, 30,000 to 56,000 pairs and 1.0 to 1.6 million triangles
before the cull, from the three cameras measured.

**What it measured** (2026-10-31, RTX 5090, `msvc-release`, 1920 × 1080, the owner's flags; a shared
machine, others at 30–100% of the CPU at every run's start or end, so differences under about 0.3 ms
are within the runs' spread). GPU median `--far-forest off` → `on`: `ridge` 5.54 → 5.74 ms (hw/csm)
and 6.36 → 6.74 (rt/rt), `south-lake` 9.63 → 9.79 and 7.58 → 7.26, an overview across the region
9.31 → 9.64 and 6.44 → 6.77. Under the cascaded maps the cost is the shadow pass (0.16–0.32 ms):
the far forest is a rigid caster and the farthest cascades reach it; the camera's raster moved 0.02
ms. **What it draws**: `ridge` looks up a slope inside the ring and sees no far tile (the same
visible pairs; 36 sampled pixels differ, a far tree's shadow); `south-lake` gains trees on the
mountain's flanks past the ring; the overview gains the whole band past the ring, the far slope and
the mountain's flank, where it drew bare ground. **The pair cap's trade**: the prefix's extra pairs
come off what the world's consumer admits — at the overview 46 outer-ring tiles were withheld with
the far forest against 33 without, and the 46 are drawn as far tiles where the 33 were drawn by
nothing. **A side effect**: 1,812 more prefix instances move every tail instance's slot, and the
masked cross-fade's dither is seeded by the slot (R91), so a fading transition keeps other pixels of
the same trees — scattered patches in every rasterized before-and-after, none of them far tiles.

**What holds it.** `far_forest_tests.cpp`: the tile key is the world's, bit for bit; the hand-off
draws exactly the tiles the tail does not hold with instances, parks and restores the right
instances, commits only an accepted move, and an empty forest is no hand-off; a streamed load with
the far forest off is the scene it was, and on builds a far tile per occupied world tile, each a mesh
and a prefix instance at its corner with no cone and its part per cluster, crosses where the oak's
star is, adds exactly its clusters to the prefix's pairs, writes entries that are **the same bytes
with one load job and with six**, and a second load reads every tile back (hits, no misses, the same
vertices); and on a GPU, with the ring holding the four tiles round the origin and a camera 230 m off
the forest's edge: **937 pixels of far trees** where the scene without the far forest drew none (tree
pixels 1,090 against 174), **no far pixel in a tile the tail holds**, none at all with every tile
held, and more with none held (RTX 5090, `msvc-debug`, 2026-10-31).

**What of it keys on its generator** (read for G198, which does not copy it): its coarsest form is
the DAG's terminal clusters, which is the whole-tree star only because the flora capability bakes
one (section 38 is written by flora alone), and the cross is found from that star's shape; its
`min_height_m` of 4 m is the forest's understory line. Neither is wrong for trees, and neither says
what a rock's far form is: a rock's terminal clusters are its DAG's top, which over a talus is most
of the mesh ([geometry](geometry.md#the-far-form)).

## The far tile

Roadmap G198 (2026-11-13; `far_tile.h`, `far_tile.cpp`; scene_gen's `far_tile.h`). **A tile mesh
that is its members' far forms** ([geometry](geometry.md#the-far-form)): a generator, or a host's
form rule, hands a recipe `<dir>/far-<hash>.far.json` — the mesh generator "far" — that names other
placement meshes exactly as a near tile hands them (a recipe's bytes, or a file and its hash) and
where each stands from the far tile's origin, in whole millimetres with a turn and a scale, and the
far form level they draw. `load_placement_mesh` answers it through `load_far_tile`, on whichever
thread builds the tile's meshes:

1. Every member is built or found as a near tile builds it (`load_placement_mesh`, the same
   derived-data entry, no textures), and its far form is the one its container carried, or the
   same bake from its finest level.
2. Each placement's level is turned, scaled and moved to its place; a normal is turned with the
   inverse of the scale. One part a distinct material: a member's materials and images are taken
   once, an image's relative path made absolute against its member's directory, and two members
   whose materials are the same record over the same images share a part — every piece of a talus
   is its own mesh with its rock's one set, so a far tile of forty pieces is one part.
3. Each part is **welded** by point and UV — a far form keeps its mesh's vertices, split wherever
   the near form had a hard edge, and a triangle that shares no corner fills a cluster's 64
   vertices with 21 triangles; a far form is drawn smooth, which at its distance is a pixel's
   shading, and an atlas seam stays a seam. A welded vertex's normal is **the mean of the near
   form's own normals at its copies** (`k_far_tile_build_version` 2): a deposit's bed carries the
   plan's gradient, the same on both sides of a piece's cut, where the first pass made normals
   again from the far form's large triangles, gave every piece its own, and the band read as
   paving from 300 m; a run whose copies cancel takes the faces' area-weighted normal. Copies
   weld only within **60 degrees** of each other (`k_far_tile_build_version` 3): a piece's top and
   the wall under its cut meet at a right angle on one point, and one vertex there took the mean
   of both and tilted every cut's top toward its wall, which drew the lines between the paving's
   slabs; a faceted stone's facets still weld (the forest tile: 1,368 clusters welded whole, 1,430
   at 60 degrees) — then
   clustered with its own DAG (`build_cluster_lod`, the load's options), the parts merged, and the
   clusters laid out leaves first as every tile mesh is; its textures are the load's pass over the
   one mesh, as every tile mesh's are.
4. **It keeps itself in the derived-data cache**, a container under a key over the recipe's
   identity (every member's recipe and place), the far form's, the recipe's and the build's
   versions and the load's LOD options. Activated again — a ring step back, another run, another host — it is read
   whole and no member is touched (33 ms for the forest tile below, debug).

So the far tile is **one instance**: one run of pairs, one bottom-level structure, one admission into
the mesh room, where the meshes it stands for were one each; and **they need not be resident** — a
far tile reads its members' containers while it builds and keeps nothing of them. It is rigid, casts
as any rigid instance does (traced shadows trace it in the frame's structures; the cascades draw it
where their frusta reach), and casts what its members cast within its error, which is under a pixel
where it is drawn. What it costs and how its hand-over reads are on the deposits' page
([rocks](rocks.md#a-deposit-past-the-first-ring)), its first user.

**What it costs to make and to hold** (the forest tile, rocks.md's table): 2.5 s of members cold
from their cached containers (15 far forms baked, none carried) and 0.8 s to build, debug, on the
pool; 33 ms read back. It holds one admission into the room (1,430 clusters, 3.6 MiB since G198's
second pass; 2,261 and 5.7 MiB at the first) and **no near
mesh**: a member is built only when its container is not in the cache, once, and its streams are let
go as soon as its far form is read.

**General purpose.** The recipe is `scene_gen`'s and names no generator but its members' paths;
nothing in the renderer, the world or the recipe reads which generator handed a tile. A file member
(a `.clusters` or a glTF) is built through the same door (`far_tile_tests.cpp` places an imported
boulder field three times, one turned, and holds the far tile to one material, three times the
level's triangles, under a quarter of the three meshes' clusters, and the same bytes whether the
container carried its far form or not). **Tonight only the deposits hand one**
([rocks](rocks.md#a-deposit-past-the-first-ring)): an imported mesh a scene file scatters is a
resident mesh, and gets **its own far form per instance** through the rings' rule (below), not yet
the merge into one instance a tile; the world-side merge — one call after `PlacementTiles::build`'s
loop that hands a far ring's tile-mesh and resident placements as one far tile — is the row that
closes it. **A scene with none of it** pays nothing: no recipe names the generator, and
`load_placement_mesh` asks one suffix of the path.

**A resident mesh's far form, offered** (G197's hook, `far_offered.cpp`): every rigid, unfitted
resident mesh of a streamed entry that does not pick its own forms has each level of its far form
made a scene mesh of its own (its source's materials and textures, its own DAG, `form_source` its
source, rigid), offered to the rule with the projected diameter it serves — the source's diameter
by the rule's own measure over the level's honest error, times the threshold — and the rule draws
it where it serves for fewer pairs than the DAG's cut. A level that keeps half the mesh or more is
not built (it would lose to the cut at every floor it serves), so a load pays the bake and the
level's DAG only for a mesh a far form can help; a mesh with a fit is not offered yet (the rule's
diameter is the fitted one about the fit's anchor). `far_offered_tests.cpp` holds the offer on an
imported field of 300 small stones; there the DAG's own cut at the ring's floor is one cluster and
wins, which is the rule doing its work.

### What path 1 costs a load

G198's second pass, on a scene that scatters **seven imported glTF meshes** (the Khronos Avocado,
BoomBox, Corset, Lantern, FlightHelmet, SciFiHelmet and Suzanne, through the scatter generator's
`mesh` kinds) over a gentle terrain, streamed in rings of 1.5, 4 and 8 tiles of 64 m, with no
deposit and no other generator's mesh (msvc-release, RTX 5090; other agents' builds were running,
so every time is an upper bound). The offer bakes the seven far forms and builds **19** offered
levels (1,235 clusters), of which the rule drew **3**:

| | Load-scene stage | Path 1 (`far forms offered … ms`) |
|---|---:|---:|
| base `61ccce67`, cold / warm | 14.2 s / 0.21 s | none |
| first pass, cold / warm (baked every load) | 14.4 s / 1.15 s | 0.73 s / 0.80 s |
| this pass, cold / warm (kept in the cache) | 15.5 s / 0.66 s | 0.90 s (7 baked, 19 built and written) / 0.35 s (19 read) |

So the first pass made a warm load of this scene five times longer: every load baked every rigid
resident mesh's far form and built every offered level's DAG again. **Each offered level is now kept
in the derived-data cache** (`far_offered.cpp`): a container of its DAG, its part map and the far
form it came from, under a key over the mesh's source identity (a glTF's file hash, or the identity
a container records of what it was built from), the load's LOD options, `k_far_form_version` and
`k_far_tile_build_version`; a warm load reads it and neither bakes nor builds. A mesh with no source
identity at all is baked every load, as before. `far offered: a resident mesh's offered levels are
kept in the derived-data cache` holds the entries and the same forms on the second load. What a warm
load still pays, 0.35 s here, is reading 19 containers of which the rule draws 3; offering only the
levels that can win a ring (the rule's own comparison before a level is built) is the row that
would take it to the reads of those 3.

**And the same bytes cold and warm.** The first bake followed its input's order: a DAG built in the
load and the same DAG read back from its container lay their clusters out differently (leaves
first), and the cold and warm loads offered 1,235 and 1,233 clusters. The bake now sorts the finest
level's vertices by their bytes and its triangles by material and corners before anything else
([geometry](geometry.md#the-far-form)), so its result is a function of the surface alone.

**What an imported mesh gets, and what a scene with none of it pays.** Any rigid, unfitted mesh a
streamed entry places as a resident mesh is offered its far form's levels, the cheaper of a level
and the DAG's cut drawn per ring; an imported boulder gets exactly what a generated one gets. A mesh
with a fit is not offered yet (a row). A scene that streams nothing pays nothing (`offer_far_forms`
returns before its loop); a streamed scene whose meshes are all deforming or fitted pays the loop
over its meshes and no bake.

## Relief

**Contract, 2026-10-26 (R105, proposed; the engine path is not started).**
[Ground relief](../experiments/ground-relief.md) records the sources, authoring choices and
sampling limits. Relief is opt-in; absence must preserve existing geometry, material bytes,
cache identities and captures.

| Tier | Representation | Picture and self-occlusion | Cascades and rays | Collision | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Authored landform | Source heightfield at its recorded spacing and filtered far chain | Actual triangles and silhouette | The selected triangles | Existing sampled ground | Selected geometry |
| Synthesized relief | Deterministic height over integer world millimetres, scene seed, mask-level substrate coverage and physical feature parameters | Near lattice vertices displaced in the terrain pool; normal from the same displaced central differences | Every consumer reads the pool's positions; no alternate shadow or RT surface | CPU double mirror at the support lattice; add after the base fields' time blend | Same displaced cut; no shading surrogate for geometry |
| Sub-lattice detail | Layer normal maps and the shared sand detail function, filtered by pixel footprint | Shading only, no silhouette or geometric self-occlusion | Alters receiver shading only, never the occluder | Does not move support | Same shading function, sampled for convergence |

No parallax tier is selected. A single-valued relief field cannot model overhangs, loose logs,
root plates or detached boulders. Those remain placed geometry. Relief coverage is mip-0 mask
coverage, independent of the camera and of texture-height blending; texture height remains
an optical blend input. A shared vertex uses the **named coarser level's** spacing, height,
relief and normal on both tiles (ADR-0050), including a corner shared by four levels.

**Sampling rule.** For feature width w and lattice spacing s, multiply its amplitude by
`F(w/s) = smoothstep(2, 4, w/s)`: zero at two samples, whole at four, continuous between.
For an enabled maximum spacing M also apply `1 - smoothstep(M/2, M, s)`; s >= M does no
relief work. The default M is four times the finest spacing, leaving the two finest dyadic
rings eligible. Each profile is bounded by A in absolute height and mask weights have total
at most one, so a point's change between spacings s and 2s is bounded by the sum of
`weight * A * abs(filter(s) - filter(2s))`, never more than the weighted amplitude budget.
This is an amplitude-continuity bound, **not proof of temporal pop-free LOD**: changing a
layout discretely still changes triangles. Ring-crossing captures must establish whether a
spatial/temporal morph is needed before accepting the result.

**Geometry pays for what it carries.** Relief must be present in rest-mesh bounds and LOD
errors, with conservative padding for the difference between the field and the rest cut.
Filtering in the pool alone over a flat simplified DAG is insufficient. Far levels and
levels past the threshold have no relief field, kernel work or allocation. The finer near
option must feed collision's spacing as well as rendering's. Lattice-point equality alone
does not establish contact equality between vertices of differently simplified triangles;
walker acceptance must check that error explicitly. Pool overflow and pair admission remain
visible refusals/counters, never evidence that the full relief was drawn.

## The sand close up

The owner walked the erg for the first time on 2026-09-28 (`engine-view --walk`): the dunes' scale read, the sand did not — from eye height a smooth shaded surface with a vertex every 50 cm to 1.5 m. He asked for a sand texture and normals, and named the difficulty: **it has to look natural and it must not create seams.** A tiled image fails both on terrain this size: it repeats, and it has edges. So the detail is **a function, not an image**: wind ripples and grain evaluated per pixel in the resolve from the pixel's world (x, z), the scene's seed and the wind, with no texture coordinates, no tiles and nothing to meet at an edge (2026-09-29; the function is gfx's, "The ground's detail" in [gfx](gfx.md), `ground_detail.slang`).

**What a scene asks for** (`engine.scene.TerrainDetail`, `Terrain` version 6, `TerrainDesc::has_detail`/`detail`). The mechanism is the engine's and the numbers are the scene's — [ADR-0046](../adr/0046-scene-generators-register-themselves.md)'s consequence, "which generators are the engine's and which a game's" — in a versioned, append-only block whose absence draws exactly what was drawn before it existed, so no golden image or hash moved:

| Field | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `ripple_wavelength` | 0.12 m | crest to crest; real wind ripples are 8 to 15 cm apart |
| `ripple_height` | 0.008 m | crest to trough, about a centimetre; 0 draws no ripples |
| `ripple_asymmetry` | 0.75 | the windward share of a wavelength: a long gentle stoss, a short steep lee |
| `ripple_defects` | 0.35 | how often a crest ends or two join, [0, 1]: sets the kernels' radius (6 to 1.5 wavelengths) and their spread about the wind (2° to 20°) |
| `ripple_slope_start_deg`, `ripple_slope_end_deg` | 22°, 30° | the ground's slope over which the ripples fade out: a slip face at the angle of repose is avalanched smooth |
| `grain_size` | 0.02 m | the grain's coarse cell; a finer octave a quarter of it lies under it |
| `grain_albedo`, `grain_roughness` | 0.08, 0.05 | how far the grain moves the albedo (a share of it) and the roughness, either way; 0 none |
| `lee_start_deg`, `lee_end_deg` | 0°, 0° (none) | version 2: the ripples' **exposure** — on ground falling away from the wind they start to go at this lee slope along the wind and are gone at that one; both 0 is no exposure, the first pass. The ergs take 10° and 18° |
| `grain_finest` | 0 (none) | version 2: the grain becomes **gradient noise** in octaves from `grain_size` halving down to this (the ergs' 1 mm is five: 20, 10, 5, 2.5 and 1.25 mm); 0 is the first pass's two octaves of value noise |
| `grain_normal` | 0 | version 2, with `grain_finest`: the root-mean-square slope the grain's height leans the shading normal by (the ergs take 0.06) |
| `streak_start_deg`, `streak_full_deg` | 0°, 0° (none) | version 2: **grainflow streaks** on ground falling away from the wind, starting at this lee slope along it and whole at that one (the ergs: 22° and 30°) |
| `streak_width`, `streak_length` | 0.4 m, 2 m | a tongue across the fall line and down it |
| `streak_albedo`, `streak_roughness`, `streak_normal` | 0.06, 0.04, 0.012 | what the tongues move, each a root-mean-square: the albedo (a share), the roughness, the normal (a slope) |
| `flow_start_deg`, `flow_full_deg` | 0°, 0° (none) | version 3: **grainflow lanes** on a slip face, starting at this lee slope along the wind and whole at that one (the ergs: 24° and 30°, with the streaks off) |
| `flow_cell`, `flow_width`, `flow_widening` | 10 m, 0.6 m, 0.3 | `flow_width` is a lane's width; `flow_cell` and `flow_widening` are **retired** by the fourth pass (read, checked, not drawn). Third pass: the world lattice's cell (about a lane's length), a lane's width, how much it widens down a cell |
| `flow_normal`, `flow_albedo` | 0.05, 0.015 | the lanes' relief as a root-mean-square slope, and their colour as a share of the albedo |
| `flow_length` | 24 m | version 4: a lane's segment, the longest a grainflow **tongue** runs (each 45–95% of it, so some stop part-way) |
| `flow_share`, `flow_turnover` | 1 (every lane, always), 0 (never changes) | the lanes are **episodes**: this share present at once, each cycling this many times per m² of the ground's transport (the ergs: a quarter, and 800, about three cycles a calm day) |
| `patch_size`, `patch_min`, `patch_max`, `patch_defects` | 0 (none), 0.7, 1.4, 0.5 | version 3: **patches** — a slow noise of position (octaves at `patch_size` and half it; the ergs 30 m) scaling the ripples' wavelength and height within [min, max] and their defects (the kernels' spread) by up to `patch_defects` either way |
| `steer_max_deg`, `steer_gain` | 0 (none), 2 | version 3: **steering** — on a slope oblique to the wind the ripples turn along its contours, at most this far (the ergs 20°) |
| `ripple_celerity`, `flatten_start`, `flatten_end` | 0 (still), 0, 0 (never) | version 3: the ripples **travel** this many metres per m² of the ground's transport (the ergs 2,000), fade by their travel per frame, and **flatten** as the wind's strength over its mean passes from start to end (the ergs 1.6 to 2.2) |
| `spacing_gain`, `spacing_min`, `spacing_max` | 0 (none), 0.8, 1.6 | version 2: the ripples' wavelength and height scaled by `1 + gain × climb`, the ground's rise into the wind as a tangent, clamped; the ergs take a gain of 2.5 (1.53 at a 12° windward slope) |

`read_scene_file` refuses a block the mechanism cannot draw with a sentence naming the field (`validate_terrain_detail`). **Its numbers never enter `terrain_hash`**: they are shading, drawn per frame from a block, and neither the mesh nor its maps depend on them. What the detail does change in the maps is the next paragraph's, and enters the hash only where it changes their bytes.

**Where the sand is.** The terrain is one material over two baked maps ([Scenes, camera paths and flythroughs](#scenes-camera-paths-and-flythroughs), "The terrain"); with the detail asked for, the metallic-roughness map's **alpha is the sand share** (`TerrainSurface::sand`, blended across the same bands as the colour: the plain's sand and the basin's are sand, the ridge rock and the basin's floor are not), the material carries `gfx::k_material_ground_detail` — and the rings' slots, which draw with the terrain's material, with it — and the detail is weighted by that alpha. Without a ridge or a basin the share is 1 everywhere and the alpha 255, exactly the byte the map always had, so the erg keeps its hash and its cache entry; a terrain with a ridge or a basin gets another (`"SANDMASK"` in `terrain_hash`).

**The wind, from the ground provider.** The ripples lie across the wind the ground says blows at the surface's time: `scene_gen::GroundOps::wind` ([scene_gen](scene_gen.md#the-two-kinds)), a unit vector over (x, z), continuous in time, which the renderer reads through `TerrainSampler::wind` and links no provider for. The dunes answer the ripple term's own rule — the day's wind, turned in from yesterday's over the day's first two hours, along the shorter arc so a day's turn is no step (`terrain::DuneField::ripple_wind`, [terrain](terrain.md#what-the-effect-needs)); the waves answer their one prevailing wind. `GpuScene` holds a sampler of the scene's ground for it (a dune field is too dear to make per frame) and the time the surface stands at: the scene's `time`, until a moving terrain's `TerrainMotion::frame` sets the surface's every frame (`GpuScene::set_ground_time`). Each frame writes one `gfx::GroundDetailParams` behind the shadow maps' block (`GpuScene::ground_detail_params`), shared by every view.

**Three readers, one function.** The rasterized resolve draws it; **the ray-traced path** writes the visibility buffer by rays and the same resolve shades it, so a pixel the two agree on is the same byte (the test below finds 23,631 such pixels and not one another colour); **the reference path tracer** includes the same file and evaluates the same function **unfiltered**, since a ray has no footprint and the jittered samples a reference pixel averages are the filter — a converged reference is what the resolve's fades and roughness transfer stand for. At a walker's feet, 64 samples, pixel centres, one bounce, the resolve is **0.0498 FLIP** from the reference with the detail and **0.0539** without it: the detail adds nothing to the disagreement the transport already has. **The second pass on a slope** (2026-09-30): the ergs' numbers, every term on, on waves steep enough to have slip faces (16 m over 60 m) laid out on a grid of a metre, at the feet on ground climbing into the wind at 12° — **0.0489** with the detail, 0.0479 without — and falling away from it at 26°, in the streaks' band — **0.0508** against 0.0476, nearly all of the difference in the picture's upper half, ten metres down the slope, where the resolve fades a 40 cm tongue by its footprint and a reference at the pixel's centre point-samples it; held to 0.01 more than without (`ground_detail_tests.cpp`). The grid was a metre because on the flat case's 4 m the same lee read 0.0691 against 0.0510: looking down at the feet, the triangles under them reach behind the camera's plane, where the resolve rebuilt a point the pixel does not see until 2026-10-03 ([gfx](gfx.md), "Where a pixel meets its triangle"), and the 2 m tongues showed it — stripes running on to the bottom of the resolved picture where the path tracer drew them ending. **Since the fix the case runs on the 4 m grid** (2026-10-03, the third pass's numbers): climbing into the wind **0.0547** with the detail against 0.0494 without, and on the 26° lee **0.0613** against 0.0587 — the detail's share spread over both halves of the picture rather than gathered at its bottom. It is more than the metre grid's share, most likely because a terrain four times the size has a 16-bit position grid four times as coarse (1.6 cm a step), and the resolve's point is on that grid where the reference's hit is on the floats, which moves the millimetre grain between them. The first comparison above was on that grid at such a camera: with the fix it reads **0.0485** with the detail, where it read 0.0498, and 0.0539 without, as it did — so 0.0013 of its disagreement was the reconstruction's.

**The filter rule, which is what makes it look natural at a distance.** A ripple fades by the larger, over the screen's two axes, of the pixel's footprint **along the wind** in wavelengths, from the reconstruction's own derivatives — a grazing footprint is long and thin and only its extent across the crests aliases — in two stages: the profile's harmonics first (the asymmetry eases to a sinusoid between eight pixels a wavelength and four, since the lee is a quarter of a wavelength and aliases an octave early), then the sinusoid (between four pixels and two). **The slope variance the stages take goes into the GGX roughness** (`α² += σ² − σ²_drawn`), so distant sand is rougher, not flatter and not a mirror; on sand already at 0.92 that is a few hundredths. The grain fades by its cells against the footprint's longest side. **What the pull-back measured** — the erg, 240 frames from a walker's 1.65 m to 350 m over the western floor at 960×540, detail on and off, every eighth frame beside a 4×4 supersampled picture of itself ([the experiment](../experiments/sand-detail-2026-09-29.md)): no moiré and no pop. Blurred by a box of radius 3 (twice), which leaves a structure's bands and shifts and removes the ripples themselves, the error against the supersampled picture is **0.20 of a level of luma with the detail and 0.17 without**; the mean brightness never moves by more than **0.09** of a level against it (the rougher-not-flatter rule's test); and the frame-to-frame change with the detail comes down to the change without it by the time the camera is 30 m up, where the fade has taken the ripples, and never spikes on the way. Near the ground the detail doubles the per-frame change (1.2 levels against 0.6 on average) because it is detail the camera moves across, not flicker. The two-stage fade was chosen by eye over the one-stage: a pixel's error against the supersampled picture is larger with it (0.89 against 0.76, since the supersampled picture still shows the asymmetric profile the eased one no longer draws) but the 1-pixel stair-stepped lee lines at four to eight pixels a wavelength are gone. The renderer's own test holds the rule on the waves at 192×108 (`ground_detail_tests.cpp`, below).

**Grainflows come and go** (2026-09-30, the owner on the preview: "I don't think the entire lee needs to be covered in streaks, just there should be some that appear and disappear over time depending on wind activity"). That is how a real face behaves. Sand arriving at the brink piles until it avalanches down a lane, and grainfall slowly buries the tongue again, so a face shows a few fresh flows over smooth sand, and more of them the harder the wind blows. Each lane of the grainflow term is therefore an **episode**:

- **A clock.** The ground's transport path length times `flow_turnover`, reduced to a fraction of a cycle in double (`gfx::ground_detail_motion`, `GroundDetailParams::flow_clock`).
- **Its own phase.** Each lane is present for `flow_share` of each cycle, at a phase of its own (`ground_episode`). It comes up over the first twentieth of that time, since an avalanche is sudden, and fades over the last seven tenths, since grainfall is slow.
- **Wind drives it.** With no wind the clock stands and so does the face. In a storm the clock runs faster. Once it advances more than a quarter of the share a frame (a storm at the game's rate, any fast time-lapse), the lanes fade by `ground_fade` exactly as the ripples do by their travel.
- **The ergs.** A quarter of the lanes and a turnover of 800: about three cycles on a calm day. On the mirror a face is 19% lanes at a time, and 28% of it changes half a cycle on.
- **Pictures.** `after_slip_20m_raking` and `after_slip_20m_clock33_*` / `clock67_*` show the same face at three readings.
- **Cost.** One more hash and a few operations per lattice point.

**Ripples that are not all alike** (version 3, 2026-09-30; the owner: "ripples are still incredibly uniform as well throughout the sand" — the spacing term moves only on a windward slope, and most of the erg is floor). Two terms, each a function the ripple kernels already take:

- **Patches.** Two octaves of the grain's gradient noise at `patch_size` and half it, two channels, each scaled to about [-1, 1] and clamped: the first scales the wavelength and the height together by `sqrt(min max) 2^(v log2(max/min)/2)` (so a ripple keeps its shape and its slope variance), the second the kernels' spread about the wind by up to `patch_defects` of itself (capped at a sine of 0.9) — a narrower spread is longer, straighter crests, a wider one more junctions. A function of position alone, so it does not slide when the normal changes; eight lattice hashes a rippled pixel. Over a kilometre of samples the scale covers 0.70 to 1.40 with a mean of 1.00.
- **Steering.** On a slope oblique to the wind the near-surface flow is turned along the contours: the ripples' direction is the wind with `min(steer_gain tan(slope), 1/2)` of its component along the fall line taken out, clamped to `steer_max_deg`. Nothing on the flat, nothing straight up or down a slope, and at most half the component so that where the wind runs nearly along the fall line the turn grows no faster than the normal turns: on a 25° slope round the compass at most 19.5° and 0.1° per 0.1° of azimuth. Arithmetic, a few dozen operations; like the spacing it multiplies only offsets from kernel centres, and a tenth of a degree of turn moves the crests at most 0.009 of a wavelength (measured where the sum stands clear of its taper). The footprint's fade reads the steered direction and the patched spread.

Along lines crossing patches over ground whose slope swings across the wind, the shaded ripple never jumps between half-millimetre steps (`ground_detail_tests.cpp`, "ripples in patches, steered by the ground …"). What these cannot give is the variation the terrain knows and the normal does not — ripples coarser on a crest where the wind is strongest, finer in a hollow — which would be a channel from the provider, as the shelter is.

**Ripples that move** (version 3, 2026-09-30; the owner, from a fast time-lapse: "it looks strange to have the surface level rising ... with the ripples staying on top"). What real ripples do is in [terrain](terrain.md#how-real-ripples-behave-and-what-the-picture-takes-from-it): they migrate downwind with the transport, stand when the wind drops, climb rather than vanish under slow deposition, and flatten in very strong wind.

- **Travel.** Every kernel's phase is taken back by `2π travel / λ`, with λ the block's base wavelength whatever the spacing or the patches scale the ripple by, so the crests move along their own direction, the kernels stay where the lattice put them, and **a ripple s times as long and as high moves 1/s as far** — a bedform's celerity is the flux over its height. The travel is `ripple_celerity` metres per m² of the ground's transport path length (`scene_gen::GroundOps::transport`, `TerrainSampler::transport`; the dunes answer from the wind record's integral in full, storm gains included, below). `renderer::terrain_detail_motion` turns the transport at this frame's surface time and the last frame's into the block — what `GpuScene::ground_detail_params` calls every frame, and a function of those two times alone, so a frame at clock value T is the same bytes however T was reached — and `gfx::ground_detail_motion` reduces the travel modulo 256 base wavelengths in double before it becomes a float, so the shader holds it to 1.6e-5 of a wavelength. A whole number of base wavelengths moves no crest at any scale, so the reduction's wrap is invisible. (Until 2026-10-04 each kernel took back its own wavenumber's phase, `2π travel / (λ s)`: the wrap stepped every scaled ripple by `256 / s` cycles, and between wraps the phase wound up wherever the scale varies — with travel near the 30.7 m period, a patch's change of scale over 15 m wound in about as many cycles a metre as the ripples have. This page said the wrap came every four game days; at the speed measured below it came every 15 to 30 game minutes.)
- **Continuous in the clock** (2026-10-04; the owner at 1x: they "only updated every few seconds instead of continuously"). The wind record's integral is whole cm² (`terrain::WindRecord::integral`, right for the dunes), and the ripples were drawn from it: at a celerity of 2,000 a cm² is 20 cm of travel, 1.67 wavelengths, so they held still while a cm² blew — 12 game seconds at desert-endless's own time, 5.5 on day 1's morning — and then jumped, and on the frame of the jump their 20 cm of "travel this frame" faded them out entirely. It was not a float: the surface time reaches the ground as a double and then as integer microseconds, and at a clock near zero the step was the same 20 cm with a period that followed the wind, not the clock's magnitude. The dunes now answer from `WindRecord::magnitude_at`, the integral's whole cm² and the fraction of the next one the record's line has reached, so the travel is a straight line in the clock within every hour of the record ([terrain](terrain.md#the-wind-record); [the experiment](../experiments/ripple-motion-2026-10-04.md) has the instrument's series before and after).
- **How fast, measured** (2026-10-04, `ground_motion_tests.cpp`). On desert-endless at its own time — day 1,095, the hour after midnight — the ripples travel **100 cm a game minute** (1.7 cm a second), and over that whole day 192 cm a minute; the year from that time averages 79 cm a minute (1,133 m a day). That is a hundred to two hundred times the "half a centimetre a minute" this page claimed until then: the celerity of 2,000 was fitted to a calm day after a storm on the storm erg (36 cm²), where an ordinary day of the record moves thousands of cm² (5,666 on that year's mean day, 13,843 on day 1,095). So what the owner sees on this scene, with the base wavelength 12 cm: **at 1x** the ripples flow downwind, crossing their own wavelength every 4 to 7 seconds; **at 60x** they move 1 to 2 m a second, 1.7 to 3.2 cm a frame, a seventh to a quarter of a wavelength, where the shutter's fade begins (below), so on the day's strong hours they soften; **at 3,600x** they move 1 to 2 m a frame, ten or more wavelengths, and are gone into the roughness. A centimetre a minute at 1x on this day would be a celerity of about 10, the first one tried ([sand, third pass](../experiments/sand-third-pass-2026-09-30.md#ripples-that-move)); `ripple_celerity` is the scene's number, and which speed the scenes should have is the owner's call.
- **A time-lapse blurs them as a shutter would.** Their travel since the last frame (`GpuScene` keeps the last frame's surface time) counts as footprint: whole at a quarter of a wavelength a frame, gone at a half, with the lost slope variance going into the roughness. At a day a second they cross a wavelength a frame and are gone, and they return as the rate comes down.
- **A storm flattens them.** Between `flatten_start` and `flatten_end` of the wind's strength over its record's mean (the ergs: 1.6 and 2.2; storm 42 peaks at 2.31), their weight falls to 0, taken from the weight so a flat bed is smooth and not rough. The strength is the hour's (`WindRecord::wind_at`), so inside that band their weight steps once an hour; that is a storm's few hours a year, and not yet smoothed.
- **Cost.** One multiply a kernel for the travel, and a max for the frame's fade.
- **Tests.** On the mirror (`domain/gfx`), a travel of 3.7 cm moves the phase by exactly that, to 5e-16 wavelengths, at scales 0.7 to 1.6 by the base wavelength's share to the same, and the reduction's period moves it by 5e-14. `ground_motion_tests.cpp` sweeps the block `terrain_detail_motion` makes for desert-endless, 3,600 frames at 0.1x, 1x, 60x and 3,600x, from the scene's time three years in and from a morning near the clock's zero: the transport on each hour's straight line to a micrometre of travel, every frame's step of the block's travel the transport's to two floats of the reduced period, no frame standing still while the transport moves, no step standing out of an hour's, and at 1x and below none a hundredth of a wavelength. Before the change every sweep failed on the line (up to 20 cm off it), and 1x's had five 20 cm jumps in its minute. On a GPU, the **instrument**: the detail view of a windward slope near the origin, with the scene's ground, drawn at two clock values three years in a fifth of a wavelength of travel apart, and the ripples' displacement along the wind read back by correlation — the second picture against the first sampled at each pixel's ground point less a trial displacement — must be the block's travel to a twentieth (24.09 mm against 24.00; before, 0.01 mm against a staircase's 0); and a frame at clock value T is the same bytes reached frame by frame over five seconds or by a jump from a day later with the same last frame. The instrument's long series, a capture a game second for 90 s, is the same file's skipped case.

**Tongues that meander and branch** (2026-10-03, the owner: "let's do that next step too"). A real tongue is not straight. Its centreline wanders as the flow finds its way down, more toward the toe; its width swells and pinches; and a lobe sometimes splits into two, each half ending in its own toe. Each tongue's shape (`ground_tongue`) now has:

- **Meander.** The centreline wanders by two harmonics: a long one of 8–16 m, with amplitude 0.13–0.42 of `flow_width`, and a short one of 2–4 m at 0.3 of that. It grows from 0.3 at the head to 1 at the toe, so it leans at most about 11° off the lane.
- **Pinch.** The half-width swells and pinches by 12% along the tongue.
- **Branching.** About three tongues in ten split part-way down, between 45% and 65% of their length. Over a quarter of the length the lobe becomes two, each 0.7 as wide and 0.55 half-widths either side, normalised so the pair is one lobe's height where it has not yet parted. Each half has its own rounded toe (`ground_lobe`).
- **Drawn once a tongue.** All of it comes from the tongue's own hash: eight more draws of the generator, no more lattice hashes.
- **Gradient by forward difference.** The shape is local arithmetic in the tongue's own coordinates (metres across its lane and down from its head), so it is exact in float anywhere in the world. Its gradient is a forward difference of 2 mm in those coordinates: hand-deriving every term would cost more errors than it saves, and three evaluations of a few dozen operations on a slip-face pixel cost little next to its hashes.
- **Still a function of position.** The normal still never moves a tongue.
- **Measured.** On the mirror, nine points in ten lean along the fall line by less than 0.29 on a direction; the meander adds about 0.07. No millimetre step jumps.

**Grainflow tongues, with soft ends** (2026-10-03, version 4; the owner on the straight lanes: "let's do the soft cutoff in a way that makes sense, we're wanting to end up with a AAA near photorealistic implementation"). A real grainflow is a tongue, not a line (Hunter 1977; Kocurek and Dott 1981): an avalanche released below the brink scours a narrow **chute** with **levees** either side, deposits a **lobe** further down that widens and thickens, and stops in a **rounded toe**, part-way down the face or at its foot. So each lane of the fixed-direction field is now a chain of tongues along its direction:

- **One tongue a segment.** Each lane has one tongue per segment of `flow_length` (24 m on the ergs), staggered from lane to lane by the golden ratio.
- **Its own measurements.** Each tongue has its own length (45 to 95% of the segment), start, width (0.7 to 1.3 of `flow_width`), lateral jitter and episode. Lanes are `2 flow_width` apart.
- **Its shape.** Its profile across eases from a chute with levees (`(1-r²)² (2.4 r² - 0.6)`) over the upper half into a lobe (`(1-r²)²`). Its half-width widens from 0.6 to 1.4 of its width toward the toe. (The fifth pass took the levees out, above: the chute is `−0.3 (1-r²)²`.)
- **Soft ends, over metres.** The head comes in over a tenth of its length and the toe goes out over a fifth, and the toe's edges end before its middle, so it is round in plan. Those are metres on a face, never a lane width.
- **No swim.** The height and its gradient are analytic, and everything is a function of position, so the fixed directions' guarantee holds.
- **Cost.** Three lanes a direction, six lattice hashes a slip-face pixel (four for the straight lanes, eight for the third pass's cells).
