On the mirror the tongues run a median 15.6 m along their lanes' centres (10th percentile 10.3 m, 90th 21.2 m). Nine points in ten lean along the fall line by less than 0.3; the heads, the chute-to-lobe transitions and the toes are the rest, and lanes of one direction stay parallel. The ergs keep half the tongues present (`flow_share` 0.5, from a quarter: with the gaps between tongues a quarter left a face nearly bare from the brink).

**The slip face, fifth pass: what the dashes were** (2026-10-04). **The owner's report**, flying the endless desert: a slip face close up was covered edge to edge in short light and dark dashes all pointing the same way, like rain on a window — the complaint the fourth pass was meant to answer. Replayed at his markers on the GPU at his pixel density (3,840 × 2,160, `fov_y` 0.96; [the experiment](../experiments/sand-fifth-pass-2026-10-04.md)):

- **What drew the dashes.** The second pass's streaks, by their albedo: switching the streaks off left a smooth face, and switching off the ripples, the grain or the streaks' roughness or normal changed nothing. Each dash is one 2 m × 0.4 m kernel, 0.91 m × 0.18 m at half height, 9 to 14 by 28 to 72 pixels from 43 m, up to 40% off the sand.
- **Why they were there.** `desert-endless` copied the erg's detail block on 2026-09-30, before the third pass changed the erg's. It kept the streaks and had no grainflow. Every later pass changed `desert-erg` alone, and every test and picture judged it alone. **The endless desert now carries the erg's block, and the rings test holds the two files equal** ("the endless desert draws the erg's sand").
- **What the fourth pass's tongues did on the GPU.** They read as long faint tongues, but with two faults:
  - The chute's **levees**, steep sides a few centimetres across that came and went along the tongue, read under a low sun as broken dashes a metre or two long.
  - The **fade by a whole lane width** let the tongues draw up to 36% more variation than the pixels hold at 10 to 20 cm. From a few hundred metres that showed as one-pixel vertical lines.
- **The chute is now a shallow scour with no levees** (`ground_tongue`: `−0.3 (1 − r²)²`), easing into the lobe as before.
- **The tongues fade by the footprint against `k_ground_flow_body`, 0.75 lane widths a period**: whole at four pixels a period and gone at two, 11 and 22.5 cm on the ergs, where the fourth pass's were 15 and 30. The number is the instrument's:
  - at a whole lane width the scour drew a fifth more variation than the pixels hold, at 15 cm;
  - at half a lane width the tongues were gone where 8 × 8 samples still held them;
  - 0.75 stays within a tenth at every size.
- **The lanes' scales**, which `flow_albedo` and `flow_normal` are divided by, are measured again: 0.213 and 0.723 per lane width (`k_ground_flow_rms`, `k_ground_flow_slope_rms`). So the scene's numbers mean what they meant.
- **The instrument** (`ground_detail_tests.cpp`, "a slip face draws a few long faint tongues, not speckle") reads a 32° face at 5 cm a sample. Features are regions more than 2% off the face's mean luminance; each is counted and measured by its second moments.
  - **In the face's own shade:** 2.0 features per 100 m², a median 3.9 m long, 3.9% of contrast at the 99th percentile. The streaks read 49, 1.7 m and 26%.
  - **Under a raking sun:** 7.2 per 100 m², 8.1 m. The fourth pass's levees read 19.2 and 1.8 m.
  - **At a distance:** over pixels of 3 to 40 cm, never more variation drawn than 1.09 times what 8 × 8 samples of each pixel hold. The fourth pass drew 1.36 times at 15 cm.
  - **Asserted:** the test holds each of these, and asserts that the streaks read as speckle.
- **Not changed:** the lanes in sixteen directions, the segments, the episodes, the meander, the pinch and the split lobes. Where two directions blend, the tongues of the neighbouring direction can be seen faintly at 22.5° from a hundred metres.

**The slip face, fourth pass: lanes that are lanes** (2026-10-03). **The owner's report**, from the brink of a face looking along and down it: "Close up (and especially looking down) the lee side streaking still looks very elliptical dottish."

**Why the third pass looked that way.** Its four cells of 10 m each drew a fan of lanes, `s0 / (1 + widening t)`, rays from the cell's centre line leaning up to 8° off the fall line at its edge. Neighbouring fans leaned the other way, so in the blend two families crossed at up to 17° and beat into ovals. No lane outlived its cell, and the windows cut what was left into dipoles. The new plan and brink views (`face_plan`, `face_brink`, `face_feet`, below) show the dashes and crossings before the change.

**The lanes now lie in sixteen fixed directions.** For each direction, a one-dimensional gradient noise of the position's own coordinate across it:

- **Position alone.** A lane is a function of position only, constant along its direction and without end; the face's weight (`flow_start_deg` to `flow_full_deg`) ends it at the brink and the toe.
- **The fall line only picks.** It chooses the nearest direction, and the two nearest blend only over the middle fifth of a sector. Everywhere else one family of straight lanes lies at most 9° off the fall line. Within 2.25° of a sector's middle, two families cross at 22.5°, each normalised to keep the contrast.
- **Nothing swims.** The normal moves only the blend's weight: a milliradian 3 km out changes the lanes by at most 11.6% of their rms at the blend's steepest, and by nothing outside a blend.
- **Episodes stay per lane.** A present lane beside absent ones is one chute with its levee, the length of the face.
- **Cost.** Four lattice hashes a slip-face pixel, where the cells took eight.
- **Retired.** `flow_cell` and `flow_widening`.
- **Measured** ([the experiment](../experiments/sand-fourth-pass-2026-10-03.md)). Along a lane the autocorrelation is 1 at 40 m. Outside a blend, the gradient's share along the fall line is under sin 9° at the 99th percentile. There is no jump across the blend's edges or a direction's own angle, and the filter keeps the mean within 0.5% at 5 to 40 cm pixels.

**The slip face, third pass: grainflow lanes** (version 3, 2026-09-30; its cells and widening were replaced by the fourth pass's fixed directions, above). The owner, of the second pass's streaks at twenty metres: "very blotchy and short streaky ... doesn't look like sand streaking down the lee side at all" — a flat face covered in 20–40 cm dashes, lighter and darker, like rain on a window, which is what 0.4 m × 2 m ellipses of 6% albedo look like from a distance (the preview's `before_slip_20m_raking` draws exactly that). A real slip face (Hunter 1977; Kocurek and Dott 1981) is smooth sand with **long tongues of avalanched sand**, from near the brink most of the way to the toe, a few decimetres to a metre or two across, widening a little downslope and ending in rounded toes, over an apron of grainfall — seen by **relief under raking light**, barely by colour. So the term is relief first and long: a lattice of `flow_cell` (10 m) fixed in the world, and in each cell a **one-dimensional** gradient noise of the coordinate *across* the fall line measured from the cell's centre, lanes `flow_width` (0.6 m) apart, constant along the fall line; each lane's lattice gradient windowed along the fall line by a start near the top of the cell and a length of 0.8 to 1.7 cells, so it begins near the brink and ends in a rounded toe; the across coordinate shrunk down the fall line so a lane widens (`flow_widening`, 30% a cell); the four nearest cells blended by quintic weights and divided by the root of their squared sum, so the blend keeps the contrast. Its height leans the normal to a root-mean-square slope of `flow_normal` (0.05) and it moves the albedo by `flow_albedo` (1.5%): the second pass had it the other way round. Every projection is of an offset from a cell's centre, so the trap below holds no danger (a thousandth of a radian of normal 3 km out moves the lanes by 6% of their root-mean-square), and a pixel pays four cells, eight lattice hashes, where the streaks paid twenty-seven kernels. It fades by the footprint across a lane, the lost slope variance into the roughness (a 32° face against 8 × 8 supersampling at 5 to 40 cm pixels: the mean within 0.13%). On the mirror the lanes' gradient along the fall line averages a tenth of their gradient across it, and no millimetre step jumps. The weights leave out the blend weights' own gradient, the cell being seventeen lanes across. **The ergs switch the streaks off and take the lanes**, as episodes (below), from a lee slope of 24° and whole at 30°; the streaks stay in the shader, unchanged, for a scene that names them. [The experiment](../experiments/sand-third-pass-2026-09-30.md) has the pictures and the author's reading.

**The slip face: streaks down the fall line** (version 2, 2026-09-29; the owner's photograph: "a slip face that is smooth, with faint streaks running down its fall line"). Where the ground falls away from the wind near the angle of repose — the streaks' weight is a smoothstep of the same fall along the wind the exposure reads, between the scene's two slopes — there are no ripples and in their place **tongues of avalanched sand**, a sum of kernels on a lattice of `streak_length` fixed in the world, each an ellipse that long down the fall line (the direction of `n.xz`) and `streak_width` across, lighter or darker, mostly albedo and roughness with a slight normal. They fade toward the brink and the toe as the slope leaves the band, and by the footprint across a tongue, the slope variance that takes going into the roughness. With the ergs' bands every weight is a smooth function of the normal — ripples to 10°, smooth lee from 18° to 22°, streaks from 22° and whole at 30° — so between rippled sand, smooth lee and streaked slip face there is never a line (the mirror's sweep from flat to 40° steps no weight and no albedo by more than 0.005 in a hundredth of a degree). **The trap**, which the fall line and item 5's spacing share: never multiply an absolute coordinate by anything that depends on the normal, since at 3 km a thousandth of a radian is metres of pattern. The tongues are the ripples' machinery turned to the fall line: the lattice is fixed in the world and only a point's **offset from a kernel's centre**, at most a tongue's half-length, is projected on the fall line, so the same thousandth of a radian 3 km out moves the tongues' sum by 1.2% of its root-mean-square. A slip face 32° steep, shaded against 8 × 8 supersampling at pixels of 5 to 40 cm: the mean holds to 0.4% and the variation is never above the supersampled picture's by more than a twentieth.

**Spacing that follows the wind** (version 2, 2026-09-29; the owner's walk: "the ripples are uniformly tight everywhere"). A ripple's wavelength follows the wind at the surface: longer where the flow speeds up climbing a windward slope toward a crest, the scene's own on the flat. The ripples' wavelength and height (so a ripple keeps its shape and its slope variance, and the roughness transfer is unchanged) are scaled by `clamp(1 + spacing_gain × climb, spacing_min, spacing_max)`, the climb being the fall along the wind with its sign turned. **Per pixel**, the brief's first way: every kernel reaching a pixel uses the pixel's own wavenumber, so the sum stays coherent and continuous wherever the normal is, and the footprint's fade uses the local wavelength. Its price is that the ripples slide a little when the normal changes (an LOD cut, a dune moving under a time-lapse): the wavenumber multiplies only a kernel's offset from its centre, so a change moves each kernel's phase by at most its radius times the change in wavenumber, `R |Δk|`. At the defaults (R = 4.4 wavelengths) that is 27.8 × gain × sec²θ / s radians of phase per radian of normal; **on a 12° windward slope at the ergs' gain of 2.5, a tenth of a degree moves a kernel's edge by 0.0086 of a wavelength, and the mirror measures the crests themselves moving by at most 0.0127** where the sum stands clear of its taper (the sum's phase moves faster than any one kernel's where kernels partly cancel) — under the twentieth that would have sent it to the brief's second way, two fixed fields blended. Nor is there a jump where the wavelength varies: over ground whose slope rises from 0 to 14° across 12 m, the scale climbing from 1 to its clamp across dozens of lattice cells, the height never changes between half-millimetre steps by more than its slope allows; and the zero crossings over 40 m confirm the local wavelength (666 on the flat, 424 at a scale of 1.53: 1.57). `ground_detail_tests.cpp`, "the ripples' spacing follows the wind". What it does not do: shorten the ripples where the flow slows (a dune's toe, an interdune floor), which would need the provider's knowledge, as the shelter above does.

**Grain that reads as sand** (version 2, 2026-09-29; the owner's walk: "the sand itself looks pixelated"). At his feet a pixel is a little under a millimetre, so the first pass's finest cells, 5 mm of value noise, were six pixels across and showed their lattice as an upscaled image, with nothing under them. With `grain_finest` the grain is **gradient noise**, which is zero at every lattice point and has its extremes between them, so it has no lattice to see: octaves from `grain_size` halving down to the finest, each faded by the footprint as the ripples are, the albedo and roughness channels scaled to the first pass's root-mean-square over all of them (so `grain_albedo` means what it meant), and a third channel, a height, whose analytic gradient leans the shading normal by `grain_normal` — so under a low sun the sand between two crests is no longer flat. The slope variance the fades take goes into the roughness by the ripples' rule. **Its filter, in a CPU form** (`domain/gfx/tests/ground_detail_tests.cpp`): seen from above at pixels of 2 mm to 3 cm against 8 × 8 supersampling, the mean brightness holds to 0.05% and the pixel-to-pixel variation is never above the supersampled picture's. **Far from the origin** a float's step is a quarter of a millimetre at 3.7 km and the reconstruction is off by a few of them, so four steps count as footprint: there the 1.25 mm octave was gone, the 2.5 mm at 0.41 of its weight (9% of its own amplitude wrong), and 5 mm whole (5%); within 900 m every octave held to 5%. Since 2026-10-04 the step is the one of the point's offset from the detail's frame origin, within 512 m of the eye, so no octave of a millimetre or more is taken by it anywhere ([The sand far from the origin](#the-sand-far-from-the-origin), below). **What it costs**: an octave is four lattice hashes, and at the feet four octaves draw (20 to 2.5 mm; the finest fades under a 1 mm pixel), sixteen hashes against the ripples' eighteen kernels, each of which is a hash, three more draws and a sine; the first pass's grain was eight. The GPU's milliseconds are the owner's to measure at the merge. No glints yet.

**The ripples fade by the ground's slope** — the shading normal's, which is continuous where the triangle's steps at every edge — between 22° and 30° by default, and by the sand share; the grain does not fade by slope, since a slip face is sand too.

**The second pass** (2026-09-29) answered the owner's first walk with four terms, each off by default so a scene naming none of them draws the first pass to the bit, each judged on the CPU mirror's preview pictures and measured there, since no GPU ran where it was written ([the experiment](../experiments/sand-detail-second-pass-2026-09-29.md)).

**And by which way the ground faces the wind** (version 2, 2026-09-29, the owner's first walk: "ripples over the crest, on the side the wind blows toward, make no sense"). The fade by steepness alone left ripples on every lee gentler than 22°, where real sand is smooth, because the condition that matters is exposure, not steepness. With `w` the wind and `n` the shading normal, `dot(n.xz, w) / n.y` is the ground's fall along the wind — the tangent of its slope down it: negative climbing into the wind, positive falling away, less on a slope facing across it — and the **exposure** is 1 on flat and windward ground, falling smoothly to 0 across the scene's band of lee slope (`lee_start_deg` to `lee_end_deg`; the ergs' 10° to 18° were chosen from the preview's dune, `after_eye_dune_*`, [gfx](gfx.md), "The ground's detail"). The ripples' weight is multiplied by it, and so the roughness transfer, which is weighted by the same weight, takes nothing from it: **sheltered sand is smooth, not unresolved**, so what the exposure removes does not come back as roughness. It needs no data, is a function of the surface and so has no seam, and follows a dune that moves. `GroundShading::exposure` carries it, and the detail view's green channel (the ripples' drawn share) shows it without a flag.

**What the exposure cannot see**, because the normal does not know it: the **flat** ground just downwind of a brink, inside the separation bubble, which has a level normal and no wind; and anything a ruin or a rock shelters. Both are fields, not functions of the normal. **Design, not built**: the ground provider knows the first from its own primitives — the distance downwind of each brink, in that dune's heights (the bubble reattaches about four to six heights downwind) — and a placement generator the second from its footprints; the provider would hand the shelter over as a channel of the terrain's maps beside the sand share (the metallic-roughness map's alpha is taken; the albedo map's alpha is free, and costs no new texture), the resolve would multiply the exposure by it, and the rings' chunks would bake it as they bake the sand share. [scene_gen](scene_gen.md#the-two-kinds) and [terrain](terrain.md#what-the-effect-needs) carry the same note for the provider's side.

**Seams, tested and not assumed** (`ground_detail_rings_tests.cpp`, with the terrain capability's rings shrunk to a 128 m terrain as the rings' own tests have them). A view five metres over the sand straddles the inner ring's border and a chunk border inside both rings, drawn in the detail view (`--view detail`): every covered pixel's ripple height and grain — each a function of (x, z) alone — is held to the CPU function (`domain/gfx/tests/ground_detail_reference.h`) at the world point its own depth says it shows. **At the ring's border the ripple is within 1 of 255 and the grain within 4, at the chunks' borders both within 1**, against 13 and 11 inside a chunk — a float depth is a few millimetres along the ground at a grazing angle, and a lee and a 5 mm grain cell change fastest there — and the share of the ripples drawn steps between neighbours by at most 9 and 7 across the borders against 12 inside. **With the second pass** (the ergs' own block, read from their scene; 2026-09-30) the grain is still a function of (x, z) alone and holds the same way — within 9 of 255 at the ring's border and 1 at the chunks', against 23 inside a chunk, where the gradient grain's coarse octave changes faster than the value noise did — and the share of the ripples drawn, which now carries the exposure, steps across a border by no more than inside a chunk (19 and 7, against 19). The ripple height is not held to the CPU there, because the spacing scales its wavelength by the level's own normal, which is the height function's only to the level's spacing: up to 0.05 of scale apart inside a chunk, near a brink, which is a fifth of a wavelength of phase. What a border adds to that is read by an instrument: the ergs' numbers with a metre-long plain sinusoid and no defects, whose height at a pixel can be solved (Newton's method on the CPU's ripple at the pixel's world point) for the scale the GPU drew it at, so the scale's difference from the height function's reads back per pixel, and its step between neighbours is the step the level's normal takes. A kernel's reach in wavelengths is the defect density's alone, so a step in scale slides a crest by the same share of a wavelength at a metre as at 12 cm, `(6 - 4.5 defects) Δs / s`. **Across the inner ring's border the scale steps by at most 0.009** (0.005 at the 99th percentile, 125 pixels read back) — the normal by at most 0.004 radians, a crest by 0.04 of a wavelength at a scale of 1, 5 mm on the ergs' ripples — **and across a chunk's border by at most 0.028** (0.017 at the 99th percentile, 549 pixels; a chunk's cut is simplified on its own), **against 0.020 at the 99th percentile between neighbours inside a chunk** (25,743 pixels), where the levels' interpolated normal cannot follow the height function's round a brink: at the 99th percentile both borders step the normal by less than the inside of a chunk moves it from one pixel to the next, and the ring's border does at its worst too. The test holds the ring's border to 0.015 and both borders' 99th percentile to the inside's. Over the rings with the detail on, occlusion culling and the cone test change no pixel and two runs are the same bytes, as they are over the waves (`ground_detail_tests.cpp`), where a block that asks for nothing also draws exactly what no block draws.

**What it costs** (RTX 5090, `msvc-release`, traced shadows, under the GPU lock with the GPU 0–2% busy before each run, so upper bounds; [the experiment](../experiments/sand-detail-2026-09-29.md) has the table): the resolve, frame by frame against the same path without the detail, **0.091 ms at the median, 0.19 at the 95th percentile and 0.23 at the 99th at 11520×2160** along the erg's own path, and 0.090 / 0.105 / 0.116 over a walk at eye height; 0.010–0.028 at the median at 1920×1080. That is under a third of a millisecond at the surround size but for one frame of 3,601 (0.42). **Under traced shadows only**: measured again at the second pass's merge, the same walk costs the resolve 0.53 ms with the cascaded maps or with no shadows and 0.11 ms with traced ones, because a resolve that traces rays spends most of its time waiting and the detail's arithmetic runs inside it ([the second pass's page](../experiments/sand-detail-second-pass-2026-09-29.md#the-cost-on-the-gpu-measured-at-the-merge-2026-09-30) has the table). **With the third pass** the same walk costs the resolve 0.86 ms under the cascaded maps and 0.24 under traced shadows: its own terms add 0.13, and its code being in the shader costs the second pass's numbers 0.10 more than they cost before it was compiled in, the baseline without the detail unchanged ([the third pass's page](../experiments/sand-third-pass-2026-09-30.md#the-cost-on-the-gpu-measured-after-the-merge)). The owner accepted that cost on 2026-10-03: it is what this quality costs, and a later detail setting scales it down in rungs rather than the default being cut. **With the fifth pass** (2026-10-04) the same walk under the cascaded maps costs the resolve 0.838 ms against 0.836 for the fourth pass, measured the same day on the same tree, where the resolve without the detail had grown to 1.15 ms from other work ([the fifth pass's page](../experiments/sand-fifth-pass-2026-10-04.md#the-cost)). The ripples are skipped wherever their fade is zero, which is most of the frame past a few tens of metres, so the cost is where they are drawn; if it had to be cut, the kernels would go first — eighteen summed a pixel, about six reaching it — then the grain's fine octave, which is under a pixel almost everywhere.

**What does not reach it yet** ([Not yet](#not-yet)): ripples that migrate with the transport integral (they stand still and turn with the wind), glints, footprints' interaction with the ripples, wet sand, and any sampled texture.

### The sand far from the origin

The owner set the fly speed to 10,000 m/s, flew the endless desert out to 460 km and dropped into walk mode at (−419070, 80, −66781): the ground's tiles refined as they arrived, and **the ripples stayed "very low resolution"** — the case of a game with fast travel or a teleport. His record says the tiles were all there (the layout's lag 0 m, nothing pending or building for the last 400 frames), and the reproduction offscreen at his pose shows why the ripples were not: staircased crests in 3.1 cm squares and no grain, because the detail was evaluated at the point's float32 world coordinate, whose step there is 3.1 cm ([gfx](gfx.md), "Far from the origin", has the instrument's numbers). Since 2026-10-04 the detail is evaluated in a **frame** near the eye with the world's offset carried exactly: the scene renderer calls `gfx::ground_detail_frame(detail, eye.x, eye.z)` on the block `GpuScene::ground_detail_params()` makes, once a frame, and the reference does the same at its camera. `ground_detail_params()` itself is unchanged — the frame is a function of the eye, which it does not know, and its motion is another change's. The picture at 420 km is the sand the origin draws; near the origin it is the bytes it was within 512 m of it (measured at a walker's view there) and within two codes elsewhere (3.9% of pixels one code off at the erg walk's start); the detail costs 0.054 ms more at 11520×2160, 0.879 ms where main's shader cost 0.825 in the same session ([the experiment](../experiments/far-from-origin-2026-10-04.md), which also surveys every other float32 absolute position on the way to the picture and the game — the eye itself among them, which at 420 km moves in 3.1 cm steps and loses a walker's motion along x outright).

## Instances that come and go

A streamed world's buildings arrive and leave with their tiles ([world](world.md)), so the resident scene has to take instances **between frames** without loading the scene again. The meshes stay — a kit is a few dozen, loaded with the scene — and only the instances change: `SceneRenderer::set_dynamic_instances(tail, blocks)`, which hands the tail to `GpuScene::set_dynamic_instances` and **does not wait for the device**. The meshes' textures stay with them, one per distinct image for the whole kit, and a tail uploads none ([One upload per distinct image](#one-upload-per-distinct-image)).

**A fixed prefix and a tail of blocks.** A scene whose `SceneData::dynamic` is set is its load's instances — the terrain, whatever the file placed — followed by a tail the caller hands over whole, **named block by block**: a `DynamicBlock` is a key and a run of the tail, and the world's placements consumer names one per tile, by the tile's key, from the ranges it builds the tail out of (`PlacementTiles::tile_ranges`, engine-view's `ViewWorld::hand_over`). A caller that names none hands the whole tail over as one block. The prefix never moves: its instances, their `first_pair`s and so their pairs keep their numbers through every change, so the terrain's occlusion history survives every tile and its ids mean what they meant. **Neither does a tile.** Each block gets a run of instance slots and a **reserved** run of pairs, laid out in the same order in both spaces (`TileLayout`, `tile_layout.h`), so the instances' `first_pair`s stay sorted and a tile that arrives, leaves or changes writes its own slots and nothing else; every other tile keeps its instances, its pairs, its ids and its occlusion history, the way the prefix always did. The instances are placed as the load places its own (`make_instance`: the mesh's fit, then the instance's transform, at the pair its block gives it; `SceneData::mesh_fit` keeps the fits, because the float positions they were measured from may be gone by then) and given their mesh's material base (kept by the GPU scene from the material table's layout). Until 2026-09-25 the tail was one prefix sum after the load's instances, so every change rewrote every tile's instances and pair entries behind the first one that moved and waited for the device to do it: [E35](../experiments/e35-world-streaming.md) measured 3.2 ms a change for a kit of boxes and 15–17 ms for E33's ashlar kit, whose tail is eight million pairs — the largest cost of a frame by two orders of magnitude, on six frames of seven along the desert flythrough.

**A block may bring its own instances and a version** (2026-10-31, roadmap W81). A `DynamicBlock` whose `instances` is set is read from there and not from the tail beside it — `first` is still its place in the tail the blocks make in order, so `tail_index` answers as before — and its `version` is the caller's number for that key's instances, changed whenever they change and never reused. A block that comes back with the key, count and version the layout holds (`TileBlock::version`) is kept **without reading one instance**; a block with no version (0), or another, is compared instance by instance against the slots' keys as it always was, and counted (`TileChange::compared`, `TileStats::compared`). The world's placements hand every tile over this way (`PlacementTiles::set_run_sink`, [world](world.md#the-consumers)), so a commit no longer writes a tail and the renderer reads only the tiles that changed: along the forest proof of concept's flight writing the tail took 6.3 s and comparing it 2.7 s of a 40 s path, every commit paying for every held tile ([the measurement](../experiments/forest-load-in-2026-10-31.md)). The fires of a game's props are found block by block (`FireSet::place(tail, blocks)`). A caller that hands a tail and blocks without either field — engine-view's handover pass, the tests — is unchanged. **What follows a change's tables costs the slots it wrote** too: the policy counts (`FloraStats::field_instances`, `casters_*`, `untraced`, the untraced pairs and the cached instances, which the chain's first sizing and estimates read) are kept slot by slot as `write_slots` writes and trims (`GpuScene::policy_count`), where every change counted the whole instance table again, twice when a tree swayed in; a debug build recounts after every change and asserts the two agree (`policy_counts_match`). The chain's drop order is still laid out over every slot of a change that wrote any (`lay_out_rt_order`).

**What a change costs is named per frame** (2026-11-01, roadmap W82). `TileStats` times the parts of `set_dynamic_instances` past the scene's own change — the props' fires placed over the new tail (`fires_ns`), the far forest's hand-off (`far_ns`, of which `GpuScene::place_instances` is `place_ns`) — beside the compare, layout, write, after and relayout times it had, and engine-view's frame record carries each frame's share as `world.handover_ms` and its parts ([apps](apps.md), "The frame record's world"). On the owner's v24 dash they were not the cost: the hand-over was 22–57 ms of a 1.5–4.5 s turn (a tight compaction's 34–49 ms of slots written, once a relayout's 102 ms wait), the rest the tiles' building on the frame's thread, which the world's build budget now bounds ([world](world.md#the-consumers)). A streamed world whose ground is the world's tiles has no activation budget on its ring, so the placements consumer's own budget is what keeps a burst of activations off one frame.

**The block rules** (`TileLayout::apply`, each counted in `Stats::tiles`):

- **Size.** A block reserves its instances' pairs rounded up to `k_block_pair_granularity` (16) and its slots rounded up to `k_block_instance_granularity` (4), and past eight granules to eight steps an octave (9, 10, …, 16, 18, 20, … granules; `block_capacity`), so at most an eighth of a large block is slack and blocks come in few enough sizes that a freed one fits the next tile of its kind. A slack pair costs the cull what a hole does (below), which is why it is an eighth and not the quarter the first version allowed: [E37](../experiments/e37-tile-instance-blocks.md) measured the ashlar world's holes at a median 16% of the dispatch with four steps an octave. Sixteen pairs is small beside an ashlar tile (tens of thousands) and not much beside a tile of one-cluster boxes (a few dozen).
- **Kept** when the key comes back with the same instances — mesh, transform and padding, compared field by field against what the slots were made from: nothing is written. **Rewritten in place** when the key comes back with other instances that still fit its block (an ashlar tile moving from sections to walls, 25,726 pairs to 24,377, stays where it was). Otherwise the old block is freed and the tile placed.
- **Placed** in the smallest free block both of whose runs hold it, split when what is left is at least a granule of each; when none does, at the end. A freed block merges with a free neighbour, and a free block at the end is given back before anything is placed, so the dispatch ends where the last tile does.
- **Numbered again** — every block's pairs given out again where its slots stand, in slot order, and no slot written — when the holes pass `k_default_compact_pct` (25%, the `renderer.tiles.compact_pct` tunable, read when the scene is created) of the pairs the cull dispatches and `k_compact_min_holes` (4,096), when a tile that fits no free run by its pairs takes one by its slots (free slots past half that share of the table), and at the cap (below, "The pairs are numbered again, and no slot moves"; T154, 2026-11-15: until then the holes laid everything out again). **Compacted** — every tile laid out again in the caller's order, as a first fill lays it, and every slot written once — only when the caller asks (`set_dynamic_instances(…, compact = true)`) — engine-view asks when its world starts over, at a flythrough's repeat, so every repeat lays its tiles out as the first fill did and inherits nothing of where the last one's ended up — or when, after a numbering, free slots pass twice the same share of the table and `k_compact_min_free_slots` (4,096) — the share itself when blocks may not move. **Moved** — the block that ends the table given back and placed by its slots in the smallest free run before it, a few blocks a change, and the pairs numbered again behind them — when free slots pass half the share (below, "Free slots close at the end, a few blocks a change"; T164, 2026-11-16: until then free slots past the share laid everything out again). A layout whose classes' slack would take it past the 2^24 pairs has its pairs numbered again where its slots stand (below, "At the cap the pairs are numbered again"). Until T137 (2026-11-14) it was packed **tight** instead — every tile laid out again, each block exactly its tile, every slot written — and **at the ceiling that was a whole rewrite every few dozen changes**: the forest proof of concept's tail holds 15.6 of the 16.8 million pairs, and along a 40 s flight its layout went tight 60 times, every slot written again each time (25–45 ms of the frame's thread, the table set rewritten on the GPU). Laying it out at the classes first, which always fits a tail admitted at its classes, was tried and measured worse — the classes leave less than a tile of room at the ceiling, so the next append compacted again: 467 whole rewrites on the same flight ([the measurement](../experiments/forest-load-in-2026-10-31.md)). What would stop it was thought to be room the admission leaves the layout, or a compaction that moves only the blocks past the cap; what was built moves none.

**At the cap the pairs are numbered again**, and no slot moves (T137, 2026-11-14). *The cause it removes.* The forest staging's walk (360 m at 4.5 m/s, 3840 × 2160, traced, batch 64's stack) held **22 frames of 71 to 108 ms**, one every hundred frames or so, and each was a tight layout: `set_dynamic_instances` wrote 298,000 to 326,000 slots in 52 to 86 ms (`world.write_ms`: every instance made again from its source — the matrix, the fit, a swaying tree's record given back and taken), and the frame's `submit_frame` then staged the whole table and a top-level record a slot for the set it flipped to in 16 to 24 ms (`cpu.tables`), with the other sets' turn of 30 ms a few frames later. Those are the jumps a walk in a window has, every couple of seconds; the same flight's 32 frames of 450 to 780 ms are the ground's, and an offscreen run's alone ([What a frame waits for](#what-a-frame-waits-for)). *Why nothing has to move.* The cap is on **pairs** — the visibility id names 2^24 — and slots are not short. A slot's `first_pair` is the sum of the clusters of the live slots before it, so with every slot where it stands the pair space closes up by arithmetic: `TileLayout::number_pairs_again` walks the blocks and the free runs in slot order and gives a block exactly its pairs and a free run none, which is the pair space a scene loaded with this tail has, and until T154 `GpuScene::number_first_pairs` gave every tail slot its first pair again in one pass of additions (a null slot keeps the pair the live ones before it end at, so the slots stay sorted and a pair nobody owns still lands on a null instance; since T154 it is runs, below). No instance is made, no tree's record moves, no key is compared; `TileLayoutChange::tight` says it happened and `TileChange::slots_renumbered` how many slots' numbers moved. *What the GPU took.* Until T154 each table set copied the slots whose number moved and expanded their pairs again when a frame next flipped to it (one range beside the pending runs); their top-level records name no pair and were left, which is the 300,000 matrices a set no longer writes. Every pair past the first hole changes its number, exactly as it did under the tight layout, so whatever is kept per pair between frames (the occlusion's flags, the fade) sees what it saw then. *From then on* a free run holds no pairs, so a tile that arrives fits none by its pairs: it takes the smallest free run that holds its **slots**, split by slots alone, and the pairs are numbered in behind it (`place`, with the cap in hand) — without that the table would grow by every tile that came. Free blocks' slots past `renderer.tiles.compact_pct` of the table (and `k_compact_min_free_slots`, 4,096) lay everything out again, as holes do under the cap; that is the only whole rewrite left. *What it cost.* Until T154 a change at the cap copied the table from the first slot whose number moved (the forest's 29 MB at worst) and expanded those pairs again on every arrival that needed pairs numbered, where a change that found a hole of its class used to copy its own slots alone: by the arithmetic a few milliseconds on many frames instead of 71 to 108 on a few; T154 measured the pass of additions alone at 3.7 to 5.8 ms (below), and takes both off the frame's thread. **Not measured on the forest yet**: on the night this was built the machine never had the 45 GB of free commit a forest load needs, so the walk's pair — main's build and this one's back to back, the 22 frames side by side — is flown by the coordinator from the scripts the row left, and its numbers belong here when it has been. Until T154 a scene under the cap never took the path; since then it does too (below). A consumer with no streamed tail has no layout at all. *What holds it.* `tile_layout_tests.cpp`'s random world runs under the cap and at it (a cap of 12,000 pairs, the world held to it as a pair budget holds one): at the cap the pairs were numbered again on 67 of its 400 changes and laid out again on 25 under T137 (155 and 0 since T154); on every change a tile that stayed keeps its slots and none of them is written, the layout never ends past the cap, the table stays sorted and every pair finds its owner by the search. `dynamic_instances_tests.cpp` holds the picture: a scene whose cap is its largest tail to the pair (`GpuScene::set_pair_limit`) takes eight changes, three of them numbered again (four since T154), with two and with three frames in flight, and after each the table is the layout's (`validate_tables`) and the frame is the loaded scene's — 0 ids, 0 depths, 0 colours different (RTX 5090, 2026-11-14) — and again with a change every frame and none waited for.

**The pairs are numbered again, and no slot moves**, under the cap as at it (T154, 2026-11-15). *The cause it removes.* On the forest staging re-planned with its lakes the tail peaks at 14.4 M of the 16.8 M pairs, under the cap, so T137's numbering never ran and the ordinary compaction did instead: along the 2,400-frame grounded walk (`--terrain-async`, 3840 × 2160, rt/rt, bounce on, batch 65's build) **five frames of 82 to 85 ms, 426 to 427 frames apart** (483, 909, 1335, 1762, 2188), each `compactions 1`, `tight 0`: `set_dynamic_instances` wrote 348,640 slots in 59.6 ms (`world.write_ms`, every instance made again from its source), then `submit_frame` staged the whole table and a top-level record a slot for the set it flipped to in 19.6 ms (`cpu.tables`), and the next frame did the second set's in 20.8 ms. Why every 427 frames: the walk crosses tiles at a steady rate, a tile that leaves frees a block whose pairs only a tile of its class fits, and the holes grow by the same share each crossing until they pass a quarter of the dispatch; then every tile was laid out again. *Why nothing has to move under the cap either.* A hole costs the cull a thread and nothing else, and closing it needs no slot to move: T137's numbering does it with every slot where it stands. So when the holes pass the share the pairs are numbered again — each block keeping its class's pairs when they all fit under the cap (so a tile rewritten with a few more clusters still fits where it is), exactly its pairs when they do not, and a free run none — and a tile that fits no free run by its pairs goes to the end, which moves no pair, unless the pairs are being numbered anyway (at the cap, or another tile of the change took a run by its slots) or the free slots pass half the share of the table (and `k_compact_min_free_slots`): then it takes the smallest run that holds its slots, its pairs numbered in behind it, as at the cap (`TileLayout::place`). Without that the free runs, which a numbering leaves with no pairs, would never be taken again and the table would grow until free slots passed the share; and without the half share every such tile would number the pairs — the engine's streamed forest, taking every run it could, numbered them on 592 of its 900 frames, each a GPU pass over the slots after the run. Laying everything out again is left to a caller's request and to free slots past the share of the table after a numbering (`k_compact_min_free_slots`). The numbering keeps the slots' order, so the order of the tiles' pairs is what it was, and **the tie rule gives a tie between two tiles to the same one before and after** ([gfx](gfx.md), "The tie rule"; a compaction laid them out in the caller's order and could change the winner of such a tie, which "The picture does not depend on where a tile's block is", below, states as the exception). *Why it costs the frame nothing.* A slot's new number is a function of the run it is in: a block's slots all move by the block's distance (its live slots keep their offsets from its first pair, its slack the live pairs' end) and a free run's null slots all take its one number. So `TileLayout::number_pairs_again` gives the change's writes their new numbers and says what moved as `PairShift` runs (`pair_shift.h`: add a value, or set one, over a run of slots), a run a block or fewer — where T137 added up every slot's number on the CPU (one pass over 349,000 records of 96 bytes, which a scratch measurement on this machine timed at 3.7 to 5.8 ms beside the night's builds, the table larger than the cache) and copied every moved record into every table set again (29 MB a set). The runs go to every table set, composed with any it has not taken yet (`compose_shifts`), and each set applies them on the GPU when a frame next flips to it: `pair_shift_main` (`pair_expand.slang`, one workgroup a run) before the frame's copies, which then give a slot the frame copies its record whole, and `pair_expand_runs_main` after them, one workgroup a slot numbered again and not copied, which writes its pairs again (the `pair shift` pass and the `pair expand` pass's second dispatch, in the render graph; `TileStats::gpu_tables` counts both). The CPU's own table takes the runs **when it is read** (`GpuScene::cpu_shift_`): a slot a change writes drops them, a run of slots a set copies is settled first, the whole table before a set is written whole (a growth's frame, which stages the whole table anyway), and `validate_tables`, `pair_cluster` and the test decode read through them (`table_first_pair`). What a numbering costs the frame's thread is the layout's walk of its blocks and a few compositions of a few thousand runs: on a tail of the forest staging's size (5,000 tiles, 360,064 slots, 15.4 M pairs, every fourth tile gone and the holes past the share) `tile_layout_tests.cpp` times the change at 0.69 to 0.86 ms in `msvc-release`, the whole of `apply` over its 3,750 blocks, and two compositions of its 2,500 runs at 0.13 to 0.19 ms (2026-11-15, the machine's processors 53 to 88% busy with other agents' builds: upper bounds), against 59.6 + 19.6 + 20.8 ms before. *What it changes.* Every pair past the first that moved changes its number, as under a compaction, so what is kept per pair between frames sees what it saw then: the occlusion's flags (a frame of culling, never a pixel); the cross-fade's table is written every frame for every drawn pair and carries nothing across. Holes now close many times more often (in the random world under the cap, 263 numberings of 400 changes where there were 70 compactions), each a GPU pass over the moved slots and their pairs per table set rather than a write of every slot; and the table keeps the free runs' slots between numberings, never more than the share. *What holds it.* `tile_layout_tests.cpp`: the random world under the cap and at it, 0 laid out again in either (70 and 25 before), every numbering's runs at most one a block or free run, a tile that stayed never written, and **a table set that lags** — brought up to date every third change from the composed runs and the writes since — equal to the table slot for slot; the runs' composition, cut and search against a table of slots taking them one at a time; and the forest-sized change above, which writes only the freed blocks' null slots and hands on 2,500 runs. `dynamic_instances_tests.cpp`'s tile-by-tile case (the holes c leaves are numbered again, the one compaction left the one asked for) and the cap case run under the cap as well (one numbering there, four at the cap, none laid out again), each step against the loaded scene: 0 id, 0 depth and 0 colour differences with two and three frames in flight (RTX 5090, 2026-11-15).

**The lists of runs are reserved to the tail's slots** (T215, 2026-11-23). *The cause it removes.* Batch 72's gate failed `engine_view.frame_loop` in `msvc-no-ecs`: 2 allocations of 448 bytes at frame 68 of the streamed trees' second flight, one growing `shift_scratch_` in `push_shift` and one growing `cpu_shift_` in `compose_shifts`' copy back, under `commit_tail` → `ViewWorld::hand_over` → `set_dynamic_instances`. Nothing reserved the lists, so each grew to what it had held so far, and how many runs a list holds follows how the tile commits bunch and which slots a set settles, which is timing: a second flight over the same tiles can cut a list past the first's. *The bound.* A change's runs are one a block or free run, but nothing smaller than the tail's slots bounds the rest: a table set's list and the CPU's are compositions, which keep the edges of every layout composed into them, and the CPU's list is cut wherever a set's copy settles a slot (`settle_first_pairs`) — a slot marked alone, by a sway or a still form's lean, settles anywhere inside a block. Every list is sorted, disjoint and of runs a slot or longer inside the tail, so `shift_run_bound` is the tail's slots, and `GpuScene::reserve_shift_lists` gives the change's list, the CPU's, the scratch, the expansion's, every set's and the carry's that room where the tail's slot capacity is set (the first fill, `reserve_table_sets`, and `fit_tables` when the capacity grows or the sets are made again), so no frame grows one. *What it costs.* 16 bytes a tail slot a list, reserved and untouched until a list fills it: on a tail with two sets, seven lists, 112 bytes a slot of address space against the instance table's own 96; at the forest's capacity of about 540,000 slots, about 60 MB of commit, none of it resident until a list runs long. *What holds it.* `tile_layout_tests.cpp`'s "lists reserved to the tail's slots allocate nothing in a second flight" drives a model of `GpuScene`'s lists (its own CPU list, two table sets and scratch, through the same `pair_shift.h` calls; not `GpuScene` itself) through a streamed world of 160 small tiles at a pair cap (131 and 132 numberings in two flights of 400 small commits), the second flight also settling six slots a change alone: unreserved, as main's lists were, the CPU's list peaks at 74 runs in the first flight and 234 in the second — past the layout's 90 blocks and free runs — and the second flight allocates 8 times; reserved by `reserve_shift_runs`, 0. That proves the bound and the reservation pattern; that `reserve_shift_lists` reaches every list `GpuScene` holds is `engine_view.frame_loop`'s to show, on the device.

**Free slots close at the end, a few blocks a change** (T164, 2026-11-16). *The cause it removes.* After T154 the one whole rewrite left under the cap was free slots past the share once the pairs were numbered, and a player's walk meets it where the engine's grounded walk never does: the owner's walk of the forest on batch 66 (`reports/lab/20261116-165619-170` of the proof of concept, a window with the wildlife game, 13,463 frames) flew from its start up and across the world at 300 to 1,000 m/s, and as the tail emptied and filled again **ten changes laid every tile out again** — 14,000 to 253,000 slots written, 5 to 60 ms of the frame's thread (`world.write_ms`) and 1 to 18 ms a table set (`cpu.tables`), six of them in the hundred frames (742 to 839) in which the tail fell from 12.4 M to 2.1 M pairs, the worst 170 ms with a relayout beside it. Each freed the table of its holes and the next crossing made new ones. *What is done instead.* While free slots pass half the share (12.5% of the table by default, and `k_compact_min_free_slots`), the block that ends the table is given back — its slots written null — and placed by its slots in the smallest free run before it that holds it, `TileLayout::place`'s rule for a block that fits no run by its pairs; what it left at the end goes back, so the table shrinks by a block, and the next block from the end follows, until the free slots are under half the share, a block fits no run before it, or the change has moved `renderer.tiles.move_slots` slots (`k_default_move_slots`, 16,384: about 4 ms of the frame's thread to write and 1 ms a table set at the forest's cost a slot). The pairs are then numbered again behind them, as T154 numbers them, so a change writes the blocks it moved and their old slots null and nothing else, and the table closes over a few changes instead of in one. Laying everything out again is left to a caller's request and to free slots past **twice** the share that the moves have not closed (one change emptying half the table); `move_slots` 0 keeps the old rule, the share itself. A moved block keeps its key, so its age for the hand-off's fade (`GpuScene::block_stamp`) and its trees' records go with it, and its writes are the ordinary slot writes every table set takes. *What it changes.* A moved block's pairs and slots change their numbers, as a reused free block's do, so the occlusion's flags for them see a frame of culling; and since the moves change the slot order of the blocks they move, the tie rule can give a tie between two tiles to the other one after a move, as it could after a compaction ("The picture does not depend on where a tile's block is", below). *What holds it.* `tile_layout_tests.cpp`: a tail of the forest staging's size (5,000 tiles of 70 slots) with every third tile gone — a third of the table free, past the share, which laid every tile out again before — closes in four changes moving 794 blocks, at most 16,344 slots written a change against the 233,310 every slot of a relayout, the table checked slot by slot after each; in `msvc-release` the layout of the change the tiles leave in took 3.3 ms and a change that only moves at most 1.9 ms (2026-11-16, the machine busy with other agents' builds: upper bounds); with `move_slots` 0 the same change still lays everything out. A random world of tiles of 300 to 2,000 slots, 200 changes with a budget of 2,048 slots, moves 57 blocks, lays nothing out again, keeps every tile that came back the same in its slots unless the change moved it, and never leaves free slots past twice the share after a numbering. *Flown* on the forest staging (3840 × 2160, rt/rt, bounce on, `--terrain-async`, batch 66's build against this one in one lease, the Windows session locked and other agents' builds beside both, so upper bounds): along a 54 s fast flight that crosses about 9 km at up to 500 m/s as the owner's walk did, batch 66's build laid every tile out again **8 times** (10,000 to 309,000 slots, up to 81.5 ms of writes and 18.8 ms of a table set, two frames of 105 and 111 ms) and this one **none**, its numberings 62 to 144 with the moves; frames with more than 20 ms of slot writes 10 to 3, the worst 81.5 to 32.1 ms. The grounded walk, whose tail never empties, has no compaction on batch 66 and none here.

**A hole is a pair nobody owns, and the cull can reject it without a search** (W6, 2026-11-15; behind `renderer.cull.pair_table`, off by default from 2026-11-16 and on again since 2026-11-17, the next paragraph says why, and read only by a run over every pair since the cull culls instances first). The slack a block keeps past its instances and a freed block are holes: the cull dispatches one thread per pair of the whole space, holes included. A block's slots past its instances, and a freed block's, hold **null instances** of a **null mesh** — one `gfx::MeshDesc` past the scene's, with no clusters — whose `first_pair` is where the live pairs end, so the slots stay sorted and the binary search over `first_pair` (`instance_of_pair` in `scene.slang`) still finds every pair's owner; the CPU's decode, `GpuScene::pair_cluster`, answers "nothing" for a hole. **The cull no longer searches**: `gfx::CullParams::pairs` names the scene's pair table — the `{instance, cluster}` per pair the resolve decodes a pixel through, written by `pair_expand.slang` for every instance whenever its slot is and once at load for a scene read whole — and `cluster_cull.slang` reads a pair's instance from it in one coalesced load, where the search was a chain of dependent loads, one a halving, which a hole paid in full before its instance said it held nothing ([E37](../experiments/e37-tile-instance-blocks.md) measured the ashlar world's cull 18% slower with a median 17.5% of its dispatch in holes). A hole's entry is **stale** — nothing writes it — so it may name anything: an instance past the table, rejected by the index; or a live instance whose pairs are elsewhere, rejected by the same test that rejected a hole after the search, `pair - first_pair >= mesh.cluster_count` (a pair below the instance's first wraps past it), which no instance passes for a pair that is not its own. A live pair's entry is always its own, because an instance's pairs are expanded with its slot, the renumbering at the cap's included, and the resolve already relied on that for every pixel. Both cull passes declare the pair table read on a frame that writes the tables, so the graph orders them after the expansion. A caller with no table (`pairs` 0: every test of `domain/gfx` but one) searches, as the pass always did. `scene: ... occlusion over instances` holds it on the GPU: the same single pass with the instance read from a table over a dispatch with 499 holes past the scene's 506 pairs, whose entries name every kind of wrong instance in turn, draws exactly the reference cut, no hole and no live pair lost. The compaction share still bounds what holes cost; a hole is now a load and a compare. **What it saved** (2026-11-15, the RTX 5090, main's release build b299cce2 against this one, flown main, this, main, this in one lease, 600 frames each, offscreen at 3840×2160; other processes held 58 to 100% of the CPU, the GPU ours, so the frame times are upper bounds and the pair is the measurement): under `--raster rt --shadows rt` with the bounce, the cull went from **0.038 to 0.029 ms** at the median on `streamed-forest` (615,000 pairs, 81,000 of them holes) and from **0.063 to 0.048 ms** on `desert-endless` (635,785 pairs, a scene read whole with 47,849 instances, no holes) — a quarter of the pass either way, because the search was most of every thread and not only a hole's; the frame's GPU total moved by less than its own run-to-run spread (4.67/4.66 against 4.68/4.67 ms, 10.85/10.93 against 10.81/11.07). With `--raster hw --shadows csm`, where the cull runs twice for occlusion and once a cascade, the camera's culls went from 0.058 to 0.044 ms and the cascades' from 0.082 to 0.059, and the frame from 1.340/1.339 to 1.290/1.313 ms. Every frame of every pair culled the same: the same visible pairs by draw, casters, shadow pairs and built structures, frame for frame. What it costs: 8 bytes a pair read per cull dispatch, where a scene with a handful of instances had its search out of the cache; no scene flown then got slower, and one the gate flew did (next paragraph).

**Where the table costs more than the search: a card at idle clocks** (batch 66's gate, 2026-11-16). The table is bytes the search never reads: 8 a pair, 5.1 MB a frame on `desert-endless` (635,785 pairs), which the first cull run of a frame pulls from memory and the later runs find in the L2, while the search reads only the instance records the instance load after it reads anyway. On a card at full clocks the shorter chain of loads wins; on a card idling its memory clock the bytes do. The frame budget `endless-1080p-csm` is flown by the gate with the Windows session locked, the displays asleep, and a light 1080p frame leaving the card idle most of each 16 ms: every zone reads 2 to 9 times what the same build reads with the session unlocked (P0, memory at 14,001 MHz), the total 2.84 against 1.13 ms and the cull 0.376 against 0.042. There the camera's culls, the first reader, pay the pull: medians of the RTX 5090 over the run's 7,201 frames, the machine quiet, the binaries flown alternately in one lease from copies outside any checkout, cull / shadow cull in ms:

| Binary | Session locked (the gate's state) | Unlocked |
|---|---|---|
| main b299cce2 | 0.335, 0.335, 0.335 / 0.100, 0.101, 0.100 | 0.051, 0.051 / 0.074, 0.074 |
| 77f67282, the stack before W6 | 0.336, 0.351 / 0.100, 0.100 | |
| d2200686, the stack with W6 | 0.374, 0.377, 0.377 / 0.079, 0.080, 0.079 | 0.041, 0.041 / 0.051, 0.051 |
| d2200686's source with the table read by no cull run | | 0.052 / 0.072 |

So the table is +0.04 ms on the camera's two occlusion runs and −0.02 on the four cascades' at idle clocks, a net +0.02 ms a frame (the frame's total moves less than its run-to-run spread), and −0.01 and −0.02 at full clocks, where the total went 1.166, 1.167 → 1.131, 1.127 ms; every frame of every binary culls the same pairs, casters and shadow pairs. **No rule by run keeps both**: whichever run reads the table first pays the pull, so the camera's culls searching and the cascades reading it (0.052 / 0.052 unlocked, the camera's gain given back) would at idle clocks move the pull into the first cascade, not remove it (reasoned, not flown: the session could not be locked for it), and searching everywhere gives back W6's gain wherever the card is awake, which is wherever the owner plays. What would keep both is fewer bytes: a 4-byte instance per pair beside the cluster rather than interleaved with it (half the pull; every reader of the table changes), or a hole marked in the table so that it is rejected without reading its instance and mesh, which is most of what the search's pull is. At the pair cap the table is 134 MB, larger than the L2, and every cull run would pull it, about 0.37 ms a frame for the views and four cascades at full bandwidth, against the search's 45 MB of instance records: unmeasured, and the case for the smaller table. The budget was not moved. **So the read is a tunable, `renderer.cull.pair_table`, off by default until R173** (read once a frame in `record_frame`): off, the camera's and the cascades' `CullParams::pairs` are 0 and the two cull passes declare no read of the pair table, so every run searches as main did; `--tunable renderer.cull.pair_table=true` gives W6's behaviour exactly as merged, for measuring the smaller table against. Off flies main's medians: with the session unlocked, main, off, main, off in one lease, the cull 0.056, 0.051 against off's 0.051, 0.051 ms and the shadow cull 0.084, 0.066 against 0.063, 0.072, with on at 0.041 / 0.052 and every frame culling the same set; no locked pair was flown, so off's locked numbers are main's by construction (the same shader path), not by measurement. **Measured at the cap since** (R173, 2026-11-17, [the measurement](../experiments/cull-by-instance.md)): on a grid of rocks at 1.01, 8.04 and 16.74 M pairs, 3840 × 2160, the table beats the search in every state flown — traced, the cull 0.053 / 0.326 / 0.752 ms searched against 0.036 / 0.183 / 0.354 read with the session unlocked and 0.063 / 0.326 / 0.766 against 0.042 / 0.199 / 0.359 locked; hw with the cascades, locked, the camera's culls 1.201 against 0.648 ms and the cascades' 1.974 against 1.139 at 16.74 M — because the cost is the threads' work and not the table's bytes. **So the tunable is on by default since then**, which matters only where a run passes over every pair: while `renderer.cull.instances` is on the cull looks no pair's instance up at all ([The cull culls instances first](#the-cull-culls-instances-first)). `dynamic instances: the cull draws the same with the pair table read and searched` flies the tiled world with its holes both ways against the loaded scene's ids, depth and colour.

**The pair table is expanded on the GPU.** The pair table — the {instance, cluster} of every pair, which the resolve decodes a pixel's id through — used to be built on the CPU for the whole tail and uploaded with every change: 66 MB for the ashlar tail, most of its 15 ms. Everything its entries hold is already in the instance table, so a change now uploads its own slots and a list of the live instances among them, and `pair_expand.slang` writes their entries: one 64-lane workgroup per listed instance, its lanes striding over the mesh's clusters. **The cull reads it too, for every pair it dispatches, where `renderer.cull.pair_table` is on** (W6: the pair's instance in one load, `CullParams::pairs`; off by default in batch 66 and 67, on since R173, and read by a run over every pair alone), so every live pair's entry is its own in every frame, and what keeps it so is named: `pair_expand_main` writes the pairs of every slot a change writes, `pair_shift_main` and `pair_expand_runs_main` those of the slots a numbering moved that the frame did not copy (T154), the terrain levels' slots' pairs are copied in with their set (`TableUpdate::pair_copies`), and a set made again is carried over on the GPU, both tables, by the frame that flips to it (T167, below), or written whole when there is nothing to carry it from. A hole's entries are never listed and keep whatever they held; the cull rejects such a stale entry by its two tests before reading a cluster — an instance past the table's count, or a pair outside the named instance's own run (`pair - first_pair` past its mesh's clusters) — and the resolve never reads one, since a hole is never drawn. A change that skipped an expansion of a live slot would break the cull, not only the resolve (corrected 2026-11-16, the review of R61: this paragraph said until then that only the resolve read the table).

**Table sets, flipped at the frame boundary.** The instance table and the pair table a frame reads are one of `GpuScene::table_sets()` **sets**, at least two and one per frame in flight (`reserve_table_sets`, which `SceneRenderer::create` calls). A change is written into the CPU's table (`instance_table_`) and marked, as runs of slots, pending for every set; the next frame to be recorded flips `GpuScene::instances` and `pair_table` to the next set and brings it up to date before anything reads it (`GpuScene::prepare_tables`): it copies that set's pending runs out of the frame slot's own staging buffer (host-visible, kept, one per slot, written after `begin_frame` has waited for the slot's previous frame) in a `table copy` transfer pass and expands their pairs in a `pair expand` compute pass, both in the render graph, and every pass that reads either table declares it. A set is written only by the frame that flips to it, and the sets are used in turn, so a set comes round again only after every other one has been current — at least as many frames as there are frames in flight — and the frames still in flight read the others. **So nothing waits for the device:** a change is CPU work on the tile's own instances and a flip, and when a change outgrows the per-pair buffers or the table sets (below) the old buffers go to `gfx::FrameContext::defer_destroy` rather than to a wait, and are freed when the frames that may read them are done. A frame with no change behind it flips nothing and declares nothing; a scene read whole has one pair table written at upload and one instance table, as before.

**A loaded instance moves through the flip** (2026-10-19, roadmap S88's remainder). The prefix is the load's, written into each set when a frame first flips to it, and until this date nothing rewrote it — so `move_instances` refused a dynamic scene, and the test game's actors, whose scene has props, could play their clips but not walk. Two routes were open: write the moved records into every set at once, or let a move ride the next flip as a tail block's change does. **The second was taken**, because it is the path the sets already have: `GpuScene::place_instances` writes the CPU's table as in a scene read whole and then marks each moved slot pending for every set (`mark_instance_written`, which the terrain levels' prefix slots already go through when a chunk changes); the next frame flips to a set no frame in flight reads and copies the slot out of its frame slot's staging with whatever the tail changed, the slot's top-level record with it, in the same `table copy` pass, and every other set takes it when a frame next flips to it. The first route would have been a device write into sets that frames in flight read — a wait, or a second rule for which sets may be written when — for the same picture. So a dynamic scene's move **waits for nothing** (and since 2026-10-22 so does one in a scene read whole, through the record upload: [Moving an instance](#moving-an-instance)), costs a slot's 96 bytes, its 64-byte top-level record and its clusters' pair entries rewritten as they were, per set, and the frames in flight keep drawing the instance where it stood. **What a move carries** is the instance record's cell and 3×4; nothing else holds the placement: the deformed-vertex pool, the static-shape caches and the joint matrices are in mesh space, the bottom-level structures are built every frame from the frame's cut, `tlas_references` writes every top-level transform from the frame's instance table, and the pair table's entries are a function of the slot and its mesh, which a move keeps. A move of a **tail slot** is refused ("instance 3 is in the dynamic tail, which set_dynamic_instances places") — a tile's instances are placed by the tail they come in — and so, as in a scene read whole, is a placement of another mesh.

**The picture does not depend on where a tile's block is — with one stated exception.** A tile's instances sit wherever its block is, so a streamed scene's instance numbers and pair numbers are not a loaded scene's; its surfaces are. The ids a capture decodes name the same (cluster, triangle) of the same instance, which `GpuScene::tail_index`/`tail_indices` turn back into its place in the tail — the loaded scene's numbering — and every depth and colour is the loaded scene's word for word ([What holds it](#instances-that-come-and-go), below). **The exception is a depth tie between two tiles' surfaces.** The tie rule gives it to the larger pair ([gfx](gfx.md), "The tie rule"), and which of two tiles has the larger pairs now depends on the order the blocks were placed in, where the one prefix sum made it tile order — a function of the set. Within a tile, and between a tile and the prefix, a tie goes where it always did, and a compaction lays the tiles out in the caller's order again. Two tiles of a streamed world are buildings on different ground and do not share coincident surfaces; a world whose tiles do would see the winner of such a tie depend on when each arrived.

**Every per-pair buffer is laid out by a stride, not by the count.** The visible list's runs, the per-view pair-to-entry tables, the occlusion flags, the vertex path's indexed-draw records and the table sets' pair tables are `GpuScene::pair_stride()` apart or long — `visible_base`, `cascade_base`, `pair_entries_address`, `vertex_records_offset` and the shaders' own run strides (`DeformAllocParams::pair_count`, `ClusterRecordParams::pair_count`, `DeformParams::max_entries`) all take it — and only the cull's dispatch and its bounds check take `pair_count()`, the end of the layout's pair space, holes included. For a scene read whole the two are one number, so its layout, its buffers and its pictures are the bytes they were; the renderer's whole suite passing unchanged is the check. A dynamic scene's stride starts at its prefix's pairs and **grows** when the layout passes it — half as much again, in whole pages of 4,096 pairs, so a world that fills its rings reallocates a handful of times and not on every tile — and the per-pair buffers and the table sets are then made again (the old ones deferred), after which the occlusion flags hold whatever the allocator left and the next frame fills both, as a first frame does, and every set is carried over by the frame that next flips to it. The instance tables keep a capacity the same way, in pages of 1,024 slots.

**A set made again is carried over on the GPU** (T167, 2026-11-17). *What it was.* After a growth every table set was made again and **written whole** by the frame that next flipped to it, in turn: on T164's fast flight over the forest staging (1,620 frames, 3840 × 2160, rt/rt, the bounce on, the session locked, batch 67's build with the startup trace's stages in these functions) each of those frames spent 44 to 61 ms of its thread in `prepare_tables` — the frame slot's staging made again at the whole table's size (22 to 28 ms: a host-visible buffer of about 120 MB, its pages faulted in), 500,000 to 600,000 records of 96 bytes copied into it (10 to 20 ms) and a top-level record written a slot (11 to 31 ms) — two such frames after each of the flight's two growths of the instance capacity. *Now.* `fit_tables` keeps the old buffers of the set the last frame read, with the runs and numberings it had not taken (`GpuScene::TableCarry`; a change before the flip adds to them), and the frame that flips to a set made again copies its two tables from those — or, for the second and third sets, from the set the last frame read, which holds every slot as of its own flip — on the GPU (the `table carry` pass, before the numbering and the copies, `TileStats::gpu_tables` counting it), then takes that set's pending runs and numberings as its own, so it costs the frame what a set that lagged would. The old set is freed once that frame has completed (`TableUpdate::retire`). The top-level records, one buffer and not a set's, are carried over the same way after a swapped relayout of the chain made them again: `lay_out_ray_tracing` keeps the old ones (`rt_records_from_`) and the next set written copies them into the new (the `record carry` pass) before its own runs' records — where until T167 every set written whole wrote a record a slot (11 to 31 ms each), and the first version of the carry still wrote them whole once (16 to 21 ms); a waited relayout uploads them whole, as it always did. Only a set with nothing to carry it from — a scene's first frame — is staged whole. The picture and every table are the same (the dynamic-instance cases below, through growths with two and three frames in flight). A change that grows nothing leaves the flags alone: a tile's stale flag only decides which occlusion pass tests its pairs, and pass 2 tests everything pass 1 did not draw, so it may cost a frame of culling and never a pixel. The vertex path's index budget is the full `k_vertex_index_budget` for a dynamic scene, since no load can bound a tail; a cut past it goes to the capacity draw, as any cut does. **Two rules the carry keeps** (batch 67's fixes, reviews A1 and A4). Every slot written between a growth and the frame that carries goes into the carried runs, a slot `mark_instance_written` marks (a loaded instance's move, which is the far forest's hand-off, a ring chunk turned on at its corner, a morph's padding, the water wind's bound) as well as a tail's: the sets are all new then and take nothing themselves, and until the mend such a slot reached no set until it was written again, so a far tile the tail drew was drawn twice (`far forest: ... not drawn twice`, 369 far pixels; `dynamic instances: a loaded instance moved right after the tables grow is in every set`; `water wind: a hand gale on the frame after the tables grow reaches every table set`). And a set a carry has read is written next by a later frame while the carrying frame may still be in flight, the one place a frame reads a set that is not its own, so that frame imports the set's two tables as last read by a transfer (`TableUpdate::after_carry_read`) and its first write waits for the read; the sets are made with `TransferSrc` for the copy.

**The 2^24-pair limit stays a stated refusal.** `k_max_pairs` is the visibility id's 2^24 (`pair << 8 | triangle` in 32 bits). `pairs_after` checks a run of instances against it — or against a caller's own budget — and `set_dynamic_instances` checks the tail's pairs before the layout is touched, and the layout's own end after it, packing the tiles tight when the classes' slack is what passes it: a tail past it is refused with a sentence and the scene is exactly as it was. So are blocks that do not cover the tail in order or repeat a key, a mesh the scene has not and a skinned instance. The world's placements consumer runs the same check before it asks — over every tile it holds, drawing the innermost rings and the nearest tiles first ([world](world.md#the-consumers)) — so a streamed world withholds its farthest tiles rather than a frame. Before any of it, `GpuScene::create` accounts the prefix, the rings' slots and the tail's floor together ([The pair accounting](#the-pair-accounting)).

**The pool and the chain over the tail** (since 2026-10-12, roadmap G59). Until then a dynamic scene was rigid and rasterized: `GpuScene::create` refused one with the ray tracing chain or the deformed-vertex pool, because both were laid out once per instance at load. Read in the code, the two refusals protected three things. **The chain's per-instance tables** — `rt_instances` (the top-level records: transform, the instance as the custom index, the mask), `instance_counts` and `blas_records`, the top-level structure and the bottom-level set — were sized by the load's instance count and written once, so a tail slot past them had no record and a slot that changed hands kept the old one. **The chain's per-pair half** — the bucketing scratch `slots` and the cluster sets' largest geometry index — was sized by the load's pairs, where a tail's visible list is laid out by the stride. **The pool** needed nothing per block: its per-frame blocks are suballocated over the cull pass's visible list (`deform_alloc.slang`), and a hole's null instance of the null mesh is never visible, so it gets no block and no entry; what the pool lays out by the stride is its per-entry slot table `deform_slots`, whose address every mesh record carries. And the terrain levels — the rings and the world's tiles — are drawn through the pool, which is why a world drawing its ground from tiles refused streamed placements. Now: the chain's per-instance tables are sized by the **instance capacity** (`rt_instance_slots_`, the table sets' 1,024-slot pages), every slot has a record from the start — `GpuScene::tlas_record`, the one function the load and a change both write through: the instance's transform at the world's origin (the frame's `tlas_references` overwrites it from the eye, with the bottom-level address), the slot as the custom index, and a mask of `0xff`, or **0 for a hole's null instance**, whose structure is empty anyway — and a block's arrival, rewrite or departure copies **its own slots' records** with its instances, out of the same frame-slot staging, in the same `table copy` pass, before the frame's `tlas_references` (`TableUpdate::rt_copies`). The per-pair half is laid out by the stride (`lay_out_ray_tracing`), and the stride is capped at `pair_limit()` — the most pairs the device's cluster geometry indices name over the views' runs, casters included — which the layout is refused past and the world's placements consumer budgets against, so a tail never makes a frame the chain cannot name. The bottom-level set is built over every slot of the capacity, so the records past the frame's instances are cleared to empty structures each frame (a 16-byte fill a slot). The emit pass already finds a hole's pair on its null instance or past a live one's slice and writes nothing, as the cull pass does, so no shader changed. A change that grows the stride or the instance capacity of a scene with the pool or the chain (`relayout_pending()`) has `GpuScene::relayout` make `deform_slots` (and the mesh records that name it) and the chain's per-instance half again, keeping the chain's capacity — rare by construction, since both grow half as much again, and counted (`TileStats::relayouts`, `relayout_ns`). Until T152 that waited for the frames in flight; since T152 it is made beside them ([below](#a-relayout-is-swapped-in)). Every other change writes its own slots and waits for nothing. The terrain levels' slots are the load's prefix: their instances are written through the table sets like a tail's (`mark_instance_written`), and their pairs — a function of the slot whatever chunk it draws, which the expansion cannot read from a slot's mesh record (it counts only the chunk's clusters) — are uploaded once and copied into each set written whole (`TableUpdate::pair_copies`). **Deformed loaded instances beside the tail** (2026-10-18, roadmap R84). Until then `GpuScene::create` also refused a dynamic scene with a skinned or morphed instance anywhere in it — the test game's two actors and its prop tail could not be one scene, so its animation was off. Read again, nothing of the three protected things needed it: the per-instance deform table is laid out once, at load, for the **load's** instances — the terrain levels already, and now a skinned or morphed authored instance — whose slots and pairs never move; a tail instance is placed with `k_invalid_deform` (`make_instance`), so it is rigid and draws, casts and is traced off the 16-bit grid and the float positions; the pool's per-frame blocks follow whatever entries the cull emits, and the per-entry slot table is laid out by the stride and made again by `relayout`.
